{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.319730+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_10ae89aad78e0fc69097f30e9fe9c191ff493e03ff3e432047db1bff53018b87","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:subdivided-graph of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] For $r\in{\mathbb N}_0$, the \emph{$2^r$-subdivision}
$G_r=(\Lambda_r,E_r)$ of $G$ is obtained by replacing every edge by a series
of $2^r$ edges as follows.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\Lambda_r$ is obtained from $\Lambda$ by adding $2^r-1$ new vertices $v_{e,2^{-r}j}$,
  $j=1,\ldots,2^r-1$ for
  any edge $e\in E$. We say that these new vertices are located on the edge $e$. 
  In particular, $\Lambda\subseteq \Lambda_r$. 
\item Every edge $e\in E$ is replaced by a series of $2^r$ edges $e_{1,r},\ldots,e_{2^r,r}$ as follows.
  For bookkeeping purposes only, we endow $e$ with a direction, and 
  call $v_{e,0}$ and $v_{e,1}$ the two vertices it consists of. Then, $e$ is
  replaced by the new edges $e_{j,r}=\{v_{e,2^{-r}(j-1)},v_{e,2^{-r}j}\}$, $1\le j\le 2^r$,
  which we view as being located on the edge $e$. Thus, 
  $E_r=\{e_{j,r}:e\in E, 1\le j\le 2^r\}$.
\end{itemize}
Note that $\Lambda_0=\Lambda$ and $\Lambda_r\subseteq\Lambda_{r+1}$. 
For technical convenience, we introduce also the set of
direct self-loops $\Delta_r:=\{\{i,i\}:i\in\Lambda_r\}$.","status":"unverified"}

For a MARTINGALE the hypothesis is equivalent to sup_n E|X_n| < infinity, since E[X_n] is constant and E|X_n| = 2E[X_n^+] - E[X_n]. Convergence is ONLY almost sure: it need not hold in L^1, and E[X_infinity] need not equal E[X_0]. Standard failure: let (X_n) be the product of independent nonnegative mean-one factors, for instance X_n = prod_{k <= n} (1 + eps_k) with eps_k = +1 or -1 with probability 1/2 each - equivalently X_n = 2^n on the event that all signs were +1 and 0 otherwise. Then X_n is a nonnegative martingale with E X_n = 1 for every n, so it is L^1-bounded and converges a.s., but the limit is 0 almost surely and E X_infinity = 0 != 1 = E X_0. Nonnegative supermartingales always converge a.s. because X_n^+ = X_n has bounded expectation; upgrading to L^1 convergence is exactly what uniform integrability supplies. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.2.11]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:28:08.660922+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_111e04d7407e518dbc2b8eb97fe19053a3cddf9ce81b560743bede5f72906e9d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 (See, e.g., {\cite[Fact~3.5) of arXiv:2607.29495, 'Fast Mixing for Low-Temperature Potts Models via Poisson Trees'] {CLV21a}}]
Let $\nu$ be a Gibbs distribution over $[q]^{V}$ and $P$ denote the Glauber dynamics for $\nu$. Let $\nu_{\mathrm{min}}=\min_{\sigma: \nu(\sigma)>0} \nu(\sigma)$. Then the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $T_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)\leq \frac{1}{\gamma}\log \frac{1}{\epsilon\nu_{\mathrm{min}}}$ where $\gamma$ is the spectral gap of $P$.
    \item $T_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)\leq \frac{1}{\alpha}\big(\log\log \frac{1}{\nu_{\mathrm{min}}}+\log \frac{1}{2\epsilon^2}\big)$ where $\alpha$ is the log-Sobolev constant of $P$
    \item $T_{\mathrm{mix}}(\epsilon)\leq \frac{1}{\hat\alpha}\big(\log\log \frac{1}{\nu_{\mathrm{min}}}+\log \frac{1}{2\epsilon^2}\big)$ where $\hat\alpha$ is the modified log-Sobolev constant of $P$.    
\end{enumerate}
It holds that $\alpha\leq \hat\alpha\leq 2\gamma$. Moreover, with $K(r)=\frac{1-2r}{\log (\frac{1}{r}-1)}$, it holds that $\alpha\geq K(\nu_{\mathrm{min}})\gamma$; for $\nu$ that is $b$-marginally bounded, it holds that $\alpha\geq K(b) \hat\alpha$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-06T03:36:16.690087+00:00","domain":"harvested statement (arXiv 2512.18592, 2025): mathematics","id":"claim_115c89f8a67d4fce88f37c87ae749bc1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2.4 (Erdős–Rényi, SBMs and logistic RDPGs) in the first version of arXiv:2512.18592, 'Wavelet Latent Position Exponential Random Graphs'] Fix $c\\in\\mathbb{R}$ and a real symmetric Hilbert–Schmidt matrix $S=(s_{rs})_{r,s\\geq 0}$, and let $G_{n}\\sim\\mathrm{WL\\mbox{-}ERG}(c,S)$ be generated as in Definitions 2.1 – 2.3. 1. (Erdős–Rényi.) If $s_{rs}=0$ for all $(r,s)\\neq(0,0)$, then $G_{n}$ is Erdős–Rényi $G(n,p)$ with $p=\\sigma(c+s_{00})$. 2. (Haar/SBM special case.) Assume the underlying wavelet system is the Haar system and fix an integer $J\\geq 0$. Let $\\{I_{\\ell,J}\\}_{\\ell=0}^{2^{J}-1}$ be the dyadic partition of $(0,1)$, define $\\phi_{\\ell,J}(x):=2^{J/2}\\mathbf{1}_{I_{\\ell,J}}(x)$, and let $V_{J}:=\\mathrm{span}\\{\\phi_{\\ell,J}:0\\leq\\ell\\leq 2^{J}-1\\}\\subset L^{2}(0,1)$. If the logit satisfies $f_{S}\\in V_{J}\\otimes V_{J}$, equivalently if there exist real coefficients $\\alpha_{\\ell k}$ such that $f_{S}(x,y)=\\sum_{\\ell,k=0}^{2^{J}-1}\\alpha_{\\ell k}\\,\\phi_{\\ell,J}(x)\\phi_{k,J}(y)\\quad\\text{in }L^{2}\\big((0,1)^{2}\\big),$ then $G_{n}$ is a stochastic block model with $2^{J}$ blocks. In particular, there are constants $\\beta_{\\ell k}:=2^{J}\\alpha_{\\ell k}$ such that $f_{S}(x,y)=\\beta_{\\ell k}$ for a.e. $(x,y)\\in I_{\\ell,J}\\times I_{k,J}$, and hence the block connectivity probabilities are $p_{\\ell k}=\\sigma(c+\\beta_{\\ell k})=\\sigma(c+2^{J}\\alpha_{\\ell k}).$ Under $U_{i}\\sim\\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$, the block proportions are $\\pi_{\\ell}=2^{-J}$. 3. (Finite-rank PSD $\\Rightarrow$ logistic RDPG.) Assume $S$ is positive semidefinite as an operator on $\\ell^{2}$ and has finite rank $d$. Then there exist functions $g_{1},\\dots,g_{d}\\in L^{2}(0,1)$ such that $f_{S}(x,y)=\\sum_{k=1}^{d}g_{k}(x)g_{k}(y)\\quad\\text{in }L^{2}\\big((0,1)^{2}\\big).$ Consequently, for a measurable representative $\\Phi(x):=(g_{1}(x),\\dots,g_{d}(x))\\in\\mathbb{R}^{d}$ (defined a.e.), $W_{c,S}(x,y)=\\sigma\\!\\bigl(c+\\Phi(x)^{\\top}\\Phi(y)\\bigr)\\quad\\text{for a.e. }(x,y).$ Therefore $G_{n}$ is a logistic random dot product graph: with latent positions $X_{i}=\\Phi(U_{i})\\in\\mathbb{R}^{d}$, the edges are independent conditional on $X$ and satisfy $\\mathbb{P}(A_{ij}=1\\mid X)=\\sigma(c+X_{i}^{\\top}X_{j})$ for all $i<j$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["characteristic 0 (over Q or a field containing Q); the criterion needs the field to contain, or to be extended by, roots of unity","'general' means indeterminate coefficients; a particular polynomial of degree >= 5 may well be solvable (x^5 - 2 is)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626563+00:00","domain":"algebra","id":"claim_115d87a98ec962f9b30fe189acf038bc99ce62e12c2461843b01819a67bf4895","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For n >= 5 the general polynomial equation of degree n, x^n + a_1 x^{n-1} + ... + a_n = 0 with independent indeterminate coefficients over Q (the field Q(a_1, ..., a_n)), is not solvable by radicals: there is no formula for its roots built from the coefficients by field operations and extraction of k-th roots. Moreover specific polynomials over Q are not solvable by radicals, for instance x^5 - x - 1 and x^5 - 4x + 2, whose Galois groups over Q are S_5. For n <= 4 the general equation IS solvable by radicals (the quadratic formula; Cardano's formula for cubics, 1545; Ferrari's method for quartics). GALOIS'S CRITERION, which subsumes the theorem: a polynomial over a field of characteristic 0 is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is a solvable group.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A a square complex matrix; eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity in the refinement","the discs are closed; a point of the union may fail to be an eigenvalue (the theorem localises, it does not characterise)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479038+00:00","domain":"linear algebra","id":"claim_118eb1edbdd586661b78b6b8a406c50d9aa31e793c06b918802f39726a6468d2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A = (a_ij) be a complex n x n matrix and for each i let R_i = sum_{j != i} |a_ij| be the i-th deleted absolute row sum and D_i = { z in C : |z - a_ii| <= R_i } the i-th Gershgorin disc. Then every eigenvalue of A lies in the union of the discs D_1, ..., D_n. Applying the theorem to the transpose, every eigenvalue also lies in the union of the column discs (radii the deleted column sums), so the spectrum lies in the intersection of the two unions. Refinement: if a union of k of the discs is disjoint from the union of the other n - k, then exactly k eigenvalues (counted with algebraic multiplicity) lie in the union of those k discs. Consequences: a strictly diagonally dominant matrix (|a_ii| > R_i for all i) is invertible, since 0 lies in no disc; a Hermitian strictly diagonally dominant matrix with positive diagonal is positive definite; and the discs can be shrunk by a diagonal similarity D^{-1} A D, which changes the radii to sum_{j != i} |a_ij| d_j / d_i.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Discrete Gaussian free field on a two-dimensional lattice domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions","Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property and lattice Green function asymptotics","Random-walk-below-a-barrier (ballot) estimates for the scale walk"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.987849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_11fcc5b0b92d4300329a446dd3a28c80e7535335cb27eaecb364b7fce9c12206","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The concentric decomposition (Biskup-Louidor) describes the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field h in a box of side N as seen from a point x where the field is near its maximum. Around x one takes nested dyadic annuli; conditioning on the values of h on the boundaries of the concentric boxes, the Gibbs-Markov property splits h into (i) a random walk S_k along the scales, whose increments are the Gaussian binding fields' values at x, with variance of order g log 2 per scale, with the maximum constraint acting as a barrier the walk must stay below (entropic repulsion), (ii) independent zero-boundary fields in the annuli, and (iii) explicit bounded error terms from the non-exact scale invariance of the lattice Green function. The maximum-at-x event becomes a ballot-type event for the walk S_k, handled by random-walk-below-a-barrier estimates, which yield tightness of the centred maximum, the local limit law of the maximum, and the description of the cluster of near-maximal points around x (the cluster law nu). It is the tool behind the full extremal process of the DGFF (Biskup-Louidor 2016, 2018) and the intermediate level sets. It does not by itself give universality for other log-correlated fields: the binding-field structure uses the DGFF's exact Gibbs-Markov property. Typical failure: Treating the annulus fields phi_k as exactly independent rather than approximately so, and carrying a multiscale second-moment computation through without tracking the coupling error terms; because the GFF is only log-correlated rather than an exact branching random walk, the independence used in the concentric decomposition is an approximation that must be explicitly controlled, and skipping this step is a common source of unjustified exponent claims for GFF level-set percolation. Canonical reference: Biskup and Louidor, 2016, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Biskup and Louidor, 2018, Advances in Mathematics; Biskup, Extrema of the two-dimensional discrete Gaussian free field, PIMS-CRM lecture notes, 2020, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.355487+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_120844a9e4d83f44ff30daf26d429f2a5182a56faf96997588561c50bbb77eb5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 223 (relaxed domains) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\dist(\cdot,\cdot)$ denote the Euclidean distance in $\R^N$, and define
\beq
\begin{aligned}
    S_N(\iota)
    &\equiv\bigg\{\bx\in\R^N :
    \frac{\dist(\bx,S_N)}{N^{1/2}} \le \iota
    \bigg\}\,, &
    \Sigma_N(\iota)
    &\equiv\bigg\{\bx\in\R^N :
    \frac{\dist(\bx,\Sigma_N)}{N^{1/2}} \le \iota
    \bigg\}\,.
\end{aligned}\eeq
We call $S_N(\iota)$ the \textbf{$\iota$-relaxed spherical domain},
and $\Sigma_N(\iota)$  the \textbf{$\iota$-relaxed Ising domain}.\footnote{While these relaxed domains are needed in the Ising setting for the notion of a Lipschitz algorithm to make sense, any point in $S_N(\iota)$ or $\Sigma_N(\iota)$ can be rounded to a point in $S_N$ or $\Sigma_N$ with nearly the same performance; see Remark~\ref{r:relaxed-wlog}.}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["G finite, connected, undirected, without isolated vertices (weighted graphs work verbatim with weighted degrees and volumes)","the spectral gap is that of the NORMALISED Laplacian; for regular graphs it is (d - mu_2)/d, and the unnormalised version scales by d","conductance is measured against volume; the vertex-count edge expansion h(G) is the same quantity only for regular graphs"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:49:11.846189+00:00","domain":"spectral graph theory","id":"claim_123dda5b10ef9e8af280ba37a63254fd3b1973ad6a342a5785086a24af3d21fc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let G = (V, E) be a finite connected graph with vertex degrees d(v), volume vol(S) = sum_{v in S} d(v), and for a vertex set S with 0 < vol(S) <= vol(V)/2 let phi(S) = e(S, V - S) / vol(S) be its conductance, where e(S, V - S) counts the edges leaving S. The conductance (Cheeger constant) of G is phi(G) = min over such S of phi(S). Let 0 = lambda_1 < lambda_2 <= ... <= lambda_n <= 2 be the eigenvalues of the normalised Laplacian L = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}. CHEEGER'S INEQUALITY (Alon-Milman, Sinclair-Jerrum, Dodziuk; the graph form of Cheeger's 1970 Riemannian inequality): lambda_2 / 2 <= phi(G) <= sqrt(2 lambda_2). For a d-regular graph with adjacency eigenvalues d = mu_1 >= mu_2 >= ..., lambda_2 = (d - mu_2)/d and the edge expansion h(G) = min e(S, V-S)/|S| (over |S| <= n/2) satisfies (d - mu_2)/2 <= h(G) <= sqrt(2 d (d - mu_2)). Both sides are sharp up to constants: the cycle C_n has phi of order 1/n and lambda_2 of order 1/n^2 (so the square root is needed), while the hypercube and expanders have phi and lambda_2 of the same order. Consequences: a graph is an expander (phi bounded below) if and only if it has a spectral gap bounded below; the mixing time of the random walk is O(log(n) / lambda_2) and at least of order 1/phi; the sweep cut of the second eigenvector (the proof of the upper bound) is the spectral partitioning algorithm, with the guarantee phi(S) <= sqrt(2 lambda_2) for the set it returns; higher-order Cheeger inequalities (Lee-Oveis Gharan-Trevisan) relate lambda_k to k-way partitions, and the improved Cheeger inequality bounds phi by lambda_2 / sqrt(lambda_3).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:51:11.463204+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_124528d929f6d734b3af9da0d623a149f8e9b2fbbd826f9c30808973fd01d0e6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 20 ({\cite[Definition~6.2, 6.9, and Proposition~6.10) of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] {MS}}]
With notation as above,
set $d:=\dim R$.
Let $(R,\Delta)$ be a log $\Q$-Gorenstein pair, and let $E_R(k)$ be the injective hull of $k$ as an $R$-module.
Fix a canonical divisor $K_R \geq 0$.
Write
$K_R +\Delta=\frac{1}{m}\divi(f)$ for some $0\neq f\in R$ and some $m\in\Z_{>0}$.
Take a representing element $f^{\frac{1}{m}}\in R^+$.
Let $B$ be a perfectoid big Cohen-Macaulay $R^{+}$-algebra and
let $\phi:H_{\m}^{d}(R(K_R)) \rightarrow H_{\m}^{d}(B)$ denote the morphism such that
the composition of the natural morphism $H_{\m}^{d}(R) \rightarrow H_{\m}^{d}(R(K_R))$ and $\phi$ is identical to the morphism induced by the multiplication by $f^{\frac{1}{m}}$.

The BCM-test ideal of $(R,\Delta)$ with respect to $B$ is defined as
\[ \tau_{B}(R,\Delta) 
:= {\Image( E_R(k) \cong H_{\m}^{d}(R(K_R)) \xrightarrow{\phi} H_{\m}^{d}(B))}^{\vee} \subset R, \]
where ${(-)}^{\vee}$ denotes Matlis duality.
The BCM-test ideal of $(R,\Delta)$ is defined as
\[ \taubcm(R,\Delta) := \bigcap_{B} \tau_B (R,\Delta) \subset R.\]
We say
that $(R,\Delta)$ is $\BCM_B$-regular if $\tau_B (R,\Delta)=R$
and
that $(R,\Delta)$ is BCM-regular if $\taubcm(R,\Delta)=R$.
These definitions are independent of the choices of $K_R$ and $f^\frac{1}{m}\in R^+$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.185383+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_124638bc797a9a4572624a22ce91ae82e81cd300580d95579507cac5f603d60d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2606.30349, 'Attenuated Poisson Dirichlet approximations for divisibility configurations'] Let \(X,Y,Z\) be \(\mathbf N(\mathbbm X)\)-valued random variables defined on a common probability space, and let \(B\subset \mathbf N(\mathbbm X)\) be measurable. \begin{align*}
p
:=
\Pb[Z\in B]\wedge \Pb[Y\in B]
>
0.
\end{align*}

{"assumptions":["mu is a product measure on {0,1}^n, or satisfies the FKG lattice condition (log-supermodular)","A and B are both increasing (or both decreasing) events; f and g both monotone in the same direction","the reversed inequality needs one increasing and one decreasing event","no conclusion for events that are not monotone, and none for a non-FKG measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.048644+00:00","domain":"percolation and correlation inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_12642faa7ec3d8f83d07d4fc84666d17c25bf65b9cb7021607d2e1967b320070","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let mu be a product probability measure on {0,1}^n (Harris 1960), or more generally a measure on a finite distributive lattice satisfying the FKG lattice condition mu(x v y) mu(x ^ y) >= mu(x) mu(y) (Fortuin, Kasteleyn, Ginibre 1971). If A and B are both increasing events, then mu(A and B) >= mu(A) mu(B); equivalently, for increasing functions f and g, E[f g] >= E[f] E[g]. The same holds when both are decreasing. If one event is increasing and the other decreasing, the inequality reverses: mu(A and B) <= mu(A) mu(B). The inequality says nothing about a pair of events that are neither increasing nor decreasing, and it fails for a general (non-FKG) measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.659256+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_126e4f1a177aa826fa23e4d73aebf2fc9d6ea0efe3bf8b478348f4cac9e263a3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 11 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] Let $S$ be a finite-dimensional Banach space. Let $\mathbf{X}\in \Omega G_p([a,b],V)$ and $\mathbf{Y}\in \Omega G_q([c,d],W)$, and set $\kappa=\lfloor p\rfloor$ and $\lambda=\lfloor q\rfloor$. Let $g\colon F\to S$ be Fr\'echet smooth, and let $Z$ be a two-parameter $(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y})$-controlled path.
Then the composition $g(Z)$ defines a two-parameter controlled path
\[
g(Z) \in \mathcal{D}^{p,q}_{\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}}([a,b]\times[c,d], S).
\]
Moreover, $g(Z)$ is characterized by the identity
\[
g(Z)_{t,v}[\eta,\xi] = g\left(Z^{(0,0)}_{t,v}\right)[\eta,\xi],
\qquad
\text{for all } \eta \in V^{\otimes 0},\ \xi \in W^{\otimes 0}.
\]

The higher level components of $g(Z)$ are given as follows. For
$\xi_j \in V^{\otimes j}$ and $\eta_k \in W^{\otimes k}$, define
\[
g(Z_{t,v})[\xi_j,\eta_k] :=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\displaystyle
\sum_{m=1}^{\kappa-1} \frac{1}{m!}
D^m g\left(Z^{(0,0)}_{t,v}\right) \circ Z_{t,v}^{\otimes m}
\circ \left(\tilde{\Delta}^m \boxtimes \mathrm{id}_{T^{<\lambda(W)}}\right)
[\xi_j,\eta_k],
& j>0,\ k=0, \\[2ex]
\displaystyle
\sum_{n=1}^{\lambda-1} \frac{1}{n!}
D^n g\left(Z^{(0,0)}_{t,v}\right) \circ Z_{t,v}^{\otimes n}
\circ \left(\mathrm{id}_{T^{<\kappa(V)}} \boxtimes \tilde{\Delta}^n\right)
[\xi_j,\eta_k],
& j=0,\ k>0, \\[2ex]
\displaystyle
\sum_{\ell=1}^{\lambda+\kappa-2} \frac{1}{\ell!}
D^\ell g\left(Z^{(0,0)}_{t,v}\right) \circ Z_{t,v}^{\otimes \ell}
\circ \widetilde{(\Delta \boxtimes \Delta)}^{\ell}
[\xi_j,\eta_k],
& j>0,\ k>0 .
\end{cases}
\]
Here, $\Delta$ denotes the shuffle coproduct, $\tilde{\Delta}$
denotes the restriction $\pi_{\geq 1} \circ \Delta$ and $\Delta^m$ denotes the $m$-fold iterate of $\Delta$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["i.i.d. observations with finite variance (Andrews states the result under moment conditions for the CLT)","the constraint is active at the true parameter (theta = 0); for theta > 0 the bootstrap is consistent"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:23:59.828365+00:00","domain":"resampling / constrained estimation","id":"claim_128317036fe4b38de221748567b9dd5e4b220bf4b14f749dabab4f8dd0bb0ff4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X_1, \\dots, X_n$ be i.i.d. with mean $\\theta \\ge 0$ and variance $\\sigma^2$, and let the estimator respect the constraint: $\\hat\\theta_n = \\max(0, \\bar X_n)$. When the true parameter is interior ($\\theta > 0$) the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the conditional law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges to $N(0, \\sigma^2)$, the law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta)$. When the true parameter is on the boundary ($\\theta = 0$) it is not: $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n - \\theta) \\Rightarrow \\max(0, Z)$ with $Z \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$, a law with an atom of mass $1/2$ at zero, whereas the bootstrap law of $\\sqrt n(\\hat\\theta_n^* - \\hat\\theta_n)$ converges, conditionally on the data, to the law of $\\max(0, Z + \\zeta) - \\max(0, \\zeta)$ with $\\zeta \\sim N(0, \\sigma^2)$ a random shift that does not vanish - so the bootstrap distribution is random in the limit and does not equal the sampling distribution (Andrews 2000, Theorem 1). The same failure holds for maximum-likelihood and least-squares estimators under inequality constraints whenever the true parameter has an active constraint, in particular for nonnegatively constrained regression and portfolio weights with coordinates at zero: the bootstrap replicates flip the constrained coordinates between zero and positive values, and the spread of the replicates is not the spread of the estimator. Consistent alternatives: the $m$-out-of-$n$ bootstrap with $m \\to \\infty$, $m/n \\to 0$, and subsampling, both of which recover the limit law at the boundary.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.740854+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_12b24723aa93f050871e7949f914605cbec33b4efdc7c35f81ec8af464b9628e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Let $\{ C_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be uniformly random elements of $[m]\coloneqq\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$, and let
$\{ U_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ be uniformly random elements of $(0, 1)$.
Assume the family $\{ U_n, C_n \}_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is independent.
The random variable $C_n$ denotes the coupon type
obtained on day $n$.
Define the random variables
\[
  L(i, n) \coloneqq \sup\{ k \leqslant n \mid C_k = i \}, \quad i \in [m], \quad n > 0.
\]
Then $L(i, n)$ is the most recent day no later than $n$ that coupon
type $i$ was issued.
For clumsiness probability $p \in [0, 1)$, the 
clumsy coupon collection time can be defined by
\[
  T_{m, p} \coloneqq \inf \{ n > 0 \mid L(i, n) > 0 \ \text{and} \ U_{L(i, n)} \leq 1 - p \ 
    \text{for all $i \in [m]$} \},
\]
the first day that every coupon type has been updated, their most
recent updates all having been non-clumsy.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.530380+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_12cada61a0fe3477c1bfafbdeb2ef3132076cda06b26983b5dd3acb4db76c1c9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition eq:residual-mixed-set of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:bulk-sparse-reduction}
Let \(V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be Borel measurable and bounded below, and let
\(0<r_N\le1\) and \(1\le k_N\le N\) be arbitrary deterministic
sequences.  Write
\[
 D_{N,r_N}
 =\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):\left\lVertx\right\rVert_\infty\le r_N\}
\]
and
\[
 \mathcal A_N(k_N,\rho)
 =\left\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):
 \text{some \(S\subset[N]\), \(\left\lvertS\right\rvert\le k_N\), satisfies }
 \norm{x_{S^c}}_2\le\rho\right\}.
\]
For \(\rho>0\), define the residual mixed-profile set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal R_N(r_N,k_N,\rho)
 :=
 \left\{x\in\mathbb S^{N-1}(1):
 \left\lVertx\right\rVert_\infty>r_N,\ 
 \inf_{\substack{S\subset[N]\\|S|\le k_N}}
 \norm{x_{S^c}}_2>\rho\right\}.
\end{equation}
Then the disjoint decomposition
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb S^{N-1}(1)
 =D_{N,r_N}\,\dot\cup\,
  \bigl(\mathcal A_N(k_N,\rho)\setminus D_{N,r_N}\bigr)
  \,\dot\cup\,\mathcal R_N(r_N,k_N,\rho)
\end{equation}
holds.  Suppose only that the exact bulk slice satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \log\mathscr C_N^J(V;D_{N,r_N})
 =:\Phi\in\mathbb R.
\end{equation}
No independence, moment matching, tail, density, or nondegeneracy
condition is needed for the decomposition itself.
For \(\rho>0\), set
\begin{align*}
 \mathscr S_N(\rho)
 &:=
 \mathscr C_N^J\bigl(
 V;\mathcal A_N(k_N,\rho)\setminus D_{N,r_N}\bigr),\\
 \mathscr R_N(\rho)
 &:=
 \mathscr C_N^J\bigl(
 V;\mathcal R_N(r_N,k_N,\rho)\bigr),
\end{align*}
and define
\begin{align}
 \overline\Phi_{\rm sp}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 &:=
 \lim_{\rho\downarrow0}\limsup_{N\to\infty}
 \frac1N\log\mathscr S_N(\rho),
 \\
 \overline\Phi_{\rm mix}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 &:=
 \lim_{\rho\downarrow0}\limsup_{N\to\infty}
 \frac1N\log\mathscr R_N(\rho).
 
\end{align}
Then
\begin{equation}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 =
 \max\left\{
 \Phi,\,
 \overline\Phi_{\rm sp}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet),\,
 \overline\Phi_{\rm mix}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 \right\}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, exact universality holds if and only if both nonbulk
upper exponents are at most \(\Phi\).

If \(k_N=o(N)\), \(({\rm PT})_p\), and
(equation eq:critical-count-ceiling of the paper) also hold, then
\begin{equation}
 \overline\Phi_{\rm sp}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 \le\Xi_p^{\rm sp}(V).
\end{equation}
In particular, whenever the explicit sparse-rate compatibility condition
\begin{equation}
 \Xi_p^{\rm sp}(V)\le\Phi
\end{equation}
holds, exact universality is equivalent to the single residual condition
\begin{equation}
 \overline\Phi_{\rm mix}^J(V;r_\bullet,k_\bullet)
 \le\Phi.
\end{equation}
When the disorder and \(V\) satisfy the hypotheses of
(thm:growing-point-cutoff of the paper), and
(equation eq:growing-Haar-zero-cost-condition of the paper) and
\(q_N^{\rm gr}\to0\) hold, that theorem supplies the corresponding
universal regularized bulk pressure.  Controlling its one-sided
de-regularization defects is one sufficient route to
(equation eq:exact-growing-bulk-slice of the paper), with
\(\Phi=\Phi_p^{\rm bulk}(V)\).","status":"unverified"}

    \]

    \[c_j\equiv \frac{\hx_j(\tbmeta^j, \by)}{M}\]

\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.178381+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_131ae949172d86ae168b2e818eabd79a5838d7728d49005f103c10b7e9b9c37a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 84 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $\acute{Y}$ be a continuous local martingale started from $\acute{Y}(0)=1$, and let $\theta$ be a stopping time with $\E\langle \acute{Y}\rangle_\theta<\infty$. If $\E [(|{{\acute{Y}}}_\theta|-1)^2] \le\epsilon$, then $\E\langle \acute{Y}\rangle_\theta \le 4\epsilon^{1/2}$.

\begin{proof}
The process
$\acute{M}(t)\equiv \acute{Y}^2(t)-\langle\acute{Y} \rangle_t$ is a continuous local martingale. It follows from e.g.\ \cite[Thm.~4.13]{MR3497465} that the stopped process $\acute{M}(t\wedge\theta)$ is a uniformly integrable true martingale, so the optional stopping theorem gives
    \[
    \E\langle \acute{Y}\rangle_\theta
    = \E\Big[ (\acute{Y}_\theta)^2-1\Big]\,.
    \]
Combining with Lemma~\ref{l:quadratic.ineq} and the hypothesis gives
    \[
    \E\langle \acute{Y}\rangle_\theta
    \le 2\epsilon^{1/2}
    + \frac{2\E[(|\acute{Y}_\theta|-1)^2]}{\epsilon^{1/2}}
    \le 4\epsilon^{1/2}\,,
    \]
as claimed.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.432703+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_13279b84b29dd341ec4ea79e17486be448a9a1e1f755f1def7f857a636231449","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 3. dfn: effective resistance between sets of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Effective resistance between sets}]  
  Fix a resistance form $(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})$ on $F$
  and write $R$ for the corresponding resistance metric.
  For sets $A, B \subseteq F$,
  we define
  \begin{equation}
    R(A,B)
    \coloneqq
    \left(
    \inf\{
    \mathcal{E}(f,f):
    f \in \mathcal{F},\
    f|_{A} \equiv 1,\
    f|_{B} \equiv 0
    \}
    \right)^{-1},
  \end{equation}
  which is defined to be zero if the infimum is taken over the empty set.
  Note that by (4. dfn cond: resistance forms condition 4 of the paper) 
  we clearly have $R( \{x\}, \{y\}) = R(x,y)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.658524+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_135d76fe090d841832a9d1ccd3f68ba7e306916f708faaae3d0d4db304d2c130","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Control and $\omega$-$p$-variation) of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] A control on $[a,b]$ is a continuous, super-additive map
$\omega:\Delta_{[a,b]}\to[0,\infty)$ vanishing on the diagonal.

Given $p\ge 1$ and $f:\Delta_{[a,b]}\to F$ set
\[
\|f\|_{p,\omega}
:=
\inf\Big\{C>0:\ \|f_{s,t}\|_F\le C\,\omega(s,t)^{1/p}
\ \text{for all }(s,t)\in\Delta_{[a,b]}\Big\},
\]
with the convention $\inf\varnothing=\infty$, and define
\[
C_\omega^p(\Delta_{[a,b]},F)
:=
\{f:\Delta_{[a,b]}\to F:\ \|f\|_{p,\omega}<\infty\}.
\]

For a path $g:[a,b]\to F$, we write $g\in C_\omega^p([a,b],F)$ if its increment map
\(
(s,t)\mapsto g_{s,t}
\)
belongs to $C_\omega^p(\Delta_{[a,b]},F)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:48:24.296466+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1385f546816d7b24554a5fa481bfafe95d74b0d238d9843baffed62269a94a4a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem q>1 of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] Consider the secretary problem for a Mallows distribution with $q=q_n>1$ in the case that the largest number is  of highest rank.

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1+\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q_n}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=0$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1+\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*\sim\frac1c\left(1-\log(e-1)\right)n^\alpha\approx0.459\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$:
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q_n}(\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M_n^*))=\frac1e.
$$
\noindent iii. Let $q>1$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\uparrow(n,M^*)$, where
$$
M^*=\begin{cases}&\max\left\{M\ge1: \sum_{j=M}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}\ge\frac q{q-1}\right\}, \ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}\ge \frac q{q-1};\\
&0,\ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}<\frac q{q-1}.\end{cases}
$$
(If  $\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}=\frac q{q-1}$, then $M^*-1$ is also optimal.)

\noindent The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
\begin{equation}
\lim_{n\to\infty}P_n^{\mathcal{M};q}(\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M^*))=\begin{cases}&\frac{q-1}q(1-q^{-M^*})\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac1{q^j-1}\ge\\
&(1-q^{-M^*}),\ \text{if}\ M^*\ge1;\\
&\frac{q-1}q>,\ \text{if}\ M^*=0.\end{cases}
\end{equation}
The limiting probability in (equation SuccessProbup of the paper) is always greater or equal to $\frac1e$ and is strictly greater than $\frac1e$ for all but at most a countable number of $q$ with no accumulation points in $(0,\infty)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["d-regular graphs on n vertices; tau_2 = the relaxation time (inverse spectral gap) of the natural random walk, maximised over all d-regular graphs on n vertices for fixed n","the d=3 (cubic) enumerations used are COMPLETE for n<=12 (counts 1,2,5,19,85 match the known sequence); the d>=4 enumerations are RANDOM SAMPLES (isomorphism-deduplicated, stopped after 4000 consecutive repeats) and are NOT certified complete, especially at n=12"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.998009+00:00","domain":"probability/Markov chains","id":"claim_13c3a894a23e44b0acdc4d79135f18d9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"The paper proving the Aldous-Fill spectral gap conjecture leaves conditional the claim that for every sufficiently large even order n, the slowest d-regular graph (maximising relaxation time tau_2) is cubic (d=3); the finite crossover point is n=8. The 2-regular cycle has tau_2 = 1/(1-cos(2 pi/n)) ~ n^2/(2 pi^2), one third of the cubic asymptotic 3n^2/(2 pi^2), so cubic graphs must eventually overtake the cycle but do not lead at first: the slowest-known regular graph by order is 2-regular (the cycle) at n=4 (tau_2=1.0000) and n=6 (2.0000), then becomes 3-regular at n=8 (3.9271, versus the cycle's 3.4142), n=10 (13.5414, cycle 5.2361), and n=12 (17.8846, cycle 7.4641). Separately, the extremal cubic maxima (0.75, 1.50, 3.93, 13.54, 17.88 for n=4,6,8,10,12) jump by a factor of 3.5 from n=8 to n=10, out of line with the surrounding steps; this is because the extremal cubic graph acquires a BRIDGE at n=10 and CANNOT do so at any earlier order. Proof that a bridged cubic graph needs n>=10: if a cubic graph has a bridge uv, deleting it leaves a component A containing u where every vertex has degree 3 except u (degree 2), so the degree sum 3|A|-1 must be even, forcing |A| odd; |A|=1 would need a loop and |A|=3 would need four edges among three vertices (both impossible for a simple cubic graph), so both sides of any bridge are odd and at least 5, giving n>=10. This matches exact enumeration: no bridged cubic graph exists at n=4, 6, or 8; at n=10 there is exactly one bridged cubic graph and it IS the extremal one (tau_2=13.5414, versus 6.8423 for the best bridgeless cubic graph on 10 vertices); at n=12 there are four bridged cubic graphs and the extremal one among them is a 5|7 split (17.8846, versus 10.3190 for the best bridgeless cubic graph), a 6|6 split being impossible by the same parity argument. So the crossover at n=8 (cubic first overtakes the cycle, still bridgeless there, via a narrow 2-edge 4|4 cut) and the jump at n=10 (the bridge becomes possible) are two DIFFERENT events. NOT CERTIFIED: whether any regular graph of degree d>=4 ever competes with the cubic extremal graphs at these orders - only suggested: a 4-regular graph would need a second eigenvalue of 0.944 to compete, and the best 4-regular graph seen has 0.890; and a parity fact (a d-regular graph has a cut of size c across a vertex subset A only if c = d|A| mod 2, checked on 8400 random cuts with zero violations) shows a bridge is impossible outright for any EVEN degree d, which is suggestive but not a proof that odd degrees d>=5 cannot compete either.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.773082+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1447ac7edeb187e1982ff160bc578d85fb9b1cf07f7630c9907d6544d4217793","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (The \JKL{} formulation of Einstein areal flows) of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] Consider four-dimensional spacetimes $(\Mcal,\guntrois)$ with spatial topology $\Tbb^3$ and two commuting spacelike Killing fields with closed orbits, admitting a foliation by the area~$|t|$ of the symmetry orbits. Consider a constitutive law $p=p(\mu)$ (pressure vs.\ mass-energy density) satisfying hyperbolicity and asymptotic conditions (stated in~\eqref{hyperbolic-eos-zero}, below). Then the following properties hold.
\bei

\item \textbf{Perfect-fluid matter model.} In the class of regular flows, the Einstein--Euler system 
\bel{equa-49F}
G^{\alpha\beta} = T^{\alpha\beta},
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha T^{\alpha\beta}=0
\ee
is equivalent to an \emph{evolution--constraint, first-order differential system} in terms of the variables \eqref{equa-phipsi}, as  given in \eqref{eq:T2-1234-def}--\eqref{equa-9385}, below, and referred to as the \JKL{} system. Its evolution subsystem has essentially \emph{quadratic nonlinearities} with a partial \emph{null structure} and, away from vacuum, is strongly hyperbolic.   All differential operators in the formulation 
remain defined on the full (closed) state space, including cavitation and near-light speed fluid propagation, although the hyperbolicity degenerates at non-zero null states.  

\item \textbf{Particle-production dissipative model.} Analogous properties hold for the following class of Einstein--Navier--Stokes systems
\bel{eq:pot-production-system0}
G^{\alpha\beta}=T_\chi^{\alpha\beta},
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}=0,
\qquad
\nabla_\alpha A_\chi^{\alpha\beta\gamma}
=-\mathscr B^{\beta\gamma}, 
\ee
namely an extension of the Einstein--Euler system by adjoining to the fluid variables a symmetric two-tensor relaxation field~$\zeta$. The tensors $T_\chi$ and $A_\chi$ are defined from second-order derivatives
of a \emph{Navier--Stokes potential} denoted by~$\chi$, which is assumed to satisfy suitable equilibrium, dominant-energy, and causal-hyperbolicity conditions in \autoref{def-pot-hyperbolic}. The relaxation rate tensor~$\mathscr B$ is prescribed and satisfies suitable stable-equilibrium and positivity conditions in \autoref{def-pot-source}. In particular, the coupled evolution equations are symmetric hyperbolic in the interior of the state space, and both Einstein equations and Bianchi equations are satisfied.  The associated particle-number current~$\vNumb_\chi$ satisfies $\nabla_\alpha \vNumb_\chi^\alpha = \zeta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}\geq 0$.

\item \textbf{Dissipated-energy dissipative model.} 
Analogous properties also hold for the following class of Einstein--Navier--Stokes systems
\bel{eq:pot-dissipated-system0}
\begin{aligned}
G^{\alpha\beta}
&=T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}+T_{\rm aux}^{\alpha\beta}, \quad
&
\nabla_\alpha T_\chi^{\alpha\beta}
&=-\sigma n^\beta, \quad
&
\nabla_\alpha A_\chi^{\alpha\beta\gamma}
&=-\mathscr B^{\beta\gamma},
\end{aligned}
\ee 
with 
\be
\begin{aligned}
T_{\rm aux}^{\alpha\beta}
&=\sigma \underline\pi^{\alpha\beta},
&
\sigma & \coloneqq \frac{\zeta_{\alpha\beta} \mathscr B^{\alpha\beta}}{-n_\alpha\beta^\alpha} \geq 0. 
\end{aligned}
\ee 
Here $\underline\pi^{\alpha\beta}$ is the (rescaled) projection onto the symmetry orbits, $n_\alpha$ is the future-directed normal to the areal foliation, and $\beta$ is the rescaled fluid momentum.
The model includes an auxiliary stress tensor~$T_{\rm aux}$ (\autoref{def-diss-en}), which compensates the mass-energy dissipated by~$T_\chi$. In particular, the coupled evolution equations are symmetric hyperbolic in the interior of the state space, and both Einstein equations and Bianchi equations are satisfied.
The associated particle-number current~$\vNumb_\chi$ is divergence-free.
\eei
\noindent For all three systems, the Einstein constraints propagate from one areal hypersurface, and the metric variables are reconstructed from the transport, constraint, and periodicity equations. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.165090+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_14c12419e48d441dc5aa5a7d5a0e080939ec89667ae7347c2f8743f09e0c5653","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 38 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] There exists a constant $C_8=C_8(\alpha,\iota)$ such that the following holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ over $\dot{\bg}_+, \hat{\bg}_+$, where $c$ is an absolute constant. 
    For any $\|\by\|^2=N$, the function
    \[
        \btheta_+ \mapsto
        \frac{2(\hbg_+,\btheta_+)}{M}
        + \frac{2\|\btheta_+\|(\dbg_+,\by)}{M\sqrt{N}}
        - \frac{((\hbD_+)^{-1} \btheta_+, \btheta_+)}{M}
    \]
    attains its supremum over $\R^{B_+}$ at some $\btheta_+$ satisfying
    $\|\btheta_+\| \le C_8N^{1/2}$.
    (We take the assertion to be vacuously true if $B_+ = \emptyset$.)

\begin{proof}
    Since the function tends to $-\infty$ as $\|\btheta_+\| \to +\infty$, the supremum is attained at a local maximizer $\btheta_+$.
    The function is differentiable everywhere except possibly at $\btheta_+=\bzero$, so the only possible local maximizer are $\btheta_+=\bzero$ and stationary points $\btheta_+$. 
    The stationarity condition gives
    \[
      \btheta_+
     =\hbD_+\bigg(   \hbg_+
        + \frac{(\dbg_+,\by) \btheta_+}{N^{1/2} \|\btheta_+\|}
        \bigg) \,.
    \]
With probability $1-e^{-cN}$, we have $\|\hbg_+\| \le 2 M^{1/2}$, $\|\dbg_+\| \le 2 N^{1/2}$, and consequently $|(\dbg_+,\by)| \le 2N$. Since the operator norm of $\hbD_+$ is at most $\hv_1$, it follows that any stationary point $\btheta_+$ must satisfy
    \[
        \|\btheta_+\|
        \le\hv_1 \bigg(
            \|\hbg_+\|
            + \bigg|
            \frac{(\dbg_+,\by) }{N^{1/2} }
            \bigg|
        \bigg)
        \le
        2\hv_1\Big( M^{1/2} + N^{1/2}
         \Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:reduced-normalization}}{\le}
        \frac{4(\alpha^{1/2}+1)}{\iota} N^{1/2}\,.
    \]
This proves the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.300829+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_150695aae1416938622114b2c4a679692c1815cb8ead848472a4025947266e99","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 6 (Main result in spatial dimension $d=1$) of arXiv:2510.22155, 'Random walks in space-time random media in all spatial dimensions: the full subcritical fl'] Let $\{K_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ denote an environment satisfying Assumption \ref{a1}, and let $\mathfrak H^N$ be as in \eqref{hn}. Assume as in Definition \ref{goodseq} that one has a good sequence of deterministic initial data $\mathfrak H^N(0,\bullet)$ converging weakly as measures to some limit $\mathfrak H_0$. There is an explicit Banach space $X$ of distributions on $\mathbb R$, which is continuously embedded in $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R)$, such that the rescaled and recentered collection $\{ \mathfrak F^N\}_{N \ge 1}$ is tight with respect to the topology of $C([0,T], X)$. Furthermore any limit point as $N\to \infty$ is as follows. 
\begin{itemize} 
\item (Bulk fluctuations in $d=1$) If $N^{1/2}\varsigma_N \to \boldsymbol{\varsigma} \text{ as } N\to\infty$, then the limit point is unique and coincides with the law of $(t,x)\mapsto e^{\varsigma\bullet x +\frac12 |\varsigma|^2 t} \mathcal U(t,x+\varsigma t)$ where $\mathcal U$ is the solution of the additive-noise SPDE \begin{equation}\partial_t \mathcal U(t, x) = \frac12\partial_x^2 \mathcal U(t, x) + \gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot \partial_x^p \big((\mathfrak H_0 *G_t)(x)\;\xi(t, x)\big),

\end{equation}started with initial data $\mathcal U(0, x)=0$. 
\end{itemize} Here $G_t(x) = G(t,x)= (2\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2t}$ is the standard heat kernel, $*$ denotes spatial convolution, and $ \xi$ is a standard space-time white noise defined on $\mathbb R_+\times \mathbb R.$ Furthermore in either case we have the noise coefficient $$\gamma_{\mathrm{ext}}^2:=  \frac1{(2p)!}\int_{I} \bigg[ \int_{I^2}( x- y)^{2p}\mu(\mathrm d x)\mu(\mathrm d y)-\int_I ( a- z)^{2p} \pdif( z,\mathrm d a)\bigg]
\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}(\mathrm d z).
$$Here $\pi^{\mathrm{inv}}$ is the invariant measure of the Markov kernel $\pdif$, under its unit normalization (see Definition \ref{def:unit}). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:39:41.409377+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_151c2cd817e606194ab584e595b3b3b6abc30d5d83801642ebb46cdd45bd57dd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2604.07207, 'Mixing times of step-reinforced random walks'] Let $G=(\ZZ_L, +)$ where $L\geq 3$ is an odd number and assume that $\mu(1)=\mu(-1)=1/2$.  $$c_3L^{\frac{1}{\alpha}} \leq  t^{(\alpha)}_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon) \leq C_3 L^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}.$$

{"assumptions":["sub-Gaussian increments with respect to the metric d","separability of the process, so that the supremum is measurable and the chaining series converges","convergence of the entropy integral"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_15319d42d2a2e77a7eb628a9a06e56b61b321dba9d4e5dfffbd869a984b61dbb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X_t)_{t in T} be a stochastic process on a metric space (T, d) with SUB-GAUSSIAN INCREMENTS, meaning P( |X_s - X_t| > u ) <= 2 exp( - u^2 / (2 d(s,t)^2) ) for all s, t and u > 0. Then there is an absolute constant C with E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C integral_0^{diam(T)} sqrt( log N(T, d, u) ) du, where N(T, d, u) is the covering number, the smallest number of d-balls of radius u needed to cover T. If the process is not centred one should read the statement for X_t - X_{t_0} with a fixed base point. {"assumptions":["(a) f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| finite","(c) the characterisation quantifies over a rich enough class of test functions","(d) the Gaussian vector must be CENTRED"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543764+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1564c803ed1f4f740d9c5f603549c04916aaed26f09262fdb378ee739b59ba18","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"(a) Let Z be standard Gaussian on R and f absolutely continuous with E|f'(Z)| < infinity. Then E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ]. (b) Multivariate: if X is centred Gaussian on R^n with covariance Sigma and f is differentiable with the appropriate integrability, then E[ X_i f(X) ] = sum_j Sigma_{ij} E[ d f / d x_j (X) ]. (c) STEIN'S CHARACTERISATION: a real random variable Z is standard Gaussian IF AND ONLY IF E[ Z f(Z) ] = E[ f'(Z) ] for every bounded, continuously differentiable f with bounded derivative. This is the identity that makes Stein's method work: to show a law is close to Gaussian, one bounds E[ Z f(Z) - f'(Z) ] over a class of test functions f solving Stein's equation. (d) ISSERLIS-WICK FORMULA: for a centred Gaussian vector, E[ X_1 X_2 ... X_{2m} ] = sum over all PERFECT MATCHINGS of {1, ..., 2m} of the product of the covariances of the matched pairs, and any odd moment vanishes. For 2m = 4 this reads E[X_1X_2X_3X_4] = Sigma_{12}Sigma_{34} + Sigma_{13}Sigma_{24} + Sigma_{14}Sigma_{23}, and in particular E[Z^4] = 3 for a standard Gaussian, which is the '3' that the fourth moment theorem tests against. Centring is essential in (d); for a non-centred Gaussian one must first subtract the means. [standard; Isserlis (1918), Stein (1972); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Chapter 3]","status":"unverified"}

	\]

	\]
(note this differs slightly from the set $S_\delta$ defined in the proof of Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.lip.trunc.to.ideal}). 
	By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_2(\R,C)$ endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric is compact.
	The set $S_\delta$ is closed with respect to the $\bbW_\fq$ metric, and therefore also compact. We may thus cover $S_\delta$ with finitely many $\bbW_\fq$-balls,
	\[S_\delta = \bigcup_{\mu \in T_\delta} \cB_{\fq,\delta/5}(\mu)
		\,,\]

		\[\cB_{q,\delta/5}(\mu) 
		\equiv\bigg\{
			\mu' \in S_\delta : \bbW_\fq(\mu,\mu') \le

	Note that for each $\mu \in S_\delta$, we have
	\begin{align*}
		\bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)

	Proposition~\ref{p:confinement}. It follows that for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[
		\inf_{\mu \in S_\delta} \bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu) \ge 
		\frac{4\delta}{5}\,.
	\]
	For each $\mu \in T_\delta$,  Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound} implies
	\[
		\E \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu\Big)
		\stackrel{\eqref{e:confinement.consequence.of.variance.bound}}{\ge} \bigg(\Big[\bbW_\fq(\mu(\cA_N),\mu)^2 - o_N(1)\Big]_+\bigg)^{1/2}
		\ge \frac{3\delta}{5}
	\]
	for sufficiently large $N$.

$\mu \in T_\delta$, we obtain
	\[
		\P\bigg(

		\bigg)

	\]
	(This $c$ depends on $\alpha,L,\delta$ only, as $\epsilon,\fq$ affect only the $N$-independent number of terms $|T_\delta|$ in the union bound.)
	On this event, we further have
	\[\bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)), S_\delta\Big)
		\ge \min_{\mu \in T_\delta} \bbW_\fq\Big(\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)),\mu\Big) - \frac{\delta}{5}
		\ge 
		\frac{\delta}{5}\,,\]
	and therefore $\mu_\bG(\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)) \not\in S_\delta$.
	Combining with \eqref{e:confinement.mu.bG.to.P2} shows that 
	\[

	\]

	On this event, we obtain the desired estimate
	\[

{"assumptions":["All hypotheses, dimensions, step restrictions and observable norms in the statement; no independent audit."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:50:21.974827+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_15ae575f5cdf6ffb959dcd4d6db118bd84cd72568d605a4fd10d69cb34b06ab0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own work draft; proof (unaudited), claim w730-T355-C009 v1; novelty unestablished.

Let d,q be finite positive integers. Let H be constant SPD with eigenvalues
in [m,M], m>0, and let sigma,D,kappa>=0. Let 0<rho<2 and

    0<eta<=rho/M, gamma=min(m,M(2-rho)/rho),
    eta kappa^2 <= gamma/2, B=I-eta H.

An adapted recursion starts from deterministic u0,v0 and satisfies

    u_{k+1}=u_k-eta xi_k^u,  v_{k+1}=B v_k-eta xi_k^v,
    E[xi_k^u | F_k]=0, E[xi_k^v | F_k]=0,
    E[|xi_k^v|^2 | F_k] <= sigma^2 tr H + kappa^2 |v_k|^2,
    E[|xi_k^u|^2 | F_k] <= sigma^2 D^2 |v_k|^2.           (1)

The filtration contains the state before the kth increment. No iid,
symmetry or moments beyond these conditional second moments are required
for the oracle estimate. If the target's on-manifold covariance identity
is desired, additionally impose Cov(xi^v | state (u,0))=sigma^2 H.
The tangent condition then forces tangent and cross covariance to vanish
there, giving sigma^2 diag(0,H), proportional to the population Hessian.

Define V=|v0|, alpha=sigma^2 tr H, and

    c_V=2(alpha+kappa^2 V^2)/gamma,
    R_T=sigma^2 D^2 (V^2/gamma+T c_V).

For F in C_b^2(R^{d+q}), let F_uu,F_uv,F_vv be the global operator-norm
bounds of its second derivative blocks. For every T>=0,

    sup_{integer 0<=K<=floor(T/eta^2)}
      |E F(u_K,v_K)-F(u0,B^K v0)| <= eta C(T,V),
    C(T,V)=F_uu R_T/2+F_uv sqrt(c_V R_T)+F_vv c_V/2.    (2)

Thus a=1, with explicit constants, in a larger normal-noise class than
C007's uniformly bounded conditional covariance class. This is not a
claim that the new constants improve those of C007 when kappa=0.

When v0=0, (2) compares against the constant slow limit (u0,0) at every
index. For general fixed v0 and F_v=sup ||D_v F||, comparison against
(u0,0) has bound eta(C(T,V)+F_v) at every integer

    ceil(log(max(1,V/eta))/(eta gamma))<=K<=floor(T/eta^2).

An empty interval covers no indices. The initial-layer cutoff is the
same deterministic contraction argument as C008; it is not a logarithm
in the weak-error constant. No comparison against (u0,0) is asserted at

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_15e330d2baaa644ec10bc714fcdd93a5b89163ac895e536f314465a8b83d5176","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 195 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, let $p^\sigma\equiv p^\sigma(\bXi)$ denote the empirical averages
	\[
	\frac1M\sum_{a\le M}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\ind \Big\{
	X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a)
	\notin  [-\trK,\trK)\Big\}\,.
	\]
Similarly, let $p^\Ising\equiv p^\Ising(\bXi)$ denote the empirical average
	\[
	\frac1N\sum_{i\le N}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	\ind \Big\{
	X^{\trunc,\Ising}(q_d,i)
	\notin  [-\trK,\trK)\Big\}\,.
	\]
Then $p^\sigma(\bXi) \le o_{\trK}(1)$
for all $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$, with probability
at least $1- \exp(-N^{1/2})$.

\begin{proof}
Let $\bar{p}^\sigma$ be defined as $p^\sigma$, but with $[-\trK+1,\trK-1)$ in place of $[-\trK,\trK)$.
Let $f:\R\to\R$ be the Lipschitz function defined by
	\[f(x)=\begin{cases}
	0 & \textup{if $|x|\le \trK-1$,}\\
	1 & \textup{if $|x|\ge \trK$,}\\
		|x|-(\trK-1)
		&\textup{if $\trK-1
			\le |x| \le \trK$}\,.
	\end{cases}\]
Since $\ind\{x\notin[-\trK,\trK)\} \le f(x)
\le \ind\{x\notin[-\trK+1,\trK-1)\} 
$, for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have
	\[p^\sigma(\bXi)
	\le
	F^\sigma(\bXi)
	\equiv
	\frac1M
	\sum_{a\le M}
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	f(X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a))
	\le \bar{p}^\sigma(\bXi)
	\,.
	\]
We first argue that the \emph{annealed} expectation of $\bar{p}^\sigma$ is small for each $\sigma$. Note that since $\vX^{\trunc,\RomI:\RomIII}$ is frozen upon leaving $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ (Definition~\ref{d:trunc}), the probability that $\vX^{\trunc,\RomI:\RomIII}(q_d,a)$ lies outside $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ is maximized at time $d=\dmax$. From the spatial rerandomization (Definition~\ref{d:rerand}), this is the same as the probability that $\vY^{\RomI:\RomIII}(q_d)$ lies outside $[-\trK,\trK)^3$ at time $d=\dmax$. This (annealed) probability can be bounded using the proof of  Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}: recall from \eqref{e:A.H} that the event $A(H)$ has probability tending to zero as $H\to\infty$. On the complement of $A(H)$, the paths
$\bar{D}^\RomI$,
$Y^\RomII$, $Y^\RomIII$, $Y^\Ising$
are all $\gamma$-H\"older with H\"older norm $O(H)$, and in particular the maximum deviation of each path must be $O(H)$.
Moreover, since $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges uniformly to zero, the discrepancy between $\bar{D}^\RomI$ and $Y^\RomI$ converges uniformly to zero, so we can conclude that the maximum deviation of $Y^\RomI$ is also $O(H)$.
If we take $H$ to be a small constant multiple of $\trK$, then we conclude that $\E[\bar{p}^\sigma(\bXi)] \le o_{\trK}(1)$ for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$. A similar argument gives 
$\E[\bar{p}^\Ising(\bXi)] \le o_{\trK}(1)$. 

The above implies that the annealed expectation of each $F^\sigma$ is also small. It remains to show that $F^\sigma$ is highly concentrated about this expectation. For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$,
it follows by Corollary~\ref{c:conc.empir.avg} 
that $F^\sigma$ is $(L^{O(1)}/(\delta N^{1/2}))$-Lipschitz on the set $U_\MAX$. It follows by 
Assumption~\ref{a:params} that this Lipschitz constant is very small, for instance,
	\[
	\frac{L^{O(1)}}{\delta N^{1/2}}
	\ll \frac{1}{N^{1/3}}\,.
	\]
By the Kirszbraun extension theorem, there exists a function $\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)$ which agrees with $F^\sigma$ for $\bXi\in U_\MAX$, but such that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is $(1/N^{1/3})$-Lipschitz on the entire space. 
It follows by standard concentration bounds (see e.g.\ Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}) that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is highly concentrated about its mean $\E[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)]$. We finally bound
	\[
	\E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	\le \E\Big[F^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	+ \E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi);(U_\MAX)^c\Big]
	\le 
	\E\Big[F^\sigma(\bXi)\Big]
	+\bigg\{ \E\Big[\tilde{F}^\sigma(\bXi)^2\Big]
	\P\Big((U_\MAX)^c \Big)
	\bigg\}^{1/2}
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,.
	\]
In the last step, we used that $\tilde{F}^\sigma$ is Lipschitz so its second moment must be bounded, while  \eqref{e.MAX.bound} implies that $\P((U_\MAX)^c)$ is very small. This proves the claim for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, and a similar argum (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287467+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1637051eb8cf9971561070e4866638ef1c48ccf7f1cba15a2067c2bee9fa4a90","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Delta-bound of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Fix $q\in[0,1)$ and let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $[-1,1]$ with
		$\int m^2\,\mu(\mathrm{d} m)=q$.
		For $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$, let $(X_t^{\mu,\zeta})_{t\in[q,1]}$ be the
		Auffinger--Chen process (equation eq:AC mu of the paper), set
		\[
		u_\zeta(t,x):=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(t,x),
		\]
		and define
		\begin{equation}
			\Delta_\zeta^\mu
			:=
			\int_{[q,1]}
			\Bigl(\mathbb{E}\bigl[u_\zeta(t,X_t^{\mu,\zeta})^2\bigr]-t\Bigr)\,\zeta(\mathrm{d} t).
		\end{equation}
		Then:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item
			For every $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$,
			\[
			|\Delta_\zeta^\mu|\le 1.
			\]
			
			\item
			Let $\zeta_\mu$ be the unique minimizer of $\mathrm{TAP}(\mu,\cdot)$ on $\mathcal P([q,1])$.
			Assume that $\mu$ is supported in $[-1+\delta,1-\delta]$ for some
			$\delta\in(0,1)$, and let $\zeta\in\mathcal P([q,1])$ satisfy
			\[
			\zeta(\{q\})\ge u_0>0.
			\]
			Then there exists $C=C(\xi,u_0)$ such that
			\[
			|\Delta_\zeta^\mu|
			\le \frac{C}{\delta}\,\mathrm{dist}(\zeta,\zeta_\mu).
			\]
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:42:16.237774+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1640493759a801066c3bc341079b93aca8a08a5c8115e39e23bc5001f57ab49f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm pd of arXiv:2607.00311, 'Thermal Concentration and Poisson--Dirichlet Edge Statistics for Random-Lattice Gibbs Ense'] Let $L_n$ be distributed according to $\mu_n$ on $\mathbb X_n$.
Let $c>1$ and put $\alpha=1/c$.
Order the sign classes of $L_n^\sharp$ by increasing $\tau_n$ and write them as $\bm u_{n,1},\bm u_{n,2},\ldots$.
Define
$$
W_{n,j}^{(c)}=
\frac{g_{n,c}(\tau_n(\bm u_{n,j}))}
{\sum_{\bm u\in L_n^\sharp}g_{n,c}(\tau_n(\bm u))}
$$
and $W_{n,c}=(W_{n,1}^{(c)},W_{n,2}^{(c)},\ldots)$.
Then, as a random element of $\ell^1$,
$$
W_{n,c}\Rightarrow W_c:=
\left(
\frac{T_1^{-c}}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}T_k^{-c}},
\frac{T_2^{-c}}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}T_k^{-c}},
\ldots
\right).
$$
Since $0<T_1<T_2<\cdots$, the sequence
$T_1^{-c},T_2^{-c},\ldots$ is already ordered in decreasing order.
Thus $W_c$ is a normalized ranked mass sequence.
Moreover, $W_c$ has the Poisson--Dirichlet distribution $\operatorname{PD}(1/c,0)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.870142+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_165ff34db6bc3cc369d91e4b314263e1ac9e3fcbd44087b4f5f843871197f4c6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop average-degree-bridge-alternatives of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Fix $\rho\in(0,1]$ and a constant $d_{\rm av}>0$. Let
\[
G^{(k)}=(I^{(k)},J^{(k)},M^{(k)})
\]
be a deterministic sequence of weighted bipartite graphs, where
$M^{(k)}\in\mathbb R^{I^{(k)}\times J^{(k)}}$.
Assume
\[
|I^{(k)}|=k,\qquad |J^{(k)}|=n_k,\qquad \frac{n_k}{k}\to\infty.
\]
Assume the following properties hold for all sufficiently large $k$:
\begin{itemize}
\item The support graph of $G^{(k)}$ has \hyperref[def:local-sparse-four-cycle-incidence]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{local sparse four-cycle incidence}}}{} with parameter $\varepsilon_k\to0$.
\item The average right degree is at most $d_{\rm av}$:
\[
\frac1{n_k}\sum_{j\in J^{(k)}}
|N_{G^{(k)}}(j)|
\le d_{\rm av}.
\]
\item The support is nonempty, and the average magnitude of the nonzero weights is at most $1$:
\[
\frac1{|E^{(k)}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in E^{(k)}} |M^{(k)}_{ij}|
\le 1,
\]
where $E^{(k)} = \{(i,j)\in I^{(k)}\times J^{(k)}:M^{(k)}_{ij}\ne0\}$ is the edge set of $G^{(k)}$; see Definition (def:weighted-bipartite-graph of the paper).
\end{itemize}
Let $r(k)$ be an integer sequence with $\rho k\le r(k)\le k$.
Then there is a sequence $m_k\to\infty$ such that, for a uniform sample
\[
\Omega_k\subseteq J^{(k)},\qquad \text{of size } |\Omega_k|=r(k),
\]
with probability $1-o(1)$ at least one of the following holds:

\begin{enumerate}
\item $G^{(k)}[\Omega_k]$ contains an isolated right vertex.

\item $G^{(k)}[\Omega_k]$ contains distinct degree-one right vertices $j,j'$ with the same unique left neighbor:
\[
N_{G^{(k)}}(j)=N_{G^{(k)}}(j')=\{i\}
\]
for some $i\in I^{(k)}$.

\item $G^{(k)}[\Omega_k]$ contains a \hyperref[def:weight-compatible-rooted-matching-tree]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{weight-compatible $m_k$-matching rooted tree}}}
whose right vertices have support degree at most $40d_{\rm av}$ and whose
incident nonzero weights have absolute value at most $10d_{\rm av}$.

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space; for the one-sided version T need not be invertible","A is measurable with log^+ ||A|| integrable","the splitting version additionally needs T invertible, A(x) invertible a.e., and log^+ ||A^{-1}|| integrable","all statements hold for mu-a.e. x; exponents depend on mu"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438459+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents, smooth dynamics","id":"claim_1676fc5d4bd4204464d67994de31ed5e2340561ded554ac315e0ddd82660b53e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \mathcal{B}, \mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \to M_d(\mathbb{R})$ a measurable cocycle with $\log^+ \|A\| \in L^1(\mu)$; write $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x)\cdots A(x)$.

ONE-SIDED (FILTRATION) VERSION - no invertibility of $T$ or of $A$ needed. For $\mu$-a.e. $x$: (a) the limit $\Lambda(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \big(A^n(x)^{\mathsf T} A^n(x)\big)^{1/2n}$ exists (a symmetric positive semidefinite matrix); (b) there are an integer $1 \le k(x) \le d$, exponents $\infty > \lambda_1(x) > \lambda_2(x) > \dots > \lambda_{k(x)}(x) \ge -\infty$ (only the smallest may be $-\infty$; this happens whenever $A$ is singular with positive probability, and can also happen for a.e.-invertible $A$ when $\log^+\|A^{-1}\|$ is not integrable), and a filtration of linear subspaces $\mathbb{R}^d = V_1(x) \supsetneq V_2(x) \supsetneq \dots \supsetneq V_{k(x)}(x) \supsetneq V_{k(x)+1}(x) = \{0\}$, measurable in $x$, such that $A(x) V_i(x) \subset V_i(Tx)$ and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x) \quad\text{for every } v \in V_i(x) \setminus V_{i+1}(x);$$
(c) $k$, the $\lambda_i$ and the multiplicities $m_i = \dim V_i - \dim V_{i+1}$ are $T$-invariant functions of $x$ (constants when $T$ is ergodic); (d) $\lim \frac1n \log |\det A^n(x)| = \sum_i m_i \lambda_i(x)$, and more generally $\lim \frac1n \log \|\Lambda^p A^n(x)\|$ (norm on the $p$-th exterior power) equals the sum of the $p$ largest exponents counted with multiplicity; (e) the $\lambda_i$ with multiplicities are exactly the limits $\lim \frac1n \log \sigma_j(A^n(x))$ of the singular values, i.e. the logarithms of the eigenvalues of $\Lambda(x)$.

TWO-SIDED (SPLITTING) VERSION. If moreover $T$ is invertible, $A(x) \in GL_d(\mathbb{R})$ a.e. and $\log^+ \|A^{-1}\| \in L^1(\mu)$, then for a.e. $x$ all exponents are finite and there is a measurable $A$-equivariant splitting $\mathbb{R}^d = E_1(x) \oplus \dots \oplus E_{k(x)}(x)$, $A(x)E_i(x) = E_i(Tx)$, $\dim E_i = m_i$, with $\lim_{n \to \pm\infty} \frac1n \log \|A^n(x) v\| = \lambda_i(x)$ for all $v \in E_i(x) \setminus \{0\}$ (the SAME exponent forwards and backwards), $V_i(x) = \bigoplus_{j \ge i} E_j(x)$, and the angles between the Oseledets subspaces decay subexponentially along orbits: $\lim_{n\to\pm\infty} \frac1n \log \sin\angle\big(E_i(T^n x), \bigoplus_{j\ne i} E_j(T^n x)\big) = 0$.

WHERE IT FAILS. (1) Without $\log^+\|A\| \in L^1$ the limits need not exist: for $d = 1$ the theorem IS Birkhoff's theorem for $\log|a|$, which fails when $\log^+|a| \notin L^1$. (2) Without $\log^+\|A^{-1}\| \in L^1$ (or with $T$ non-invertible) there is in general NO equivariant splitting, only the forward filtration: the subspaces of vectors with exponent exactly $\lambda_i$, $i \ge 2$, are not canonically defined and the 'slow' directions are not invariant under $A$. (3) The exponents depend on the measure $\mu$: different ergodic measures for the same $T$ and $A$ generally have different exponents, and a point outside the full-measure set need not have exponents at all. (4) Convergence is not uniform in $x$, and the Oseledets subspaces are only measurable, in general not continuous, in $x$. (5) The theorem is about $\|A^n(x)v\|$ along ONE orbit; it says nothing about eigenvalues of $A^n(x)$ or about $\|A^n\|$ averaged over $x$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:02:08.103281+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16bbb74aece97d597e566a5e4c0446b9db38717ddf87291027c3feced1cbe59f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 17 of arXiv:2608.27374, '\Large \bf Distribution-constrained optimal multiple stopping: the Root-type solution'] For every \(i=0,\ldots,n\) and \(y\in\mathbb R\), we have

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.815410+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16c4740aba5042f3ad9a84b6ae1bd62bd1bf991539a3fb69e1d53e6dcfa0170f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:cyclic-suspension of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Put $C=\Sigma_{\ell,c}A$ and $D=\max A$.  For
$q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$, let $L_q(A)$ be the real span of the homogeneous
relation vectors of relation degree at most $q$, and put
$r_q(A)=\dim L_q(A)$.  Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For every $q\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}$,
\begin{equation}
 |qC|=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(q,\ell-1)}|(q-j)A|.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, for $X\in\{A,C\}$ put
\[
 \mathcal H_X(z)=\sum_{q\geq0}|qX|z^q.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal H_C(z)=\mathcal H_A(z)[\ell]_z,\qquad
 [\ell]_z=1+z+\cdots+z^{\ell-1}.
\end{equation}

\item Let
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_A&=K[x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}],&
 \psi_A&:S_A\longrightarrow K[u,v],\\
 \psi_A(x_i)&=u^{D-a_i}v^{a_i},&
 I_A&=\ker\psi_A,\qquad R_A=S_A/I_A.
 \end{aligned}
\]
be the standard-graded projective semigroup ring of $A$.  Put
$S_C=S_A[y]$, and let $I_C$ be the kernel of the homogeneous toric map
\[
 x_i\longmapsto u^{\ell(D-a_i)}v^{\ell a_i},\qquad
 y\longmapsto u^{\ell D-c}v^c,
\]
so that $R_C=S_C/I_C$.  Then
\begin{equation}
 R_C\cong
 R_A[y]\big/\bigl(y^\ell-x_0^{\lambda_0}\cdots
 x_{m-1}^{\lambda_{m-1}}\bigr).
\end{equation}
The displayed polynomial is homogeneous and regular.  In particular, if
$R_A$ is Cohen--Macaulay, then so is $R_C$.

\item Define the ambient $K$-polynomials by
\[
 \mathcal K_A(z)=(1-z)^m\mathcal H_A(z),\qquad
 \mathcal K_C(z)=(1-z)^{m+1}\mathcal H_C(z).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal K_C(z)=\mathcal K_A(z)(1-z^\ell).
\end{equation}
If $\beta^A_{i,j}$ and $\beta^C_{i,j}$ are the standard-graded Betti
numbers over $S_A$ and $S_C$, respectively, extended by zero outside their
natural homological and internal degree ranges, then
\begin{equation}
 \beta^C_{i,j}
 =\beta^A_{i,j}+\beta^A_{i-1,j-\ell}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, with $\xi$ an indeterminate recording homological degree, put
\[
 \mathcal B_A(\xi,z)=\sum_{i,j}\beta^A_{i,j}\xi^iz^j,
 \qquad
 \mathcal B_C(\xi,z)=\sum_{i,j}\beta^C_{i,j}\xi^iz^j.
\]
Then
\[
 \mathcal B_C(\xi,z)=\mathcal B_A(\xi,z)(1+\xi z^\ell).
\]

\item Label the coordinates of $C$ by the tuple
$(\ell a_0,\ldots,\ell a_{m-1},c)$.  They need not be in increasing order;
this changes $L_q(C)$ only by a coordinate permutation.  Put
\[
 w_{\ell,c}=(\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_{m-1},-\ell).
\]
Under the old-coordinate embedding,
\begin{equation}
 L_q(C)=
 \begin{cases}
  L_q(A),&q<\ell,\\[2mm]
  L_q(A)\oplus\mathbb Rw_{\ell,c},&q\geq\ell.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Hence
\begin{equation}
 r_q(C)=r_q(A)+
 \begin{cases}
  0,&q<\ell,\\
  1,&q\geq\ell,
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
and the multiset of active-relation birth degrees is the old multiset with
$\ell$ adjoined.

\item Define the order-$q$ Freiman dimension by
\[
 \operatorname{fdim}_q(A)=m-1-r_q(A).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{fdim}_q(C)=
 \begin{cases}
  \operatorname{fdim}_q(A)+1,&q<\ell,\\
  \operatorname{fdim}_q(A),&q\geq\ell.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}

\item One has
\begin{equation}
 \max C=\ell D,\qquad
 \operatorname{ndiam}(C)=\ell\operatorname{ndiam}(A).
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:07.256165+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16cd630722365cf9146136827d4da45014dde4e13d8a0c3651edeb6f14791a5a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 of arXiv:2604.19220, 'Split merge dynamics for expanding intervals and point processes on the real line.'] For a given family of splitting proportions

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:52:57.675242+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16cd9a22835cdde01668d655408aed5023a2d9dbb36f5d83b0c61f0a74e6d30e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 10 of arXiv:2609.02686, 'The Bonnet-Myers theorem on Finsler manifolds with integral weighted Ricci curvature bound'] Let $(M, F, m)$ be an $n$-dimensional $(n\geq 2)$  forward complete connected Finsler metric measure manifold with $\Lambda_{F}<\infty$. Given $p\in (\frac{n}{2}, n]$, $\alpha\in [\frac{1}{2},1)$. Then we can get the following results.
\ben
\item[{\rm (1)}] There exists a nonnegative constant $\varepsilon_{0}=\varepsilon_{0}(n,p,\Lambda_{F},\alpha,R_{0})$ such that when $\overline{\left\|{\rm{Ric}}_{\infty}^{\Lambda_{F}^{2}}\right\|}_{p, R_{0}, 0}\leq \varepsilon_{0}$,

\be
{\rm{diam}}(M)\leq \frac{\Lambda_{F}^{-1}(\Lambda_{F}+1)\pi}{2}.

\een","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:18:13.277070+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16dda0c9f10a17bae81a21c9f5039052877abed640c4e00fc3901e62325f3ad2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:survival of arXiv:2507.14676, 'On the critical parameters of branching random walks'] Let $(X,\mu)$ be a BRW starting from one particle at $x\in X$ and let $A\subseteq X$.
	We say that
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item 
		the process \textsl{survives locally wpp} in $A$ 
		if 
		$
		{\mathbf{q}}(x,A)<1
		
		
		
		$;
		\item
		the process \textsl{survives globally wpp} if
		
		$
		
		
		
		{\mathbf{q}}(x,X) <1$;
		
		
		\item
		there is \textsl{strong local survival wpp} in $A$ 
		if
		$ 
		{\mathbf{q}}(x,A)={\mathbf{q}}(x,X)<1$

		$.
	\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["E X^2 < infinity (finite variance); with only a finite mean use Markov on |X - mu|","t > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.625865+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_16e67a3e90398ddbb9bc39a2380f27c36c12b66fd99444ceee8f8badbc90a232","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random variable with finite mean mu = E X and finite variance sigma^2 = Var X. Then for every t > 0, P(|X - mu| >= t) <= sigma^2 / t^2; equivalently P(|X - mu| >= k sigma) <= 1/k^2 for every k > 0. The inequality is sharp: for t >= sigma the variable taking the values mu - t and mu + t with probability sigma^2 / (2 t^2) each and the value mu otherwise has mean mu, variance sigma^2 and P(|X - mu| >= t) = sigma^2 / t^2 exactly. It gives no information for t <= sigma, and it is the classical route to the weak law of large numbers: for i.i.d. X_i with finite variance, P(|(X_1 + ... + X_n)/n - mu| >= eps) <= sigma^2 / (n eps^2) -> 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:25:55.462440+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_16ea751e5943e18cc7592d103569423dca46eba43154b303be250342e8d24d23","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 19 (Large deviation principle) of arXiv:2607.28238, 'Well-posedness and large deviations for the obstacle problem of first-order stochastic con'] The family $\{X^\varepsilon\}$ is said to satisfy the large deviation principle with rate function $I$ if for each Borel subset $A$ of $\mathcal{E}$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.580419+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1735778aaca10a65189fbd741cefd1c48f000341d27b9831055fcfa73b29880f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 18 (Bethe verification) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] On $T_d$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red} is exact.) By vertex-transitivity all transmission probabilities equal a single $p=p^{\ex}$, the harmonic measure is uniform on the end space $\Sigma^{\mathbb N}$, $\Sigma=\{1,\dots,d-1\}$, there is no failure-strength heterogeneity across siblings (all forcings identical), and the failed cluster is exactly a Galton--Watson process with offspring law $\mathrm{Bin}(d-1,p)$. The mean matrix is the scalar $M=(d-1)p$, so $\rho(M)=(d-1)p$.
\item (Theorem~\ref{thm:gap} is an equality.) The boundary is homogeneous, $p_ew_e\equiv p$, so $\ell=\log(d-1)+\log p$ and $e^{\ell}=(d-1)p=\rho(M)=p_{\min}^{-\dimH}$ with $p_{\min}=1/d$; the Jensen gap is zero. At criticality $(d-1)p=1$ the weighted dimension is $0$.
\item (Theorem~\ref{thm:32}.) At criticality the offspring law is $\mathrm{Bin}(d-1,1/(d-1))$, mean $1$, variance $1-1/(d-1)<\infty$ for $d\ge3$, giving $C_d=(2\pi(1-1/(d-1)))^{-1/2}>0$ and the $n^{-3/2}$ tail. The binary tree $d=2$ is the degenerate variance-zero case and is excluded.
\item (Theorem~\ref{thm:stab}.) $\rho=(d-1)p(\theta,\gamma)$ with $p$ decreasing in $\theta$ and increasing in $\gamma$; $\mathcal M_+=\{p>1/(d-1)\}$ is convex, $\mathcal M_-$ its complement is contractible by the $\gamma$-retraction, the critical curve is smooth, and $(1-(d-1)p)^{-1}$ is the explicit expected cluster size.
\item (Theorems \ref{thm:pressure}, \ref{thm:dimS} and \ref{thm:crt}.) The pressure is affine, $\varphi(\beta)=\log(d-1)+\beta\log p$, so the convexity gap vanishes, consistent with item 2. In the supercritical regime $(d-1)p>1$ the failed boundary has $\dimH(\partial S)=\log((d-1)p)<\log(d-1)=\dimH(\partial T)$: the cascade survives along an exponentially thin bundle of rays, of relative codimension $\log(1/p)$. At criticality, the cluster is single-type with bounded offspring, so the exponential-moment hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:crt} is automatic and the conditioned cluster rescaled by $\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{off}}}{2\sqrt n}$, $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{off}}=1-\frac{1}{d-1}$, converges to the CRT by Aldous' theorem \cite{Ald93}.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Recurrent symmetric Markov process; base point o; inverse local time at o","GFF with covariance the Green function of the process killed at o, independent of the process","Identity in law, not a pathwise coupling"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988309+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_178ab0e20429fbcabddf72bded46fbdf579084e30b0d6607f8a57c199cde4f8b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Generalised second Ray-Knight theorem (Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000): let X be a recurrent symmetric Markov process on a countable state space (for instance continuous-time random walk on a finite connected graph, or on Z^2), started at a base point o, and let tau(u) be the inverse local time at o, the first time the local time at o reaches u. Let (phi_x) be the Gaussian free field on the state space with covariance the Green function of X killed at o, independent of X. Then the field (L^{tau(u)}_x + (1/2) phi_x^2)_x has the same law as ((1/2)(phi_x + sqrt(2u))^2)_x. Dynkin-type isomorphisms exist for transient processes killed at an independent exponential time (there the shift is absent). Uses: transfer of DGFF extremal results to local-time level sets and cover times (Ding-Lee-Peres via the Gaussian free field maximum), thick points of random walk, and the Sabot-Tarres and Lupu loop-soup couplings. Limits: the isomorphism identifies laws, not couplings, of the two sides unless the stronger Lupu coupling is used; the sign of phi is lost in the square, so events about level sets of the local time correspond to two-sided level sets of phi + sqrt(2u). Typical failure: Using the generalized second Ray-Knight isomorphism but omitting or misplacing the additive shift sqrt(2T) term that appears when T is a fixed constant rather than an inverse-local-time stopping time, as in the classical Brownian motion Ray-Knight theorems; dropping or mislocating this shift silently changes which boundary or starting condition the isomorphism is actually describing. Canonical reference: Ray, 1963, Illinois Journal of Mathematics; Knight, 1963, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society; Eisenbaum, Kaspi, Marcus, Rosen and Shi, 2000, Annals of Probability; Lupu, 2016, Annals of Probability.","status":"unverified"}
