{"assumptions":["T_n is an ordered rooted tree, and its one-vertex fringe subtrees are leaves."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363466+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fb16adade5b99b6afb4fbfd858b71d368ab5f3b8075f27b19a7efee1501cb95","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the negative part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.4 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Problem 20.4 asks for a Gaussian extension of Theorem 7.12, the law of large numbers for fringe-subtree counts. Let T_n be the simply generated tree, equivalently the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, with n vertices. Let N_T be the number of vertices whose fringe subtree equals a fixed finite ordered rooted tree T, and let N_d be the number of vertices with d children. For the one-vertex tree bullet, N_bullet = N_0 exactly, since its occurrences are precisely the leaves. In both constructions of the companion memo on Problem 20.2, the subcritical law of its Theorem A (nu < 1) and the critical infinite-variance law of its Theorem B (nu = 1, sigma^2 = infinity), the bulk of the vertices has degree 0 or 1. Hence N_0 = n - N_1 + O(1), and N_bullet inherits the non-Gaussian limit of (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n): a two-point law in the first construction and a mixture of two Gaussians in the second. Assuming those two theorems, fringe-subtree counts are not asymptotically normal in general when nu < 1, nor when nu = 1 with sigma^2 = infinity. The finite-variance critical case is resolved in the literature by Janson (Random Structures Algorithms 48, 2016, Theorem 1.5) and is not included here as own work. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:30:28.827360+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fb655af0af51c6fd1c94e68562250b7d6520db202e17d88f0a7aea05e01d7a5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 15 of arXiv:2609.02105, 'Contact fundamental forms and \\ adjoint varieties'] Let $M$ be a complex manifold  with a contact structure $H \subset TM$. 
\begin{itemize} \item[(i)]
For each $z \in M$, define $\fn_{z, 1} := H_z$ and $\fn_{z, 2} := T_z M/H_z$. Then $\fn_z = \fn_{z,1} + \fn_{z, 2}$ has a graded Heisenberg algebra structure given by Lie brackets of vector fields. We call it the {\em symbol algebra} of the contact structure $H \subset TM$ at $z \in M$.  Its universal enveloping algebra $U(\fn_z)$ has a grading coming from the grading $\fn_z = \fn_{z,1} + \fn_{z, 2}$ (this grading is not compatible with the natural filtration of the universal enveloping algebra), which we denote by $$U(\fn_z) \  = \ \oplus_{k \geq 0} U_k(\fn_z).$$  As $z$ varies, it defines a vector bundle $U(\fn)$ on $M$ with the fiber $U(\fn)_z = U(\fn_z)$  and a vector subbundle $U_k(\fn)$ for each $k \geq 0$ with the fiber  $U_k(\fn)_z = U_k(\fn_z)$.
\item[(ii)] For each $z \in M$,  define the {\em weighted order} ${\rm ord}_z(\varphi)$ of a local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M, z}$ to be  zero.
The {\em weighted order} ${\rm ord}_z (\xi)$ of a nonzero local vector field $\xi$ is defined to be 1 if it is a local section  of $H$ and 2 otherwise.  A local monomial  differential operator  on $M$ of the form $\xi_1 \cdots \xi_r$ has weighted order $${\rm ord}_z (\xi_1 \cdots \xi_r) \ := \ {\rm ord}_z (\xi_1) + \cdots + {\rm ord}_z(\xi_r).$$ A local differential operator on $M$ is {\em of weighted order $\leq k$} at $z$ if each of its monomial terms has weighted order at most $k$. 
\item[(iii)]
A local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M,z}$ has {\em weighted vanishing order $\geq k+1$} at $z \in M$, if $P\varphi$ vanishes at $z$ for any local differential operator $P$ of weighted order $\leq k$. Denote by $\bm^k_z \subset \sO_z$ the ideal of local holomorphic functions with weighted vanishing order $\geq k$ at $z$ and set $ J^k_z := \sO_z / \bm^{k+1}_z.$ The vector bundle $J^k$ on $M$ whose fiber at $z$ is $J^k_z$ is called the {\em bundle of contact $k$-jets}. 
A local holomorphic function $\varphi \in \sO_{M,z}$ naturally determines a local section $j^k(\varphi) \in \sO(J^k)_z$, called the {\em contact $k$-jet} of $\varphi$ at $z$. 
There is a natural surjective homomorphism of vector bundles $ \pi^{k}_{k-1}: J^{k} \to J^{k-1}$ yielding an exact sequence of  vector bundles 
$$0 \to U_{k}(\fn)^* \longrightarrow J^{k} \stackrel{\pi^{k}_{k-1}}{\longrightarrow} J^{k-1} \to 0,$$ where $U_k(\fn)^*$ denotes the dual of the vector bundle $U_k(\fn)$.  \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.751928+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fc20a5681643b475f0f39f7026b6a8536ea7fa315fd2f91358dbeb6b84e3c43","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 26 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Fix $c > 0$ and let $Q_t$ be the birth-death process
  with
  \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $Q_0 \sim \operatorname{Poisson}(c)$;
    \item $n \mapsto n +1$ transitions of rate $c$; and
    \item $n \mapsto n - 1$ transitions of rate $n$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Then the first hitting time of $0$,
  \[
    \tau_c \coloneqq \inf\{ t \geqslant 0 \mid Q_t = 0 \},
  \]
  has Laplace transform
  \[
    \E e^{-s\tau_c} = e^{-c}
    \left[1 - c\int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^{s} e^{-cx} \, dx
    \right]^{-1},
    \quad s \geqslant 0.
  \]
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $s > 0$. By total expectation,
    \[
      \E e^{-s \tau_c}
      = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty
      \E\left(e^{-s\tau_c} \middle| Q_0 = n\right)
      \PP(Q_0 = n)\\
      = e^{-c} \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{c^n}{n!}\, \phi_n(s)
    \]
    where $\phi_n(s) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}(e^{-s\tau_c} \mid 
    Q_0 = n)$. So if $\Phi_s$ is defined on $[0, c]$ by
    \begin{equation}
      
      \Phi_s(y) \coloneqq \sum_{n=0}^\infty
      \phi_n(s) \, \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \quad \text{then} \quad
      \E(e^{-s\tau_c}) = e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c).
    \end{equation}
    Clearly $\phi_0(s) = 1$ and first-step analysis gives
    \[
      (c+n+s) \, \phi_n(s) = 
      n \, \phi_{n-1}(s) + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s),
      \quad n > 0.
    \]
    By taking a weighted sum of this recurrence,
    \[
      \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \left(c + n + s \right)
      \phi_n(s) = \sum_{n = 1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!}
      \left[ n \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \, \phi_{n+1}(s)\right].
    \]
    The left-hand side is
    \[
      (c+s) \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_n(s)
      + y \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_n(s)
      =
      (c+s)\left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
    \]
    while the right-hand side is
    \[
      y \sum_{n=1}^\infty
      \frac{y^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} \, \phi_{n-1}(s)
      + c \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{y^n}{n!} \, \phi_{n+1}(s)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[ \Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s)\right].
    \]
    We are left with the differential equation
    \[
      (c+s) \left[\Phi_s(y) - 1\right]
      + y \, \Phi_s'(y)
      = y \, \Phi_s(y) + c
      \left[\Phi_s'(y) - \phi_1(s) \right]
    \]
    or equivalently,
    the initial value problem
    \begin{align}
      
      \left(c-y\right) \Phi_s'(y)
      + \left(- c + y - s\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= \overbrace{c \, \phi_1(s) - c - s}^{-K}\\ \notag
      \Phi_s'(y) + \left(-1-\frac{s}{c-y}\right) \Phi_s(y)
      &= -\frac{K}{c-y}
    \end{align}
    with condition $\Phi_s(0) = 1$.
    Use the integrating factor $I_s(y) = e^{-y} \, (c-y)^s$ to write
    \begin{align*}
      \left[e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)\right]'
      &= \frac{-K}{c-y} \, e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s\\
      e^{-y} \left(c-y\right)^s \Phi_s(y)
      - e^{-0} \left(c - 0\right)^s \Phi_s(0) 
      &= \int_0^y \frac{-K}{c-x} \, e^{-x} \left(c - x\right)^s \, dx
      \intertext{for any $y < c$. It's clear from \eqref{eq:Phi} that
      $\Phi_s$ is continuous, so take the $y \uparrow c$ limit:}
      \frac{c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}
      &= K.
    \end{align*}
    Finally, the $y \uparrow c$ limit of \eqref{eq:IVP}
    informs us $-s \, \Phi_s(c) = -K$, thus
    \begin{align*}
      \E e^{-s\tau_c}
      &= e^{-c} \, \Phi_s(c)
      = \frac{e^{-c}\, c^s}{\int_0^c e^{-x} \, s \left(c-x\right)^{s-1} dx}\\
      &= \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^c e^{-x} \left(c-x\right)^s dx}
      = \frac{e^{-c} \, c^s}{c^s - \int_0^1 c \, e^{-cx} \left(c-c\,x\right)^s dx}\\
      &= e^{-c} \left[1 - c \int_0^1 \left(1-x\right)^s e^{-cx}\, dx \right]^{-1}.
      \qedhere
    \end{align*}
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["psi(lambda) = log E e^{lambda X} finite for some lambda > 0 (otherwise the bound is vacuous)","for the i.i.d. rate statement: independent and identically distributed summands"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627588+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1fe4f3b747b727689cb17f579418ee4b2fd98070d9ff3fa9527f2e43df172cf8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a random variable with cumulant generating function psi(lambda) = log E[exp(lambda X)], finite on an interval containing 0 in its interior on the right. Then for every t, P(X >= t) <= exp(-psi^*(t)) where psi^*(t) = sup_{lambda >= 0} (lambda t - psi(lambda)) is the (one-sided) Legendre transform of psi. If X = sum_{i=1}^n X_i with the X_i independent and identically distributed with cumulant generating function psi_1, then psi = n psi_1 and P(X >= n t) <= exp(-n psi_1^*(t)): the exponent is LINEAR in n with rate psi_1^*(t), the Cramer rate function. Cramer's theorem says this exponential rate is exactly right, that is (1/n) log P(X >= n t) -> -psi_1^*(t) for t > E[X_1] under a finiteness condition on psi_1 near 0, so the Chernoff bound loses nothing at the level of the exponential rate although it can lose polynomial factors. The method requires SOME finite exponential moment: without it psi^* is identically 0 for t above the mean and the bound is vacuous, which is the correct behaviour for heavy-tailed laws. [standard; e.g. Dembo and Zeitouni, Large Deviations Techniques and Applications, 2nd ed., Chapter 2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:09.854550+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_1ff93fade75195c2bc7aad8a3619cd72ef7f7e316a358b40e32608f81ba88a58","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2605.20026, 'Quasihelix properties\\ of selected Volterra Gaussian processes'] \leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[1),left=5pt]
\item 
 \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item For any fixed $\lambda > 0$ and $\alpha\in(-1/2, 1/2)$ the process $U^{(1)}$ is a local $(\alpha+\frac12, 0, T)$-quasihelix for any $T>0$.
    \item Let $\alpha = 1/2$. Then for any fixed $\lambda > 0 $ and any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ the process $U^{(1)}$ is a  local $(1, 1 - \varepsilon, 0, T)$-generalized quasihelix for any $T>0$.  
    \item Let $\alpha > 1/2$. Then for any fixed $\lambda > 0$ the process $U^{(1)}$ is a local $(\alpha+\frac12, 1$, $0, T)$-generalized quasihelix  for any $T>0$ and $(1, T_1, T_2)$-quasihelix  for any  \mbox{$0 < T_1 < T_2$}.
\end{enumerate} 

\item

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a probability space (or a finite measure space)","G convex, nondecreasing, superlinear at infinity; the constant sup_i E[G(|X_i|)] must be uniform over the family"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751629+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_2009470175a95a3c30c51a0b9029476dfd66707c810383993ea647e49b0c988a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space and {X_i : i in I} a family of random variables. The family is uniformly integrable if and only if there exists a nondecreasing convex function G : [0, infinity) -> [0, infinity) with G(t)/t -> infinity as t -> infinity such that sup_{i in I} E[G(|X_i|)] < infinity. The sufficiency direction is the one used in practice: a uniform bound on any superlinear moment, for example sup_i E[|X_i|^p] < infinity for a single p > 1, or sup_i E[|X_i| log^+ |X_i|] < infinity, forces uniform integrability. A uniform bound on the FIRST moment does not: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) the family X_n = n 1_{(0,1/n)} has E|X_n| = 1 for all n and is not uniformly integrable. [standard; e.g. Dellacherie and Meyer, Probabilities and Potential, or Williams, Probability with Martingales, Section 13.3]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.686380+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20379a5dab6d932dbb7f2d5de4b388201a8eeacc73402556dcd59bdc4ce9d0cc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 15 (Resonant skew-Hermitian endpoint identity) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $\Lambda\subset 2\pi\Q$ be finite and symmetric, and choose $m\geq1$ such that

 =\ell(a)D

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348858+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_208f7c4d1a65f4167efac3277e11eddaa90b1e153739b4d3e12334ae49c18c70","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 165 ($\by$ is Lipschitz) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Take $\by\equiv \by(q_{d+1})$ as in \eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y}, so it is measurable with respect to $\cG(q_{d+1})$, as defined by \eqref{e:gaus.filt}. 
Conditional on $\cG(q_d)$,
the random vector $\by$ has mean zero, and is subgaussian with variance proxy $L^{O(1)}$.

\begin{proof} Let us abbreviate
	\[
	\bXi
	\equiv \bXi^{d+1}
	\equiv \frac{\bG(q_{d+1})
		-\bG(q_d)}{\sqrt{p_{d+1}-p_d}}\,,
	\]
so this is a gaussian independent of $\cG(q_d)$. Then we can express
	\begin{align*}
	\sqrt{\delta_d}\by
	&\stackrel{\eqref{e:normalized.vectors.y}}{=}
	\E\bigg[ \cA\Big(
		\bG(q_d)
		+(p_{d+1}-p_d)^{1/2}\bXi
		+ (1-p_{d+1})^{1/2} \bG'\Big)\,\bigg|\,\bG(q_d),\bXi
		\bigg]\\
	&\qquad-\E\bigg[ \cA\Big(
		\bG(q_d)
		+(p_{d+1}-p_d)^{1/2}\bXi
		+ (1-p_{d+1})^{1/2} \bG'\Big)\,\bigg|\,\bG(q_d)\bigg] \,.
	\end{align*}
Thus, conditional on $\cG(q_d)$,
the vector $\by$ has mean zero.
It follows by the assumption on $\cA$ together with assumption~\eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} that
 $\by$ is $L^{O(1)}$-Lipschitz in $\bXi$, so the subgaussian claim follows using Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.592384+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2092f4f49ea0d52063ec02bc8e3f7158aa9283d9f4c1bbf8e17c9a7aebe64b24","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.03466, 'Least-Favorable Location for Binomial Top-$t$ Selection'] Consider $k$ independent Bernoulli populations, each sampled $n$ times, and select the $t$ populations with the largest success counts, breaking ties uniformly. Classical monotonicity reduces the worst case over the preference zone with separation $\\delta$ to the slippage family with levels $p$ and $p+\\delta$, leaving only its absolute location $p\\in[0,1-\\delta]$ undetermined. A Gaussian approximation suggests the symmetric center $p_{\\mathrm c}=(1-\\delta)/2$, and the exact two-population problem is uniquely centered there for every $n\\ge2$. For fixed $k,t$ and $\\delta\\in(0,1)$, we prove that exact eventual centering holds precisely when $k=2t$. When $k\\ne2t$, the least-favorable location $p_{n,k,t}^*$ satisfies \\[ p_{n,k,t}^*-p_{\\mathrm c} =(k-2t)C_\\delta n^{-1/2}e^{-n\\Gamma_\\delta}\\{1+o(1)\\}, \\] where $C_\\delta$ and $\\Gamma_\\delta$ are explicit and positive. In either case, the least-favorable location is eventually unique. The proof writes incorrect selection as a union of pairwise misrankings and applies inclusion--exclusion, yielding a bipartite graph expansion. A single misranking has its exact maximum at the symmetric center and determines the central curvature; two-edge intersections sharing one population determine the central slope through their multiplicity imbalance; all remaining graphs have higher large-deviation rates.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space and T: X → X a map","for the orbit-closure characterization, T is continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111010+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics","id":"claim_20ab9dec4c9cbfd28df1fff4fca5251efcaf20965cb1e82ec6c01020cfd918be","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and T: X → X a map. A set A ⊂ X is (forward) invariant if T(A) ⊆ A. A minimal set is a nonempty closed invariant set M that contains no proper nonempty closed invariant subset. Some authors require T(M) = M (strict invariance); for a continuous T on a compact Hausdorff space a minimal set in the above sense automatically satisfies T(M) = M, since T(M) is then itself nonempty, closed (compact image) and invariant, hence equal to M. Characterization (T continuous): a nonempty closed invariant M is minimal if and only if for every x ∈ M the forward orbit {Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is dense in M. Proof of the equivalence: for x ∈ M the orbit closure cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} is nonempty, closed, contained in M, and invariant because continuity gives T(cl O) ⊆ cl T(O) ⊆ cl O; so minimality forces it to equal M; conversely, if every orbit in M is dense and N ⊂ M is nonempty closed invariant, any x ∈ N has its orbit inside N, so M = cl(orbit) ⊆ N. The system (X,T) itself is called minimal if X is a minimal set, i.e. every forward orbit is dense. Examples: a periodic orbit is a minimal set; an irrational rotation of the circle is minimal; the closure of a non-periodic orbit is in general NOT minimal (e.g. the orbit closure of a point of the doubling map whose orbit is dense contains the fixed point 0 as a smaller minimal set). Continuity is used in the orbit-closure characterization; the definition of a minimal set itself does not need it. For flows and group/semigroup actions the same definitions apply with 'orbit' read as the (semi)group orbit.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0129-recurrence-transience-criterion-for-excited-random-walks-under-station","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.048084+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20d91e1f2f967bd5c7191a2142a497f6f5c041cbfb86f3a0ac001391879cb602","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Examine the branching-process-with-migration proof and where i.i.d. is used. Result: The proof of Theorem 3.10 under (3.10) translates the walk into a branching process with migration whose offspring law at site k is determined by the cookie stack at k; under (IID) the branching process is homogeneous in space and the criterion delta > 1 is the criterion for the branching process to die out... under (SE) the process is a branching process in a stationary ergodic environment (BPRE with migration), whose survival criterion is governed by the Lyapunov exponent of the environment, i.e. by an ergodic average of log-means, not by the mean delta of the drift. So the natural (SE) analogue is NOT 'delta in [-1,1]' with delta = E sum_i (2 omega(0,i) - 1) but a criterion involving the annealed versus quenched growth rate of the associated BPRE; for i.i.d. environments the two coincide because the migration term is affine. I tested this on the simplest non-i.i.d. case: an environment alternating deterministically between two cookie stacks a and b (period 2, hence SE after a random shift): the branching process with migration is then periodic and its two-step transition is again a branching process with migration with delta_2 = delta_a + delta_b; the criterion becomes delta_a + delta_b > 2 for transience, i.e. the average delta > 1, consistent with the naive extension. For genuinely random ergodic environments a similar averaging holds if the migration is additive, which it is (the number of cookies eaten per visit adds). So the expected answer is YES for (SE) with the same delta, and the obstruction to a proof is that the branching-process comparison uses independence between the offspring at different sites when computing the extinction probability of the process with migration; with dependence one needs an ergodic theorem for the total progeny, available via the Kesten-Kozlov-Spitzer approach only for i.i.d.. Recorded: periodic environments satisfy the naive extension; the general (SE) case reduces to an ergodic total-progeny theorem for branching with migration in stationary environments. Key identity: Periodic two-stack environment: transient iff delta_a + delta_b > 2, i.e. the averaged delta criterion holds. Obstruction: Ergodic total-progeny theorem for branching processes with migration in stationary environments.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["INFINITE exchangeability; the theorem is false for finite exchangeable sequences","values in a Polish space, so that regular conditional distributions and a countable determining class exist"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781914+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_20e7e94fd93a2e51ba5becdbc47068b21245cc7d9d4def4e9e32ec611d9265ad","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be an INFINITE exchangeable sequence of random variables taking values in a Polish space S, meaning that for every n the law of (X_1, ..., X_n) is invariant under permutations of the n coordinates. Then there is a random probability measure Theta on S, measurable with respect to the exchangeable sigma-algebra, such that CONDITIONALLY on Theta the X_i are i.i.d. with common law Theta. Equivalently the law of the sequence is a MIXTURE of i.i.d. laws, and Theta is the almost sure limit of the empirical measures (1/n) sum_{i <= n} delta_{X_i}. The theorem is FALSE for finite exchangeable sequences. Counterexample with n = 2: let (X_1, X_2) be uniform on {(0,1), (1,0)}. This is exchangeable, but any mixture of i.i.d. Bernoulli sequences has Cov(X_1, X_2) = E[p^2] - (E p)^2 = Var(p) >= 0, whereas here E[X_1] = E[X_2] = 1/2 and E[X_1 X_2] = 0 give Cov = -1/4 < 0. Sampling without replacement is exactly the mechanism, and it produces the negative correlation that no mixture of i.i.d. can. What DOES survive in finite length is a quantitative approximation, due to Diaconis and Freedman: an exchangeable sequence of length n, restricted to k of its coordinates, is close in total variation to a mixture of i.i.d. sequences, with an error of order k/n. So infinite exchangeability is the hypothesis and it is not decorative; 'exchangeable' alone, applied to a finite sample, does not license treating the data as conditionally i.i.d. [de Finetti (1931); Hewitt and Savage (1955) for the general Polish case; Diaconis and Freedman (1980) for the finite version]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the chain is reversible with respect to pi (real eigenvalues); the bounds are stated for the absolute spectral gap","aperiodicity (e.g. laziness) so that gamma* > 0","the upper bound carries the factor log(1/pi_min); the lower bound holds for epsilon < 1/2"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049135+00:00","domain":"Markov chains and mixing (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_2114caacee9ef704ca7243abee0f8be7a280413638cb34b387097351ec0f2be3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be the transition matrix of an irreducible, reversible Markov chain on a finite state space with stationary distribution pi, and let gamma* = 1 - max{|lambda| : lambda an eigenvalue of P other than 1} be the absolute spectral gap, with relaxation time t_rel = 1/gamma*. Then for every epsilon in (0, 1/2) the total-variation mixing time satisfies (t_rel - 1) log(1/(2 epsilon)) <= t_mix(epsilon) <= t_rel log(1/(epsilon pi_min)), where pi_min is the smallest stationary probability (Levin, Peres, Wilmer, Theorems 12.4 and 12.5). Mixing time is therefore the relaxation time up to a factor between log(1/(2 epsilon)) and log(1/(epsilon pi_min)); on a state space of size N the gap between the two sides can be as large as log N, and neither side can be dropped in general. For a lazy chain (holding probability at least 1/2) all eigenvalues are nonnegative, so the absolute gap equals the ordinary gap 1 - lambda_2; a periodic chain (a simple random walk on a bipartite graph) has an eigenvalue -1, gamma* = 0, and never mixes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:31:57.866085+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_215bdd42b029f2faca44ec2589e5bd0f812548361f87037ecf3ccc313ab831c8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition d:dirstructure of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] A \emph{Dirichlet structure}  $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu,\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})$ 	is a probability space $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu)$ along with a quadratic form $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ on $L^2(X,\mu)$ that satisfies the following properties.
		\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
			\item (densely defined, non-negative definite, quadratic form) $\mathcal{E}: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}$ is bilinear, where $\mathcal{F}$ is a dense subspace of $L^2(X,\mu)$ and $\mathcal{E}(f,f) \ge 0$ for all $f \in \mathcal{F}$.
			\item (closed form) $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ is a \emph{closed} form; that is, $\mathcal{F}$ is a Hilbert space equipped with the inner product
			\[
			\mathcal{E}_1(f,g):= \mathcal{E}(f,g)+ \langle f,g \rangle_{L^2(\mu)}, \quad \mbox{for all $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$}.
			\]
			\item (Markovian property) $f \in \mathcal{F}$ implies that $\widetilde{f}:=0 \vee (f \wedge 1) \in \mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{E}(\widetilde{f},\widetilde{f}) \le \mathcal{E}(f,f)$.
			\item $\mathds{1} \in \mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{E}(\mathds{1},\mathds{1})=0$, where $\mathds{1}$ is the constant function on $X$ that is identically one.
			\item (existence of carr\'e du champ operator) For all $f \in \mathcal{F} \cap L^\infty(m)$, there exists $\gamma(f,f) \in L^1(m)$ such that for all $h \in \mathcal{F} \cap L^\infty(m)$, we have 
			\[
			\mathcal{E}(fh,f)- \frac{1}{2}\mathcal{E}(h,f^2)= \int h \gamma(f,f) \,d\mu.
			\]
			\item (strong locality) For all $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$ and $a \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $(f+a)g =0$ implies $\mathcal{E}(f,g)=0$.
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.910289+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_21931244b4db91d736e19507a99eae5d45246650639f17658377c90a511ac411","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:shifted-contours of arXiv:2608.26745, 'Moderate Deviations for the Largest Eigenvalue of a Randomly Deformed Gaussian Unitary Ens'] There exist constants $c,C,\eta>0$ such that, uniformly for
$\bm\xi\in\mathcal G_N$, the following statements hold for all sufficiently large
$N$.

If $r=d+t(1\pm {\rm i})\in\Gamma^\pm$, then
\begin{align}
 \Re\Phi_N(r)
 &\le C-ct^3,
 &&0\le t\le T_N^*,                                    \\
 \Re\Phi_N(r)
 &\le-cN-cN^{2/3}(t-T_N^*),
 &&T_N^*\le t<\infty.                                          
\end{align}

If $s=-d-t\pm {\rm i}t\in\Sigma^\pm$, then
\begin{align}
 -\Re\Phi_N(s)
 &\le C-ct^3,
 &&0\le t\le T_N^*,                                    \\
 -\Re\Phi_N(s)
 &\le-cN-cN^{2/3}(t-T_N^*),
 &&T_N^*\le t<\infty.                                          
\end{align}

On the local pieces $0\le t\le N^\eta$,
\begin{align}
 \Big|e^{\Phi_N(r)}-e^{r^3/3}\Big|
 \le CN^{-c}(1+t^4)e^{-ct^3},                          \\
 \Big|e^{-\Phi_N(s)}-e^{-s^3/3}\Big|
 \le CN^{-c}(1+t^4)e^{-ct^3}.                          
\end{align}

Moreover, after decreasing $\eta$ if necessary, for every fixed integer
$m\ge0$ there is a constant $C_m>0$ such that, whenever
$L^3\le c\log N$, uniformly for $0\le q\le L$,
$\rho\ge0$, and either choice of sign,
\begin{align}
 &\int_{N^\eta}^{\infty}(1+t^m)
 \exp\!\left\{\Re\Phi_N(d+t(1\pm {\rm i}))+q(d+t)-\rho(d+t)\right\}\,\mathrm d t
 \le C_m e^{-cN^{3\eta}}e^{-d\rho},  \\
 &\int_{N^\eta}^{\infty}(1+t^m)
 \exp\!\left\{-\Re\Phi_N(-d-t\pm {\rm i}t)+q(d+t)-\rho(d+t)\right\}\,\mathrm d t
 \le C_m e^{-cN^{3\eta}}e^{-d\rho}. 
\end{align}

The same estimates hold with $\Phi_N(\zeta)$ replaced by $\zeta^3/3$.  For a
nonnegative spatial variable (denoted by $x$ on $\Sigma$ and by $y$ on
$\Gamma$), the corresponding estimates hold after extracting $e^{-dx}$ or
$e^{-dy}$, respectively, and omitting the positive term $q(d+t)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Nonzero rank-one target and exactly noiseless labels; full-row-rank design","Nonzero initial sample-gradient projection, automatic almost surely for independent nondegenerate Gaussian input-factor initialization","Measurable constant step chosen from the data and realized initializer and meeting both displayed bounds","For expectation: independent standard Gaussian inputs, n>p+3; comparison is a limit of expected risks with the zero RRR benchmark"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:56:41.473119+00:00","domain":"LoRA rank-one convergence and deficiency margins","id":"claim_21c6842180ec6ca8f1000ef2b6555029537399fe396caf4bb9b4cf553b55014c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; T419-C021 v1, proof (unaudited), no novelty claimed. Let Delta=u w^T be a real m-by-p nonzero rank-one target, ||u||=1, w nonzero. Let X be p-by-n full row rank, and let Z=Delta X exactly, without label noise. Set C=XX^T/n, lambda=lambda_min(C)>0, c=||C||op. Initialize b0=0 and any finite a0 in R^p with g0=w^T C a0 nonzero. Put

 q0=w^T C w/2>0,
 J=||a0||^2+1,
 R=||Delta||F+sqrt(2q0/lambda),
 K=J+2R,
 ell=||Delta C||op=||C w||.

Choose one constant step

 0<eta<=min{1/(1+2q0),1/(6Kc+ell)}.

Then simultaneous empirical factor GD has, for every t>=1,

 q_t:=||(b_t a_t^T-Delta) C^(1/2)||F^2/2
 <=q0 exp[-eta^3 lambda g0^4(t-1)/(8q0 cK)],

and therefore

 ||b_t a_t^T-Delta||F^2
 <=(2q0/lambda)exp[-eta^3 lambda g0^4(t-1)/(8q0 cK)].

This is fitting from the prescribed zero output factor at arbitrary input-factor scale; it does not require near-identity covariance or a spectral initializer. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.530224+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_21d2a5018cf74284bf204467cf2d5730a77c94fcd7b28d93caf66cb23f5f62f9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition eq:cutoff-event of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[proposition]{prop:quenched-cutoff}
Fix \(0\le\varepsilon<1/2\) and a Borel set \(B\subset\mathbb R\), with no
independence, identical-distribution, density, or genericity condition.
Set
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon}
 =\left\{\max_{I\in[N]^p}|J_I|
 \le N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\right\},\qquad
 \delta_{N,\varepsilon}
 =\mathbb P(\mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon}^c),
\end{equation}
and, whenever the conditioning event has positive probability, write
\(\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}
:=\mathbb P(\,\cdot\mid\mathcal T_{N,\varepsilon})\).  If merely
\(\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1)\), then the event has positive probability
for all sufficiently large \(N\), and
\[
 \left\lVert\nu-\nu'\right\rVert_{\mathrm{TV}}
 :=\sup_A\left\lvert\nu(A)-\nu'(A)\right\rvert
\]
satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \left\|
 \mathcal L_{\mathbb P}\bigl(Q_N^J(B)\bigr)
 -\mathcal L_{\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}}
 \bigl(Q_N^J(B)\bigr)
 \right\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\delta_{N,\varepsilon}.
\end{equation}
Consequently, for every deterministic sequence \(a_N\), every
\(\eta>0\), and every bounded measurable
\(\varphi:[0,\infty]\to\mathbb R\),
\begin{align}
 &\left|
 \mathbb P\bigl(\left\lvertQ_N^J(B)-a_N\right\rvert>\eta\bigr)
 -\mathbb P_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}
  \bigl(\left\lvertQ_N^J(B)-a_N\right\rvert>\eta\bigr)
 \right|
 \le\delta_{N,\varepsilon},\\
 &\left|\mathbb E\varphi(Q_N^J(B))
 -\mathbb E_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}\varphi(Q_N^J(B))\right|
 \le2\left\lVert\varphi\right\rVert_\infty\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1).
 
\end{align}
In particular, convergence of \(Q_N^J(B)\) in probability to a
deterministic limit is equivalent under the original and conditioned
laws.

The hypothesis \(\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1)\) follows, for example,
from the marginal bound
\[
 \sup_{I\in[N]^p}\mathbb E\exp(J_I^2/K^2)\le2,
\]
which requires no independence and gives
\begin{equation}
 \delta_{N,\varepsilon}
 \le2N^p\exp\{-K^{-2}N^{1-2\varepsilon}\}=o(1).
\end{equation}
Mean comparison needs only a separate integrability input.  In
particular, if \(0\le Q_N^J(B)\le M_N\) almost surely and
\(M_N\delta_{N,\varepsilon}\to0\), then
\begin{equation}
 \left|\mathbb E Q_N^J(B)
 -\mathbb E_{N,\varepsilon}^{\mathrm{cut}}Q_N^J(B)\right|
 \le M_N\delta_{N,\varepsilon}=o(1).
\end{equation}
The critical-count ceiling \({\rm(CC)}_p\) is sufficient, with
\[
 M_N=\frac1N\log(1+D_{N,p})=O(1).
\]
Algebraic genericity gives the explicit \(N\)-independent choice
\begin{equation}
 M_N=M_p:=
 \log(p-1)+\log\left(1+\frac2{p-2}\right).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:19:47.300957+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_21d4f49bfcd68c408ad18811bd2404c7533fb5adcca2d0064c2d79ca3e22ca91","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition The distributions $\wishart$ and $\gaussmat$ of arXiv:2602.11129, 'Information-Theoretic Thresholds for Bipartite Latent-Space Graphs Under Noisy Observation'] We let $\mathbb{W}(n, m, p, d)$ be the distribution over $n \times m$ matrices with entries in $\{0,1\}$ obtained as follows.     Define further the threshold $\tau = \tau(d, p)$ such that for any $u \in L, v \in R$, we have $

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:32:20.761755+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2247540e3bd73e1f9ac070e833ce77db0f12f0ee46a5765eaef048b9e6d5d91f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 21 of arXiv:2609.00448, 'Equivariant formality and representation theory'] Let $G$ be a compact connected Lie group of rank $n$, $S$ a torus subgroup of dimension being $n-1$, $T$ a maximal torus of $G$ containing $S$, $\mu\in \chi(T)$ a primitive character of $T$ such that $S=\text{ker }\mu$, $L$ a primitive weight in the weight lattice $\mathfrak{t}^*_\mathbb{Z}$ corresponding to $\mu$ after exponentiation, and $W$ the Weyl group of $G$. Define
	\[\Phi_L:=\left(\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}} wL\right)^{n(L)}\in \text{Sym}^*(\mathfrak{t}^*)^W,\]
	where $W_{[L]}$ is the stabilizer of $[L]:=\{\pm L\}\in \mathfrak{t}^*/\{\pm 1\}$, $n(L)=1$ or 2 depending on whether $\displaystyle\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL$ is $W$-invariant or $W$-anti-invariant, i.e. 
	\[\displaystyle w'(\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL)=\text{sgn}(w')\prod_{w\in W/W_{[L]}}wL\text{ for all }w'\in W.\] 
	Then $(G, S)$ is isotropy formal if and only if $\Phi_L\notin (f_1, \cdots, f_n)^2$, where $f_1, \cdots, f_n$ are the fundamental $W$-invariant homogeneous polynomials on $\mathfrak{t}$, i.e. $\text{Sym}^*(\mathfrak{t}^*)^W=\mathbb{R}[f_1, \cdots, f_n]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["characteristic zero (or the general polynomial over any field of characteristic zero)","n >= 5","coefficients are independent indeterminates: particular degree-5 polynomials over Q may still be solvable by radicals"],"created_at":"2026-08-29T02:26:24.137447+00:00","domain":"algebra / Galois theory","id":"claim_2256ca4481d9e0acf08c9c091382001ee523cf5d05e7ef315770d80b729f7390","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let n >= 5 and let K = Q(a_0, ..., a_{n-1}) be the field of rational functions in independent indeterminates. The general polynomial x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + a_1 x + a_0 over K is not solvable by radicals: no root of it lies in any radical extension of K (a tower K = K_0 < K_1 < ... < K_m in which each K_{i+1} = K_i(r) with r^{k} in K_i for some k >= 1). The reason is Galois' criterion: a polynomial is solvable by radicals exactly when its Galois group is a solvable group, and the general polynomial has Galois group the full symmetric group S_n over K, which is not solvable for n >= 5. For n <= 4 such formulas exist.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.020004+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_22579e0013e3790d51f813ba1becd014cb593a5097ee0a2b9087ed0d03bfb032","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 35 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(Z\) be a connected normal complex space whose dense analytic
regular locus \(\cR\) carries a K\"ahler structure \((g,J)\).  Assume
that the analytic and metric topologies agree, that \(d|_{\cR}\) is the
intrinsic length distance, and that \((Z,d)\) is a complete locally
compact length space equal to the metric completion of \((\cR,g)\).
Assume also that \(Z\) is klt, that \(\omega_g\) extends locally as a
positive current with bounded potential, and that every point has a
local closed holomorphic embedding
\(V\hookrightarrow\Omega_V\subset\C^L\) for which
\begin{equation}
                     \omega_g\ge c_V\omega_{\C^L}
                     \quad\text{on }V\cap\cR.
\end{equation}
Let $G:Z\to\C^r$ be continuous and holomorphic, and
assume on $\cR$ that
\begin{equation}
 \nabla dG^a=0,\qquad
 \left[\langle dG^a,d\overline{G^b}\rangle_{g^{-1}}\right]_{a,b=1}^r
 \text{ is positive definite}.
\end{equation}
Then, after composing \(G\) with an element of
\(\mathrm{GL}(r,\C)\), without translating the target, there is a global
biholomorphic isometry
\begin{equation}
                         Z\cong\C^r\times Z'
\end{equation}
under which $G$ is the projection.  The factor $Z'$ is connected, complete,
normal, and klt; write \(g'\) for its induced regular K\"ahler metric.
It inherits the bounded-local-potential K\"ahler current
and the local ambient metric lower bound of $Z$, and
\begin{equation}
                         \Sing Z=\C^r\times\Sing Z'.
\end{equation}

If, in addition, $f$ is locally Lipschitz on $Z$, smooth on $\cR$, and
satisfies \(\Rc+\nabla^2f=g/2\) on $\cR$, then
\[
                 f(z,y)=\frac{|z|^2}{4}+\ell(z)+f'(y),
\]
where $\ell$ is real affine-linear and $f'$ is locally Lipschitz; if $f$
is proper, then $f'$ is proper.  If also
\begin{equation}
                         \int_{\cR}e^{-f}\,dV_g<\infty,
\end{equation}
then \(\int_{\Reg Z'}e^{-f'}\,dV_{g'}<\infty\).  Finally, assume that
the flow of \(\nabla f\) is complete and preserves \(\cR\), and that its
canonical self-similar maps extend to the metric completions.  Then the
same Euclidean factor is static on every negative-time slice in that
canonical gauge. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli percolation on the discrete torus, d > 6","Mean-field cluster geometry (intrinsic diameter m^{1/2}, Euclidean diameter m^{1/4})"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T07:48:45.952251+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2279334a78f40f9f470203698541f2090e13571639d4fc686f5a52efb3646d33","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE MECHANISM NOTE, author-recorded. On the torus T_{n,d} with volume V, a critical cluster of size V^{2/3} has intrinsic geometry of a critical tree embedded four-dimensionally, so its Euclidean diameter is of order (V^{2/3})^{1/4} = V^{1/6}, while the torus side is V^{1/d}. Since V^{1/6} > V^{1/d} iff d > 6, above six dimensions the window clusters wrap around the torus many times and see the torus uniformly; this is why the exploration process should have the same global (mass-proportional) depletion as in G(n,p), which is what the multiplicative-coalescent scaling limit (Heydenreich-van der Hofstad Open Problems 13.3 and 13.5) needs. The torus plateau theorem (Hutchcroft-Michta-Slade) is the two-point version of this uniformity; the open step is the exploration-level (higher-point) version. Same reason makes eps >> V^{-1/3} lie above the correlation-length crossover eps >> V^{-2/d} for d > 6 (Open Problem 13.2).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5","consistent equivariant flow rule choosing uniformly among same-coloured children"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.450036+00:00","domain":"probability, trees, ergodic theory","id":"claim_22df461caf6d08479ba0f1da9d8fdedbb4603bca52d4395ae62573d0bad9bec1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (version 19 August 2026), Question 17.18 (p. 575) asks whether a consistent equivariant flow rule admitting a stationary measure EQUIVALENT to Galton-Watson measure must induce an ergodic Markov chain; their Proposition 17.17 proves it when all child weights are strictly positive, and Exercise 17.22 gives a non-ergodic example whose stationary measure is only absolutely continuous, so equivalence is the point of the question. Our result (id P0033, 2026-09-08): NO. Take Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5 (mean 12/5) and an isomorphism-invariant colour in {0,1} defined by AND at two-child vertices and OR at three-child vertices; both preserve unanimity, so every vertex has at least one child of its own colour, and the flow chooses uniformly among those. Galton-Watson measure is stationary, the root colour is invariant along the chain and takes each value with probability 1/2 - a non-constant invariant function, hence no ergodicity - and the stationary measure equals Galton-Watson measure, trivially equivalent to it. The colour exists because F(p) = (3/5) p^2 + (2/5)[1 - (1-p)^3] fixes 1/2, and r_n = E[q_n^2] satisfies r_{n+1} = 3/10 + (3/5) r^2 + (2/5) r^3 whose increment factors as (r - 1/2)[(2/5) r^2 + (4/5) r - 3/5], driving r_n from r_0 = 1/4 up to 1/2 and giving E[q(1-q)] = 0. Verification as the source words it: the step the proof leaves implicit, and which was checked, is that Galton-Watson really is stationary - it holds because, conditioned on the children's colours, the child subtrees are independent, each distributed as Galton-Watson conditioned on its own colour, so the chosen subtree is exactly GW given colour = c, the uniform choice adds no bias, and mixing over c returns GW. Prior art unchecked; the tree-automaton and factor-of-iid literature is where to look.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:37:15.060495+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_22e3220c4d656df74b5d8f73283dcfda6cb7f51a72f552e1865f5f268dc96bb6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 20 of arXiv:2607.11756, 'Full replica symmetry breaking in the Sherrington--Kirkpatrick model'] Let $\nu$ be a Borel probability measure on $[0,1]$, and write
\[
 \alpha_\nu(s)=\nu([0,s]),\qquad u=u_\nu.
\]
Let $X^\nu$ be the optimal diffusion
\[
 \dd X_s^\nu
 =\beta^2\alpha_\nu(s)u_x(s,X_s^\nu)\dd s+\beta\dd W_s,
 \qquad X_0^\nu=0.
\]
For every $s>0$, the law of $X_s^\nu$ has a strictly positive
$C^\infty$ density $p_\nu(s,\cdot)$. Define
\begin{equation}
 r_\nu(s,x)
 =\exp\{-\alpha_\nu(s)u(s,x)\}p_\nu(s,x),
 \qquad
 V_\nu(s,x)=-\log r_\nu(s,x).
\end{equation}
Then, for every $s>0$,
\begin{equation}
 r_\nu(s,x)
 =g_{\beta^2s}(x)
 \E_{\mathrm{br}}\exp\left\{
 -\int_{[0,s]}
 u\left(t,\frac tsx+\beta\mathfrak b_t^{\,s}\right)
 \nu(\dd t)
 \right\}.
\end{equation}
If $\alpha_\nu\equiv m$ on an open interval $(a,b)$, then
\begin{equation}
 (r_\nu)_s=\frac{\beta^2}{2}(r_\nu)_{xx}
 \qquad\text{on }(a,b)\times\R.
\end{equation}
If $q\in(0,1]$ is an atom of $\nu$ of size $c=\nu(\{q\})$, then
\begin{equation}
 r_\nu(q,x)=\e^{-cu(q,x)}r_\nu(q-,x),
\end{equation}
where
\[
 r_\nu(q-,x)
 =\e^{-\alpha_\nu(q-)u(q,x)}p_\nu(q,x).
\]
Finally, $r_\nu(s,\cdot)$ is even and log-concave, and
\begin{equation}
 (V_\nu)_x(s,x)\ge0,
 \qquad
 (V_\nu)_{xx}(s,x)\ge0,
 \qquad
 (V_\nu)_{xxx}(s,x)\le0,
 \qquad x>0.
\end{equation}
By parity,
\[
 (V_\nu)_x(s,0)=(V_\nu)_{xxx}(s,0)=0.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:05:52.484116+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_232ad64da67b53b2162d8c096bfce0dbcf0c9f8dd1389336552f8794cebade9f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eq:v-grad of arXiv:2505.02685, 'On the Spectral Expansion of Monotone Subsets of the Hypercube'] We say that $F : L^2(V) \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ is \emph{Fréchet differentiable} at $f \in L^2(V)$ if there
    exists a bounded linear operator $A : L^2(V) \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$ such that
    \[
        \lim_{\|h\|_{2} \to 0} \frac{\abs*{F(f+h) - F(f) - Ah}}{\|h\|_{2}} = 0 \,.
    \]
    In this case, we call $DF(f) \vcentcolon= A$ the \emph{Fréchet derivative} of $F$ at $f$. Moreover,
    by the Riesz representation theorem there exists a unique vector $v \in L^2(V)$ satisfying
    \begin{equation}
        
        Ah = \inp{h}{v}
    \end{equation}
    for all $h \in L^2(V)$. We call $\nabla F(f) \vcentcolon= v$ the \emph{gradient} of $F$ at $f$.
    Finally, we say that $F$ is (Fréchet) $C^1$ if it is Fréchet differentiable at every $f \in
    L^2(V)$ and the map $f \mapsto DF(f)$ (from $L^2(V)$ to the space of bounded linear operators
    $L^2(V) \to \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$) is continuous.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["k is an algebraically closed field","R = k[x_1, ..., x_n]"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T06:33:58.360339+00:00","domain":"algebraic geometry","id":"claim_23762cd326b445e39e634e7e4b65878c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let k be an algebraically closed field and R = k[x_1, ..., x_n]. Weak form: every proper ideal of R has a common zero in k^n; equivalently, every maximal ideal of R is (x_1 - a_1, ..., x_n - a_n) for some a in k^n. Strong form: for every ideal I of R, the ideal of polynomials vanishing on V(I) is the radical of I, I(V(I)) = sqrt(I). {"assumptions":["X compact metric, T continuous and topologically exact","T is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres, so that L maps C(X) into C(X)","the weight w is continuous and strictly positive everywhere","there exist lambda > 0 and h in C(X) with h > 0 everywhere and L h = lambda h","there exists a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu (used only for algebraic simplicity)","the conclusion is about the eigenvalues of L acting on C(X); no Banach space of Holder or bounded-variation functions and no quasi-compactness is assumed"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090835+00:00","domain":"thermodynamic formalism, transfer operators, Perron-Frobenius theory","id":"claim_237e639d0e9ed9df151e70d43e37add45d9d02ba588674ca6999612a5fb36cf3","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"SETTING: X a compact metric space; T : X -> X a continuous, topologically exact map which is a local homeomorphism with finite fibres (so that the operator below sends continuous functions to continuous functions); w : X -> (0, infinity) a continuous weight. Define the transfer (Ruelle) operator on complex continuous functions by (L f)(x) = the sum of w(y) f(y) over the finitely many y with T(y) = x; L is a bounded positive operator on C(X). Assume the Perron data exist: a number lambda > 0 and a strictly positive h in C(X) with L h = lambda h, together with a Borel probability measure nu with L* nu = lambda nu, i.e. the integral of L f with respect to nu equals lambda times the integral of f with respect to nu for all f in C(X). CONCLUSION: (1) if f in C(X) is complex-valued and L f = z f with |z| = lambda, then z = lambda and f is a constant multiple of h - so lambda is the only eigenvalue of modulus lambda in C(X) and its eigenspace is one dimensional; (2) lambda is ALGEBRAICALLY simple: there is no f in C(X) with L f - lambda f = h, hence no Jordan block at lambda. WHERE THE HYPOTHESES BITE: (i) exactness cannot be weakened to minimality, unique ergodicity or transitivity. Take X the circle, T an irrational rotation and w identically 1, so that L f = f composed with T^{-1}: every character exp(2 pi i n x) is an eigenfunction with an eigenvalue of modulus 1, so the peripheral spectrum is infinite - and the system is minimal and uniquely ergodic but not exact (it is invertible, hence never exact). (ii) Strict positivity of the weight is essential. If w may vanish, the irreducibility can become periodic: in the finite-state model, where L is a nonnegative matrix, the statement above is the PRIMITIVE case of the Perron-Frobenius theorem, and an irreducible matrix of period p > 1 has exactly p eigenvalues of modulus equal to its spectral radius, so simplicity of the peripheral eigenvalue genuinely fails. (iii) The conclusion concerns the peripheral eigenvalue only and gives NO spectral gap: to place the rest of the spectrum in a strictly smaller disc one needs quasi-compactness (a Lasota-Yorke or Ionescu-Tulcea-Marinescu inequality on a Holder or bounded-variation space), a separate hypothesis on the regularity of w and the expansion of T. (iv) The existence of h and nu is assumed here, not proved; producing them is the other half of the Ruelle-Perron-Frobenius theorem and needs its own hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A finite with at least two elements (for N = 1 the maximum has mean 0)","the signs are independent and symmetric; the bound is on the expectation over the signs only, the vectors are fixed"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706093+00:00","domain":"probability and learning theory","id":"claim_238153b7dd2c94196c2f503107fe4086af1bd720d344b15f76689b1605667c76","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be a finite subset of R^n with N = |A| >= 2 elements, and let r = max_{a in A} ||a||_2. Let sigma_1, ..., sigma_n be independent Rademacher signs (uniform on {-1, +1}). Then E_sigma [ max_{a in A} sum_{i=1}^{n} sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N), and consequently E_sigma [ max_{a in A} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i a_i ] <= r sqrt(2 log N) / n. Two consequences used constantly in learning theory: (1) for a finite class F of functions bounded by B on a sample x_1, ..., x_n, the empirical Rademacher complexity satisfies R_hat_S(F) = E_sigma sup_{f in F} (1/n) sum_i sigma_i f(x_i) <= B sqrt(2 log |F| / n), since each vector (f(x_1), ..., f(x_n)) has Euclidean norm at most B sqrt(n); (2) for a class C of sets of VC dimension d, restricting to the sample leaves at most s(C, n) <= (e n / d)^d distinct indicator vectors (Sauer-Shelah), each of norm at most sqrt(n), so R_hat_S(C) <= sqrt(2 d log(e n / d) / n) for n >= d. The logarithm cannot be removed at this generality: for A = {-1, +1}^n (N = 2^n, r = sqrt(n)) the maximum is exactly n while the bound reads n sqrt(2 log 2), so the lemma is sharp up to the constant sqrt(2 log 2) = 1.18; for VC classes Dudley's chaining removes the logarithm, R_hat_S(C) <= C sqrt(d / n).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583278+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_2391dac5df9a90395b1af7a294eca603716608168823cf2e7908d46e42b93d6a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In any bipartite graph, the maximum size of a matching (a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint) equals the minimum size of a vertex cover (a set of vertices meeting every edge). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:05.832712+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_23fec3e9fa8457461adb98074a2fe51ba41e458fdb7b27e5aa082d223348f60e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 7 (Hardness of exact quantile and lower-buffered quantile evaluation) of arXiv:2608.22227, '\fontsize{18pt}{20pt}\selectfont \bf Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning with Smoothed Q'] The following decision problems are PP-hard under polynomial-time Turing
reductions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item exact finite-horizon QMDP evaluation, i.e., deciding whether
    \(Q_\tau(R^\pi)\le c\) for the return \(R^\pi\) of a fixed deterministic
    policy;
    \item exact lower-buffered quantile evaluation, i.e., deciding whether
    \(Q_\tau^\beta(R^\pi)\le c\) for the return \(R^\pi\) of a fixed
    deterministic policy.
\end{enumerate}
The hardness holds even for finite-horizon MDPs with two states, one action,
binary transition probabilities, and deterministic rational rewards in
\([0,1]\). Consequently, the corresponding exact planning problems are also
PP-hard under polynomial-time Turing
reductions. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:28:49.115169+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_243e514c75f244b768e672633a227325552613a8147ea9c26ece25d23a5b112e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm THM52 of arXiv:2608.16170, '\bf On hitting time distributions of Markov processes with sub-Gaussian heat kernel bounds'] Let $X$ be a Borel right process on $(E,d)$ that satisfies (AC), (H2a) and (H2b).

 Further assume that $X$ admits the following short-time heat kernel lower bound at a fixed point $x\in E$: For some $T>0, \alpha>0,\beta>1$, there exist constants $C_1,C_2>0$ such that
\begin{equation}
p(t,x,y)\ge \frac{C_1}{t^{\alpha/\beta}}\exp\left\{-C_2\left(\frac{d(x,y)}{t^{1/\beta}}\right)^{\beta/(\beta -1)}\right\}, \quad \forall t\in (0, T], \, y\in E.
\end{equation}
Let $B\subset E$ be a nearly Borel set with compact closure $\overline{B}$. 
Then for any $\delta,\rho>0$ and any $\lambda>0$ ($\lambda\geq 0$ if $X$ is transient),
 \[
        \mathbb{P}^x[\sigma_B\leq t]\geq \frac{\nu^{(\lambda)}_{B_{x,\delta}}(\overline{B}_{x,\delta})}{\mathrm{e}^{\lambda T}}\cdot \frac{C_1C_3}{ t^{(\alpha-\beta)/\beta}}\exp\left\{-(1+\rho)C_2\left( \frac{\widetilde{d}(x,B)+\delta}{t^{1/\beta}}\right)^{\beta/(\beta-1)}\right\},\quad 0<t\leq T,
    \]
    where  $B_{x,\delta}:=\{y\in B:d(y,x)\leq \widetilde{d}(x,B)+\delta\}$, $\nu^{(\lambda)}_{B_{x,\delta}}$ is the measure obtained in Lemma~(LM51 of the paper), $C_1$ and $C_2$ are as in (equation eq:55 of the paper), and $C_3=(\beta-1)\rho\cdot \min\{(1+\rho)^{\alpha-\beta-\alpha/\beta}, 1\}>0$ is a constant depending on $\alpha, \beta,\rho$.","status":"unverified"}

Set
\[

\]
Then, for every pair of mappings
\[
f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k),
\quad
g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k),
\quad
f_j,g_j\in \mathcal P_d(\gamma),
\]
satisfying
\[
\int_E \Delta_f\,d\gamma \ge a

\text{and}

d_{\rm TV}(f,g)

where $C_1>0$ is an absolute constant.
	
In particular, optimizing over $\beta$, we obtain
\[
d_{\rm TV}(f,g)
\le
C_2k^5d
\bigl(1+\bigl|\ln\bigl(a^{-1}b^{\frac{2k-1}{2}}\max_{1\le j\le k}\|f_j-g_j\|_{L^2(\gamma)}\bigr)\bigr|\bigr)^s
\bigl(a^{-1}b^{\frac{2k-1}{2}}\max_{1\le j\le k}\|f_j-g_j\|_{L^2(\gamma)}\bigr)^\varkappa

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:14:37.637559+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2474c39324432340e948b01fcc2e3ca33d7c61618c625150fa62f220524fb6ff","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 5 (Volterra-resolvent comparison) of arXiv:2608.19151, 'Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Controlled Hawkes Jump-Diffusions'] Let $k\in L^1([0,T];\mathbb R_+)$, and let $R$ be the solution of the Volterra equation
\[
    R(t)=k(t)+\int_0^t k(t-s)R(s)\,\dd s, \ t\in [0,T].
\]
Suppose $f,F$ are nonnegative integrable functions on $[0,T]$ and
\[
    f(t)
    \le
    F(t)+\int_0^t k(t-s)f(s)\,\dd s,
    \qquad 0\le t\le T.
\]

Then
\[
    f(t)
    \le
    F(t)+\int_0^t R(t-s)F(s)\,\dd s.
\]
Consequently,
\[
    \int_0^t f(u)\,\dd u
    \le
    \left(
        1+\int_0^T R(u)\,\dd u
    \right)
    \int_0^t F(s)\,\dd s,
    \qquad 0\le t\le T.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Every definition and fixed-nu spectral clock premise in the statement","Balanced four-point frozen full-kernel GD with independent Gaussian hidden weights and iid readouts +/-nu; fixed0<nu<=1","Width limit precedes e->0; unit-norm single-index teacher, noise-averaged risk with rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e)","Simple-root event kappa^2>4aB; peak location refers to real spectral interpolation of discrete GD","No claim of nonlinear transfer, continuous iid-input extension, fixed label-noise amplitude or full Target1 closure"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T18:16:40.848916+00:00","domain":"epochwise double descent; ReLU full-kernel risk with random initial output","id":"claim_2493a9214e35c7702fb0aa74303c41f864042d4e37f5786d1c0242c56c7ed61b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft: proof (unaudited); independent mathematical and novelty review pending. Balanced four-point frozen-model spectral interpolation only; actual nonlinear transfer remains open.

# C017 v1: rescaled noise restores two roots in the iid-head frozen precursor
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: bound. Target:1. Novelty unestablished.
A supporting frozen-model result, not full Target1 and not yet a nonlinear-network result.

## 1. Model and precise limit
For 0<e<1/4 set D=1+e^2+e^4 and x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D), s,t=+/-1.
Use the uniform four-point population and teacher direction
u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2). The letter u_e denotes this direction, not
nu, the fixed readout magnitude in (0,1]. Set c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)),
alpha=c_e/2, g(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Its Walsh coefficients in modes
0,s,t,st are (0,alpha,alpha,alpha).
Initialize independent neurons with W_j~N(0,I_3) and heads independently +/-nu.
First take width to infinity at every fixed e, obtaining initial Gaussian
Walsh coefficients Z_(e,h). This is the ordinary fixed-width CLT of C016.
Then train the FROZEN deterministic full kernel
 H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z]
with discrete step1/2. Write b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2) for the normalized
four-point eigenvalues lambda_h. Use the settled clock premises
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), b_0 bounded away from0.
Thus eta=(b_t+b_st)/b_s~e and b_t/(b_t+b_st)->1/2.

For fixed kappa>0 choose effective Walsh noise variance alpha^2 rho_e,
 rho_e=kappa/sqrt(e).
Four independent errors +/-sigma_e with sigma_e=2alpha sqrt(rho_e)
realize exactly this variance. In particular sigma_e~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4),
so label noise remains <=1 for small e, but is not fixed as e decreases.
The noise-averaged clean risk conditional on initialization, in real-time
spectral interpolation of discrete GD, is
 Q_e(t)=sum_h [exp(-2b_h t)(Z_(e,h)-theta_h)^2
             +alpha^2 rho_e(1-exp(-b_h t))^2].             (1)
At integer t this is exactly discrete kernel GD. Real t is used only to
locate extrema of its spectral interpolation; no GD-to-flow limit is taken.

## 2. Joint initial-output covariance, on the relevant scales
Let phi_h(W)=(1/4)sum_(s,t) h(s,t) ReLU(W.x_(s,t)), and
lambda_h^RF=E phi_h(W)^2. The initial covariance is diagonal in Walsh modes,
Var(Z_(e,h))=nu^2 lambda_h^RF, by Gaussian coordinate sign symmetry.
In the Gaussian limit these modes are therefore independent.
C016 establishes lambda_s^RF/e^2->1/2 and the bounds
|phi_t|,|phi_st|<=e^2|W_2|/sqrt(D).
For W_0!=0, all four preactivations eventually have its sign. Consequently
phi_t/e^2 -> W_2 1{W_0>0}, and phi_st/e^2 ->0 almost surely.
Dominated convergence with the preceding bounds gives
 lambda_t^RF/e^4->1/2, lambda_st^RF/e^4->0.                (2)
On one probability space take independent standard normals G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st
and set Z_(e,h)=nu sqrt(lambda_h^RF)G_h for every e. This coupling has exactly
the required Gaussian law at each e. Since alpha~e^2/2, writing
A_(e,h)=(Z_(e,h)/alpha-theta_h/alpha)^2, we get almost surely
 e^2 A_(e,s)->a=2nu^2 G_s^2,
 A_(e,t)->(sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2, A_(e,st)->1.                (3)
Define B=((sqrt(2)nu G_t-1)^2+1)/2 >=1/2.
Here a>0 almost surely and a is independent of B. Independence is used only
after the joint Gaussian limit, not for finite-width output coefficients.

## 3. The new central derivative limit
For real s in a fixed compact interval set
 t_e(s)=((3/2)log(1/e)+s)/b_s, z=exp(-s).
Then q_s=exp(-b_s t_e(s))=e^(3/2)z exactly.
Normalize the risk derivative by 2alpha^2(b_t+b_st). Its fast contribution is
 [rho_e q_s-(A_(e,s)+rho_e)q_s^2]/eta
 =kappa(e/eta)z-[(e^2 A_(e,s))(e/eta)+kappa e^(5/2)/eta]z^2
 -> kappa z-a z^2.                                      (4)
For each slow mode q_h=1-O(e log(1/e)) uniformly on the compact interval.
Thus rho_e q_h(1-q_h)=O(sqrt(e)log(1/e))->0, while A_(e,h)q_h^2
has the limits in (3). The rate weights tend to1/2, giving their combined
contribution -B. The constant-mode contribution vanishes: its exponent
decays faster than every power of e and Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.
The same calculation after differentiating in s is valid: slow terms gain
a factor b_h/b_s=O(e), and even rho_e times that factor tends to0;
constant-mode exponentials dominate the additional polynomial factors.
Hence, almost surely in this coupling, uniformly on each compact s interval,

 Q'_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2(b_t+b_st)) -> H_kappa(s)
                                      =kappa exp(-s)-a exp(-2s)-B,
 and the derivatives in s converge too.                  (5)

## 4. Two-root criterion and peak time
On the event Delta=kappa^2-4aB>0 define
 z_+=(kappa+sqrt(Delta))/(2a), z_-=(kappa-sqrt(Delta))/(2a).
Both are positive and z_+>z_-. The classification is the elementary quadratic
criterion already used in C012, now with random coefficients a and B.
As s increases, H is negative, positive, then negative across
 s_min=-log z_+ and s_max=-log z_-.
The roots are simple. Uniform C1 convergence in (5) gives, for every such
fixed Gaussian realization, one nearby minimum and one nearby maximum of
the frozen interpolation for all sufficiently small e, converging to these
locations. Derivative convergence also gives strict decrease immediately
after the maximum. Thus there are two descents separated by a rise.
More precisely the peak satisfies
 b_s t_peak-(3/2)log(1/e) -> -log z_-,
 t_peak~(6pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                         (6)
The statements are pathwise in the coupling, on Delta>0. Random compact
neighborhoods are allowed: convergence on every integer-sized compact set
holds on one probability-one event. No deterministic width rate is asserted.
On Delta<0, H is negative on every compact s interval; this only addresses
this particular time window, not global absence of DD. Delta=0 is not treated.

For value-based nonlinear transfer, a useful additional consequence is this:
 d/ds [Q_e(t_e(s))/(2alpha^2 eta)] converges to H_kappa(s).
Therefore differences of the normalized risks converge to differences of
 V(s)=-kappa exp(-s)+(a/2)exp(-2s)-Bs.
Values across the two simple extrema have strict gaps of order alpha^2 eta.
An o(alpha^2 eta) uniform risk error over a containing compact interval would
preserve appropriately chosen decrease/rise/decrease witnesses and interval
peak localization. Such a nonlinear error is NOT supplied in this claim.

## 5. A tunable probability lower bound
The Gaussian independence in Section2 gives E a=2nu^2 and E B=1+nu^2,
so E[4aB]=8nu^2(1+nu^2). Markov's inequality yields
 P(Delta>0) >= 1-8nu^2(1+nu^2)/kappa^2.                   (7)
Choose kappa^2>8nu^2(1+nu^2)/delta for any prescribed delta in (0,1).
Then the frozen limiting construction has two simple central extrema with
probability greater than1-delta. The noise amplitude still tends to zero.
This is an initialization probability bound, with risk already averaged over
labels; it is not concentration for one realized label vector.
For fixed kappa the exact event probability need not equal this lower bound.

## 6. Scope and next unpaid step
C016's failed rho~1 route is avoided by changing BOTH noise scale and time
center; fixed nu and the unit-norm single-index teacher are retained.
This lemma concerns the balanced four-point frozen precursor only. It does
not yet prove the result for actual nonlinear GD, continuous iid input laws,
fixed label-noise amplitude, macroscopic feature learning, or full Target1.
The next step is a uniform-in-time risk transfer at order o(alpha^2 eta),
with nonzero iid initial output retained. C009's finite-horizon strategy is
a candidate; C015's zero-output paired argument cannot simply be substituted.
Independent mathematical and novelty review is pending. No paper-level
priority claim is made. Sources: own C009 clocks, C012 quadratic-root tool,
C016 Gaussian covariance and exact risk formula; the added slow-mode limits
and derivative scaling are proved above.","status":"unverified"}

\begin{equation}

 the driving function $\theta(t)$ evolves as

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:46:25.367094+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_252ee2f030f8cf94be73408951bb9a3732895c52f357735d1b18e740fa213d2b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem annuli_lemma of arXiv:2604.14122, 'The scaling limit of random walk and\\ the intrinsic metric on planar critical percolation'] Fix $m\in \mathbf{N}$, and let $i,j\in \mathbf{N}$ with $i\leq j-10$. Let $B(0,R^{-i}/2)$ be the box centered at the origin with side length $R^{-i}$, and tile it with boxes of side length $n^{-1}R^{\kappa-j}$. Let $K$ be the set of centers of such boxes that are fully contained inside $B(0,R^{-i}/2)$. Suppose that $z_1,\ldots, z_m\in K$ are distinct. Then there exist $n_{u}\in \{1,\ldots,m\}$ 
for each $1\leq u\leq m$ and $s_{u,l},r_{u,l} \in \mathbf{R}_{\geq 0}$ such that $0<s_{u,l}<r_{u,l} \leq n^{-1}R^{\kappa-i}$ for $1\leq l\leq n_{u}-1$ and $0=s_{u,n_{u}}< \frac{1}{2}n^{-1}R^{\kappa-j}\leq r_{u,n_{u}}$ so that all the annuli $A(z_u;s_{u,l},r_{u,l})$ are pairwise disjoint and
\[ \prod_{u=1}^{m} \frac{\prod_{l=1}^{n_{u}-1} s_{u,l}}{\prod_{l=1}^{n_{u}} r_{u,l} } \leq C(R,m)\prod_{u=1}^{m} \frac{1}{R^{-i} \wedge \min_{1\leq v<u} |z_{u}-z_v|} , \]
where $C(R,m)$ is a constant depending only on $R,m$. We use the convention that $\prod_{l=1}^{n_{u}-1} s_{u,l}=1$ if $n_{u}=1$, and the minimum of an empty set is infinite.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:00:46.822597+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_25d0ebf9f483b8c580212f3e0ad5e9867056252c8bd3c689d12ac82eac4e7189","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 24 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] Fix $\omega\in\Omega_{0}$. We construct a legal
path $\omega_{0}=\omega,\omega_{1}=\omega_{0}^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}},\dots,\omega_{2n+1}=\omega_{2n}^{x_{2n}-1,x_{2n}}=\omega^{-1,0}$
(with $n$ depending on $\omega$). We do it in three phases:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Begin with a path $\omega_{0}=\omega,\omega_{1}=\omega_{0}^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}},\dots,\omega_{n}=\omega_{n-1}^{x_{n-1}-1,x_{n-1}}$,
whose last configuration satisfies $c(-1,0,\omega_{n})\neq0$ (here
$c=c^{\land}$ by Observation \ref{obs:D_and}). Recall Lemma \ref{lem:and_move_0},
and that $(k+1)F_{l(\omega)}(\omega)<l(\omega)$. If $c(-1,0,\omega)\neq0$
we are done (taking $n=0$). Otherwise, there exists $x\in[2,l(\omega)]$
with $\omega(x)=0,\ \omega(x-1)=1,\ c(x-1,x,\omega)=1$. Set $x_{0}$
to be the minimal such $x$, and $\omega_{1}=\omega^{x_{0}-1,x_{0}}$.

Continue by induction: assume that we constructed $\omega_{m}$. If
$c(-1,0,\omega)\neq0$ we move to phase 2. Otherwise, set $x_{m}$
to be the minimal $x\in[2,l(\omega)]$ such that $\omega_{m}(x)=0,\ \omega_{m}(x-1)=1,\ c(x-1,x,\omega_{m})=1$,
and $\omega_{m+1}=\omega_{m}^{x_{m}-1,x_{m}}$.

This procedure is valid, since we only exchange sites in $[1,l(\omega)]$,
so the condition $(k+1)F_{l(\omega)}(\omega_{m})<l(\omega)$ holds
for all $m$. Moreover, it must end: at each step the center of mass
$\sum_{x=1}^{l(\omega)}x\eta(x)$ increases by $1$, and it cannot
exceed $\sum_{x=1}^{l(\omega)}x\cdot1\le l(\omega)^{2}.$
\item Next, exchange $-1$ and $0$, choosing $x_{n}=0$ and $\omega_{n+1}=\omega_{n}^{-1,0}$.
\item Finally, wind back the path of phase 1: for $m\in\{n+1,\dots2n\}$
we set $x_{m}=x_{2n-m}$, and $\omega_{m+1}=\omega_{m}^{x_{m}-1,x_{m}}$.
Since all these transitions are in $[1,L]$ they do not depend on
the configuration at $-1$ and $0$, hence they are all legal and
end at $\omega_{2n+1}=\omega^{-1,0}$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.840260+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_25dfdb6ad36272428c7e68c2c5843725634bd26c6d40216b47d99e3b6123e27d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 4 of arXiv:2607.20714, 'High Minima of Gaussian Processes: Overshoots and Minimizer Locations'] The probability measure
\(\mu\in\cM(K)\) is optimal
if and only if

\[
        k_\mu(t)\ge \mathcal E_R(\mu),
        \qquad t\in K.
\]

Moreover, if \(\mu\) is optimal, then
\[
        k_\mu(t)=\mathcal E_R(\mu),
        \qquad t\in\supp(\mu).
\]

In particular, if \(k_\mu\) is constant on \(K\), then \(\mu\) is
optimal. If, in addition,
\[
        \mathcal E_R(\eta)>0
\]
for every nonzero finite signed measure \(\eta\) on \(K\) satisfying
\(\eta(K)=0\), then the optimal measure is unique.

\(k_\mu\) is constant on \(K\).","status":"unverified"}

Not independently checked.
# T422 Target 1: explicit constants for the optimal constant step

Status: candidate proof; independent review pending. The theorem concerns expected
risk. Its first hitting index is deterministic, not a pathwise stopping time.

## Model and statement

Use the exact Gaussian second-moment recurrence established in the row diagnostics.
The covariance eigenvalues are h_j=j^(-alpha), alpha>1. The initial mode energies
are h_j a_j(0)=j^(-gamma), gamma>1. Labels have independent, mean-zero noise with
variance sigma2>=0. Each step uses B independent fresh examples, B a positive
integer. The batch gradient is their average. Put

    v_t = sum_j h_j a_j(t) = twice expected excess risk,
    Z_r = zeta(r),  v_0=Z_gamma,
    p=(gamma-1)/alpha >0, q=(2alpha-1)/alpha in (1,2).

This follows the existing diagnostics' gamma convention. If the target exponent
beta specifies a_j(0)=j^(-beta), then gamma=alpha+beta. If beta specifies the
risk mode energy h_j a_j(0)=j^(-beta), then gamma=beta. The two conventions must
not be interchanged. In Wang et al.'s Assumption 3.3, alpha is their beta and
p is their source exponent s.

Let S*(B,epsilon) be the minimum first hitting index of v_t<=epsilon v_0 over
ALL constant steps eta>0. No stability restriction is imposed on that minimum.
Define E*=B S*. For delta=epsilon Z_gamma, set

    eta_eff = min( 2B/Z_alpha, 2/(1+1/B), 4 delta B/(sigma2 Z_alpha) ),

where the third entry is omitted if sigma2=0, and

    Phi_1=epsilon^(-1/p)/eta_eff,
    Phi_2=(B epsilon)^(-1/q) eta_eff^(-(1-1/q)),
    Phi=max(Phi_1,Phi_2).

Here are explicit constants, all depending only on alpha,gamma:

    d=2^(-gamma-1-p)/(gamma-1),
    k=2^(-2alpha-1-q)/(2alpha-1),
    N=ceil(max(1, [2/((alpha-1) Z_alpha)]^(1/(alpha-1)))),
    T=N^alpha/2,
    epsilon_0=min(1/(8 Z_gamma), d/(2 Z_gamma T^p)).

For r>1 write s_r=(r-1)/alpha and define

    C(r)=2^s_r max( Z_r,
                   Gamma(s_r)/alpha + 2 [r/(e alpha)]^(r/alpha) ).
    C_D=C(gamma), C_K=C(2alpha).

If p<=q, define

    H=1+1/(1-p)                 if 0<p<1,
    H=1+1/(e(q-1))              if p=1,
    H=1+1/(p-1)                 if 1<p<=q,
    kappa=ceil(max(32, 1+4*2^p, 8*2^q C_K H/Z_alpha)),
    U=kappa (8 C_D/Z_gamma)^(1/p).

If p>q, define

    kappa=ceil(max(32, 1+4*2^p)),
    A=2^(q+4) C_K Z_(gamma-alpha),
    U=max( kappa (8 C_D/Z_gamma)^(1/p),
           kappa^(1-1/q) (A/Z_gamma)^(1/q) ).

Finally set

    c_minus=min( (d/Z_gamma)^(1/p)/4,
                 (k/(4 Z_gamma))^(1/q) 4^(-(1-1/q)) ),
    c_plus=2+U.

For every B>=1, sigma2>=0, and 0<epsilon<=epsilon_0, the claimed bounds are

    c_minus Phi <= S*(B,epsilon) <= c_plus Phi,
    c_minus B Phi <= E*(B,epsilon) <= c_plus B Phi.              (THEOREM)

The upper bound is achieved to these constants by the explicit stable choice
eta=eta_eff/kappa. The lower bound covers even a step that reaches the target
before subsequently diverging. Constants are deliberately conservative.



Model convention: the full gamma>1 range uses finite-risk Gaussian L2 series predictions, or the exact nonnegative second-moment recurrence. If the target coefficient sequence must belong to ordinary l2, impose gamma>alpha+1. The theorem does not assert an ordinary l2 target outside that range.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform measure","R_1, ..., R_r linearly independent over F_2","eps_j in {-1, 1}"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:29:33.705628+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_26395867dbb037c8c4660e450acf5d46bab82d6df5661e46b44a4c0ff038bfec","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On {-1, 1}^n (n >= 1) with the uniform probability measure mu, chi_S(x) = prod over i in S of x_i for S inside [n], and f^(S) = E[f chi_S] is the Walsh-Fourier coefficient of a real function f, so f = sum over S of f^(S) chi_S. Let R_1, ..., R_r be subsets of [n] whose incidence vectors are linearly independent over F_2, let eps_1, ..., eps_r be signs and A = {x : chi_{R_j}(x) = eps_j for every j}. Then 1_A = 2^(-r) prod over j of (1 + eps_j chi_{R_j}) = 2^(-r) sum over u in F_2^r of (prod over j with u_j = 1 of eps_j) chi_{R(u)}, where R(u) is the symmetric difference of the R_j with u_j = 1, and u -> R(u) is injective. Hence mu(A) = 2^(-r) and |A| = 2^(n-r); 1_A^(R(u)) = 2^(-r) prod over j with u_j = 1 of eps_j on the span L = {R(u)}, 1_A^(S) = 0 for S outside L, and sum over S of 1_A^(S)^2 = 2^r 4^(-r) = mu(A), as Parseval requires of an indicator. For one constraint, 1_A = (1 + eps chi_R)/2, with coefficient 1/2 at the empty set and eps/2 at R. The signed encoding sigma_A = 2 1_A - 1 has sigma_A^(empty) = 2^(1-r) - 1 and sigma_A^(S) = 2 1_A^(S) for nonempty S, of magnitude 2^(1-r) on the nonempty part of L and 0 off it; for r = 1, sigma_A = eps chi_R.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H and K are Hilbert spaces","T: H -> K is a compact linear operator"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571346+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator ideals","id":"claim_268f267d3a7f9fc6940b6a4871070cfb6e23bc7b6f5580744ad369b2454b3628","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H and K be Hilbert spaces and T: H -> K a compact operator. Then T*T is a compact positive self-adjoint operator on H, and |T| = (T*T)^{1/2} is compact and positive. The singular values (s-numbers) s_1(T) >= s_2(T) >= ... >= 0 of T are the eigenvalues of |T| (equivalently, the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of T*T), listed in nonincreasing order and repeated according to multiplicity; if |T| has only finitely many nonzero eigenvalues the list is completed by zeros. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352618+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_26a0e199958afa07f34bccaf6e73beada948f08f75c064be8df303e9bac5ec01","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 196 (subsequential limits for piecewise constant processes) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Analogously to $\mu_{\bG^N}$ and $\Q_N$, let $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$ denote the law of the piecewise constant processes
	\[\Big(
	\Gamma^{\bullet,N},\Upsilon^{\bullet,N},\mathcal{E}^{\bullet,N}
	\Big)\]
conditional on $\bG^N$, and let $\Q_{\bullet,N}$ denote the law of $\mu_{\bullet,\bG^N}$. Suppose $\Q_N\to\Q$ along an integer subsequence $N\to\infty$, as guaranteed by Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}. Then $\Q_{\bullet,N}\Rightarrow\Q$ along the same subsequence. The ``$\frozen$'' variant of the statement also holds.

\begin{proof}
By Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}, for any sequence of integers $N\to\infty$, there exists a further subsequence along which $\Q_N$ converges weakly to $\Q$, with $\mathcal{E}^N$ converging almost surely to the zero path. Take any such subsequence:
to simplify notation, we can assume (by re-indexing) that it is the entire sequence of integers $N\ge1$. 
This means there exists a Skorohod coupling of the disorder matrices $\bG^N$ for which, with probability one over $(\bG^N)_{N\ge0}$, we have $\mu_{\bG^N}\Rightarrow\mu$ along the same subsequence, where $\mu_{\bG^N}$ is the law of the process $(\Gamma^N,\Upsilon^N,\mathcal{E}^N)$ conditional on $\bG^N$. Moreover $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges almost surely to the zero path, which implies
that $\mathcal{E}^{\bullet,N}$ does also.

Now abbreviate $\Xi^N\equiv(\Gamma^N,\Upsilon^N)$
and $\Xi\equiv(\Gamma,\Upsilon)$.
 Let $L^\infty([0,1],\R^8)$ denote the space of (not necessarily continuous) functions $[0,1]\to\R^8$, equipped with the uniform metric. If $\Phi$ is a bounded Lipschitz functional on this space, then we have
	\beq
	\lim_{N\to\infty} 
	\bE_{\bG^N} \Phi(\Xi^N)
	=\bE \Phi(\Xi)
	\eeq
almost surely (along the subsequence, under the Skorohod coupling).
Let $\Xi^{\bullet,N}$ be the piecewise constant variant of $\Xi^N$, and let $\mu_{\bG_\bullet,N}$ be the law of $\Xi^{\bullet,N}$. To conclude the result, it suffices to show that
	\[
	\lim_{N\to\infty} 
	\bE_{\bG^N} \Phi(\Xi^{\bullet,N})
	=\bE \Phi(\Xi)
	\]
almost surely for all bounded Lipschitz functionals $\Phi$, possibly after passing to a further subsequence of integers $N_k\to\infty$, as long as the subsequence does not depend on $\Phi$. In light of \eqref{e:observable.a.s.conv}, it suffices to show that
	\[\lim_{N\to\infty} 
	\bE_{\bG^N} \Big[
	\Phi(\Xi^N)
	-\Phi(\Xi^{\bullet,N})
	\Big]=0
	\]
almost surely along the subsequence $N_k$, for all bounded Lipschitz functionals $\Phi$.

Recall the proof of Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}. For any sequence $\epsilon_N\to0$, for each $N$ we have a compact set
 $\mathcal{K}_N=\mathcal{K}((H_{N,k})_{k\ge0})$ defined by \eqref{e:compact.K}, such that $\Q_N(\mathcal{K}_N^c) \le \epsilon_N$ for all $N \ge N_0$. We can take $\epsilon_N\to0$ slowly enough so that $H_{N,1} \delta^\gamma \to0$, where $\gamma=1/5$ is the H\"older exponent from the proof of Proposition~\ref{p:tightness}. We then have
 	\begin{align*}
	&\bigg|\bE_{\bG^N} \Big[
	\Phi(\Xi^N)
	-\Phi(\Xi^{\bullet,N})
	\Big] \bigg|
	\le
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \ind\{ (\mathcal{K}_N)^c\}
	+\ind\{\mathcal{K}_N\}
	\bigg|
	\bE_{\bG^N} \Big[
	\Phi(\Xi^N)
	-\Phi(\Xi^{\bullet,N})
	\Big] 
	\bigg| \\
	&\qquad\le
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \ind\{ (\mathcal{K}_N)^c\}
	+\ind\{\mathcal{K}_N\}\bigg\{
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \mu( A(H_{N,1}))
	+ \|\Phi\|_{\textup{Lip}}
	\bE_{\bG^N}\Big[
	\|\Xi^N-\Xi^{\bullet,N}\|_\infty
	; A(H_{N,1})^c
	\Big]
	\bigg\} \\
	&\qquad\le
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \ind\{ (\mathcal{K}_N)^c\}
	+\bigg\{
	2\|\Phi\|_\infty \frac{17\mathscr{C}}{H_{N,1}}
	+ \|\Phi\|_{\textup{Lip}} O(1) H_{N,1} \delta^\gamma
	\bigg\}\,.
	\end{align*}
If we now take a subsequence $N_k\to\infty$ such that $\epsilon_{N,k}$ is summable, then the above converges to zero almost surely along this subsequence. This concludes the proof of the non-``$\frozen$'' version of the statement. The ``$\frozen$'' variant follows by the same argument, since all the preceding results of this section were also proved for this setting. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
