{"assumptions":["Gaussian observation with known noise covariance","k >= 3","the target mu_0 is fixed (not data-chosen)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.943999+00:00","domain":"estimation theory","id":"claim_2d47bd4398f93195c40d1d09827060e0250226eeff222b67b0e734c505237ec9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $X \\sim N(\\theta, \\sigma^2 I_k)$ in $\\mathbb{R}^k$ with $k \\ge 3$ and $\\sigma^2$ known, and let $\\mu_0 \\in \\mathbb{R}^k$ be any fixed target. Define $$\\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}} = \\mu_0 + \\Big(1 - \\frac{(k - 2)\\sigma^2}{\\|X - \\mu_0\\|^2}\\Big)(X - \\mu_0), \\qquad \\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}+} = \\mu_0 + \\Big(1 - \\frac{(k-2)\\sigma^2}{\\|X - \\mu_0\\|^2}\\Big)_+ (X - \\mu_0).$$ Then for every $\\theta$: (i) $E\\|\\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}} - \\theta\\|^2 = k\\sigma^2 - (k-2)^2\\sigma^4\\, E\\big[\\|X - \\mu_0\\|^{-2}\\big] < k\\sigma^2 = E\\|X - \\theta\\|^2$, so the shrunk estimator strictly dominates the observation itself in total squared error, with the largest gain when $\\theta$ is near $\\mu_0$ (risk $\\to 2\\sigma^2$ at $\\theta = \\mu_0$); (ii) the positive-part version dominates the plain one, $E\\|\\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}+} - \\theta\\|^2 \\le E\\|\\hat\\theta_{\\mathrm{JS}} - \\theta\\|^2$ with strict inequality. The shrinkage amount $s = (k-2)\\sigma^2/\\|X - \\mu_0\\|^2$ is the ratio of the expected squared noise norm to the observed squared distance from the target; it is small exactly when the observation sits far from the target relative to its noise. When the noise covariance is a known $\\Sigma$ rather than $\\sigma^2 I$, apply the lemma to $\\Sigma^{-1/2}(X - \\mu_0)$ (so $s = (k - 2)/\\big((X - \\mu_0)^T \\Sigma^{-1}(X - \\mu_0)\\big)$) - the Mahalanobis form; a mis-specified $\\Sigma$ that understates the noise gives an $s$ that is too small.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:47:12.028201+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2d48e8e4700c4fe5fea19eaf5a4eec5ce2e7a85053fdff72ff0385c07fa0fd7d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition thm:theorem_uniqueness_lqg_metric of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] {GM21}}]
  
  Let $h$ be a whole-plane GFF. Fix $\nu>0$ and $0 < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 \leq \lambda_3 \leq \lambda_4 < \lambda_5$. Then there exists $\mathbbm{p} \in (0,1)$ such that the following is true.  Suppose that for each $z\in \mathbb{C},r>0$, we have events $E_r(z) \in \sigma(h)$ and additionally for any points $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z} ,  \text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w} \in \mathbb{C}$, and any simple path $\eta$ from $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z}$ to $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}$, we have events $\mathfrak{C}_r^{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w},\eta}(z) \in \sigma(h)$, satisfying, for a deterministic constant $\Lambda > 1$, the following properties.

\begin{enumerate}[(1)]

  For all $z \in \mathbb{C}$ and all $r >0$,  the event $E_r(z)$ is determined by $(h-h_{\lambda_5 r}(z))|_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}A}_{\lambda_1 r ,  \lambda_4 r}(z)}$,  and for all $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w} \in \mathbb{C}$,  the event $\mathfrak{C}_r^{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w},\eta}(z)$ is determined by $h|_{B_{\lambda_4 r}(z)}$ and the path $\eta$ stopped at the last time that it exits $B_{\lambda_4 r}(z)$.
\item 
For all $z \in \mathbb{C}$ and all $r >0$, we have $\mathbb{P}(E_r(z)) \geq \mathbbm{p}$.
\item 
For all points $z \in \mathbb{C},r >0$ and $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}$ satisfying $\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}\notin B_{\lambda_4 r}(z)$, we have
\begin{align*}
\Lambda^{-1} \mathbb{P}(E_r(z) \cap \{\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}} \cap B_{\lambda_2 r}(z) \neq \emptyset\} \lvert h|_{\mathbb{C} \setminus B_{\lambda_3r}(z)}) \leq \mathbb{P}(\mathfrak{C}_r^{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w},\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}}}(z) \cap \{\Gamma_{\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}z},\text{\usefont{U}{bboldx}{m}{n}w}} \cap B_{\lambda_2 r}(z) \neq \emptyset\} \lvert h|_{\mathbb{C} \setminus B_{\lambda_3r}(z)}).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:47:22.242763+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2d491f32f6e8e9fc015c925f6a2fbeed183e35a2ec07c615929f7ed4999170c1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 7 of arXiv:2605.25762, 'Brownian Convergence of Planar Domains and Stability of the Planar Skorokhod Embedding Pro'] Let $f$ be analytic on the unit disc $\mathbb{D}$ and $p>0$. The
$p$-th Hardy norm of $f$ is 
\begin{equation}
\Vert f\Vert_{\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})}:=\sup_{0\le r<1}\Big\{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{2\pi}_{0}\big|f(re^{i\theta})\big|^{p}\,d\theta\Big\}^{\frac{1}{p}}.
\end{equation}
The supremum is well-defined\cite{Rudin2001}. The Hardy space, denoted
by $\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})$, consists of analytic $f$ with $\Vert f\Vert_{\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})}<+\infty$.
A key fact of Hardy spaces is the boundary trace: if $\Vert f\Vert_{\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})}<+\infty$,
then the radial boundary values $f^{*}(e^{i\theta}):=\lim_{r\to1}f(re^{i\theta})$
exists a.e.\ on $\mathbb{S}$. Moreover 
\[
\|f^{*}\|_{L^{p}(\mathbb{S})}=\Vert f\Vert_{\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})}.
\]
When $p>1$, $\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})$ identifies with $L^{p}_{2\pi}$
in the following way: if $\xi\in L^{p}_{2\pi}$ then the map
\begin{equation}
\Psi(re^{\theta i})=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int^{2\pi}_{0}\frac{1+re^{(\theta-t)i}}{1-re^{(\theta-t)i}}\xi(t)dt
\end{equation}
belongs to $\mathbf{H}^{p}(\mathbb{D})$ and $\Re(\Psi^{*})=\xi$.
When $p=1$, $\Psi$ is analytic in the unit disc but not necessarily
an element of $\mathbf{H}^{1}(\mathbb{D})$. We recommend \cite{duren2000theory,butzer1971hilbert,king2009hilbert,mcgovern1980hilbert,pandey2011hilbert}
for a concise background on Hardy spaces as well as their connections
with the Hilbert transform. The following result illustrates a deep
connection between Hardy spaces and planar Brownian motion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:35:05.841419+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2d5d8d8914af787ee83778361158e9f94956132c4083ecc262f8ab6e7d689087","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:ratio-characterization-general of arXiv:2606.27073, 'Retention Profiles and KL Contraction Bounds in Finite Markov Chains'] \leavevmode\par\noindent
Assume $M:=\max_{x\in S} r(x)>0$,
$Y:=r(X)/M\in[0,1]$,
and let $\nu$ be any probability distribution on $S$.
If $X\sim \nu$, define
$m_\nu := \mathbb{E}_\nu[Y] = \sum_{x\in S}\nu(x)\,r(x)/M$.
Then, for every $\tau\in(0,1)$,
\[
  \max\!\left\{0,\frac{m_\nu-\tau}{1-\tau}\right\}
  \le
  \nu\!\left(\{x\in S:\, r(x)\ge \tau M\}\right)
  \le
  \min\!\left\{1,\frac{m_\nu}{\tau}\right\},
\]
and equivalently,
\[
  \max\!\left\{0,1-\frac{m_\nu}{\tau}\right\}
  \le
  \nu\!\left(\{x\in S:\, r(x)\le \tau M\}\right)
  \le
  \min\!\left\{1,\frac{1-m_\nu}{1-\tau}\right\}.
\]
These bounds are sharp: given only $m_\nu$ and $M$, no stronger universal
tail bounds can be obtained. Depending on weak versus strict threshold
conventions, the extremal constants are either attained or approached by
two-point laws supported at endpoint/threshold values.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:52:17.375544+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2da9d27fddd36d48d293427abcd1737efb9dfc551ae57ccd8773f20f8bb5f6e6","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 12 of arXiv:2606.04636, 'A Thomson-type variational principle for diffusion coefficients'] For almost any $\omega\in\Omega$, $\omega(0)\neq\omega(1)$,
there exists a path $\omega_{1},\dots,\omega_{N}$, for $N=N(\omega)\in2\N$,
and a sequence of sites $x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1}$ in $[0,X(\omega)]$,
such that $\omega_{N}=\omega^{0,1}$, $\omega_{i+1}=\omega_{i}^{x_{i},x_{i}+1}\neq\omega_{i}$,
and $c(x_{i},x_{i+1};\omega_{i})=1$ for any $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$.
Moreover, the following properties are satisfied:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x_{1},\dots,x_{N/2-1}$ are all in $[2,X(\omega)],$ $x_{N/2}=0$,
and $x_{i}=x_{N-i}$ for any $i\ge N/2+1$.
\item $\omega_{j}(0)-\omega_{j}(1)=\omega(0)-\omega(1)$ for $j\le N/2$
and $\omega_{j}(0)-\omega_{j}(1)=\omega(1)-\omega(0)$ for $j>N/2$.
\item For all $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$, $\omega_{i}(x)=\omega(x)$ if $x\notin[0,X(\omega)+1]$.
\item For all $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$, $X_{-}(\omega)=X_{-}(\omega_{i})$.
\item For all $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$, $X_{+}(\omega)\le\min\{x\ge x_{i}+4:\omega_{i}(x)=\omega_{i}(x+1)=0\}$.
\item Let $\eta\in\Omega$, and assume that there exists $i\in\{1,\dots,N-1\}$
such that $\tau_{x_{i}}\eta=\omega_{i}$. Then 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $X_{-}(\omega)=X_{-}(\eta)+x_{i}$;
\item $X_{+}(\omega)\le X_{4}(\eta)+x_{i}\le X_{4}(\eta)-X_{-}(\eta)$.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $\eta\in\Omega$, $x,x'\in\Z$, $\zeta=\pm1$. Then there is at
most one possible configuration $\omega$ and one possible $i\in\{1,\dots,N(\omega)\}$
such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item $x=x_{i}$ and $\eta=\eta_{i}$,
\item $X(\omega)=x'$, and
\item $\omega(0)-\omega(1)=\zeta$.
\end{enumerate}
\item For $\omega'=\omega^{0,1}$, the path $\omega'_{1},\dots,\omega_{N}'$
beginning with $\omega'$ is given by the reversed path $\omega'_{k}=\omega_{N-k}$;
and the associated sites $x_{1}',\dots,x_{N-1}'$ are the same as
$x_{N-1},\dots,x_{1}$, which are also the same as $x_{1},\dots,x_{N-1}$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The growth bound must be uniform in t on the time strip","Continuity at t = 0 and smoothness for t > 0 do not substitute for it","Nonnegativity (Widder) is an alternative hypothesis"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106842+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations","id":"claim_2db58f26b351f116cd637cc5b251283a346f12914a601ac338aa36ad4b299c46","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The load-bearing hypothesis in uniqueness for the Cauchy problem $u_t=\\Delta u$ on $\\mathbb R^n\\times(0,T)$, $u(\\cdot,0)=g$, is the growth bound $|u(x,t)|\\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ with $A,a$ independent of $t$ (the Tychonoff class); smoothness of $u$ and continuity down to $t=0$ are not enough. Tychonoff's counterexample ($n=1$): let $g(t)=e^{-t^{-2}}$ for $t>0$, $g(0)=0$, and $u(x,t)=\\sum_{k\\ge0}\\frac{g^{(k)}(t)}{(2k)!}x^{2k}$. The Cauchy estimates for $g$ ($|g^{(k)}(t)|\\le k!\\,(\\theta t)^{-k}e^{-\\frac12t^{-2}}$ for some $\\theta>0$) make the series converge locally uniformly together with all its derivatives, and termwise differentiation gives $u_{xx}=u_t$; $u$ is continuous on $\\mathbb R\\times[0,\\infty)$ with $u(x,0)\\equiv0$, yet $u\\not\\equiv0$. So the zero initial datum admits the two distinct solutions $0$ and $u$, and by the uniqueness theorem $u$ cannot satisfy any uniform bound $|u|\\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ on a strip. Two corollaries an auditor should apply: (1) a solution of the heat equation is not determined by its initial data unless a class is specified -- 'the' solution of a Cauchy problem is meaningless without one; (2) the Tychonoff solution necessarily changes sign, because nonnegative solutions with zero initial data are unique by Widder's theorem, so one-sided bounds are an alternative (and weaker) substitute for the growth class. The class is essentially sharp: the counterexample family with $g(t)=e^{-t^{-\\alpha}}$, $\\alpha>1$, shows uniqueness fails as soon as growth $e^{a|x|^{2+\\varepsilon}}$ is allowed, while $|u|\\le Ae^{a|x|^2}$ suffices.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["both measure spaces are sigma-finite","f is nonnegative (values in [0, infinity]) and measurable for the product sigma-algebra A (x) B","the product measure is the one determined by mu(A) nu(B) on rectangles (unique under sigma-finiteness)"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.251243+00:00","domain":"measure theory, integration, product measures","id":"claim_2db60f088285630433ee3f96f70f2774756e63f25313788bb43c846a2b2b7abe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{A}, \\mu)$ and $(Y, \\mathcal{B}, \\nu)$ be $\\sigma$-FINITE measure spaces and let $f: X\\times Y \\to [0, \\infty]$ be measurable with respect to the product $\\sigma$-algebra $\\mathcal{A}\\otimes\\mathcal{B}$ (the $\\sigma$-algebra generated by the measurable rectangles $A\\times B$). Then: (i) for every $x \\in X$ the section $y \\mapsto f(x,y)$ is $\\mathcal{B}$-measurable and for every $y$ the section $x \\mapsto f(x,y)$ is $\\mathcal{A}$-measurable; (ii) the functions $x \\mapsto \\int_Y f(x,y)\\,d\\nu(y)$ and $y \\mapsto \\int_X f(x,y)\\,d\\mu(x)$ (with values in $[0,\\infty]$) are $\\mathcal{A}$- resp. $\\mathcal{B}$-measurable; (iii) $\\int_{X\\times Y} f\\,d(\\mu\\times\\nu) = \\int_X\\Big(\\int_Y f(x,y)\\,d\\nu(y)\\Big)d\\mu(x) = \\int_Y\\Big(\\int_X f(x,y)\\,d\\mu(x)\\Big)d\\nu(y)$, all three possibly $= +\\infty$, where $\\mu\\times\\nu$ is the (unique, by $\\sigma$-finiteness) product measure with $(\\mu\\times\\nu)(A\\times B) = \\mu(A)\\nu(B)$. Fubini's theorem is the companion for signed/complex $f$: if $f \\in L^1(\\mu\\times\\nu)$ - which by Tonelli applied to $|f|$ can be checked by ONE iterated integral of $|f|$ - then the sections are integrable for a.e. $x$ (resp. $y$), the partial integrals are integrable, and the three integrals agree as finite numbers. Sharp edges: (1) $\\sigma$-finiteness cannot be dropped: $X = Y = [0,1]$, $\\mu$ = Lebesgue, $\\nu$ = counting measure, $f = \\mathbf{1}_{\\{x = y\\}}$ (measurable for the product $\\sigma$-algebra since the diagonal is closed hence Borel); then $\\int_X\\int_Y f\\,d\\nu\\,d\\mu = 1$ while $\\int_Y\\int_X f\\,d\\mu\\,d\\nu = 0$; (2) nonnegativity (or integrability) cannot be dropped: $f(x,y) = (x^2 - y^2)/(x^2+y^2)^2$ on $(0,1)^2$ has iterated integrals $\\pi/4$ and $-\\pi/4$, and $f(x,y) = \\mathbf{1}_{\\{x = y\\}} - \\mathbf{1}_{\\{x = y+1\\}}$ on $\\mathbb{N}\\times\\mathbb{N}$ with counting measures has iterated sums $1$ and $0$ - in both $\\int|f| = \\infty$; (3) joint measurability cannot be dropped: assuming the continuum hypothesis there is a set $S \\subset [0,1]^2$ (Sierpinski) with every vertical section countable and every horizontal section co-countable, so the iterated integrals of $\\mathbf{1}_S$ are $0$ and $1$ - $S$ is not Lebesgue measurable in the plane; (4) for the COMPLETED product (Lebesgue measure on $\\mathbb{R}^{m+n}$ is the completion of $\\mathcal{L}^m\\otimes\\mathcal{L}^n$) the sections are measurable only for a.e. $x$ and the partial integral is defined a.e.; the equalities in (iii) still hold with this proviso; (5) the theorem gives equality of the iterated integrals with the DOUBLE integral - the existence and equality of the two iterated integrals of a signed function does not by itself imply integrability (example (2) reversed: symmetrise to make both iterated integrals 0).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.820401+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2dd4b8c52b190bc42f14fd283cd4b4624d439f3725cd340e9d5cebece7984642","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:endpoint-acm-type-two of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq4$.  The lower bound in (equation eq:endpoint-local of the paper) already counts
distinct degree-$h$ Hilbert values of arithmetically Cohen--Macaulay
projective monomial curves in $\mathbb P^{k-1}$ of Cohen--Macaulay type two.
More precisely, for $t=k-4$ and with $\xi$ recording homological degree, the
witnesses have graded Betti polynomial
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \mathcal B_{A_t}(\xi,z)
 ={}&\bigl(
  1+\xi(z^p+z^{q+s}+z^{r+s})
  +\xi^2(z^{p+s}+z^{q+r+s})
 \bigr)\\
 &\hspace{18mm}\cdot
 \prod_{i=1}^t(1+\xi z^{\ell_i}).
 \end{split}
\end{equation}
Writing $\beta_i(A_t)=\sum_j\beta^{A_t}_{i,j}$, their total Betti polynomial
depends only on $k$:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
  \sum_{i=0}^{k-2}\beta_i(A_t)\xi^i
  &=\mathcal B_{A_t}(\xi,1)=(1+2\xi)(1+\xi)^{k-3},\\
  \beta_i(A_t)&=\binom{k-3}{i}+2\binom{k-3}{i-1}.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here out-of-range binomial coefficients are zero.  In particular, the
homogeneous prime toric ideal $I_{A_t}$ has
\[
 \operatorname{ht}I_{A_t}=k-2,
 \qquad
 \mu(I_{A_t})=k-1=\operatorname{ht}I_{A_t}+1,
\]
so it is an almost complete intersection.  Thus the witnesses have ACM
coordinate rings of type two.  Their defining ideals are prime toric almost
complete intersections, all with the same total Betti format.  As
$h\to\infty$, they realize $h^{k-1+o_k(1)}$ distinct degree-$h$ Hilbert
values; at $k=4$, they realize a positive proportion of the ambient interval.
The internal degree shifts in
(equation eq:endpoint-betti-tower of the paper) vary with the parameters.
Their Hilbert numerator is obtained by setting $\xi=-1$ in
(equation eq:endpoint-betti-tower of the paper); equivalently,
\begin{equation}
 \operatorname{HS}_{R_{A_t}}(z)=
 \frac{
  (1-z^p-z^{q+s}-z^{r+s}+z^{p+s}+z^{q+r+s})
  \prod_{i=1}^t(1-z^{\ell_i})}
 {(1-z)^k}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:57:28.219164+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2e5a6151cb07c965b938ba4ac449ef6ff08cd5c9c1516ec448a180757a9f0ef3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 2 (continuous R\'enyi and Tsallis entropies) of arXiv:2607.17576, 'How much randomness is needed to symmetrize a random variable?'] Let $X$ be a real-valued random variable with density $f$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure. For $\alpha\in (0, 1)\cup (1, \infty)$, the R\'enyi entropy $h_\alpha(X)$ of order $\alpha$ is defined by
$$
h_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log \int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)^\alpha dx
$$
and the Tsallis entropy $T_\alpha(X)$ of order $\alpha$ is defined by
$$
T_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)^\alpha dx-1\right).
$$
Taking the limit $\alpha\to 1$, both entropies are reduced to the Boltzman-Shannon entropy 
$$
h(X)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x)\log f(x)dx.
$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:39:41.442209+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2ea3abbcc68ee92866b7e06145087b96647b88f831aa508a65652775d819c5b9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 12 of arXiv:2604.07478, 'Mixing Times and Cutoff for the Rook's Walk'] Let $P$ be the transition matrix of a reversible Markov chain; That is, $P$ satisfies,
   \[\pi(x) P(x,y) = \pi(y)P(y,x),\quad \forall x,y\in \Omega\]
   where $\pi$ is the stationary distribution. Then,
   \[\langle Pf,g\rangle_\pi = \langle f,Pg\rangle_\pi,\quad \forall f,g \in \mathbb{R}^\Omega\]
   \begin{proof}
     \begin{align*}
      \langle Pf, g\rangle_\pi &= \sum_{x\in \Omega}(Pf)(x)g(x)\pi(x)\\
      &= \sum_{x\in \Omega}\sum_{y\in \Omega}P(x,y)f(y)g(x)\pi(x)\\
      &= \sum_{x\in \Omega}\sum_{y\in \Omega}P(x,y)f(y)g(x)\pi(x)\\
      &= \sum_{y\in \Omega}\sum_{x\in \Omega}P(y,x)g(x)f(y)\pi(y)\tag{By reversibility}\\
      &= \sum_{y\in \Omega}(Pg)(y)f(y)\pi(y)\\
      &=  \langle f, Pg\rangle_\pi
     \end{align*} 
   \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:13:22.516162+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2ea9e2f768087d5f0eb788e32f8de31d492f709f7c075bc991aede9b9974d100","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm random coordinate change of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] Assume the setting of Theorem~(Loewner coordinate change in H of the paper), and suppose the driving function \( W_t \in \mathbb{R} \) evolves according to the stochastic differential equation

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.188469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2ec5da81fe4cd2bf3338598e43e8f927a872bec8bec1db320915c7db24db5994","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 100 (comparison of Fokker--Planck equations) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let
$\hvY(t) = \vY(t-\sss)+\xxx$
where $(\sss,\xxx)\sim\varphi$.
Let $\hvX$ be the SDE solution from Definition~\ref{d:intro.SDE.coefs}.
Assume the coefficients $B^i$ and $\Sigma^{ij}$ of \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv} are bounded and Lipschitz. Then the processes $\hvX$ and $\hvY$ satisfy the same Fokker--Planck equations. Consequently, for each fixed $t$, the marginal law of $\hvX(t)$ agrees with the marginal law of\/ $\hvY(t)$.

\begin{proof}
Abbreviate $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation density of $\vY$, and recall from Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.smoothed.occ.msr} that $\hvY$ has occupation density $\nu\equiv\rho_{\vY}*\varphi$.
Let $\mu$ denote the occupation density of $\hvX$.
 Let $f:\R^d\to\R$ be a smooth compactly supported test function. 
\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Fokker--Planck equations for $\hvY(t) = \vY(t-\sss)+\xxx$.} We will calculate
	\[
	\bE\Big[ f(\vY(T))-f(\vY(0))\Big]
	= \int_{s,x} \varphi(s,x)
	\bE\Big[ f(Y(T-s)+x)
	-f(Y(-s)+x)\Big]
	\,ds\,dx
	=\textup{(dr)}+\textup{(qv)}
	\]
where $\textup{(dr)}$
and $\textup{(qv)}$
denote the contributions from the drift and covariation respectively:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(dr)}
	&= \sum_{i=1}^d \textup{(dr)}^i
	= \sum_{i=1}^d
	\int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{-s}^{T-s}
	\partial_i f(Y(t)+x)\,dD^i(t)
	\,ds\,dx \,,\\
	\textup{(qv)}
	&= \sum_{i,j=1}^d \textup{(qv)}^{ij}
	= \frac12
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{-s}^{T-s}
	\partial_i\partial_j
	f(Y(t)+x)\,dQ^{ij}(t)
	\,ds\,dx\,.
	\end{align*}
Abbreviate $I_T(s)\equiv \ind\{s\in[0,T]\}$. The above can be further simplified as follows:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(dr)}^i
	&= \int_{s,x}\varphi(s,x)
	\int_{t,y} I_T(t+s)
	\partial_i f(y+x)
	\,\rho_{D^i}(dt\,dy)\,ds\,dx \\
	&=
	\int_{s',x'}
	I_T(s')\partial_i f(x')
	\bigg\{\int_{t,y} 
	\varphi(s'-t,x'-y)
	\,\rho_{D^i}(dt\,dy)
	\bigg\}\,ds'\,dx'\\
	&=
	\int_{t,y}
	I_T(t)\partial_i f(y)
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,y)}
	{\rho*\varphi(t,y)}
	\nu(dt\,dy)\,,
	\end{align*}
recalling at the last step that $\nu=\rho*\varphi$ is the occupation density of $\hvY$.\smallskip

\noindent
\textbf{Fokker--Planck equations for SDE solution $\hvX$.}
 If $f:\R^d\to\R$ is a smooth compactly supported test function, define
	\[
	L_t f(x)
	= \sum_{i=1}^d
	B^i(t,x)
	\partial_i f(x)
	+\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	A^{ij}(t,x)
	\partial_i\partial_j f(x)
	\]
Then, by It\=o's formula, the process
	\[
	N(t)
	= f(\hvX(t))-f(\hvX(0)) - \int_0^t L_s f(\hvX(s))\,ds
	\]
is a local martingale. Since we assumed the coefficients are bounded, we can conclude that $N$ is a true martingale, and the optional stopping theorem gives
	\[
	\bE\Big[ f(\hvX(T))-f(\hvX(0))\Big]
	= \bE \int_0^T L_t f(\hvX(s))\,ds
	= \textup{(Dr)}+\textup{(QV)}\,,
	\]
where $\textup{(Dr)}$ and $\textup{(QV)}$ denote the contributions from the drift and covariation respectively:
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(Dr)}
	&= \sum_{i=1}^d \textup{(Dr)}^i
	=\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bE \int_0^T \partial_i f(\hvX(t))
	B^i(t,\hvX(t))\,dt\,,\\
	\textup{(QV)}
	&= \sum_{i,j=1}^d \textup{(QV)}^{ij}
	=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bE \int_0^T 
	\partial_i\partial_j f(\hvX(t))
	A^{ij}(t,\hvX(t))\,dt\,.
	\end{align*}
Again abbreviate $I_T(s)\equiv \ind\{s\in[0,T]\}$. The above can be further simplified as
	\begin{align*}
	\textup{(Dr)}^i
	&= \int I_T(t)
	\partial_i f(y) 
	\frac{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi(t,x)}
		{\rho*\varphi(t,x)}
	\mu(dt\,dy)\,,\\
	\textup{(QV)}^{ij}
	&= \int I_T(t)
	\partial_i\partial_j f(y)

Let eps_1, ..., eps_n be independent Rademacher signs, independent of the X_i. Then E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i f(X_i) |, and in the other direction E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n eps_i ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) | <= 2 E sup_{f in F} | sum_{i=1}^n ( f(X_i) - E f(X_i) ) |. The constant 2 in the first inequality is the standard one and is not claimed sharp. Symmetrization is what allows one to work CONDITIONALLY on the data, replacing an empirical process by a Rademacher process whose conditional law is sub-Gaussian with an explicit variance proxy, which is the entry point for chaining bounds and Rademacher complexity. The X_i need not be identically distributed. Note the direction of the useful inequality: it bounds the centred empirical process by the Rademacher process, which is the one that can be chained. {"assumptions":["Exact stratified four-point shrinking-input model and finite-witness meaning in proofs/SINGLE_LABEL_SHIFTED_PEAK.md","Unit-norm single-index centered ReLU teacher; four independent Rademacher errors with sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e))","Fixed0<nu<=1 and kappa>0; iid Gaussian hidden weights and independent iid signed heads; both layers trained by simultaneous step1/2 GD","Width tends to infinity at each fixed e and finite horizon before e decreases","Unaudited C009/C016/C017/C018/C019 premises"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T18:17:15.475149+00:00","domain":"epochwise double descent; single-index ReLU teacher and actual both-layer GD","id":"claim_2f2729bd12f96b12d82dcd858aede16b15cb919c69481c751269e8cd65589a19","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft: proof (unaudited); independent correctness and novelty review pending. Positive-probability restricted four-atom single-label result, not full Target1.

# C020 v2: a shifted peak for ONE realized label vector
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: narrowed. Target: 1. Novelty unestablished.
General T267 remains open. This is a restricted four-atom width-first theorem.

## 1. Model and precise probability statement
For 0<e<1/4 put D=1+e^2+e^4, x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D),
s,t in {-1,1}. The population is uniform on these four atoms and the
training set contains one observation at each atom (stratified, not iid).
Set u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2), c_e=e^2/sqrt(D(1+e^2)), alpha_e=c_e/2,
and g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2. Thus ||u_e||=1 and its four Walsh
coefficients (0,s,t,st) are (0,alpha_e,alpha_e,alpha_e).
Fix 0<nu<=1 and kappa>0. Independently draw four noise signs xi_(s,t),
each uniform {-1,1}, and label y_i=g_e(x_i)+sigma_e xi_i, where
 sigma_e=2alpha_e sqrt(kappa/sqrt(e))~sqrt(kappa)e^(7/4).
Initialize f_m(x)=m^(-1/2)sum_j a_j ReLU(w_j.x), with iid w_j~N(0,I_3)
and independent iid a_j uniform {-nu,nu}. Both layers undergo simultaneous
GD with step gamma=1/2 on loss (1/8)sum_i(f_m(x_i)-y_i)^2, using gate
derivative zero at zero. The individual clean risk is
 R_(e,m,xi)(k)=(1/4)sum_i(f_(m,xi)(x_i;k)-g_e(x_i))^2.
There is NO noise average anywhere in the claim.

Let H(x,z)=E[ReLU(W.x)ReLU(W.z)+nu^2 1{W.x>0,W.z>0}x.z], and let
lambda_h be the Walsh eigenvalues of H(X,X)/4, b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2),
eta_e=(b_t+b_st)/b_s. C009's clock premises are
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi), eta_e~e,
with b_0 bounded away from zero.
For epsilon>0 let E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon) mean that there exist integer
k0<k1<k2<k3 with k0>=0, satisfying
 R(k0)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k1), R(k2)>R(k3),                   (1)
 |k1/((3pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
 |k2/((9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e))-1|<epsilon,
and k2 is an interior maximum on a nontrivial integer interval [l,k3]
with k1<l<k2<k3 and both endpoint risks strictly below R(k2).
Ties between interior maximizing indices are allowed. The claim is
 liminf_(e downarrow0) liminf_(m to infinity)
 P_(xi,initialization)(E_(e,m,xi)(epsilon)) >= 1/16.       (2)
For each fixed chi in {-1,1}, conditional on xi_(s,t)=chi*s, the lower
bound over initialization alone is 1/2. The time k1 is a low-risk
cancellation WITNESS, not a claimed uniquely located stationary minimum.
The time k2 is an interval peak, not a unique stationary point theorem.
Equation (1) is the finite-witness meaning of two descents separated by a rise;
no monotonicity of every intervening nonlinear GD step is asserted.

## 2. Gaussian-width precursor and its exact unaveraged risk
C016/C017 supply, after the fixed-e width limit, independent Gaussian
Walsh initial outputs Z_(e,h) with covariance nu^2 lambda_h^RF. Couple them
for all e using independent standard G_0,G_s,G_t,G_st. Set
 U_(e,h)=Z_(e,h)/alpha_e-theta_h/alpha_e.
Then almost surely
 e U_(e,s)->L=sqrt(2)nu G_s,
 U_(e,t)->L_t=sqrt(2)nu G_t-1, U_(e,st)->-1.
These convergences are uniform when the four Gaussian coordinates range
over a fixed bounded set; the scalar variance coefficients are deterministic.
The constant initial output Z_(e,0)=O(1) in this coupling.

Fix the single label branch xi_(s,t)=chi*s. Its only nonzero normalized
noise Walsh coefficient is N_s=d e^(-1/4), d=2sqrt(kappa)chi;
N_0=N_t=N_st=0. Write N=N_s. The exact frozen clean risk is
 Q_(e,chi)(t)=alpha_e^2 sum_h [q_h U_(e,h)+(1-q_h)N_h]^2,
 q_h=exp(-b_h t).                                       (3)
At integer times this is discrete kernel GD, not gradient flow. In real
time it is only the spectral interpolation used to select integer witnesses.
Use the favorable initialization event chi*L<0, of probability1/2.
Every assertion below first refers to a fixed Gaussian realization in
this event, then is made probabilistic through compact exhaustion.

## 3. Early cancellation and two large value gaps
For small e, N and U_(e,s) have opposite signs. Thus
 q_*=-N/(U_(e,s)-N) belongs to (0,1),
 q_*~(-d/L)e^(3/4).
The fast residual N+q_*(U_(e,s)-N) is EXACTLY zero. Define
 t_1=-log(q_*)/b_s, t_0=-log(2q_*)/b_s.
Both are nonnegative for small e, t_0<t_1, and
 b_s t_1=(3/4)log(1/e)-log(-d/L)+o(1).                 (4)
Round these to nearest integers k0,k1. Their separation is (log2)/b_s,
which tends to infinity, so rounding preserves their order. A time change
of at most1/2 multiplies q_s by exp(O(b_s))=1+O(e). The residual error at
k1 is therefore O(|N|e)=O(e^(3/4)); at k0 it is -N+O(|N|e).
Slow-mode q_h tend to1 at both times and their U_h stay bounded. The
constant-mode residual is negligible faster than every power of e because
its initial normalized coefficient is O(e^(-2)) and b_0 is positive.
It follows that
 Q(k1)/alpha_e^2 -> L_t^2+1=2B,
 Q(k0)/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa,
where B=(L_t^2+1)/2>=1/2. In particular Q(k0)>Q(k1).
This proves the first descent witness and its leading clock; no derivative
argument or minimum uniqueness is needed.

## 4. The later single-label peak
Set t_e(v)=((9/4)log(1/e)+v)/b_s and z=exp(-v). Then q_s=e^(9/4)z.
Differentiate (3), using the exact derivative identity of C019:
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st))
 =sum_h [b_h/(b_t+b_st)]
   [q_h N_h(N_h-U_h)-q_h^2(U_h-N_h)^2].                 (5)
The fast term -q_s N U_s/eta_e converges to -dL z=A z,
with A=-dL>0. Its other four expansion terms vanish uniformly on bounded
v intervals. Their orders are respectively e^(3/4), e^(3/2), e^(9/4), e^3,
for q_s N^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s^2/eta_e, q_s^2 U_s N/eta_e,
and q_s^2 N^2/eta_e. The slow terms, with N_t=N_st=0, tend to -B,
since their weights tend to1/2 and q_t,q_st=1-O(e log(1/e)).
The constant term is again exponentially negligible. Hence locally uniformly
 Q'(t_e(v))/(2alpha_e^2(b_t+b_st)) -> A exp(-v)-B.         (6)
Integration on bounded intervals gives convergence of centered risk differences:
 [Q(t_e(v))-Q(t_e(0))]/(2alpha_e^2 eta_e)
 -> V(v)-V(0), V(v)=-A exp(-v)-Bv.                     (7)
The function V is strictly concave, with its unique maximum at
 v_*=log(A/B), and has strict value gaps to either endpoint of any compact
interval containing v_* in its interior. Also, uniformly on compact v sets,
 Q(t_e(v))/(alpha_e^2 e^(-1/2)) -> d^2=4kappa.            (8)
Indeed q_s U_s=O(e^(5/4)) is negligible relative to N=O(e^(-1/4));
slow risk is O(alpha_e^2) and the constant-mode risk is negligible.
Equations (8) and Section3 give the second strict gap Q(peak)>Q(k1).
Equation (7) gives the third strict gap to a later time, now of order
alpha_e^2 eta_e. It is much smaller than the two early value gaps.

Round all central t_e(v) to the integer grid. The mesh in v is b_s->0,
so (7) remains uniform on the grid. On a fixed compact interval containing
v_* inside, an integer maximizing index is interior and its v coordinate
tends to v_*. This uses the positive gap between V(v_*) and the compact
complement of any neighborhood of v_*, not derivatives of nonlinear GD.
The central maximizing time consequently has leading term
 (9pi/nu^2)e^(-1)log(1/e).                              (9)
The early cancellation witness (4) precedes the entire central interval,
since their b_s-scaled time separation is (3/2)log(1/e)+O(1).
This completes the Gaussian frozen-array witness construction.

## 5. Probability and transfer to the actual BOTH-layer nonlinear updates
For an integer M>=1 restrict to the compact Gaussian event
 K_M={chi L<=-1/M, |G_0|,|G_s|,|G_t|,|G_st|<=M}.
These increasing events exhaust {chi L<0}. On K_M, A is bounded above
and away from zero and B is bounded above and below. Thus v_*, the offset
in (4), and all coefficients used above lie in deterministic bounded sets.
All estimates in Sections3-4 are uniform on K_M: the U limits have deterministic

{"assumptions":["the sequence is independent AND identically distributed","A invariant under permutations of finitely many coordinates"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:40.781848+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2f498bfa2a2e45261395e21060f28261d050042661f5980c3c3857ba42765667","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be INDEPENDENT AND IDENTICALLY DISTRIBUTED. Call an event A EXCHANGEABLE if it is invariant under every permutation of finitely many indices, that is A is unchanged when the values of any finite set of coordinates are permuted. Then P(A) is 0 or 1 for every exchangeable A. This is strictly stronger than Kolmogorov's 0-1 law, which applies to TAIL events: every tail event is exchangeable, but not conversely. The standard separating example is A = { S_n = 0 for infinitely many n } for a simple random walk, which is exchangeable but NOT a tail event, since changing X_1 changes every partial sum. Identical distribution is essential and cannot be relaxed to mere independence. Minimal counterexample: let X_1 be Bernoulli(1/2) and let X_n = 0 deterministically for every n >= 2. These are independent but not identically distributed, and the event A = { x : x_n = 1 for some n } is invariant under every finite permutation of the coordinates, hence exchangeable, yet P(A) = P(X_1 = 1) = 1/2. The proof below breaks exactly where one needs it to: the permutation swapping the first n coordinates with the next n is not measure preserving unless the coordinates share a law. A standard use: for an i.i.d. sequence the events {limsup S_n = + infinity} and {liminf S_n = - infinity} are exchangeable, because permuting finitely many summands changes S_n for only finitely many n, so each has probability 0 or 1; for a non-degenerate mean-zero law a short further argument then shows both probabilities are 1, but that conclusion is NOT delivered by the 0-1 law alone. [Hewitt and Savage (1955); see Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.1.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["two independent reversible chains as specified (four states in total)","g standardized: E g = 0, E g^2 = 1, sup norm 2, tau2 = 1","t = s, epsilon = s^-2, R = s^4"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:11:19.448756+00:00","domain":"probability, Markov chains, central limit theorems","id":"claim_2f5fba596bf3bb76486989dcf7046859666f85075bfa74849c51f0164cce95ba","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Aldous and Fill, Open Problem 4.30 (p. 137) asks whether there is an explicit function psi(b,s) tending to 0 as s tends to infinity, not depending on the chain, with sup_x |P(S_t/(sigma sqrt t) <= x) - P(Z <= x)| <= psi(||g||_inf, t/tau2) for standardized g and continuous-time reversible chains. Then exactly, at every s: E g = 0, E g^2 = 1, ||g||_inf = 2 and tau2 = 1. Taking t = s sends t/tau2 to infinity with the sup norm pinned at 2, yet normality fails: S_t is compound Poisson with vanishing intensity (the mean number of visits to the rare state is epsilon t = 1/s, tending to 0), so with probability 1 - O(1/s) no visit occurs and S_t sits near the deterministic value -B epsilon t while the whole variance is carried by one rare excursion. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T00:34:53.675721+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_2f7fe3b1c2bda0d848da12d7cb43374464f19fb1a854d454abd88bc194ef8e17","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematical analysis, a function of bounded variation, also known as BV function, is a real-valued function whose total variation is bounded (finite): the graph of a function having this property is well behaved in a precise sense. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.299162+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2f8e16c491ace49efc0c7433368b2458998903fd02e3c7486aa78f9a95d89ba1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 (Joint score orthogonality and Fisher-energy decomposition) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Under the joint law of $(X_t,R)$, assume the relevant squared scores are
integrable and that differentiation may be passed under the \(\nu\)-integral
in \(p_t(x)=\int p_t(x,r)\,\dd\nu(r)\).  Write
$s_t^R(X_t)=s_t^r(X_t)|_{r=R}$.  Then
\begin{equation}

\E[g_t(X_t,R)\mid X_t]=0,
\end{equation}
and therefore the score second-moment matrices obey
\begin{equation}

\E\!\left[s_t^R(X_t)s_t^R(X_t)^\top\right]
=
\E\!\left[s_t^{\rm prior}(X_t)s_t^{\rm prior}(X_t)^\top\right]
+
\E\!\left[g_t(X_t,R)g_t(X_t,R)^\top\right].
\end{equation}
Taking the trace gives
\begin{equation}

\E\|s_t^R(X_t)\|^2
=
\E\|s_t^{\rm prior}(X_t)\|^2
+
\E\|g_t(X_t,R)\|^2,
\end{equation}
and, for every deterministic vector $v$,
\begin{equation}

\E|v^\top s_t^R(X_t)|^2
=
\E|v^\top s_t^{\rm prior}(X_t)|^2
+
\E|v^\top g_t(X_t,R)|^2.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.176790+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_2fdcbd29342bc81581ff221e1335d681186fe635fa373907a7fd8c6b9238e08b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 72 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have 
\begin{align*}
\sM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0) 
&\subseteq \sM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)\,,\\
\sM^{\six}(\alpha,q_0) 
&\subseteq \sM^{\sidealast}(\alpha,q_0)\,.
\end{align*}

\begin{proof}
We repeat the most relevant part of Definition~\ref{d:SDE.classification} for this proof:
	\begin{center}
	\begin{tabular}[h]{r|cccccccc}
	\MSRheader\\
	\hline
	\PRFTWOdefn\\
	\PRFFOURdefn\\
	\PRFONEHALFdefn\\
	\SUPERPERFECTASTdefn
	\end{tabular}
	\end{center}
The classes only differ in the conditions on the function $p$.

    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ where $\epsilon < 1/2$. 
    Then $\mu$ is of the form $\mu = \mu(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,p,\zeta = \delta_0)$ for some $(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta = \delta_0,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$.
    Since $p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1}, $p$ is twice differentiable and therefore continuous, and further satisfies $p(q_0) \le \epsilon$.
    So we can find $q' \in (q_0,1)$ such that $p(q') = 2\epsilon$, and define $\tilde p \in \incr([q_0,1];[0,1])$ by
    \[
        \tilde p(t) = \begin{cases}
            2\epsilon (t - q_0) / (q' - q_0) & t \in [q_0,q')\,, \\
            p(t) & t \in [q',1]\,.
        \end{cases}
    \]
    In particular $\tilde p(q_0) = 0$, so $\tilde p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.5withzero}, as required for the $\sxii$ class.
    Since $p$ and $\tilde p$ agree on $[q',1]$, we have
    \[
        \|p'-\tilde p'\|_1
        = \int_{q_0}^{q'} |p'(t) - \tilde p'(t)|\,dt
        \le \int_{q_0}^{q'} (p'(t) + \tilde p'(t))\,dt
        \le p(q') + \tilde p(q')
        = 4\epsilon\,.
    \]
Recalling Definition~\ref{d:X.adm}, we have $\mu \in \cM(q_0;p,f)$ for budget function
$f(t) = (\E w_t)^2 / \alpha$. Applying
    Proposition~\ref{p:continuity.in.p} gives the existence of a measure
    \[
        \tilde\mu \in \cM(q_0;\tilde p,f)
        \subseteq \cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)
    \]
    with $\bbW_2(\mu,\tilde \mu)^2 \le 6(1+1/\alpha) \cdot 4\epsilon$.
    Since this holds for all $\mu \in \cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ with $\epsilon < 1/2$, we conclude
    \[
        \cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)\Big)
    \]
    for some $\tilde\epsilon$ tending to $0$ with $\epsilon$.
    By adjusting $\tilde\epsilon$ we can also ensure
    \[
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big) \subseteq \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)\Big)\,.
    \]
 Recall \eqref{e:measure.classes.simplification.without.L0}: taking a union over $L$ and an intersection over $\epsilon$ proves the first assertion, $\sM^{\sx}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\sxii}(\alpha,q_0)$.

    The proof of the second assertion $\sM^{\six}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\sidealast}(\alpha,q_0)$ is very similar, so we only describe the differences.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\six}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$ where $\epsilon < 1/2$, realized by controls $(q_*=q_0,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta = \delta_0,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\six}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$.
    In this case $p$ satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.1concave}, so $p$ is concave in addition to the properties of condition~\ref{it:3.1} used above.
    Let $q'$ and $\tilde p$ be defined as above.
    Since $p(q_0) \ge 0$ and $p(q') = 2\epsilon$, the concavity of $p$ implies $p(t) \ge \tilde p(t)$ for all $t\in [0,q']$.
    Thus $\tilde p$ is also concave, and in particular satisfies condition~\ref{it:3.3}, as required for the $\sidealast$ class.
Then, arguing identically as above completes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:21:52.490680+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_300b42551ccc128bb28f1e385adec7e50dc5dc948351ab2fb1f9af6aab00adfb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 224 of arXiv:2601.16377, '2601.16377'] Consider the master Riemann--Hilbert problem with sources $(D_h(z))_{h = 1}^H$. In addition, choose $\boldsymbol{\kappa} \in \amsmathbb{C}$ and rational functions $(L_h(z))_{h=1}^H$ that can have poles at $z = \alpha_h,\beta_h$ and such that $L_h(z) = O(\frac{1}{z})$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$ for each $h\in[H]$.

Then there exists a unique solution $(F_h(z))_{h = 1}^H$ to the master Riemann--Hilbert problem such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\displaystyle \left(F_h(z) - \sigma_h^{-1}(z) L_h(z) - \frac{1}{2\theta_{h,h}}D_h(z)\right)_{h = 1}^H$ is tame with exponent $1$; and
\item $\displaystyle\oint_{\gamma_h} \frac{\dd z}{2\ii\pi}\,F_h(z) = \kappa_h$ for all $h\in[H]$.
\end{enumerate}
The solution is given by the formula:
\[
F_h(z) = \sum_{g = 1}^H \big(\kappa_g \mathfrak{c}^{\textnormal{1st}}_{h;g}(z) - r(\alpha_g)\mathfrak{c}_{h;g}^{\textnormal{3rd}}(z;\alpha_g) - r(\beta_g)\mathfrak{c}^{\textnormal{3rd}}_{h;g}(\z;\beta_g)\big) - \sum_{\textnormal{J} \in \{\textnormal{I},\textnormal{II},\textnormal{III}\}} \mathfrak{F}_h^{\textnormal{J}}[\boldsymbol{f}^{\textnormal{J}}](z).
\]
The $H$-tuple of functions $\boldsymbol{f}^{\textnormal{J}}$ and the constants $(r(\alpha_g),r(\beta_g))_{g = 1}^{H}$ are determined by
\[
\forall g \in [H]\qquad f_g^{\textnormal{II}}(z) = \frac{2}{\sigma_g(z)} \int_{z}^{\infty} \frac{L_g(\zeta)}{\sigma_g(\zeta)}\dd \zeta,
\]
and the (unique up to addition of a constant to $f^{\textnormal{I}}_g$) decomposition of the source
\begin{equation}

\forall g \in [H]\qquad D_g(z) = \partial_z f^{\textnormal{I}}_g(z) + \frac{r(\alpha_g)}{z - \alpha_g} + \frac{r(\beta_g)}{z -\beta_g} + \partial_z f^{\textnormal{III}}_g(z),
\end{equation}
where the function $f_g^{\textnormal{I}}(z)$ is holomorphic in a complex neighborhood of $\overline{\amsmathbb{B}}_g$ and $f^{\textnormal{III}}_g(z)$ is a rational function with possible poles at $\alpha_g,\beta_g$ and such that $f^{\textnormal{III}}_g(z) = O(\frac{1}{z})$ as $z \rightarrow \infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751901+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_302068305216ae5c066735895bb24468a7e83b19c56defd1453da6e28734f134","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TYPEWRITER (L^p convergence does not imply almost-everywhere convergence). On [0,1] write n = 2^k + j with 0 <= j < 2^k and let f_n be the indicator of [j 2^{-k}, (j+1) 2^{-k}). Then ||f_n||_p^p = 2^{-k} -> 0, so f_n -> 0 in L^p for every p < infinity and in measure. But for every x in [0,1) and every k there is exactly one j with f_{2^k + j}(x) = 1, so f_n(x) equals 1 for infinitely many n and 0 for infinitely many n: the sequence converges at NO point. This is why one extracts an a.e. convergent subsequence rather than hoping for the full sequence. SLIDING BUMP (pointwise convergence does not imply L^1 convergence). On [0,1] let g_n = n 1_{(0, 1/n)}. Then g_n(x) -> 0 for every x in (0,1], indeed the convergence is pointwise everywhere on (0,1], yet integral g_n = 1 for every n. The mass does not disappear, it concentrates. The dominated convergence theorem excludes exactly this: no integrable g dominates all g_n, since any such g would satisfy g >= n on (0,1/n) for every n, forcing integral_{(0,1/n)} g >= 1 for all n and contradicting absolute continuity of the integral. ESCAPING MASS is the third, distinct failure and lives on infinite measure spaces: h_n = 1_{[n, n+1]} on R is uniformly bounded, converges to 0 everywhere, and has ||h_n||_1 = 1. Three different mechanisms, three different repairs: a subsequence, a dominating function, and a tightness condition. [standard; the typewriter sequence is sometimes attributed to Kolmogorov]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a normed space (Banach for the uniform boundedness step in the failure remark and for the dual statement)","X* is the topological dual with the weak-star topology sigma(X*, X)","B is the closed unit ball of X*, or any bounded weak-star closed subset - the equivalence concerns bounded sets only","for the dual statement (weak metrizability of the ball of X iff X* separable), X is Banach"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.401830+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, duality and weak topologies","id":"claim_3068dbe8a1de19437f2a1e5ddde4699f874618668f487ef7075cce85ce2b6a54","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed space with dual X* carrying the weak-star topology sigma(X*, X). Then the closed unit ball B of X* is metrizable in the relative weak-star topology if and only if X is separable; in that case every bounded subset of X* is weak-star metrizable, and a compatible metric is d(f,g) = sum over n of 2^(-n) min(1, |f(x_n) - g(x_n)|) for any dense sequence (x_n) of the unit sphere of X. Combined with Banach-Alaoglu (B is weak-star compact), separability of X gives that B is weak-star compact and metrizable, hence weak-star SEQUENTIALLY compact: every bounded sequence in X* has a weak-star convergent subsequence. The dual statement also holds: for a Banach space X, the closed unit ball of X is metrizable in the weak topology sigma(X, X*) if and only if X* is separable. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) 'bounded' is essential - the weak-star topology on ALL of X* is metrizable only when X is finite dimensional; indeed if it were metrizable with countable base (U_m) at 0 and X is infinite dimensional, each U_m contains a nonzero subspace (it is cut out by finitely many functionals), so one can pick f_m in U_m with ||f_m|| >= m, and then f_m converges weak-star to 0 while being unbounded, contradicting the uniform boundedness principle; (b) the two directions are not interchangeable - separability of X does not imply separability of X*: X = l^1 is separable, so B of (l^1)* = l^infinity is weak-star metrizable, but (l^1)* = l^infinity is not separable, so the unit ball of l^1 is NOT weakly metrizable; (c) the metric above is not translation-invariantly compatible on the whole of X* and the equivalence is genuinely a statement about the relative topology on bounded sets; (d) for X = l^infinity, which is not separable, the unit ball of (l^infinity)* is weak-star compact but not weak-star metrizable, and weak-star compactness there is not sequential compactness.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:49.204148+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_306e084e1cb887edf036fb5c0c3c7f11d4d1df89e4517f85f314907966879a51","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Sampling active subspaces~\protect{\cite[Thm.~3.7) of arXiv:2604.27119, '\Large Applied Random Matrix Theory\relatedversion'] {Con15:Active-Subspaces}}]
Let $f : \R^d \to \R$ be $L$-Lipschitz and differentiable.
As in~\cref{eqn:sensitivity-matrix,eqn:empirical-sensitivity},
consider the sensitivity matrix $\mtx{\Sigma} \in \Sym_d(\R)$

determined by $n$ gradient samples.  The expectation of the relative approximation error satisfies
\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.346979+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3083b9a91b3bfb645dd1208a02f4f9ee20f6b1c4e5780669c6f1d7c2726f9b6f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 149 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix $(b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}. 
Fix any vectors $\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}\in\bbR^M$, and let $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ be the centered IAMP specified by Definition~\ref{d:centered.iamp}. 
Then, for $C\equiv C(L,\epsilon,\delta)$, 
there exists a $C$-Lipschitz map $\cA^\dagger$ which agrees
with $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ with probability $1-\exp(-cN)$, and satisfies
	    \[
    \cA(-\bG,-\bg^\aux)
    =
    -\cA(\bG,\bg^\aux)\,.
    \]
In particular, it follows that $\bbE[\cA(\bG,\bg^{\aux})~|~\bx^{\dagger,0},\prxbx^{\dagger,0}]=\bzero\in\bbR^N$.
\begin{proof}
    Let $(\hat\by^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxby^{\dagger,k},\hat\bx^{\dagger,k},\hat\prxbx^{\dagger,k})$ be the IAMP iterates corresponding to $(-\bG,- \bg^{\aux})$.
    We claim that for all $0\leq k\leq \ubl$ we have
    \begin{align*}
    (\hat\prxby,\hat\by,\hat\bu,\hat\bw)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (-\prxby,-\by,-\bu,\bw)^{\dagger,k}
      \,\\
    (\hat\prxbx,\hat\bx,\hat\bv,
    \hat\bm,\hat\bsig,\hat\bb)^{\dagger,k}
    &=
    (\prxbx,\bx,\bv,
    \bm,\bsig,\bb)^{\dagger,k}\,.
    \end{align*}
Indeed, the base case for the first statement above holds easily since
$w$ is even by the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main} \eqref{i:IAMP-main-centered}, the functions
 $\psi$ and $\prxpsi$ are odd (Lemma~\ref{lem:even-manual-init}), 
the vectors $(\by,\prxby,\hat{\by},\hat{\prxby})^{\dagger,0}$ are defined by \eqref{eq:mean-0-initialization},  and  we defined $\bu^{\dagger,0}=\hat{\bu}^{\dagger,0}=\bzero\in\R^M$.
The remaining statements follow by 
induction, using the formulas \eqref{eq:proxy-y-amp-def}--\eqref{eq:x-amp-def}. 

The above shows the desired symmetry for the mapping $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$, and we must now transfer it to $\cA^\dagger$. This proceeds similarly as in the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}, using the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, except that we now need to ensure that the symmetry requirement is satisfied. 
First, we have by easy induction that $\tilde{\cA}^\dagger$ is $C$-Lipschitz on a subset $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\subseteq \bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$, similarly to the \hyperlink{proof:t.IAMP.main.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-main}}. To be precise, 
    \[\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}
    =\bigg\{
    \begin{array}{c}
    (\bG,\bg^\aux) : 
    \textup{$\bG_\circ$
    satisfies \eqref{eq:Brownian-bridge-condition},
    $\|\bG\|_\textup{op}\le C_0
    (M^{1/2}+N^{1/2})$,}\\
    \textup{$\|\bar\bg^{\ell}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$
    for all $0\le\ell\le\ubl$, and
    $\|\bar\bg^{\init}\|\leq 2\sqrt{N}$}
    \end{array}
    \bigg\}\,.
    \]
In particular, this choice of $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}$ is origin-symmetric. 
(Again, see e.g.\ the discussion on ``standard optimization algorithms'' in \cite{HuangSellke2021} for the Lipschitz bound on such a domain.)

Thus, let $S=\{\bg_1,\bg_2,\dots\}$ be a countable dense set in $\bbR^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
    For each $\bg_i$, we assume $\tilde\cA^{\dagger}$ has been extended to a $C$-Lipschitz function on $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\equiv \mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\cup \{\bg_1,-\bg_1,\dots,\bg_i,-\bg_i\}$.
    Then by the Kirzsbraun extension theorem, there exists a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}\cup \{\bg_{i+1}\}$.
    Since 
  $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i}$ is symmetric,  
the unique odd extension to $\mathcal{U}^{\dagger,i+1}$ is still $C$-Lipschitz. Continuing in this way yields a $C$-Lipschitz extension to $ \mathcal{U}^\dagger\cup S\cup -S$. This set is dense by definition of $S$, so the result follows by continuously extending to all of $\R^{MN+N_{\aux}}$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.811321+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_309034f24e28f39b10d843d08c83c6536dabbe1cbcc2c3e65e9ffa83d7c21f3b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop_prop_SL of arXiv:2603.26307, '\LARGE The incompressible Navier--Stokes--Fourier system with thermal noise'] Let Assumption (Ass:noise of the paper) hold, $(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space equipped with a filtration $\mathscr{F}$ satisfying the usual conditions and $3$-dimensional standard $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(W_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ and $3\times 3$-matrix valued $\mathscr{F}$-Brownian motions $(B_n)_{n\in \mathbb{Z}^3}$ with covariance structure (equation Eq_noise_matrix_covariation of the paper) be independent. 		\setcounter{enumi}{2}
		\item 
		For every $\eta\in C^{{\infty}}( \mathbb{T}^3)$ it holds
		\begin{align}\begin{split}
				&

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:27:56.778420+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3094139d6c32ee053ca7cdcf1a48243f534a519ed5d8e61476f08327de9b8c55","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 16 of arXiv:2608.31171, '\bf Finite-energy spacetimes with torus symmetry. \\ \Large Cauchy stability of Einstein--'] A \textbf{Navier--Stokes triple} \((\mathscr F,\chi,\mathscr B)\) is called \textbf{admissible} provided the following \textbf{invariant-domain property} holds for each of the two associated Einstein--Navier--Stokes models 
\eqref{eq:pot-production-system} and \eqref{eq:pot-dissipated-system}, as follows. 

Let \(\{\Sigma_t\}_{t_0\leq t<t_1}\) be a spacelike foliation of a compact spacetime slab, and let \((g,\beta,\zeta)\) be a regular solution of the corresponding hyperbolic evolution-constraint system\footnote{A gauge must be chosen to deal with the spacetime metric and formulate a well-posed initial value problem; this is a standard topic, not reviewed here \cite{Choquet-book}.} on \([t_0,t_1)\). Assume that
\be
\zeta(t_0,\Sigma_{t_0})\subset\mathcal K_0
\qquad\text{for some closed fiber subset }\mathcal K_0\Subset\mathscr F.
\ee
Then one has
\be
\zeta(t,\Sigma_t)\subset\mathscr F
\qquad\text{for every }t_0\leq t<t_1.
\ee
Moreover, if the fields admit a continuous limit in the ambient bundles as \(t\uparrow t_1\), while the nonsingular coefficients in the equation for~\(\zeta\) remain bounded, then the terminal relaxing field satisfies
\be
\zeta(t_1,\Sigma_{t_1})\subset\mathscr F,
\ee
rather than merely taking its values in~\(\overline{\mathscr F}\). Equivalently, the constitutive boundary~\(\del\mathscr F\) cannot be the first cause of breakdown of a regular solution.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.186720+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_31199ef303ea3dc048a12dfd4ffe05c9131d850a43b8c0ee851330f431bc4f9f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field, any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:25:39.085567+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_314c60f51b3c162d281248f74ddda1383da7af322728a078102cbbd15c592d5f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:flow of arXiv:2606.12143, 'Continuous stochastic flows driven by white noise and their duals'] A \textbf{stochastic flow} driven by $\mathcal W$ is a family of processes 
$$
\mathcal S = \left\{\bigl(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x \ge r\bigr)\right\}_{(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2}
$$
such that, for each $(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2$, the process $(\mathcal S_{r,x}(a),\, x \ge r)$ is the almost sure unique strong solution to~(equation eq:SDE_gener of the paper), and the following properties hold almost surely:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(R\arabic*)}, nosep]
    \item $\mathcal S_{r,r}(a) = a$ for all $(a,r) \in {\mathbb R}^2$. 
    \item For every $r \le x$, $a \mapsto \mathcal S_{r,x}(a)$ is c\`adl\`ag. 
    \item For any $(a_1,r_1), (a_2,r_2) \in {\mathbb R}^2$ and any $z \ge y \ge \max\{r_1,r_2\}$,
    $$
        \mathcal S_{r_1,y}(a_1) < \mathcal S_{r_2,y}(a_2) 
        \ \Longrightarrow\ 
        \mathcal S_{r_1,z}(a_1) \le \mathcal S_{r_2,z}(a_2).
    $$ 
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{-1.2em} 
A stochastic flow is said to be \textbf{continuous} if, almost surely, all flow lines are continuous. 
It is said to be \textbf{unique} if any other stochastic flow associated with~(equation eq:SDE_gener of the paper) satisfying the above properties is equal to $\mathcal S$ almost surely.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358403+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_3164e6f087edcf03d0ed5dc5b5362a181abb5563823cfe1cedcf020aa6b01bc9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fitting a per-output affine stack directly in the per-sample relative metric - weighted least squares with case weights $1/\\|y_i\\|^2$, or a per-output simplex fit with the same weights - overfits badly: the weights concentrate the effective sample on the handful of smallest-norm cases and $M + 1$ coefficients fitted to them are unusable out of sample (measured on the EMIT pool, seed 101: 0.1236 against 0.0465 for ordinary least squares on Y1, 0.1591 against 0.1292 on Y2; cross-validation on the weighted fit chooses to discard it entirely). The same objective becomes the best available estimator when it is reached through the error covariance rather than through the regression: form the error covariance in the relative metric, replace its sample eigenvalues by the Ledoit-Peche nonlinear-shrinkage values (floored at a small fraction of the bulk level), and take the sum-to-one minimum-variance weights with the intercept closing the weighted mean error, with no cross-validation anywhere. Measured on the same three cells (Y1, Y2, Y4): 0.0451 / 0.1190 / 1.799 against ordinary least squares 0.0465 / 0.1292 / 1.898 (+3.0 / +7.9 / +5.2 percent), matching the cross-validated best heuristic of the pool twice and beating it once; with the residual shrink toward the pooled simplex weights on top (cross-validated amount 0.2-0.4) it is the best estimator on all three cells, +4.1 / +11.7 / +6.7 percent over least squares and +3.4 to +3.9 percent over the pool's best. Two ingredients do the work: the nonlinear shrinkage tames the heavy-tailed spectrum that the small-norm cases create, and the sum-to-one constraint removes the scale and intercept freedom those cases exploit. In this metric the random-matrix cleaning is not a small correction on top of least squares; it is the difference between an unusable fit and the best one. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:47:41.428399+00:00","domain":"Riemannian geometry","id":"claim_31b886d6ae5e89d7ba86732be244fd5ceb8c845f680edca8ffdf80a466f188ad","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (M,g) be a Riemannian manifold with Levi-Civita connection nabla. A smooth curve gamma: I -> M on an interval I subset R is a geodesic if its velocity field is parallel along itself: nabla_{gamma'(t)} gamma'(t) = 0 for every t in I. Equivalently, in local coordinates x^1,...,x^n a curve gamma(t) = (x^1(t),...,x^n(t)) is a geodesic iff it satisfies the second-order ODE system d^2x^k/dt^2 + sum_{i,j} Gamma^k_{ij}(gamma(t)) (dx^i/dt)(dx^j/dt) = 0 for k=1,...,n, where Gamma^k_{ij} are the Christoffel symbols of g. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.142189+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_31bf23c8569447ad87fe2691c4a7ab91","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, Schur's lemma is an elementary but useful statement in representation theory of groups and algebras. In the group case it says that if M and N are two finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G and φ is a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group, then either φ is invertible, or φ = 0. An important special case occurs when M = N, i.e. φ is a self-map; in particular, for representations over an algebraically closed field (e.g. $\\mathbb {C}$), any element of the center of a group must act as a scalar operator (a scalar multiple of the identity) on M. The lemma is named after Issai Schur who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations and develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. Schur's lemma admits generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the most common of which are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen.","status":"unverified"}

Y. Shmalo, Supermodular ordering of speeded-up Markov chains without stochastic monotonicity (October 2026). For a stationary continuous-time Markov chain with real values, let the chain run at speed c. Leskela (Queueing Systems 100 (2022), 213-215, Problem 3) asked whether some stationary ergodic chain that is not stochastically monotone becomes smaller in the supermodular order of processes as it is speeded up. The paper shows that such chains exist on three states: a chain that leaves its smallest value for either of the other two values at any positive rates and returns from both at a common rate has this property and is not stochastically monotone. If the largest value returns faster than the middle one, the property fails already for pairs of sampling times. For reversible three-state chains with two distinct nonzero eigenvalues, the pairs are ordered exactly when the slow left eigenvector does not have the same strict sign at the two extreme states. Exact certificate identities, symbolic spectral formulas, linear programs over supermodular functions and a Lean 4 file accompany the paper. Paper and code: https://github.com/yspennstate/supermodular-speed-ordering (commit e1afd4de9728). Not refereed.","status":"unverified"}

		\qquad 1\le i\le N.
		\]
		Let \(\rho\) be a finite-step probability measure on \([r,q]\), and write
		\[
		\bar x_\rho(t)
		=
		\theta+(1-\theta)\rho([r,t]),
		\qquad r\le t<q.
		\]
		Let \(\phi_\rho\) solve on \([r,q]\)
		\begin{equation}
			\begin{aligned}
				\partial_t\phi_\rho
				+\frac{\xi''(t)}2
				\left(
				\partial_{xx}\phi_\rho
				+\bar x_\rho(t)(\partial_x\phi_\rho)^2
				\right)&=0,\\
				\phi_\rho(q,x)&=\Phi_\zeta(q,x).
			\end{aligned}
		\end{equation}
		For
		\[
		Z\sim\mathcal N\left(
		0,\xi'(r)-\frac{\xi'(r)^2}{\xi'(q)}
		\right),
		\]
		define
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\mathcal J_{N,\mathbf{m},q,r}(\rho)
			:={}&
			\theta\bigl[\xi(r)-r\xi'(r)-\xi(q)+q\xi'(q)\bigr]
			-\frac1N\sum_i\Phi_\zeta(q,b_i)\\
			&+\frac1N\sum_i
			\mathbb{E}_Z\phi_\rho\left(
			r,Z+\frac{\xi'(r)}{\xi'(q)}b_i
			\right)
			-\frac12\int_r^q t\xi''(t)\bar x_\rho(t)\,\mathrm{d} t.
		\end{aligned}
		\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:24:34.422868+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_322c6b7a0bc172a33d5ac4535a0d202800889fd44bdad751b4a36dbd712a25bd","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 (Signed transport and one-side-fixed composition) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] The following operations preserve affine dependence of network parameters on a

\begin{enumerate}[label={\textup{(\roman*)}}]
 \item A signed scalar $u$ may be transported through any number of hidden
 layers as the nonnegative pair

 $(u_+,u_-)\mapsto(u_+,u_-)$ and recovery $u=u_+-u_-$.
 \item Finitely many networks may be copied or run in parallel.  Their widths
 add.  A $q$-dimensional state is transported coordinatewise by $2q$
 nonnegative channels, so shorter branches can be extended to a common
 depth by fixed signed transport.  If a branch already terminates in a
 nonnegative state or a signed pair, its existing depth gap is filled by fixed
 identity layers.  If only a signed scalar affine readout
 $u=\bmw(\bmxi)^\ts\bmh+b(\bmxi)$ is available, compose that readout with the

 is preserved.  This split layer must be included in the interface depth
 ledger.
 \item Two adjacent affine layers with no intervening activation may be
 merged without losing affine code dependence whenever at least one of the

{"assumptions":["l^p norm on R^2","axis direction","d/r -> 0 asymptotics"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T04:06:41.000000+00:00","domain":"convex geometry / first-passage percolation limit shapes","id":"claim_32cba36e9ea9ba0c5d9ba247f3e15cf592fb208e4bcf772a85f058485b81ff96","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the l^p norm on R^2 and the axis direction e_2, the dogleg excess of a midpoint-displaced point v = (d, r/2) is exactly asymptotic to (2^p/p) d^p / r^{p-1} as d/r -> 0 (second-order Taylor of (1 + x^p)^{1/p}). Consequently the enclosing-ball (quadratic lower) curvature condition excess >= c d^2/r holds at the axis if and only if p <= 2: for p < 2 the excess is of larger order than quadratic (the condition holds with room), at p = 2 it is exactly quadratic with constant 2, and for every p > 2 the contact is quartic or flatter and the enclosing-ball constant is ZERO. The curvature hypothesis consumed by localization arguments is therefore genuinely restrictive - entire familiar norm families fail it at their axis directions - and cannot be discharged by convexity or symmetry alone. Numerically verified: measured excess/predicted ratios 0.9995-1.0000 across p in {1.5, 2, 3, 4} at two offsets, and the quadratic test excess/(d^2/r) converges to a constant for p <= 2 and to zero for p > 2.","status":"derived_in_campaign_refereed"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T07:57:26.300439+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_32db5e05c2234ca8a4c051e226a841c9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the free group $F_{S}$ over a given set $S$ consists of all words that can be built from members of $S$, considering two words to be different unless their equality follows from the group axioms (e.g. $st=suu^{-1}t$ but $s\\neq t^{-1}$ for $s,t,u\\in S$). The members of $S$ are called generators of $F_{S}$, and the number of generators is the rank of the free group. An arbitrary group $G$ is called free if it is isomorphic to $F_{S}$ for some subset $S$ of $G$, that is, if there is a subset $S$ of $G$ such that every element of $G$ can be written in exactly one way as a product of finitely many elements of $S$ and their inverses (disregarding trivial variations such as $st=suu^{-1}t$).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.857052+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_32e958db18a4be44f23532fc88b129366075f86c021934c666451af981293060","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 (Standard properties of Friedrichs mollifiers,
		see \cite{Li-Liu-Tang-2021-SPA,Taylor-2011-PDEbook3}) of arXiv:2609.02019, '2609.02019'] Let $J_n$ be defined by \eqref{Define Jn}. Then the following properties
		hold.
		\begin{enumerate}[label={\bf (\arabic*)},leftmargin=0.79cm]
			\setlength\itemsep{0.2em}
			\item For every $r\in\mathbb R$, $J_n$ is self-adjoint on $H^r$:
			\[
			\langle J_nf,g\rangle_{H^r}
			=
			\langle f,J_ng\rangle_{H^r},
			\quad f,g\in H^r.
			\]
			Moreover, $J_n$ commutes with every Fourier multiplier; in particular,
			it commutes with $\mathcal D^r$, $\partial_x$, and $\mathcal H$ whenever

			\]
			In addition,
			\[

			\]
			
			\item For every $a,b\in\mathbb R$ with $a>b$,
			\[
			\|\mathbf I-J_n\|_{\mathscr L(H^a;H^b)}

			\]
			whereas, for $a<b$,
			\[
			\|J_n\|_{\mathscr L(H^a;H^b)}
			\lesssim

			\]

{"assumptions":["N>=3,K>=2,1<=r<K,0<=s<r integers","One unresolved A/S pair, remaining known S contexts; uniform contexts then uniform truths; arbitrary A has uniform r-subset prior","Observed truth unions of sizes s,r from actual untagged factual samples and optional independent partial verifier; no orientation labels","Robust exact-level source Mis_infinity=0 in every compatible support/orientation; arbitrary generators"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:03:59.558789+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; calibrated generation; integer bin counts","id":"claim_33473ffb4e038cd31db014d9a7c4c10c9d09d2ada7aea2449896c78659aa2510","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited), independent mathematical, priority and target-scope review pending. # Exact saturated single-pair frontier from integer bin counts

T379-C018 v2: proof (unaudited), exact checks PASS; independent audit pending.
Target 1, secondary target 2. Conditional robust ZERO calibration only;
arbitrary VC dimension with several saturated pairs remains open here.

## Model and exact candidate

Let N>=3,K>=2,1<=r<K,0<=s<r be integers. There is one unresolved A/S
pair L,R and N-2 fixed known S contexts. S has all K truths; A has an
independent uniform r-subset. The source p chooses contexts uniformly
and then truths uniformly. Actual untagged iid factual samples and an
optional independent partial verifier give known truth unions C_L,C_R
of sizes s and r respectively. Both orientations are still compatible.
If R is A its support is fully known; if L is A it contains C_L but
its r-s residual truths vary over the other K-s candidates.

All generators are allowed. Require source Mis_infinity=0 in EVERY
compatible world, using exact output-probability score bins.
Put F=K-r, G=gcd(r,F), lambda=1/(NK). For j=0,...,G define

 k_j=min(s,r*j/G),
 L_j=K+K*j/G-2*k_j,
 a_j=(j/G)*(F/r)*k_j/L_j.                                (1)

All counts are integers and all L_j>0. The proposed exact conditional
worst-world false-mass frontier is

 V_sat(0)=F*lambda*(1-max_{0<=j<=G}a_j).                  (2)

This is a finite optimization of G+1 explicit rational values, not a
numerical estimate or an unbounded partition search. It includes every
score partition, mixed safe atoms and arbitrary output probabilities.
No optimal positive-budget or global expected frontier is claimed.

## Lower bound for every robustly calibrated generator

Fix g and its exact score partition Pi. Robust zero calibration makes
every p(B)=g(B) invariant across all compatible worlds. Since s<r<K,
swapping two residual L candidates in an A support forces all K-s
uncertified L atoms into a single score bin B*. Let k be the number
of known L truths OUTSIDE B*, so 0<=k<=s. In B* let u be the number
of known R truths, v the number of the F candidates outside C_R,
and w the number of fixed S atoms. Flipping orientation yields

 F*(u+k)=r*v.

Consequently v=F*j/G and u=r*j/G-k for an integer 0<=j<=G, with
k<=r*j/G. The size of B* is

For completeness the divisibility step uses Bezout: r/G and F/G are
coprime; a*(r/G)+b*(F/G)=1. Multiplying by v and using (F/G)|(r/G)*v
gives (F/G)|v, then the displayed parametrization. The brain returned
this standard identity in recall/walk004.txt, full card id
claim_63c5ddfd2e7e4d178b7628c572034232. It did not supply the frontier.

 L=K+K*j/G-2k+w,

and its common calibrated score, computed in the L-A world, is

 q*=lambda*(1-k*F/(r*L)).                               (3)

In any other bin let a be its known-L-truth count, u its known-R-
truth count and v its outside-C_R count. Orientation invariance gives
F*(u-a)=r*v. Its calibrated score is

 q=lambda*(1+a*F/(r*|B|))>=lambda.

Therefore in the actual compatible world R=A (whose support is C_R),
the false mass is at least

 H_R>=v*q*+(F-v)*lambda
    >=F*lambda*[1-(j/G)*(F/r)*k/(K+K*j/G-2k)].            (4)

The second inequality uses w>=0, which can only raise q* in (3).
For fixed j the function k/(K+K*j/G-2k) increases with k on the
feasible positive-denominator range: cross multiplication cancels the
quadratic terms and leaves K*(1+j/G)*(k_2-k_1)>=0. Thus its maximum
is at k=k_j. Formula (4) proves max_world H(g)>=the value (2).
It does not assume arbitrary bins are homogeneous in truth status.

## Attainer for each j

Fix any j and k=k_j. Choose k known L truths for a safe group T;
put all other L atoms in B*. In R put r*j/G-k known truths and
F*j/G outside-C_R atoms into B*. Put k of the remaining known R
truths in T alongside its k known L truths. Put all remaining R atoms
in Z. These choices are possible: k<=s and k<=r*j/G; also j<=G
ensures enough R known truths remain for T.

The groups have these source-invariant counts and scores:

* B*: K+K*j/G-2k atoms, score (3) with w=0;
* T: 2k known true atoms, score (1/r+1/K)/(2N), omitted if k=0;
* Z: r*(G-j)/G known R truths and F*(G-j)/G outside atoms,
  total K*(G-j)/G atoms, score lambda, omitted if j=G;
* fixed S atoms: score lambda.

T has source mass k/(Nr)+k/(NK). Z has source mass (G-j)/(GN)
in either orientation. B* has the remaining pair mass, or its
invariance follows directly from F*(u+k)=r*v. Thus every group has
an invariant p mass and g is its uniform coarsening; equal lambda
scores merge harmlessly. The total is one and g is robustly calibrated
with zero budget in every compatible world.

If L=A its F false atoms all lie in B*, giving H_L=F*q*. If R=A,
H_R=(F*j/G)*q*+F*(1-j/G)*lambda. Since q*<=lambda, H_R>=H_L.
The worst risk is exactly F*lambda*(1-a_j). Maximizing a_j attains
the lower bound, proving (2).

The attaining rule uses only the observed known-truth unions and the
given model parameters: choose j by the explicit optimization, and
choose the displayed subsets of those known unions. It never reads
the hidden orientation or unobserved truth labels. Those labels enter
only the subsequent all-world verification and lower-bound argument.

## Consequences and relation to the earlier obstruction

If G=1, the only improving choice is j=1,k=s. Formula (2) becomes
the earlier smaller-count expression (K-r)*b_s. Thus the saturated
unequal case still has that expression when r and K-r are coprime.
When G>1, additional neutral truth/false bundles may improve it.

For C016's family K=3m,r=3(m-1),s=2(m-1),m>=5, G=3. The reductions
a_j for j=1,2,3 are respectively

 1/[6(m+1)], 4/[3(m+4)], 1/(m+2).

The middle value is largest: it beats the last iff m>4 and beats
the first since 24(m+1)>3(m+4). Thus C016's feasible generator is
in fact OPTIMAL in the conditional zero-budget game, with exact value

 V_sat(0)=lambda*(3m+8)/(m+4).                           (5)

This upgrades a route obstruction to an exact infinite-family frontier,
within the stated single-pair regime. It does not solve the full
arbitrary-d/global expected targets. Together with the unsaturated
C017 result and the fully-known-both-sides C013 case it gives an exact
single-pair zero-budget case map, but no larger claim is inferred.

{"assumptions":["all examples are for Lebesgue measure on [0,1] or R, and counting measure on N"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553628+00:00","domain":"real analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_33568bddd455c11696bbce09e0ff678cc9dd457d94aed6dcd3a4a493975ad160","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"There is NO inclusion between L^p and L^q on a general measure space, and the two familiar inclusions run in OPPOSITE directions. (a) Finite measure (mu(X) < infinity), p < q: L^q is contained in L^p, with ||f||_p <= mu(X)^{1/p - 1/q} ||f||_q; the inclusion is strict, e.g. on [0,1], f(x) = x^{-1/2} is in L^1 but not L^2. (b) Counting measure, p < q: l^p is contained in l^q, with ||a||_q <= ||a||_p - the reverse containment; strictness: a_n = 1/n is in l^2 but not l^1. (c) Lebesgue measure on R^n: NEITHER containment holds. On R, |x|^{-1/2} 1_{{|x|<1}} is in L^1 but not L^2, while (1 + |x|)^{-1} is in L^2 but not L^1 - the first fails by a local singularity, the second by slow decay at infinity. What IS always true is the interpolation statement: for p_0 < p < p_1, L^{p_0} intersect L^{p_1} is contained in L^p, with ||f||_p <= ||f||_{p_0}^{1-theta} ||f||_{p_1}^{theta}. So a step 'f in L^2 hence f in L^1' is only legitimate after the measure has been declared finite (with the factor mu(X)^{1/2} exhibited), and 'f in L^1 hence f in L^2' only on an atomic space with atoms bounded below.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(M, g) complete, dimension n >= 2, Ric >= (n - 1) K","for K > 0 the radii are restricted to r <= pi/sqrt(K) (Myers' theorem bounds the diameter by this)","balls are metric balls; the comparison is with the constant-curvature space form of the same dimension"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626870+00:00","domain":"Riemannian geometry","id":"claim_338d9bb13af1cd024dea87103676ffb3c1862ce9e236975fc0480f3bdfa4ae16","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (M, g) be a complete Riemannian manifold of dimension n whose Ricci curvature satisfies Ric >= (n - 1) K g for a constant K, and let V_K(r) denote the volume of a geodesic ball of radius r in the simply connected complete space of constant curvature K (the sphere of radius 1/sqrt(K) for K > 0, Euclidean space for K = 0, hyperbolic space of curvature K for K < 0; for K > 0 take r <= pi / sqrt(K)).
