{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:19:42.467530+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3a217c1aff33f2b41fb20ced6168cd81f5e50cfb1eeeb59eacc432e5a04588d9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 1 (Full-space reduction and its interior equality case) of arXiv:2609.03466, 'Least-Favorable Location for Binomial Top-$t$ Selection'] For $p\in[0,1-\delta]$, let $P_{n,k,t,\delta}(p)$ be the PCS for $k-t$ probabilities equal to $p$ and $t$ probabilities equal to $p+\delta$. For each $\boldsymbol\theta\in\ThetaPZ$, define
\[
 p(\boldsymbol\theta)=\theta_{[k-t+1]}-\delta\in[0,1-\delta].
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
 \PCS_n(\boldsymbol\theta)
 \ge P_{n,k,t,\delta}\bigl(p(\boldsymbol\theta)\bigr).
 
\end{equation}
If $p(\boldsymbol\theta)\in(0,1-\delta)$, equality holds if and only if
\[
 \theta_{[1]}=\cdots=\theta_{[k-t]}=p(\boldsymbol\theta),
 \qquad
 \theta_{[k-t+1]}=\cdots=\theta_{[k]}
 =p(\boldsymbol\theta)+\delta.
\]
Consequently, for every $n,k,t$ and $\delta\in(0,1)$,
\begin{equation}
 \inf_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\ThetaPZ}\PCS_n(\boldsymbol\theta)
 =\min_{0\le p\le1-\delta}P_{n,k,t,\delta}(p).
 
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.869570+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3a2208c3223e3a9b72a41a781c8d3f9662256b012cbe5aa3edd387241c9dd104","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theor thm:c4-finite-subgraph of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] There exists a universal constant
$C_{\ifmmode\text{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\else{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\fi}\ge1$ such that the following holds.
Fix an integer $d\ge2$, a real $\rho\in(0,1]$, and positive integers $k,r,n$ with  
 $$2 \le \rho k \le r\le k\le n.$$

Let $G=(I,J,M)$ be $C_4$-free with $|I|=k$, $|J|=n$, and right degrees satisfying
\[
2\le |N_G(j)|\le d
\qquad\forall j\in J.
\]

Define
\[
K_\star:=
\max\left\{
K\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:
K\log K\le \Lambda 
\right\}, \quad \mbox{ where } \Lambda :=\min\left(\frac r2,\frac nk\right). 
\]
and let $m_\star$ be a positive integer satisfying
\[
\left(\frac{C_{\ifmmode\text{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\else{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\fi}d^4m_\star}{\rho}\right)^{C_{\ifmmode\text{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\else{\tiny(thm:c4-finite-subgraph of the paper)}\fi}d^3m_\star}
\le K_\star.
\]
Assume such an $m_\star$ exists.
If $\Omega\subseteq J$ is chosen uniformly from $\binom Jr$, then
\[
\mathbb P\bigl(\text{$G[\Omega]$ contains a \hyperref[def:weight-compatible-rooted-matching-tree]{\textcolor{PineGreen}{\emph{weight-compatible $m_\star$-matching rooted tree}}}}\bigr)
\ge
1-\exp(-\sqrt{K_\star})-\frac{32d}{\log K_\star}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:24:20.972873+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3a26f7a21ae85b9aa2ebfc410ab19afa16bb1567b02f945f465a1ed1531a73e3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem6.11 of arXiv:2508.12951, '\textbf{On the central limit question for strictly stationary, reversible Markov chains}'] Suppose $\phi: [1,\infty) \to (-\infty, 0]$ is a function
that satisfies the following conditions: \hfil\break
(a) $\phi$ is continuous, strictly decreasing, and convex 
on $[1, \infty)$; \hfil\break
(b) $\phi$ is continuously differentiable on the open 
half line $(1, \infty)$; and \hfil\break 
(c) one has that
\begin{equation}

\lim_{x \to \infty} \phi(x)\ =\ -\infty 
\indent {\rm and} \indent
\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac {\phi(x)} {x}\ =\ 0.
\end{equation}

   For each $y \in (1, \infty)$ (the open half line), let 
$L^{(y)}: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ denote the affine function whose graph is tangent to that 
of $\phi$ at the point $(y, \phi(y))$ --- that is, the affine function that satisfies
\begin{equation}

L^{(y)}(y)\ =\ \phi(y) \indent {\rm and} \indent 
L^{(y)}(x)\ \leq\ \phi(x)\ \ {\rm for\ all}\ x \in [1, \infty). 
\end{equation}
 
   Then the following statements (I), (II), and (III) hold:
\medskip

   (I) The following statements hold: \hfil\break
(i) For each $x \in (1, \infty)$,
$\phi(x) < \phi(1) \leq 0$ and $\phi'(x) < 0$.  \hfil\break  
(ii) The function $x \mapsto \phi'(x)$ for $x \in (1, \infty)$, 
is nondecreasing. \hfil\break  
(iii) One has that $\lim_{x \to \infty} \phi'(x) = 0$. \hfil\break
(iv) For each $y \in (1, \infty)$,  
$[{\rm slope\ of}\ L^{(y)}] = \phi'(y) < 0$. \hfil\break 
(v) For each $y \in (1, \infty)$, 
$L^{(y)}(0) = \phi(y) + y \cdot (-\phi'(y)) > \phi(y)$.
\medskip

   (II) For any negative number $D$ and any positive number 
$s$, there exists a number    
$T = T(\phi, D, s) > 1$ with the following property:

   For each $y \geq T$, the affine function 
$L^{(y)}$ in (the entire sentence of) eq.\ ((eq6.112 of the paper))
satisfies 
\begin{equation}

-s\ \leq\ [{\rm slope\ of}\ L^{(y)}]\ =\ \phi'(y)\ <\ 0 
\indent {\rm and} \indent
L^{(y)}(0)\ \leq\ D. 
\end{equation}
  
   (III) Suppose also that $\psi: [1, \infty) \to [0, \infty)$ is a  
function such that $\lim_{x \to \infty} \psi(x) = \infty$.
 
Then for any negative number $D$ and any positive numbers
$B$ and $s$, there there exists a real number 
$T^* := T^*(\phi, \psi, B, D, s) > 1$ with the following 
property:
\smallskip

For each $y \geq T^*$, the affine function 
$L^{(y)}$ in (the entire sentence of) eq.\ ((eq6.112 of the paper))
satisfies ((eq6.113 of the paper)) and also 
[strengthening part of ((eq6.113 of the paper))] satisfies  
\begin{equation}
  
L^{(y)}(0) + B\ \leq\ D \indent {\rm and} \indent
L^{(y)}(x) + B\ \leq\ \phi(x) + \psi(x)\ \ 
{\rm for\ all}\ x \geq 1.    
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.337040+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3a2e6aa3cebda1036ba0d57e8d5e47cb62be72857ede9c53f56de3de0b1f9294","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 27 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] Let $\mathcal L\subset(0,\infty)$ be open and assume $\mathrm{(A_{an})}$. Then $\lambda_p(L)=\Lp(\cA_L)$ is real analytic on $\mathcal L$. More precisely, if $v_L(\xi)=\phi_L(L\xi),\qquad -1\le\xi\le1$,
and $v_L(0)=1$, then $L\mapsto v_L$ is real analytic from $\mathcal L$ into $C^1([-1,1])$. After pull-back and a fixed nonzero normalization, the adjoint eigenfunction depends real analytically on $L$ as well.

At every $L_0\in\mathcal L$, writing $h=L-L_0$, one has convergent expansions
\[
\mathscr A_{L_0+h}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty h^n\mathscr A_n,\qquad
\lambda_p(L_0+h)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty h^n\lambda_n,\qquad
v_{L_0+h}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty h^nv_n
\]
in $\mathcal L(C^1,C)$, $\R$ and $C^1([-1,1])$, respectively. The coefficients are determined recursively by
\[
(\mathscr A_0+\lambda_0)v_n+\lambda_nv_0
=-\sum_{k=1}^n\mathscr A_kv_{n-k}
-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\lambda_kv_{n-k},
\qquad v_n(0)=0,
\]
for $n\ge1$. If $v_0^*$ is the adjoint eigenfunction normalized by $\int_{-1}^{1}v_0v_0^*=1$, then
\[
\lambda_n=-\int_{-1}^{1}v_0^*(\xi)
\left(
\sum_{k=1}^n\mathscr A_kv_{n-k}
+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\lambda_kv_{n-k}
\right)(\xi)\,d\xi.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:06:21.713064+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3a3fb26c1e16caea54b4848c2d2d343a09fb1be6ec0927dde293c7d6032fbdbe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Let \(a_n\to\infty\) be any deterministic sequence of positive real numbers.

{"assumptions":["Bernoulli bond percolation on the hypercube {0,1}^d","Critical window width 2^{-d/3}"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3a7116d434f2c28df46cdf038009eb62d3472655392fb61aeca9584693ef8aec","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE REDUCTION, author-recorded. Heydenreich-van der Hofstad Open Problem 13.4 asks that the second largest cluster at p_c(1 + eps) on {0,1}^d match, to leading order, the largest cluster at p_c(1 - eps), eps >> 2^{-d/3}. G(n,p) has this through the discrete duality principle: after the giant is removed, the rest is close in law to a subcritical G(n', p) with the dual mean (an asymptotic statement, not an exact symmetry); the hypercube has no such principle, so it must come from tails: the subcritical largest cluster is Theta(eps^{-2} log(eps^3 2^d)) once the tail P(|C| >= k) >= c k^{-1/2} exp(-c' eps^2 k) holds with the SHARP rate in eps^2 k (the upper bound is known, the sharp lower bound is the missing half), and the supercritical second-largest needs the same tail for the clusters after removal of the giant, which is the geometric-depletion question of the exploration process. So the duality principle is reduced, heuristically, to two tail statements, one subcritical with a sharp rate and one post-giant; turning tails into the size of the largest cluster also needs control of the number of clusters and of their dependence, so this is not an equivalence.","status":"unverified"}

The ORNSTEIN-UHLENBECK SEMIGROUP is defined by MEHLER'S FORMULA P_t f(x) = integral f( e^{-t} x + sqrt(1 - e^{-2t}) y ) gamma(dy) for t >= 0. It is a Markov semigroup: P_0 = identity, P_{s+t} = P_s P_t, P_t 1 = 1, P_t preserves nonnegativity, gamma is INVARIANT (integral P_t f dgamma = integral f dgamma), and P_t is SELF-ADJOINT on L^2(gamma). Its generator is L f = Laplacian f - x . grad f, which satisfies the integration-by-parts identity integral (L u) v dgamma = - integral grad u . grad v dgamma. The Hermite polynomials diagonalise it: L He_alpha = - |alpha| He_alpha and P_t He_alpha = e^{-|alpha| t} He_alpha, so the n-th Wiener chaos is the eigenspace of eigenvalue -n. The COMMUTATION RELATION grad P_t f = e^{-t} P_t grad f follows by differentiating Mehler's formula under the integral. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.820761+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3ab938b4d4cb0291e52c58efecec41c9b61657b15af69c0bf3f08bdc1bef47be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:root-sweep-dictionary of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Let $h\geq1$ and $k\geq2$.  One has the exact difference identity
\begin{equation}
 E_{h,k}-E_{h,k}=h\mathsf R_{k-1}\cap\mathsf A_{k-1}.
\end{equation}
For an ordered real tuple $a=(a_1<\cdots<a_k)$, write
\({\bf1}=(1,\ldots,1)\in\mathbb R^k\) and let
$a^\circ=a-k^{-1}(\sum_i a_i){\bf1}$ be its centered representative.  Let
$F_h(a)$ be the face of $\mathfrak Z_{h,k}$ exposed by $a^\circ$.  The
following data determine one another:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item the total preorder on $E_{h,k}$ induced by $u\mapsto u\cdot a$
      (equivalently, its ordered weak partition into level sets);
\item the complete ordered $h$-addition table of $a$, including ties;
\item the face $F_h(a)$.
\end{enumerate}
The dimension of $F_h(a)$ is the active relation rank $r_h(a)$.  In the
ambient space ${\bf1}^{\perp}$, its normal cone has dimension
$k-1-r_h(a)$, and the relative interior of that cone consists precisely of
the centered weights inducing the same complete table.  Moreover, the same
face determines every ordered addition table in degrees $1\leq j\leq h$.

Fix any field $K$.  If $a\in\mathbb Z^k$, put
$A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}$ and define
\[
 \varphi_a:K[x_1,\ldots,x_k]\longrightarrow K[u,t,t^{-1}],
 \qquad x_i\longmapsto u t^{a_i},
 \qquad I_a=\ker\varphi_a,
\]
where $\deg u=1$ and $\deg t=0$.  Then the number of blocks in the face
label is the Hilbert value
\begin{equation}
 |hA|=\dim_K\bigl(K[x_1,\ldots,x_k]/I_a\bigr)_h.
\end{equation}
Thus the face records the equality rank and Hilbert/block label, while its
normal cone encodes the normalized shape, realization frequency, and integer
compression developed below.","status":"unverified"}

A bounded operator T: H -> K is Hilbert-Schmidt if sum_{i in I} ||T e_i||^2 < infinity for some orthonormal basis (e_i)_{i in I} of H. The sum is then the same for every orthonormal basis of H, and ||T||_2 = (sum_i ||T e_i||^2)^{1/2} is the Hilbert-Schmidt norm. Equivalently, T is compact and sum_n s_n(T)^2 < infinity, with ||T||_2^2 = sum_n s_n(T)^2. Properties: ||T|| <= ||T||_2; ||T*||_2 = ||T||_2; every Hilbert-Schmidt operator is compact (it is the ||.||_2-limit, hence operator-norm limit, of finite-rank operators); the Hilbert-Schmidt operators S_2(H,K) form a Hilbert space under <A,B>_2 = sum_i <A e_i, B e_i> = tr(B*A), independent of the basis; and they form an ideal: ||A T B||_2 <= ||A|| ||T||_2 ||B|| for bounded A, B. Basis independence follows from sum_i ||T e_i||^2 = sum_i sum_j |<T e_i, f_j>|^2 = sum_j ||T* f_j||^2 for any orthonormal basis (f_j) of K.","status":"unverified"}

For Bernoulli percolation, and more generally for FKG-satisfying, translation-invariant models with finite energy (including the random-cluster model for cluster weight q>=1), the sharpness-of-phase-transition theorem shows that below the critical point p_c, the probability of connection to distance n decays exponentially in n, proved without duality via a finite-size criterion: a box functional phi_p(S), built from crossing probabilities and a weighted sum over pivotal edges, is shown to satisfy a differential inequality in p that forces it to either stay bounded (subcritical, exponential decay) or blow up past a threshold (supercritical), with the threshold identified as p_c. This unifies and reproves the classical results of Menshikov and of Aizenman-Barsky with a single argument that is robust enough to extend to Z^d for every d, to general transitive graphs, and to the random-cluster model. The theorem does not give the exact value of p_c, does not determine critical behavior exactly at p_c (critical exponents are a separate, generally much harder, question), and the exponential-decay rate produced is not claimed to be sharp or explicit. Typical failure: Assuming the Duminil-Copin-Tassion argument extends automatically to a non-FKG regime, such as random-cluster parameters q<1 or certain long-range or antiferromagnetic models, where positive association fails; the driving differential inequality depends essentially on FKG-type monotonicity and on finite energy, and dropping either hypothesis breaks the exponential-decay conclusion outright rather than merely weakening it. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544171+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3b43ec8f5d0fa6d27d0e5752777028d785fae794a67b64a293ba500ca12736e7","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The GAUSSIAN ORTHOGONAL ENSEMBLE GOE_n is the law of a real symmetric n by n matrix H whose entries are independent up to symmetry with H_{ii} distributed as N(0, 2/n) and H_{ij} distributed as N(0, 1/n) for i < j. Its density with respect to Lebesgue measure on the space of real symmetric matrices is proportional to exp( - (n/4) trace(H^2) ), and the law is invariant under H -> O H O^T for every orthogonal O. The GAUSSIAN UNITARY ENSEMBLE GUE_n is the law of a Hermitian H with H_{ii} distributed as N(0, 1/n) real and, for i < j, H_{ij} = x + i y with x and y independent N(0, 1/(2n)), so that E|H_{ij}|^2 = 1/n; its density is proportional to exp( - (n/2) trace(H^2) ) and it is invariant under H -> U H U^* for every unitary U. With THESE normalisations the empirical spectral distribution of either ensemble converges to the semicircle law on [-2, 2], the largest eigenvalue converges to 2, and the edge fluctuations are of order n^{-2/3} with Tracy-Widom limits (beta = 1 for GOE, beta = 2 for GUE). The DIAGONAL VARIANCE DIFFERS BETWEEN THE TWO ENSEMBLES - 2/n for GOE, 1/n for GUE - and that is what makes both densities come out as the invariant exponential of the trace; getting it wrong changes the density but not the limiting spectral law. Normalisation conventions vary widely across the literature: some authors use unnormalised entries of variance 1 and divide by sqrt(n) afterwards, some put the semicircle on [-1,1] or [-2 sqrt(2), 2 sqrt(2)], and some use exp(-trace(H^2)/2) with n absorbed elsewhere. Any imported constant must be checked against the convention it was derived under. [standard; e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Sections 2.5 and 2.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:00:46.819743+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3b587371cf631eb291613b05dab51097d529d27dc0b183b1d5fa8c0a7277305f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 1 of arXiv:2608.13208, 'Universality in dimension $1$ of kinetically constrained lattice gases'] A kinetically constrained lattice gas is a Markov
process on $\Omega=\{0,1\}^{\Z}$ with generator 
\begin{equation}
\cL f(\eta)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in\Z}c(x,y,\eta)(f(\eta^{xy})-f(\eta)),
\end{equation}
where $\eta^{xy}$ is the configuration after exchanging $x$ and
$y$. The rates are given by the \emph{constraint function} $c:\Z\times\Z\times\Omega\to[0,\infty]$
satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Nearest-neighbor jumps: $c(x,y,\eta)=0$ if $\left|x-y\right|\neq1$.
By convention $c(x,y,\eta)=c(y,x,\eta)$.
\item Translation invariance: $c(x,y,\eta)=c(x+z,y+z,\tau_{z}\eta)$ for
all $x,y,z$, where $\tau_{z}$ is the translation by $z$.
\item $c(x,y,\eta)$ does not depend on the occupation at $x$ and $y$,
i.e., $c(x,y,\eta)=c(x,y,\eta^{xy})$.
\item Finite range: there exists $r>0$ such that $c(x,y,\eta)$ depends
only on the configuration in $x+[-r,r]$.
\item Monotonicity: if $\eta(x)\le\omega(x)$ for all $x$, then $c(x,y,\eta)\ge c(x,y,\omega)$.
That is, adding vacancies speeds up transitions.
\end{enumerate}
We can also define the process on a finite segment $[a,b]$ of $\Z$
by fixing boundary conditions; in this article we always consider
filled boundary, i.e., for $x,y\in[a,b]$ the constraint in the segment
is given by $c_{[a,b]}(x,y,\eta)=c(x,y,\tilde{\eta})$ where $\tilde{\eta}$
agrees with $\eta$ on $[a,b]$ and equals $1$ outside.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:15:54.903423+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3b6077a432a793f0a80f87dc5e6644dd149f2797ff4b881d43f56274b79cacdb","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:block of arXiv:2608.28007, 'Exact Risk Ratios for Weighted Data Selection in Linear Regression'] A whitened system $\{(\xi_i,\eta_i)\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has \emph{orthogonal

{"assumptions":["f integrable on R","the pointwise identity is claimed at a specific point (typically x = 0)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264346+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_3b718e0037a91db9c64b0a4706cc1000aa0a6e3fe12673010be7f29fee1bf2dc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: the periodization $Pf(x)=\\sum_nf(x+n)$ must be continuous at the point where the identity is evaluated, and its Fourier series must converge there (absolute summability of $(\\hat f(k))_k$ is the usual sufficient condition). For a general $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb R)$ all that is true is $\\widehat{Pf}(k)=\\hat f(k)$, i.e. Poisson summation as an identity of Fourier series of an $L^1(\\mathbb T)$ function - which says nothing pointwise. Concrete failure: $f=\\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$ (with $f(0)=f(1)=1$). Then $\\sum_nf(n)=f(0)+f(1)=2$, while $\\hat f(0)=1$ and $\\hat f(k)=\\int_0^1e^{-2\\pi ikx}dx=0$ for $k\\ne0$, so $\\sum_k\\hat f(k)=1\\ne2$. The periodization equals $1$ off $\\mathbb Z$ and $2$ on $\\mathbb Z$: it is discontinuous exactly where the identity is being evaluated, and the Fourier series converges to the midpoint $1$. Redefining $f(0)=f(1)=1/2$ restores the identity. Second trap: pure decay of $f$ is not enough - one needs decay (or summability) on the transform side as well, since the right-hand series must converge; $f$ continuous and integrable with $\\hat f$ merely tending to zero gives no pointwise statement. When quoting a rate, the clean hypothesis is $|f(x)|\\le C(1+|x|)^{-1-\\delta}$ and $|\\hat f(\\xi)|\\le C(1+|\\xi|)^{-1-\\delta}$ with $f$ continuous, or simply $f\\in\\mathcal S$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:22:46.471076+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3b8085876cb651677834928140bd514720eac881bd988ff4b4fafd0a51027fc0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 96 (Geometric forms and related integrals) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] \hfill
	\begin{itemize}
		\item Recall that $\gnulltori$ is the first fundamental form of the torus $\doublenulltoritwoarg{\ubar}{u}$.
		We define the canonical area form of $\doublenulltoritwoarg{\ubar}{u}$ 
		induced by $\gnulltori$
		in the double-null coordinates $(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3)$ by:
		\begin{align} 
			\voldoublenulltori 
			& = \voldoublenulltori(\ubar',u',x^2,x^3) 
			\eqdef 
			\sqrt{\det \gnulltori (\ubar',u',x^2,x^3)} \, \mathrm{d} x^2 \mathrm{d} x^3,
		\end{align}
		where $\det \gnulltori(\ubar',u',x^2,x^3)$ is the determinant of the $2 \times 2$ matrix
		$\left(\gnulltori(\ubar',u',x^2,x^3) \left(\nullgeop{x^A},\nullgeop{x^B}\right) \right)_{A,B=2,3}$
		(see RHS\,\eqref{E:DOUBLENULLTORIFIRSTFUNDRESTRICTEDTODOUBLENULLTORI}).
		\item We define the (non-canonical) area form $\volingoingnullhypersurface$ of $\ingoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\ubar}{J}$ 
		in the double-null coordinates $(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3)$ by: 
		\begin{align} 
			\volingoingnullhypersurface 
			& = \volingoingnullhypersurface(\ubar,u',x^2,x^3) 
			= \voldoublenulltori(\ubar,u',x^2,x^3) \, \mathrm{d} u'.
		\end{align}
		\item We define the (non-canonical) area form $\voloutgoingnullhypersurface$ on $\outgoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{u}{I}$ 
		in the double-null coordinates $(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3)$ by:  
		\begin{align} 
			\voloutgoingnullhypersurface 
			= 
			\voloutgoingnullhypersurface(\ubar',u,x^2,x^3) 
			& \eqdef \voldoublenulltori(\ubar',u,x^2,x^3) \, \mathrm{d} \ubar'.
		\end{align} 
		\item We define the (non-canonical) volume form $\voldiamond$ of $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{I}{J}$ 
		in the double-null  coordinates $(\ubar,u,x^2,x^3)$ by:
		\begin{align} 
			\voldiamond 
			= \voldiamond(\ubar',u',x^2,x^3) 
			& 
			\eqdef 
			\voldoublenulltori(\ubar',u',x^2,x^3) \, \mathrm{d} u' \, \mathrm{d} \ubar'.
		\end{align}
	\end{itemize}
	
	Unless we explicitly indicate otherwise, 
	all integrals along 
	$\doublenulltoritwoarg{\ubar}{u}, \, \outgoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{u}{I}, \, \ingoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\ubar}{J}$, and $\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{I}{J}$
	are defined with respect to the above forms. 
	Moreover, we will often suppress the variables with respect to which we integrate, 
	e.g., we write:
	\begin{subequations} 
		\begin{align}
			\int_{\doublenulltoritwoarg{\ubar}{u}} 
			f 
			\, \voldoublenulltori 
			& 
			\eqdef

			\int_{(x^2,x^3) \in \T^2} 
			f(\ubar',u,x^2,x^3) \, \voldoublenulltori(\ubar',u,x^2,x^3)
			\, \mathrm{d} \ubar', 
			 \\
			\int_{\ingoingcharacteristicsurfacetwoarg{\ubar}{J}} 
			f 
			\, \volingoingnullhypersurface 
			& \eqdef 
			\int_{u' \in J} \int_{(x^2,x^3) \in \T^2} 
			f(\ubar,u',x^2,x^3) 
			\, \voldoublenulltori(\ubar,u',x^2,x^3) \, \mathrm{d} u', 
			 \\
			\int_{\characteristicdiamondtwoarg{I}{J}}

We say that $\bs{a}_N$ {\bf converges strongly to $\bs{a}$} if, in addition to converging in $\ast$-distribution, also

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0054-localisation-of-all-bulk-states-for-two-dimensional-random-band-matric","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.042114+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3bf6be9ae3842b9ca1fdd761e2056571214bc8ce381c2922ab547980201cf160","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Band matrices have no rank-one structure: the randomness at a site is a W^2-dimensional block, and the decoupling lemma degrades by a factor that grows with W^2, so the method proves localisation only for W <= W_0 small (large disorder regime), not for every fixed W. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.651862+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3c2a73cc53296bd38cbc69e9d18f9715c6a949b5dec9214a445ecf905510450a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 11 of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] Suppose that the random variables $\{ P^{(n)}_{ij} \}_{i<j}$ ($n=1, 2, 3, 4$) satisfy the following:

\item For any $n$, $\E[P^{(n)}_{d,kk}] = 0$ and $\E[(P^{(n)}_{d,kk})^2] = \cn'_n$ for some ($N$-independent) constants $\cn'_n$.

	\Omega_\caX^\epsilon := \{ \max_{1 \leq k \leq N} |x_k| \leq N^{-1/2 +\epsilon} \} \cap \{ | \| \bsx \| - 1 | \leq N^{-1/5} \}.

Suppose that Assumption \ref{assump:second_moment} holds with $\SNR_c$. If $\F < \SNR_c$,

as $N \to \infty$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X,B,mu) is a probability space and T preserves mu","the partitions P_k are countable, measurable, and increasing: P_{k+1} refines P_k","H_mu(P_k) < infinity for each k","the union of the P_k generates B modulo mu-null sets","h_mu(T) is defined as the supremum of h_mu(T,Q) over countable partitions Q of finite entropy"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090319+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, entropy, generators","id":"claim_3c3e128038c699e9bd64175dd57d1489d79b6bc2f84bbdbc616d67a216487a92","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, B, mu) be a probability space and T : X -> X measure-preserving (invertibility is not assumed). Let P_1 <= P_2 <= ... be an increasing sequence of countable measurable partitions (each P_{k+1} refines P_k) with H_mu(P_k) < infinity for every k, and assume the sequence GENERATES: the sigma-algebra generated by the union of the P_k equals B up to mu-null sets. Then h_mu(T) = lim_k h_mu(T, P_k) = sup_k h_mu(T, P_k), where h_mu(T) is the supremum of h_mu(T,Q) over all finite-entropy partitions Q. The classical generator form is the special case: for an invertible T and a partition P with H_mu(P) < infinity whose two-sided join over all integer translates generates B, take P_k = the join of T^{-n}P over |n| <= k and conclude h_mu(T) = h_mu(T,P); for non-invertible T take the one-sided join over 0 <= n <= k. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) generation is the entire content. If the union of the P_k generates only a proper sub-sigma-algebra, the limit computes the entropy of the corresponding sub-process and can be strictly smaller than h_mu(T); with every P_k trivial the limit is 0 for a system of arbitrarily large entropy. In particular a partition that separates points topologically but only generates a smaller sigma-algebra modulo mu is not enough. (ii) Monotonicity of the sequence (or at least H_mu(Q | P_k) -> 0 for every finite-entropy Q) is used; an arbitrary sequence of partitions that 'converges' in some other sense need not have monotone entropies and the comparison step breaks. (iii) H_mu(P_k) < infinity is needed for the comparison inequality. (iv) Generation is modulo mu-null sets only, and the conclusion says nothing pointwise. (v) For non-invertible T the one-sided generator computes h_mu(T); using the two-sided join for a non-invertible map is meaningless.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:23:58.630711+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3c4566fd35441bef8f16cb73953085085804d9c9ec05b5967079bb81e6177085","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 244 (ALE coordinates are identical to acoustical geometric coordinates) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $\eta, n, \tau$ be as in \eqref{E:DEFINITIONOFSTEVEFLOWMAP}--\eqref{E:DEFINITIONOFTANGENTVECTORSFORSTEVEOUTGOINGCHAR}, where we recall that equation \eqref{E:DEFINITIONOFSTEVEFLOWMAP} is solved in conjunction with the compressible Euler equations. Let $\mathbf{n}= (n_0,n_1,n_2)$ be the $\mathbf{g}$-null one-form from 
	\eqref{E:OUTGOINGCOCHARCHOICE}, let $\Lunit^{ALE}$ be as in \eqref{E:ALELUNIT}, 
	and let $\Lambda_{ALE}$ be the flow-map of $\Lunit^{ALE}$ as in \eqref{E:FLOWMAPOFALELUNIT}. 
	Then for $C^1$ solutions to the compressible Euler equations, the following hold:
			\begin{enumerate}
				\item \underline{\textbf{The flow of $\Lunit^{ALE}$}}. The flow map $\Lambda_{ALE}$ satisfies $\Lambda_{ALE}^0 = t$ and $\Lambda_{ALE}^i = \eta^i$ for $i = 1,2$.
				\item \underline{\textbf{$\Gamma_{x^1}(T)$ are characteristics in the sense of Def.\,\ref{D:CHARACTERISTICSURFACESCANONICAL}}}. 
				Recall that $\Gamma_{x^1}(T)$ is the surface defined in \eqref{E:CHARACTERISTICS}.
				For any $\Gamma_{x^1}(T)$-tangent vectorfield $W$, we have $\mathbf{n}_\alpha W^\alpha = 0$. Hence, $\Gamma_{x^1}(T)$ is a characteristic surface as in Def.\,\ref{D:CHARACTERISTICSURFACESCANONICAL}.
				\item \underline{\textbf{$\Gamma_{x^1}(T)$ are $\gfour$-null hypersurfaces}}. There exists a $\Gamma_{x^1}(T)$-tangent vectorfield $V$ 
					that is $\gfour$-orthogonal to the tangent space of $\Gamma_{x^1}(T)$. In particular, $\gfour(V,V) = 0$.
				\item \underline{\textbf{The geometric coordinates are identical to ALE coordinates}}. Suppose that $u$ is the solution to the eikonal equation $(\gfour^{-1})^{\alpha\beta}\p_\alpha u \p_\beta u = 0$ with $u \restriction_{t=0} = x^1$ and\footnote{For the proposition to be correct, $\partial_t u < 0$ is the right sign; $\partial_t u > 0$ would correspond to constructing the ingoing characteristics. A pair (q,r) is wave-admissible (in the sense of Keel–Tao) if 2 ≤ q ≤ ∞, 2 ≤ r ≤ ∞, 1/q + (n−1)/(2r) ≤ (n−1)/4, and (q,r,n) ≠ (2,∞,3). It is sharp wave-admissible when equality holds, 1/q + (n−1)/(2r) = (n−1)/4. The exponent (n−1)/2 is the dispersive decay rate of frequency-localized waves; the associated regularity s is fixed separately by the scaling relation 1/q + n/r = n/2 − s. Examples in n = 3: (4,4) with s = 1/2, (5,10) and (4,12) with s = 1, and (∞,2) with s = 0, which is the bound ‖u‖_{L^∞_t L²_x} ≲ ‖u0‖_{L²} + ‖u1‖_{Ḣ^{−1}}. Note that the energy bound ‖u‖_{L^∞_t Ḣ¹} + ‖∂_t u‖_{L^∞_t L²} ≲ ‖u0‖_{Ḣ¹} + ‖u1‖_{L²} is not a different admissible pair: it is the pair (∞,2) applied at regularity s = 1, i.e. to |∇|u. The scaling relation always ties s to (q,r), so s = 0 is the only value that goes with (q,r) = (∞,2) in the Lebesgue-norm form of the estimate. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.221997+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3c9dbb84370f01449a45a358af3c4e2180aca4413319da51186af6baec056e3a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Unique finite-time limit) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Let $F\colon[0,T)\times\Sigma\to\Sph^3$ be a smooth MIWF of a compact
torus, where $T<\infty$, and write $F_t:=F(t,\cdot)$.  Let $A_t^0$
denote the trace-free second fundamental form of $F_t$.  Put
\[
 W(t):=\Will(F_t),\qquad W_0:=W(0),\qquad
 \mu_t:=\mu_{F_t^*g_{\Sph^3}}.
\]
Assume that
for some $c_0>0$,
\[
 \inf_{0<t<T}\min_{x\in\Sigma}|A_t^0(x)|^2\geq c_0.
\]
Let $\Var_t$ denote the multiplicity-counting integral two-varifold in
$\R^4$ induced by $F_t$, and set
$\lambda_t:=\lVert\Var_t\rVert=(F_t)_\#\mu_t$.
Then there exists a unique integral two-varifold
$\Var_T$ in $\R^4$, possibly the zero varifold, such that, with
$\rightharpoonup$ denoting weak varifold convergence,
\begin{equation}
 
 \Var_t\rightharpoonup\Var_T
 \qquad\text{as }t\nearrow T.
\end{equation}
No reparametrizations of $\Sigma$ and no M\"obius transformations of
$\Sph^3$ are required.

More precisely, there are finite nonnegative Radon measures $\mu_T$ on
$\Sigma$ and $\lambda_T=\lVert\Var_T\rVert$ on $\Sph^3$ such that
$\mu_t\to\mu_T$ in total variation and
$\lambda_t\to\lambda_T$ in the bounded-Lipschitz distance
$d_{\BL}$ defined in \eqref{eq:bl-distance}.  Setting
\[
 W_T:=\lim_{t\nearrow T}W(t),
\]
there holds, for every $0<s<T$,
\begin{align}
 
 \lVert\mu_T-\mu_s\rVert_{\TV}
 &\leq \frac{2\sqrt{W_0}}{c_0}
 \sqrt{(T-s)\bigl(W(s)-W_T\bigr)},\\
 
 d_{\BL}(\lambda_T,\lambda_s)
 &\leq \frac{2\sqrt{W_0}}{c_0}
 \sqrt{(T-s)\bigl(W(s)-W_T\bigr)}.
\end{align}
Moreover, $\Var_T$ has generalized Euclidean mean-curvature vector
$H_{\Var_T}^{\R^4}\in L^2(\lVert\Var_T\rVert;\R^4)$ and
\begin{equation}
 
 \frac14\int_{\R^4}|H_{\Var_T}^{\R^4}|^2
 \dd\lVert\Var_T\rVert\leq W_T.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

For statistical mechanics models on a torus whose Hamiltonian and lattice satisfy reflection positivity across midplanes between sites, the Gaussian domination (infrared) bound gives an upper bound on the Fourier transform of the two-point function: hat{G}(k) <= C / (beta E(k)), where E(k) is the quadratic energy form of the interaction (e.g. E(k)=sum_i (1-cos k_i) for nearest-neighbor coupling) and C is an explicit constant (often 1/2; exact value depends on normalization and is not always recalled precisely across variants). Combined with a spin-wave/Gaussian domination inequality this yields, for models such as the classical Heisenberg or XY model in dimension d>=3, or the Ising model in sufficiently high dimension, existence of long-range order at low temperature via a second-moment argument applied to the infrared-bounded Fourier integral. It does not give critical exponent values, does not apply in dimension d<=2 where the infrared integral diverges (consistent with the Mermin-Wagner theorem ruling out continuous-symmetry breaking there), and requires the specific reflection-positive algebraic structure; it gives no control for models lacking this symmetry, such as many disordered, frustrated, or non-bipartite systems. Typical failure: Assuming reflection positivity survives a seemingly minor modification of the Hamiltonian, such as adding next-nearest-neighbor terms, a random field, or working on a non-bipartite lattice, without re-checking the checkerboard decomposition; reflection positivity is a delicate algebraic property that most natural perturbations destroy, so the infrared bound and everything built on it, including the Frohlich-Simon-Spencer long-range order conclusion, silently stops applying. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.626929+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3d2eccef094bb69e406fac092e701dccd48b74c6119162e597a97768bad97898","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, P) be a probability space with a filtration (F_n)_{n >= 0}, an increasing family of sub-sigma-algebras of F. A sequence (X_n)_{n >= 0} of random variables is a MARTINGALE with respect to (F_n) if (i) X_n is F_n-measurable for every n (adapted), (ii) E|X_n| < infinity for every n (integrable), and (iii) E[X_{n+1} | F_n] = X_n almost surely for every n. It is a SUBMARTINGALE if (iii) is weakened to E[X_{n+1} | F_n] >= X_n almost surely, and a SUPERMARTINGALE if E[X_{n+1} | F_n] <= X_n almost surely. Mnemonic: a supermartingale decreases in expectation, so it is what a gambler faces in an unfair game. All three notions are relative to a specified filtration; a process can be a martingale for its own natural filtration and fail to be one for a larger filtration. Integrability in (ii) is part of the definition, not a consequence: without it the conditional expectation in (iii) need not exist. If (X_n) is a martingale and phi is convex with phi(X_n) integrable for every n, then (phi(X_n)) is a submartingale by conditional Jensen; in particular |X_n| and X_n^2 are submartingales when integrable. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Chapter 10]","status":"unverified"}

    attraction of an $\alpha$-stable law for some $\alpha\in(1,2]$. Let $(d_n)$ be a sequence of positive integers such that

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.685575+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3d503c6327a83a68e621770de7b4c70c36649a0faac6888735187552b9fc9369","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 11 (Exact matrix isospectrality) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, let $\gamma:[0,T]\to V$ be continuous and of bounded variation, put $g=S(\gamma)$, let $l=\log g=\sum_{n\geq 1}l_n$, and put $v=l_1$.
Assume $R(l)=\infty$.
For every $q\geq1$ and every complex-linear map $\Phi:V_{\C}\to M_q(\C)$, write $I=I_q$ and define
\[
A_{\Phi}(z)=\sum_{n\geq 1}z^n\Phi^{(n)}(l_n).
\]
Then
\begin{equation}
\det(\zeta I-A_{\Phi}(z))
 =\det(\zeta I-z\Phi(v))
\end{equation}
for all $z,\zeta\in\C$.
Thus $A_{\Phi}(z)$ and $z\Phi(v)$ have the same eigenvalue multiset, counted with algebraic multiplicity, and
\[
\tr\bigl(A_{\Phi}(z)^p\bigr)
 =z^p\tr\bigl(\Phi(v)^p\bigr)
\qquad (p\geq1).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:37:25.962857+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3d5328bdd4ebe6b72b68f980656a4c0448e98ebdec29d3620703043d747138a8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 9 of arXiv:2608.29713, '\textbf{A Cartan geometry from a correspondence space in Riemannian geometry}'] Let $(p:\mathcal P\to N,\omega)$ be a Cartan geometry of type $(G,H)$, and let $K^\omega=d\omega+\frac12[\omega,\omega]$ be its curvature form.  The torsion of $\omega$ is the $\mathfrak m$-part of its curvature function
$\kappa^\omega$, that is, the map
\[
T^\omega:=\operatorname{pr}_{\mathfrak m}\circ\,\kappa^\omega\colon
\mathcal P\longrightarrow\Lambda^2\mathfrak m^*\otimes\mathfrak m,
\qquad
T^\omega(u)(X,Y)=\operatorname{pr}_{\mathfrak m}\left[K^\omega(u)\big(\omega^{-1}(X)(u),\omega^{-1}(Y)(u)\big)\right].
\]
We say that $\omega$ is normal if $\partial^*T^\omega=0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:21:06.854980+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3dd4e2e00dbffc7780fc1c0b58d0423d8eadfa4e8badf857585ab6ead31ff62e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 5 (Local solution) of arXiv:2608.21014, 'The stochastic Cahn--Hilliard equation in critical spaces'] Suppose that Assumption~\ref{Assumption:semilinear:evolution:equation} is satisfied for some $p\in[2,\infty)$ and $\kappa\in[0,p/2-1)\cup\{0\}$. 
     \begin{enumerate}
         \item A pair $(u,\sigma)$ is called an $L^p_\kappa$-\emph{local solution to~\eqref{eq:semilinear-stochastic-evolution}} if $\sigma\colon\Omega\to[a,\infty]$ is a stopping time, $u\colon[a,\sigma)\to X_0$ is a strongly progressively measurable process, there exists an increasing sequence of stopping times $(\sigma_n)_{n\ge 1}$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty} \sigma_n=\sigma$ a.s., and for all $n\ge 1$ it holds that $(u|_{[a,\sigma_n]},\sigma_n)$ is an $L^p_\kappa$-strong solution to~\eqref{eq:semilinear-stochastic-evolution}. The sequence $(\sigma_n)_{n\ge 1}$ is called \emph{a localising sequence} for $(u,\sigma)$.
         \item An $L^p_\kappa$-local solution $(u,\sigma)$ is called \emph{unique} if for every $L^p_\kappa$-local solution $(v,\tau)$ one has $u=v$ a.s.\ on $[a,\tau\wedge \sigma)$.
         \item An $L^p_\kappa$-local solution $(u,\sigma)$ is called \emph{$L^p_\kappa$-maximal} if for any other unique $L^p_\kappa$-local solution $(v,\tau)$ to~\eqref{eq:semilinear-stochastic-evolution} one has that a.s.\ $\tau\le \sigma$ and $u=v$ on $[a,\tau)$.
         \item An $L^p_\kappa$-local solution $(u,\sigma)$ to~\eqref{eq:semilinear-stochastic-evolution} is called \emph{global} if $\sigma=\infty$ a.s.
     \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:19:46.234096+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3e2d31e3bc198f6d34f24b118f4490d0f89d373545b5951f6c3c16244281aa2d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 68 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] Fix $\A$, $\tau$, and $\l$ as above, let $\Delta := \Delta_\tau$, and consider the functionals

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:21:56.726055+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3e382077a8e3267c7aec8426a2ccc3d45c3a67f766318c2182b13accd2e90a2c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:tightness_in_nice_bubble of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] There exists $\zeta > 0$ such that the following is true. Fix $0<r<1$. 
Suppose that $h$ is a GFF on $\mathbf{D}$ with zero boundary conditions. Let $u,v \in B(0,r)$, and let $\eta_u$ be the flow line of $h$ starting from $u$. Given $\eta_u$, let $\eta_{u,v}$ be the flow line of $h$ starting from $v$ and reflected off $\eta_u$ in the opposite direction. Let $x,y \in \eta_{u,v} \cap \eta_u$ be chosen such that the segment of $\eta_{u,v}$ from $v$ to $y$ intersects $\eta_u$ only on the right side of $\eta_u$ with angle difference $0$ (before reflecting off), and $x$ is on the segment between $v$ and $y$. Let $U_{x,y}$ be the region bounded between the segments of $\eta_{u,v}$ and $\eta_u$ from $x$ to $y$. Let $\Gamma_{x,y}$ be the collection of conditionally independent ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa'}$ naturally coupled with $h$ in each of the components of $U_{x,y}$. Let $\Upsilon_{\Gamma_{x,y}}$ denote the gasket of $\Gamma_{x,y}$. 

Let $E_\delta$ be the event that there exist $u,v,x,y$ as above such that
\begin{itemize}
 \item $U_{x,y} \subseteq B(0,r)$,
 \item $\Upsilon_{\Gamma_{x,y}} \subseteq \Upsilon_\Gamma$,
 \item $\mathrm{diam}(U_{x,y}) \le \delta$,
 \item $D_\epsilon^{\partial U_{x,y}} \ge \delta^\zeta+\epsilon^{a_0}$.
\end{itemize}
Let $\widehat{x}$ be the first point where $\eta_{u,v}$ hits $\eta_u$. Fix $c_1>0$, and let $E^1_\delta$ be the event that $E_\delta$ occurs and additionally the segment of $\eta_u$ from $x$ to $\widehat{x}$ has diameter at least $\delta^{1+c_1}$.
Then
\[ \mathbf{P}[E^1_\delta] = o^\infty(\delta) \quad\text{as } \delta \searrow 0 . \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:59:58.458182+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3e40d3a9d0e01e833a1e84320cebea234afaa20b4ee62bf25b1244d1b2fb5ef0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem calculus of arXiv:2605.14910, 'Sharp Phase Transition for the Formation of Infinite Tubes'] {DRT2019}}]

{"assumptions":["A and B are linear operators in the same Banach space","D(A) ⊂ D(B)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769951+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, perturbation theory of operators","id":"claim_3e4fa40fff097dc9c86af5298ab723946a61639931a25125440e3ee34a2b916e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A and B be linear operators in a Banach space X. B is relatively bounded with respect to A (A-bounded) if D(A) ⊂ D(B) and there are constants a, b ≥ 0 with ‖Bx‖ ≤ a‖Ax‖ + b‖x‖ for all x ∈ D(A). The infimum of all admissible a is the A-bound (relative bound) of B; the corresponding b usually grows as a approaches the infimum, and the infimum itself need not be attained. In a Hilbert space the condition ‖Bx‖² ≤ a'²‖Ax‖² + b'²‖x‖² defines the same relative bound. Relative bound 0 means: for every ε > 0 there is b_ε with ‖Bx‖ ≤ ε‖Ax‖ + b_ε‖x‖. If A is closed, B is closable, and D(A) ⊂ D(B), then B is automatically A-bounded (closed graph theorem applied to B on the Banach space (D(A), graph norm of A)). The form analogue: for A ≥ 0 self-adjoint with form q_A(x) = ‖A^{1/2}x‖² on Q(A) = D(A^{1/2}), a symmetric form β is A-form-bounded with bound a if Q(A) ⊂ D(β) and |β(x, x)| ≤ a q_A(x) + b‖x‖² for x ∈ Q(A). Operator-boundedness with bound a implies form-boundedness with bound at most a, not conversely.","status":"unverified"}

C006 v1. Novelty unestablished.

Let d,q>=1 be finite, H a constant symmetric positive definite q by q
matrix, and 0<m<=lambda(H)<=M. Fix sigma,D>=0, 0<rho<2 and
0<eta<=rho/M. Let (F_k) be a filtration and (u_k,v_k) adapted, with
deterministic u_0 and v_0=0. At each step let the jointly sampled oracle
noise (xi_k^u,xi_k^v) in R^d x R^q be F_{k+1}-measurable, with

    E[xi_k^u|F_k]=0, E[xi_k^v|F_k]=0,
    E[xi_k^v (xi_k^v)^T|F_k] <= sigma^2 H,
    E[|xi_k^u|^2|F_k] <= sigma^2 D^2 |v_k|^2.           (1)

The matrix inequality is in Loewner order and holds almost surely.
The two noise components may be dependent; their law may depend on the
entire past and on k. No iid, Markov, symmetry or higher-moment hypothesis
is imposed. Consider the unbiased stochastic-gradient oracle recursion
for the population loss L(u,v)=v^T H v/2:

    u_{k+1}=u_k-eta xi_k^u,
    v_{k+1}=B v_k-eta xi_k^v, B=I-eta H.               (2)

Here "oracle" means an unbiased estimator of grad L; this theorem does
not assert that every allowed noise field is the gradient of an individual
random sample loss. The label-gradient models of C005 are included.

For F in C_b^2(R^{d+q}), let f(u)=F(u,0), a(u)=D_v F(u,0), and define

    F_2=sup ||D^2 f||_op,
    F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||_op,
    F_uv=sup ||D_u a||_op,
    c=sigma^2 q/(2-rho), gamma=min{m,M(2-rho)/rho}.

Then, for every T>=0,

    sup_{integer 0<=K<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_K,v_K)-F(u_0,0)| <= eta C(T),
    C(T)=c[F_vv/2+T sigma^2 D^2 F_2/2+F_uv sigma D/gamma]. (3)

Thus a=1. If, in addition, the normal conditional covariance equals
sigma^2 H on the event v_k=0, then (1) forces xi_k^u=0 there almost
surely. Consequently the full noise covariance on the minimizing
manifold is sigma^2 diag(0,H), proportional to the population Hessian.
That equality is the target-compatible subclass; the estimate itself
uses only domination. No global covariance proportionality is asserted.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X, Y Banach spaces"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492197+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator theory","id":"claim_3ecf47d2e1941e3ed3b704c1615dceb455e30d7da6c0085069f13dc22e065c98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X, Y be Banach spaces. A linear operator K : X → Y is compact if it maps the closed unit ball of X onto a relatively compact subset of Y; equivalently, for every bounded sequence (x_n) in X the sequence (Kx_n) has a norm-convergent subsequence. Compact operators are bounded. They form a norm-closed two-sided ideal in the bounded operators: norm limits of compact operators are compact, and BK and KB are compact whenever K is compact and B is bounded. Every bounded finite-rank operator is compact; in a Hilbert space (and in every Banach space with the approximation property) every compact operator is a norm limit of finite-rank operators. K is compact iff its adjoint K* is compact (Schauder). The identity of an infinite-dimensional space is not compact (Riesz), so on an infinite-dimensional space a compact operator never has a bounded inverse. A compact operator maps weakly convergent sequences to norm-convergent sequences; the converse (complete continuity implies compactness) holds when X is reflexive, e.g. a Hilbert space, but fails in ℓ^1 (Schur property).\n\nExamples: diag(λ_n) on ℓ^2 is compact iff λ_n → 0; integral operators with L^2 kernels (Hilbert–Schmidt operators) are compact; the embedding H^1_0(Ω) → L^2(Ω) for bounded open Ω is compact (Rellich), so the inverse of the Dirichlet Laplacian is a compact self-adjoint operator on L^2(Ω). Non-examples: the shift operators on ℓ^2; multiplication by a function f on L^2[0,1] is compact only when f = 0 a.e.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.632723+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3f2a27cd682ee0d5c317e0d7af12a3f1c8654de548c0f8a755c4fc28db0c0893","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:prior.W.logconcave of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] For $d \ge (1+\epsilon)n$, the prior distribution $W\sim\mathbb{P}_{0}$ conditioned on ${\mathcal{H}}$ in \prettyref{eq:calH}
is $(c_0 d)$-strongly log-concave, where $c_0$ is a positive constant depending on $\epsilon$.

\begin{proof}
Under the prior distribution $\mathbb{P}_{0}$, 
the density of $W$ is given by (see e.g.\ [anderson2003introduction])
\begin{align*}
\mathbb{P}_0(W) 
&\propto e^{-V(W
)} \mathbf{1}\{ I+W \succ 0\}\,, \\
V(W) &= - \frac{d-n-1}{2}\log \det(I+W)\,.
\end{align*}
Abbreviate ${\widetilde{W}}=I+W$, and denote by 
$\nabla^2$  the Hessian with respect to the lower triangular elements of $W$. Let $H$ be an $n\times n$ symmetric matrix with zero diagonal. Then
    \begin{align*}
    \log\det({\widetilde{W}}+\epsilon H)
    &=\log\det({\widetilde{W}})
    +\log\det(I+\epsilon B)\,,\\
    B &= {\widetilde{W}}^{-1/2}H{\widetilde{W}}^{-1/2}\,.
    \end{align*}
$B$ is a symmetric matrix. Denoting its eigenvalues by $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$, we have
    \begin{align*}
    \log\det({\widetilde{W}}+\epsilon H)
    &= \log\det({\widetilde{W}})
    +\sum_{i=1}^n\log(1+\epsilon\lambda_i) 
    = \log\det({\widetilde{W}})
    +\epsilon \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i
    -\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}
    \sum_{i=1}^n (\lambda_i)^2\\
    &= \log\det({\widetilde{W}})
    +\epsilon \mathop{\rm tr}(B)
    -\frac{\epsilon^2}{2}
    \mathop{\rm tr}(B^2)\,.
    \end{align*}
It follows that
\begin{equation}
-H^\top\nabla^2 \big[\log\det \widetilde{W} \big] H =\mathop{\rm tr}(\widetilde{W}^{-1}H\widetilde{W}^{-1}H)=\|\widetilde{W}^{-1/2}H\widetilde{W}^{-1/2}\|_{\operatorname{F}}^2\ge \frac{\|H\|_{\operatorname{F}}^2}{\|\widetilde{W}\|_{\operatorname{op}}^2}\,,

\end{equation}
that is to say, the log-determinant function is strongly log-concave.\footnote{From  \prettyref{eq:hess-prior} we see that 
as long as $d\geq n+1$,
the prior distribution $\mathbb{P}_{0}$ is always strongly log-concave with constant $\Theta(\frac{d-n-1}{n^2}$); this is tight when all $x_i$'s are aligned. Lemma~(l:prior.W.logconcave of the paper) improves the curvature to $\Theta(d)$ by truncating on the typical behavior of $W$.} Next recall from \prettyref{eq:calH} that 
${\mathcal{H}}=\{\|\widetilde{W}\|_{\operatorname{op}} \leq 4\}$, which is a convex set in $W$. 
For each $W \in {\mathcal{H}}$, the right-hand side of \prettyref{eq:hess-prior} is further lower bounded by $\|H\|^2/16$, and hence
\[
\nabla^2 V(W)\succeq \frac{d-n-1}{16}I_{n(n-1)/2}\succeq c_0 d I_{n(n-1)/2}\,,
\]
for a constant $c_0>0$ depending on $\epsilon$. This proves the claim.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

			If $(\mathsf{t},\mathsf{x})$ is above or below $\mathcal{W}$, we have $d(\Delta x)=0$ and $a(\Delta x)=-1$, that is, the

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T is continuous","the metric enters only through the compact topology"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438163+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_3fe95da80d1756dae2bb8c43b479ad29fb9efff8bf12406c39a668547d7335d9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T: X \\to X$ be a continuous map of a compact metric space $(X, d)$. For $n \\ge 1$ define the dynamical metric $d_n(x, y) = \\max_{0 \\le k < n} d(T^k x, T^k y)$. A set $E \\subset X$ is $(n, \\varepsilon)$-separated if $d_n(x, y) > \\varepsilon$ for all distinct $x, y \\in E$; let $s(n, \\varepsilon)$ be the maximal cardinality of such a set (finite by compactness). A set $F$ is $(n, \\varepsilon)$-spanning if every $x \\in X$ has $d_n(x, y) \\le \\varepsilon$ for some $y \\in F$; let $r(n, \\varepsilon)$ be the minimal cardinality. The topological entropy is\n$$h_{top}(T) = \\lim_{\\varepsilon \\to 0} \\limsup_{n \\to \\infty} \\frac{1}{n} \\log s(n, \\varepsilon) = \\lim_{\\varepsilon \\to 0} \\limsup_{n \\to \\infty} \\frac{1}{n} \\log r(n, \\varepsilon) \\in [0, \\infty],$$\nusing $r(n,\\varepsilon) \\le s(n,\\varepsilon) \\le r(n, \\varepsilon/2)$; the limit in $\\varepsilon$ exists by monotonicity, and replacing the $\\limsup$ in $n$ by a $\\liminf$ gives the same value. The value is independent of the compatible metric (this uses compactness) and coincides with the open-cover definition $h_{top}(T) = \\sup_{\\mathcal{U}} \\lim_n \\frac1n \\log N(\\mathcal{U}^n_0)$ where $N$ counts the minimal subcover of the join $\\mathcal{U}^n_0 = \\bigvee_{k<n} T^{-k}\\mathcal{U}$. Basic properties: $h_{top}(T^m) = m\\, h_{top}(T)$ for $m \\ge 1$; $h_{top}(T^{-1}) = h_{top}(T)$ for homeomorphisms; $h_{top}$ is an invariant of topological conjugacy; a Lipschitz map of a compact metric space of finite box dimension has finite entropy, but a continuous map of a compact metric space can have $h_{top} = \\infty$. On a NON-compact space the separated-set quantity depends on the metric, not merely on the topology, and the equalities above can fail.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.674398+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_3ff619da11f26838eeebd63e4e7ab7d17c07daa25e94177b4f2168ecd887ce56","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 42 (Difference equation for two Ricci--DeTurck solutions) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(s(t)\) be a Ricci-flow background and let \(v_0(t)\) and \(v_1(t)\)
be two positive definite solutions of the Ricci--DeTurck equation relative to
\(s(t)\) on the same time interval.  Put
\[
        U=v_1-v_0,
        \qquad v_\vartheta=v_0+\vartheta(v_1-v_0),
        \quad 0\leq\vartheta\leq1,
\]
and assume that every \(v_\vartheta\) is positive definite.  With \(\nabla\)
the connection of \(s(t)\), the difference satisfies a homogeneous linear
system
\begin{equation}
        \partial_tU-P^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qU
        =B^p\nabla_pU+CU,
\end{equation}
where the second-order part is diagonal in the tensor components: in a fixed
frame, every component \(U^A\) is acted on by the same operator
\(P^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_q\), and no second derivative of a different component
occurs.  More precisely, for
\[
        \mathcal Q_s(v)=-2\Ric(v)+\Lie_{W(v,s)}v,
\]
one has the structural formula
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \mathcal Q_s(v)
        ={}&v^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qv
        +v^{-1}*v^{-1}*\nabla v*\nabla v \\
        &\quad+\mathcal R(\Rm(s),v,v^{-1}),
\end{split}
\end{equation}
and the mean-value identity
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \partial_tU
        &=\mathcal Q_s(v_1)-\mathcal Q_s(v_0)\\
        &=\int_0^1D\mathcal Q_s|_{v_\vartheta}[U] \,d\vartheta.
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Differentiating \eqref{eq:rdt-structural-form} gives
\begin{equation}
        D\mathcal Q_s|_{v_\vartheta}[Z]
        =v_\vartheta^{pq}\nabla_p\nabla_qZ
          +\mathcal B_\vartheta^p\nabla_pZ+\mathcal C_\vartheta Z,
\end{equation}
with
\begin{equation}
\begin{split}
        \mathcal B_\vartheta
        &=v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*\nabla v_\vartheta,\\
        \mathcal C_\vartheta
        &=v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*\nabla^2v_\vartheta
          +v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}*v_\vartheta^{-1}
             *\nabla v_\vartheta*\nabla v_\vartheta\\
        &\qquad+\mathcal R_1(\Rm(s),v_\vartheta,v_\vartheta^{-1}).
\end{split}
\end{equation}
Here \(*\) denotes universal tensor contractions, and \(\mathcal R\) and
\(\mathcal R_1\) are algebraic in the displayed arguments; in particular,
\(\mathcal R_1\) contains no derivatives of \(v_\vartheta\).  The
coefficients in \eqref{eq:rdt-difference-system} are
\[
 P^{pq}=\int_0^1v_\vartheta^{pq}\,d\vartheta,
 \qquad B^p=\int_0^1\mathcal B_\vartheta^p\,d\vartheta,
 \qquad C=\int_0^1\mathcal C_\vartheta\,d\vartheta.
\]
Consequently, uniform metric equivalence and finite-order bounds for
\(v_0,v_1\), and \(s\) give the corresponding ellipticity and H\"older bounds
for \(P,B,C\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.537240+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_402cc7a17e09582be87b6b33999c970f349a537eefdc570e9d42f1df8933d920","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 8 of arXiv:2603.28226, '2603.28226'] Let \(f\ge0\) belong to \(L^1(\mathcal F_\infty)\), let \(\lambda>0\), and let
\(\theta\ge0\). Retain the notation of Section~\ref{sec:proof} and
\eqref{eq:s-theta}; thus
\[
r:=\inf\{n\ge1:\ f_n>\lambda\},
\qquad
\varepsilon_n:=d f_n\,\mathbf1_{\{r=n\}},
\qquad
\gamma_n:=d f_n\,\mathbf1_{\{r>n\}},
\]
\[
\Lambda_0:=0,
\qquad
\Lambda_m:=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\mathbb E_k[\varepsilon_{k+1}],
\qquad
s_\theta:=\inf\{m\ge1:\ \Lambda_m>\theta\lambda\},
\qquad
t_\theta:=r\wedge s_\theta.
\]
Also set
\[
r^-:=r-1 \ \text{on }\{r<\infty\},
\qquad
r^-:=\infty \ \text{on }\{r=\infty\}.
\]

Define
\[
g_\theta:=f-f_{t_\theta},
\]
\[
h_{\theta,n}:=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}
\bigl(\varepsilon_j-\mathbb E_{j-1}[\varepsilon_j]\bigr)\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta\ge j\}},
\qquad n\ge1,
\]
\[
k_{\theta,n}^{\mathrm{st}}
:=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\gamma_j\,\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta\ge j\}},
\qquad
k_{\theta,n}^{\mathrm{pr}}
:=
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbb E_{j-1}[\varepsilon_j]\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta\ge j\}},
\qquad n\ge1.
\]
Then \(h_{\theta,n}\) converges almost surely and in \(L^1\) to a limit
\(h_\theta\in L^1(\mathcal F_\infty)\), and the sequences
\[
k_{\theta,n}^{\mathrm{st}},
\qquad
k_{\theta,n}^{\mathrm{pr}}
\]
converge almost surely and in \(L^1\) to limits
\[
k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}},
\qquad
k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}
\in L^1(\mathcal F_\infty).
\]
Moreover,
\[
f=g_\theta+h_\theta+k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}+k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}.
\]

\medskip
\noindent\textup{(a)}
\[
\mathbb P\Bigl(\sup_{n\ge1}|\mathbb E_n[g_\theta]|>0\Bigr)
\le \frac{\|f\|_1}{\lambda},
\qquad
\|g_\theta\|_1\le 2\|f\|_1.
\]

\noindent\textup{(b)}
\[
\Bigl\|\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\bigl|\mathbb E_n[h_\theta]-\mathbb E_{n-1}[h_\theta]\bigr|
\Bigr\|_1
\le 2\|f\|_1.
\]
In particular,
\[
\|h_\theta\|_1\le 2\|f\|_1.
\]

\noindent\textup{(c)}
\[
k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}=f_{s_\theta\wedge r^-},
\qquad
0\le k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}\le \lambda
\quad\text{a.s.}
\]

\noindent\textup{(d)}
\[
k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}
=
\Lambda_{s_\theta-1}\,\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta<\infty\}}
+
\Bigl(\sup_{m\ge1}\Lambda_m\Bigr)\mathbf1_{\{s_\theta=\infty\}},
\qquad
0\le k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\le \theta\lambda
\quad\text{a.s.}
\]

\noindent\textup{(e)}
\[
\mathbb E[h_\theta]=\mathbb E[\varepsilon_1],
\]
\[
\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}\|_1+\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\|_1
=
\|f\|_1-\mathbb E[\varepsilon_1]
\le \|f\|_1,
\]
\[
\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}\|_2^2
\le \lambda\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}\|_1,
\qquad
\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\|_2^2
\le \theta\lambda\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\|_1,
\]
and
\[
\|k_\theta^{\mathrm{st}}+k_\theta^{\mathrm{pr}}\|_2^2
\le (1+\theta)\lambda\|f\|_1.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726542+00:00","domain":"dispersive partial differential equations","id":"claim_4035e0f47d8f89385856e3a0fa89ee495b32f2ab6d982252999b8813bc8feedd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: finite speed of propagation and the domain-of-dependence cone are properties of the wave equation (and of symmetric hyperbolic systems), proved by a local energy identity on the cone. The Schrödinger equation has no such identity and propagates instantaneously. Concrete counterexample: let f ∈ L¹(R^n) be nonzero and compactly supported and let t ≠ 0. By the kernel formula, e^{itΔ}f(x) = (4πit)^{−n/2} e^{i|x|²/(4t)} · G(x/(2t)) where G is the Fourier transform of the compactly supported integrable function y ↦ e^{i|y|²/(4t)}f(y). By the Paley–Wiener theorem G extends to an entire function on C^n, and it is not identically zero, so its zero set contains no nonempty open set. Hence e^{itΔ}f is nonzero almost everywhere on every open subset of R^n at every t ≠ 0: compactly supported data instantly become globally supported. The same phenomenon rules out any cone-shaped domain of dependence, and the heat equation behaves the same way. What survives for Schrödinger are local smoothing, dispersive decay and (pseudo)locality statements about wave packets moving at velocity ≈ 2ξ, not a finite propagation speed; the wave equation's finite-speed argument must never be transplanted to a dispersive or parabolic equation.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:06:07.078127+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_40499db85848ffefdfdcd5e77731522500404a4250fb26b00f2814cc03ed372c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 9 (Weak stability of positive \(L^2\) Stein kernels) of arXiv:2608.27657, '\bfseries Stein Kernels and Normal Approximation\\ for Log-Concave Bilinear Forms'] Let \(\mu_k\Rightarrow\mu\) weakly on \(\R^n\), where each \(\mu_k\)
is centered and has finite second moments.  Let \(Y_k\sim\mu_k\), and
suppose that \(\mu_k\) admits a symmetric positive-semidefinite Stein
kernel \(\tau_k\) such that
\begin{equation}
  L:=\sup_k\E\|\tau_k(Y_k)\|_{\HS}^2<\infty.
  \tag{4.2}
\end{equation}
Then \(\mu\) is centered, \(\mu_k\to\mu\) in \(W_2\), and \(\mu\)
admits a symmetric positive-semidefinite Stein kernel \(\tau\) satisfying
\begin{equation}
  \E\tau(Y)=\Cov(Y),
  \qquad
  \E\|\tau(Y)\|_{\HS}^2
  \leq
  \liminf_{k\to\infty}\E\|\tau_k(Y_k)\|_{\HS}^2,
  \tag{4.3}
\end{equation}
where \(Y\sim\mu\).  The same kernel may be chosen with the following
additional permanence properties.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item
If \(F:\mathsf S_n\to[0,\infty]\) is convex and lower semicontinuous and
\(\sup_k\E F(\tau_k(Y_k))\leq C_F\), then
\[
  \E F(\tau(Y))\leq C_F.
\]

\item
If, for every \(A\in\mathsf S_n\),
\[
  \Var\!\left(\Tr(A\tau_k(Y_k))\right)
  \leq C_{\rm tr}\Tr(A^2),
\]
then
\begin{equation}
  \Var\!\left(\Tr(A\tau(Y))\right)
  \leq C_{\rm tr}\Tr(A^2)
  \qquad(A\in\mathsf S_n).
  \tag{4.4}
\end{equation}

\item
If, for every \(A\in\mathsf S_n\),
\[
  \E\Tr(A\tau_k(Y_k)A\tau_k(Y_k))
  \leq C_{\rm en}\Tr(A^2),
\]
then
\begin{equation}
  \E\Tr(A\tau(Y)A\tau(Y))
  \leq C_{\rm en}\Tr(A^2)
  \qquad(A\in\mathsf S_n).
  \tag{4.5}
\end{equation}

\item
If a constant \(C_{\rm wp}\) satisfies
\[
  \Var_{\mu_k}g
  \leq
  C_{\rm wp}\,
  \E\langle
    \tau_k(Y_k)\nabla g(Y_k),\nabla g(Y_k)
  \rangle
\]
for every \(k\) and every \(g\in C_c^\infty(\R^n)\), then
\begin{equation}
  \Var_\mu g
  \leq
  C_{\rm wp}\,
  \E\langle
    \tau(Y)\nabla g(Y),\nabla g(Y)
  \rangle
  \qquad(g\in C_c^\infty(\R^n)).
  \tag{4.6}
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:42.312267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_40871787fc45aea8c87bcfc71952dd37f18724345a7ff0c0c4b0ecef144b6d99","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 20 of arXiv:2608.05931, 'Effective Lagrangian regularity and the uniqueness threshold for random H\"older velocity '] For a function $g : X \to Y$, where $X = \T^d$ or $\R^d$ and $Y$ is a Banach space, we define for $s \geq 0$ the (semi)norm space $\mathcal{C}^s$ as follows. For $s=0$, we let
    \[\|g\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(X) Y} := \sup_{x \in X} \|g(x)\|_Y.\]
    For $s \in (0,\infty)$---letting $s = n + r$ where $r \in (0,1]$ and $n \in \N$---we define $\mathcal{C}^s(X)$ as a seminorm on a subspace of $C^n(X)$ by
    \[\|g\|_{\mathcal{C}^s(X) Y} := \sup_{x,x' \in X, x \ne x'} \frac{\|\nabla^n g(x) - \nabla^ng(x')\|_Y}{|x-x'|^r}.\]
    We note in particular that $\mathcal{C}^1$ is the Lipschitz seminorm and that $\mathcal{C}^0$ is the natural norm on the space of bounded functions---rather than $C^1$ and $C^0$ which have additional qualitative regularity hypotheses that we do not want to require, as we will frequently be working with Lipschitz functions that are not $C^1$.

    We also consider for $p \in [1,\infty), s\geq 0$ the fractional Sobolev (semi)norm spaces $W^{s,p}$. For $s \in \N$, we just let $\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(X)Y} := \|\nabla^s g\|_{L^p(X)Y}$, and for $s>0$ and $s \not \in \N$, we again write $s = n+r$ where $r \in (0,1)$ and $n \in \N$ and define
    \[\|g\|_{W^{s,p}(X) Y} := \Big(\int_X \int_X \frac{\|\nabla^n g(x) - \nabla^n g(x')\|^p_Y}{|x-x'|^{d + rp}}\,dx\,dx'\Big)^{1/p}.\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Fixed L>0 and eta>0; deterministic square X with operator norm at most L.","Independent standard Gaussian feature-weight vectors; coordinates of the resulting ReLU column need not be independent.","Each symmetric R_j excludes w_j from its measurability and has norm at most 1/eta.","Any auxiliary randomness is independent of all Gaussian feature weights.","Random-input extension requires independence from feature weights and a tight input norm; only convergence in probability is claimed there.","Owner-work proof (unaudited), w737 T385-C13 v1; no independent PASS or novelty claim."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T17:02:46.507882+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory; nonlinear random features; conditional concentration","id":"claim_40f4831c7471e288197440d464ad019ecdc928316db1ec18bf8e195faef67995","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work METHOD DRAFT; proof (unaudited), attributed to w737 T385-C13 v1; no independent PASS or novelty claim. Fix L>0 and eta>0. For each n let X be a deterministic real n by n matrix with operator norm at most L, and w_1,...,w_n independent N(0,I_n) vectors. Put h_j=ReLU(Xw_j), mu=E h_j, z_j=h_j-mu, Phi=E[h_j h_j^T], and Sigma=E[z_j z_j^T]. Let R_j be real symmetric, measurable in X and the columns w_k with k!=j (and optionally auxiliary randomness independent of all feature weights), with operator norm at most 1/eta almost surely. The recorded unaudited derivation gives, for each fixed epsilon>0, P(max_j |z_j^T R_j z_j/n-Tr(Sigma R_j)/n|>epsilon)<=C n exp[-c n min(epsilon^2,epsilon)], with C,c depending only on L,eta. The centering step uses the exact identity z^T R z-Tr(Sigma R)=h^T R h-Tr(Phi R)-2 mu^T R(h-mu) for deterministic symmetric R. Louart-Liao-Couillet quadratic-form concentration controls the raw term. Gaussian Lipschitz concentration controls the mean correction. Indeed mu_i=||x_i||/sqrt(2 pi), ||mu||^2<=n L^2/(2 pi), and w->mu^T R ReLU(Xw) is Lipschitz with constant at most sqrt(n/(2 pi))*L^2/eta. Condition on all columns except j before applying those bounds; integrate and take a union bound, without asserting independence between deviation events. Thus the method allows correlations among coordinates within each feature column, but R_j must exclude the tested column. For X=I and eta=1, taking the same-column R=zz^T/||z||^2 makes z^T R z/n tend to kappa=1/2-1/(2 pi)>0 while Tr(Sigma R)/n=kappa/n, illustrating failure if this independence hypothesis is removed. For random X independent of all w_j with tight operator norm, conditioning first on ||X||<=L and then letting L grow gives convergence in probability, rather than a uniform unconditional exponential rate. This is a fixed-positive-ridge concentration ingredient; it supplies neither an edge law nor a justification for a ridge tending to zero. The underlying source-based proof draft and all proposed uses remain subject to independent review.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A measurable, uniformly parabolic with constants lambda, Lambda (no continuity assumed)","divergence form (the analogous statement for nondivergence form with merely measurable coefficients is a different theory)","s < t; for equations with lower-order terms or on a finite time interval, constants also depend on T and those bounds"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:49.106308+00:00","domain":"parabolic partial differential equations / heat kernel estimates","id":"claim_410506486d1fb1210e085fe9677cd4acaa4ae438a0aa72b12c79fd1a43a41833","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $A(x,t)$ be real measurable on $\\mathbb R^n\\times\\mathbb R$ and uniformly parabolic with constants $0<\\lambda\\le\\Lambda<\\infty$, and consider $\\partial_tu=\\mathrm{div}(A(x,t)\\nabla u)$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:47:22.245900+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_414774552018474bc5ee76321ba5e7b66cb73ff5fb105f49125c1862c38a7ec9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 of arXiv:2605.26664, 'Mixing times for Glauber dynamics of lozenge tilings of the hexagon'] [Liquid and frozen region, arctic boundary]
  Given any open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, we call a function $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ \emph{admissible} if $F$ is $1$-Lipschitz and satisfies $\nabla F (z) \in \overline{\mathcal{T}}$ for Lebesgue almost every $z \in \Omega$. Let $\Adm (\Omega)$ denote the set of admissible functions $F : \overline{\Omega} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and, for any function $f : \partial \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, let $\Adm (\Omega; f)$ denote the set of $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ satisfying $F |_{\partial \Omega} = f$.  Define the \emph{liquid region} $\mathfrak{L}_F \subseteq \Omega$ associated with an admissible height function $F \in \Adm (\Omega)$ by 
         \begin{flalign*}
         	\mathfrak{L}_F = \big\{ z \in \Omega : \nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T} \big\},
         \end{flalign*}
         where the condition $\nabla F(z) \in \mathcal{T}$ in particular implies that $\nabla F(z)$ exists.

         In particular, we define the liquid region of $\cH_{q;a,b,c}$ as
         \[\mL_{q;a,b,c}:=\mL_{\cH_{q;a,b,c}}.\] The  boundary
        $\mathfrak A_{q;a,b,c}:=\partial\mL_{q;a,b,c}$ is called the
        \emph{arctic boundary} and the interior of
        $\mX_{a,b,c}\setminus\mL_{q;a,b,c}$ is called the \emph{frozen
        region}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.740632+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_41918c410806fda3d6ce81068e83f01a2801742dd5d07ae6173c787e38cd6ca1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:rw_reset of arXiv:2603.24803, 'Critical Spectral Invariants in Random Walks with Geometric Resetting'] Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})$ be a probability space. 
Fix $a \in \mathbb{N}$ and $z \in \{1,\dots,a-1\}$. 
Let $\{X_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be a discrete-time stochastic process on 
$\{0,1,\dots,a\}$ with initial condition $X_0=z$.

Let $\{\xi_n\}_{n\ge1}$ be i.i.d.\ random variables, independent of 
everything else, with
\[
\mathbb{P}(\xi_n=+1)=p, 
\qquad 
\mathbb{P}(\xi_n=-1)=q=1-p.
\]

Let $\{\sigma_i\}_{i\ge1}$ be i.i.d.\ geometric random variables with 
parameter $\gamma\in(0,1)$, supported on $\{1,2,\dots\}$:
\[
\mathbb{P}(\sigma_i=k)=\gamma(1-\gamma)^{k-1}, 
\qquad k\ge1,
\]
independent of $\{\xi_n\}$. Define reset times recursively by
\[
\mathbf{t}_0:=0,
\qquad
\mathbf{t}_i := \sum_{j=1}^{i} \sigma_j,
\quad i\ge1.
\]

Then the process evolves according to
\[
X_n =
\begin{cases}
z, & \text{if } n \in \{\mathbf{t}_i\}_{i\ge1}, \\[6pt]
X_{n-1}+\xi_n, & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad n\ge1,
\]
and is absorbed upon first hitting $0$ or $a$. Equivalently, at each 
step the walker resets to $z$ with probability $\gamma$ or performs a 
standard biased step with probability $1-\gamma$, independently of its 
current position.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:01:39.423732+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_41ec281780e228555015ad321135da7c10041d8812e04a31bc646c231f823757","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:max_lh of arXiv:2607.22291, 'Rare subtree patterns in size-conditioned Bienaymé trees: Poisson approximation and declum'] Assume that $\mu$ is critical and belongs to the domain of attraction of a stable law.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)]  Assume that $\mu_{1}>0$. There exists a constant $C_{\mu}>0$ such that the following holds. Set

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces","T is linear on a linear subspace D(T) of X"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.769166+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_41fdcf41b301c72abeac970dc8d13d7e8412473ffc482e2582494edf964e1f49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X, Y be Banach spaces and T: D(T) ⊂ X → Y a linear operator defined on a linear subspace D(T). Its graph is G(T) = {(x, Tx) : x ∈ D(T)} ⊂ X × Y. T is closed if G(T) is closed in X × Y; equivalently, whenever x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → x in X and Tx_n → y in Y, then x ∈ D(T) and Tx = y. Equivalently, D(T) is complete under the graph norm ‖x‖_T = ‖x‖ + ‖Tx‖. S is an extension of T (written T ⊂ S) if D(T) ⊂ D(S) and Sx = Tx for x ∈ D(T). T is closable if it has a closed extension; equivalently, x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y imply y = 0; equivalently, the closure of G(T) is the graph of an operator, called the closure T̄ (the smallest closed extension). If T is closed, a subspace D_0 ⊂ D(T) is a core for T if D_0 is dense in D(T) for the graph norm, i.e. the closure of T restricted to D_0 equals T. A closed operator need not be bounded, and being closed says nothing about D(T) being dense; by the closed graph theorem a closed operator with D(T) = X is bounded.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.349563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4227cc72423df9e86220706666cf0c5942ecb93c47543ebc0343a142107821ab","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 171 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let indices $a(q_d),a^\frozen(q_d)$
be sampled as in Definition~\ref{d:rerand}, and let
indices $i(q_d),i^\frozen(q_d)$

For $N$ large enough, we have
	\[\max_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}
	\E\bigg[
	\max_{r\in[s,t]} 
	\bigg|
	\sum_{\ell=s}^{r-1}
	\Delta X^\sigma(q_\ell,a(q_{\ell+1}))

	\bigg]
	\le L^{O(1)} (q_t-q_s)^4
	\]
for all $0\le s\le t\le \dmax$.

	with $\Delta X^{\trunc,\sigma}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$
	or $\Delta X^{\frozen,\sigma}(q_d,a^\frozen(q_{d+1}))$
	in place of $\Delta X^\sigma(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))$.

	\[

	\Delta X^{\Ising}(q_\ell,i(q_{\ell+1}))

\begin{proof}
This follows by a very similar argument as for Lemma~\ref{l:martingale.sup.bound.X.II.III.Ising}. We will describe the proof for $X^\RomII$. {"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T15:38:23.784925+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_424daabf6bab4c23b100ce5671977a4d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]\n\nFor every neighborhood U of 0 in X, its polar U^circ = {phi in X^*: |phi(u)| <= 1 for every u in U} is weak-* compact. Here X^* is the continuous dual and the weak-* topology is pointwise convergence on X; neither completeness nor separability of X is needed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_n => X in distribution","Y_n -> c in probability with c a CONSTANT (not a random variable)","for the quotient: c != 0"],"created_at":"2026-10-07T01:09:09+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_42d5d8144efc7c7815ae88f7a13799ed","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_n converge in distribution to a real random variable X and let Y_n converge in probability to a real constant c. Then (X_n,Y_n) converges jointly in distribution to (X,c). Consequently X_n+Y_n converges in distribution to X+c, X_n Y_n converges in distribution to cX, and, if c!=0, X_n/Y_n converges in distribution to X/c. For the quotient, define its value arbitrarily on {Y_n=0} when necessary; that event has probability tending to zero. Convergence Y_n=>c in distribution is equivalent to convergence Y_n->c in probability, so either hypothesis gives the same conclusion for a constant target. With a nonconstant target, separate marginal convergence alone does not identify the joint limit: if X is a nondegenerate symmetric random variable, X_n=X and Y_n=-X, then both marginal laws converge to the law of X, but X_n+Y_n=0 does not converge to the law of 2X. A random second limit is allowed when joint convergence (X_n,Y_n)=>(X,Y) is supplied; the continuous mapping theorem then gives the corresponding sum and product limits, and the quotient limit if P(Y=0)=0. [Re-derived local source, M9; textbook cross-reference: van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics, Theorem 2.8.]","status":"unverified"}
