where $\mathsf{S}_{v,e}$ is the weighted sum over all graphs on vertex set $[v]$ with $e$ edges, such that each vertex is covered by at least one edge:
\begin{align*}
\mathsf{S}_{2,1} &= W_{12}\,,\\
\mathsf{S}_{3,2} &= W_{12} W_{13}
    +W_{12} W_{23}+W_{13} W_{23}\,,\\
\mathsf{S}_{4,2} &= W_{12} W_{34}
+
W_{13} W_{24}
+
W_{14} W_{23}\,,\\
\mathsf{S}_{5,3} &= \sum_{h=1}^5
\sum_{\{i,j\}\subset [5]\setminus\{h\}}
W_{hi}W_{hj}W_{uv},
\qquad
\{u,v\}=[5]\setminus\{h,i,j\}\,.
\end{align*}
Define the residuals $R_k\equiv \eta_k-E_k$. On the event $a^2\delta_k \le c$,

{"assumptions":["phi_i 1-Lipschitz with phi_i(0) = 0","eps_i independent Rademacher signs","T bounded so the suprema are finite; constant 1 WITHOUT absolute values, 2 WITH them"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628629+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4d71e82701baa0652e97a3150c16f319f1bfdeca9e4a8d8cfae7f2157af90f94","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let T be a bounded subset of R^n, let eps_1, ..., eps_n be independent Rademacher signs, and let phi_i : R -> R be 1-Lipschitz with phi_i(0) = 0 for every i. Then E sup_{t in T} sum_{i=1}^n eps_i phi_i(t_i) <= E sup_{t in T} sum_{i=1}^n eps_i t_i. With ABSOLUTE VALUES inside the supremum the same statement holds with a factor 2: E sup_{t in T} | sum_i eps_i phi_i(t_i) | <= 2 E sup_{t in T} | sum_i eps_i t_i |. The distinction between the constants 1 and 2 is a standard source of misquotation; the constant 1 belongs to the version WITHOUT absolute values. The hypothesis phi_i(0) = 0 is needed for the version without absolute values and can be arranged by subtracting a constant, which is harmless for a symmetric process. In statistical learning the principle is what lets one strip a Lipschitz loss off a function class without changing the Rademacher complexity by more than a constant. [Ledoux and Talagrand, Probability in Banach Spaces, Theorem 4.12]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:13:31.905266+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4d8003e49784b18c586de709c2adcd02545ce254f2856efb4e7ae221eb7d7b74","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary prop:conditioned_Bernoulli1 of arXiv:2506.10765, 'A General Coupling for Ising Models and Beyond'] Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite graph, $x_e\in (0,1)$ for each $e\in E$. Let $\Omega = \{0,1\}^E$, $\Sigma \subset \Omega$ , $f:\Omega\to 2^{\Sigma}$ be defined by $f(\omega)= \Sigma^{\downarrow}(\omega):=\{\eta \in \Sigma: \eta \subset \omega\}$ as well as
	$$\rho[\omega] \propto \mathbb{P}_{x}[\omega], ~\forall \omega\in \Omega, ~\gamma[\eta]\propto 1, ~\forall \eta\in \Sigma. $$
    	Then, under the coupling measure $\mathscr{P}$ defined in Theorem (thm:generalcoupling of the paper), 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(a)] The marginal of $\mathscr{P}$ on $\Sigma$ is $\mathscr{P}_{\Sigma}[\eta]=\mathbb{P}_{\frac{x}{1+x}}[\eta \mid \Sigma] \propto \prod_{e\in \eta} x_e$. 
        For each $\omega\in\Omega$ with $\mathscr{P}_\Omega[\omega] \neq 0$, the  conditional measure $\mathscr{P}[\;\cdot \mid \omega]

{"assumptions":["F entire on C (or C^d)","claims of band limitation require the growth bound off the real axis","L^2 version needs square integrability on R; distributions need the polynomial-growth version"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264631+00:00","domain":"complex and harmonic analysis, common errors","id":"claim_4d88e0d15b6e8881d2eb18cd54107f75b8c1834afa521c13029e34cc2e348e2d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypotheses: (1) the growth bound $|F(z)|\\le Ce^{A|z|}$ must hold for all complex $z$, not merely on $\\mathbb R$; (2) $F$ must be square integrable on $\\mathbb R$ (for the $L^2$ version) or have controlled polynomial growth (for the distributional version). Failure of (1): $F(z)=e^{-z^2}$ is entire and its restriction to $\\mathbb R$ is in $L^2$, yet $|F(iy)|=e^{y^2}$, so $F$ is of order 2, not of exponential type; its Fourier transform is a Gaussian, supported everywhere - no band limitation. Failure of (2): $F(z)=\\cos(Az)$ is entire of exponential type exactly $A$ and bounded on $\\mathbb R$, but not in $L^2(\\mathbb R)$; it is not $\\int_{-A}^A\\varphi(t)e^{itz}dt$ for any $\\varphi\\in L^2$, only for the measure $\\frac12(\\delta_A+\\delta_{-A})$ - the correct statement in that regime is the Paley-Wiener-Schwartz theorem for compactly supported distributions, with a polynomial factor $(1+|\\zeta|)^N$ allowed. Similarly $F(z)=e^{Az}$ has type $A$ but grows on the real axis. Two further traps: the exponential factor in Paley-Wiener-Schwartz measures the support of the transform only through the supporting function of its convex hull, so the theorem detects $\\operatorname{ch}(\\operatorname{supp}u)$, not the support itself; and no such function can have both itself and its transform compactly supported, since a nonzero entire function cannot vanish on an open set (see Benedicks' theorem for the measure-theoretic strengthening).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X_1, ..., X_n independent","Z = f(X) nonnegative with E[Z log Z] finite"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627951+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4dc336ffe1859932768872cd898d8a70b2b6935d4bd7b90c575ded181869d08f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) be a nonnegative random variable with E[Z log Z] finite. Write Ent(Z) = E[Z log Z] - E[Z] log E[Z] and let Ent^{(i)}(Z) denote the same functional computed with respect to X_i alone, with the other coordinates held fixed. Then Ent(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ Ent^{(i)}(Z) ]. The same statement with variance in place of entropy is the Efron-Stein inequality, and the two are the p = 2 and p = 1 members of a family of phi-entropies that all tensorize. Tensorization is what converts a ONE-DIMENSIONAL functional inequality into an n-dimensional one with no loss of constant: if each coordinate's law satisfies a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant C, then the product law satisfies it with the SAME constant C, independent of n. That dimension-free feature is the whole reason the entropy method produces concentration bounds that do not degrade as n grows. Independence of the coordinates is essential. [standard; e.g. Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 4.10 and Section 4.1]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.635894+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4dc3f1bcec7db304a707ed1904c1873b2db694de992292bd0c81d99a5696c2e8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma terms_in_signature_first of arXiv:2411.13707, 'High-degree cubature on Wiener space \\ through unshuffle expansions'] \[

as required, where we use \(\xi_{0ii}=\xi_{ii0}\) (reversal property) to obtain the final equivalence.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.695099+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4e2841da640a398408c72f98a4c00ba304f3a51379b2beecfbd04e38294d3c1f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:whole-plane-persistence of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Fix $\kappa,M,R>0$.  Then there exists $C=C(\kappa,M,R)>0$ such that the following
holds.  For $\varepsilon>0$, let
$\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy
\begin{equation}
  \omega_{\varepsilon,0}\geq0,\qquad
  \int_{\mathbb R^2}\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\,\mathrm d\mathbf x=\kappa,
  \qquad
  \|\omega_{\varepsilon,0}\|_\infty\leq M\varepsilon^{-2},
  \qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\omega_{\varepsilon,0}
  \subset B_{R\varepsilon}(\mathbf0).
\end{equation}
Let $\omega_{\varepsilon,t}$, $t\in\mathbb R$, be the corresponding Yudovich
solution of the two-dimensional Euler equation in $\mathbb R^2$.  Then
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})^2
  \leq C\mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,0}).
\end{equation}
If, in addition,
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,0})\leq\frac{\kappa^2}{C},
\end{equation}
then, with
\[
  \mathbf X_\varepsilon
  :=\frac1\kappa\int_{\mathbb R^2}\mathbf x
  \omega_{\varepsilon,0}(\mathbf x)\,\mathrm d\mathbf x,
\]
one has
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})}
  |\mathbf b-\mathbf X_\varepsilon|
  \leq (1+\sqrt2)R\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{\mathbf b\in\mathsf C(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})}
  |\mathbf b|
  \leq(2+\sqrt2)R\varepsilon.
\end{equation}
In particular, for any family of initial data satisfying
(equation eq:whole-plane-initial-data of the paper) with the same $\kappa,M,R$, if
$\mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,0})\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$, then
\[
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\mathcal A(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})\longrightarrow0,
  \qquad
  \sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\ \sup_{\mathbf b\in
  \mathsf C(\omega_{\varepsilon,t})}|\mathbf b|\longrightarrow0.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["both sequences (or functions) monotone in the same direction; opposite directions reverse the inequality","no independence or product structure needed beyond the single variable; the n-variable generalization is Harris-FKG"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049386+00:00","domain":"correlation inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_4e33e7a855f3b1ed38c5b184f81787d0bc6049fa0a51bfd8ff8f2972faba1f89","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"If a_1 >= a_2 >= ... >= a_n and b_1 >= b_2 >= ... >= b_n (both sequences sorted the same way), then (1/n) sum a_i b_i >= ((1/n) sum a_i) ((1/n) sum b_i); if one sequence is increasing and the other decreasing, the inequality reverses. The integral form: for f and g both monotone in the same direction on [0,1], the integral of f g is at least the product of the integrals. This is the one-dimensional case of the Harris-FKG inequality (a product of two increasing functions of one uniform variable has nonnegative covariance), and its proof is the identity 2(n sum a_i b_i - sum a_i sum b_j) = sum_{i,j} (a_i - a_j)(b_i - b_j) >= 0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Y = sum_{k>=0} B_k (2/3)^k with i.i.d. digits B_k, P(B_k=1)=p (the biased-coin Bernoulli convolution at contraction ratio lambda=2/3, equivalently the same non-Pisot ratio 3/2 used elsewhere in this campaign)","elementary dimension bound only: Hochman's theorem is NOT used; only the entropy-over-Lyapunov upper bound on dimension and the fact that a measure on R of dimension below 1 cannot be absolutely continuous"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:46:59.956588+00:00","domain":"probability/Bernoulli convolutions","id":"claim_4e3f794ecd634c87b21e676f1227583d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the biased Bernoulli convolution at ratio 2/3 - the law of sum_k B_k (2/3)^k with B_k i.i.d., P(B_k = 1) = p - the measure is singular for every p < p* = 0.140277, where p* solves H(p) = log(3/2) in natural logarithms (H(p)/log(3/2) = 0.4896, 0.8018, 1.2341, 1.7095 at p = 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 1/2). Proof: the dimension of the measure is at most the entropy-over-Lyapunov ratio H(p)/log(3/2), and a measure on the line of dimension below one is not absolutely continuous; Hochman's theorem is needed only for the matching lower bound dim = min(1, H(p)/log(3/2)), which this does not use. Two further thresholds govern the Fourier criterion at this ratio. The biased factor |(1-p) + p e^{i phi}|^2 = 1 - 2p(1-p)(1 - cos phi) has arithmetic mean 1 - 2p(1-p) over the phase, which gives the annealed (main-term) exponent alpha(p) = 1 + log(1 - 2p(1-p))/log(3/2), zero at p(1-p) = 1/6, i.e. p = (1 - 3^{-1/2})/2 = 0.211325; and log-mean 2 log(1-p), which gives the quenched (typical) threshold (3/2)(1-p)^2 = 1 at p = 0.183503. As a calibration control for statistics on the unbiased Bernoulli convolution at 2/3 (the same ratio, frequencies and arithmetic, only the weights changed): below p* the measure is singular and a detection is expected; above 0.2113 the main term decays and a pass is expected; between 0.1403 and 0.2113 the measure has dimension one while the main term already diverges, so a reading there means nothing - controls belong at p <= 0.12 and p >= 0.35. Unlike the Pisot control lambda = 1/phi, where one localised cell forces the reading a priori, the absence of such a cell at ratio 3/2 is Mahler's open problem on ||(3/2)^m xi||, so the control's genuineness rests on an empirical extensiveness test: a flat per-step rate means one cell forces the reading, a wobbling rate means a real measurement (flat to 0.0005 at 1/phi from K = 8; wobbling by 0.028 at the unbiased 2/3).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:51:11.471805+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4e48e536a83a43df0f28d7463c2f2b582bdc348a6b07de64b0af0bcef2522415","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 35 ({\cite[Definition~3.6) of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] {LX}}]
Let $f: X \rightarrow S$ be a projective surjective morphism of integral excellent schemes with $X$ normal. Let $D$ be a $\Q$-Cartier $\Q$-divisor on $X$, and let $v$ be a divisorial valuation over $X$.
Take a projective birational morphism $\mu :Y \rightarrow X$ from a normal integral scheme, a prime divisor $\Gamma$ on $Y$, and $\lambda\in\R_{>0}$ such that $v=\lambda\cdot\ord_{\Gamma}$ (Remark~\ref{excval}).
We define the asymptotic vanishing order $v(\| D/S \|)$ of $D$ along $v$ as
\[ v(\| D/S \|) := \lambda\cdot\ord_{\Gamma}(Y/S,\|\mu^{*}D\|) = \lambda\cdot\ord_{\Gamma}(\|\mu^{*}D\|,Y/S). \]
This definition is independent of the choice of $Y$ and $\Gamma$ by Lemma~\ref{ordaffine} and Remark~\ref{ordrem}.
When $S$ is affine, we write $v(\| D/S \|)$ by $v(\| D\|)$ since it is independent of the choice of $S$ by Remark~\ref{ordrem}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving","f is integrable","the sets are defined through the partial sums S_n f, n >= 1"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438013+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, maximal inequalities","id":"claim_4e5da40826ced68e04e188001f421a2ff04ef2165ef899ef0c91ed9c71f6fc4c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu)$ be a probability space (a finite or even $\\sigma$-finite measure suffices here), $T: X \\to X$ measure-preserving, $f \\in L^1(\\mu)$ real-valued. Write $S_n f = \\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f \\circ T^k$ and $F_N = \\max_{1 \\le n \\le N} S_n f$. Then\n$$\\int_{\\{F_N > 0\\}} f\\,d\\mu \\ \\ge\\ 0 \\quad \\text{for every } N \\ge 1,$$\nand consequently $\\int_{\\{\\sup_n S_n f > 0\\}} f\\,d\\mu \\ge 0$. The maximal inequality follows: for $\\alpha > 0$, $\\mu\\big(\\{ \\sup_{n} \\tfrac{1}{n} S_n f > \\alpha \\}\\big) \\le \\tfrac{1}{\\alpha} \\int_{\\{\\sup_n S_n f / n > \\alpha\\}} f\\,d\\mu \\le \\tfrac{1}{\\alpha}\\|f\\|_1$ (apply the first statement to $f - \\alpha$; for the last step in infinite measure one needs $f \\ge 0$ or $\\mu$ finite, since $\\int (f - \\alpha)$ over the set is where $\\mu$ finite is used). This is the only analytic input needed for the pointwise ergodic theorem. It fails if $T$ does not preserve $\\mu$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.723939+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4e92ce6e9b8fc59cb1d4748bc8c36496d4a69b015f697587300eb89a24e12c0a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 22 of arXiv:2609.01190, 'Rough differential equations on manifolds via natural bundles'] Let $f:\Rsf^m\to\Rsf$ be a smooth, compactly supported function and let $\varepsilon, \tilde{\varepsilon}, \delta, \zeta\in [0,\infty)$ and $a,b, \tilde{a},\tilde{b}\in\Rsf^m$ be such that 
	\[
		|b-a|\leq \varepsilon, 
			\quad 
		|\tilde{b}-\tilde{a}|\leq \tilde{\varepsilon}, 
			\quad 
		|\tilde{a}-a|\leq \delta, 
			\quad\mbox{and}\quad 
		|\tilde{b}-\tilde{a} - (b-a)| \leq \zeta.
	\]
Let also $T_0,T_1: \Rsf^m\times\Rsf^m\to\Rsf$ be defined by 
	\begin{align*}
		& T_0(x,y):= f(y)-f(x),\\
		& T_1(x,y):= f(y)-f(x)- \frac{\partial f}{\partial x^j}(x)(y^j-x^j)
	\end{align*}
for $x,y\in\Rsf^m$. Then
	\[
		\left|T_0(a,b)\right|  \lesssim \varepsilon 
		\quad\mbox{and}\quad
		|T_0(\tilde{a},\tilde{b})-T_0(a,b)| \lesssim \varepsilon(\delta + \zeta) + \zeta,
	\]
and
	\[
		 |T_1(a,b)| \lesssim \varepsilon^2
		 \quad \mbox{and}\quad 
		 |T_1(\tilde{a},\tilde{b})-T_1(a,b)| \lesssim \varepsilon^2(\delta + \zeta) + (\varepsilon + \tilde{\varepsilon})\zeta
	\]
where the constants are non-decreasing functions of $C^1$, $C^2$, $C^2$, and $C^3$ norm of $f$, respectively. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:25:49.855602+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4eb4b78d554fab8ddb9fc9612ccfe67c15dcb1b6da850a01422157eecbf91919","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 of arXiv:2609.02019, '2609.02019'] Let $s>\frac{3}{2}+\max\{2\delta_{\mathcal Q},1\}$.Let $\tau^*$ be a stopping time with $\mathbb P(\tau^*>0)=1$.
		An $H^s$-valued progressively measurable process
		\[
		v=(v(t))_{0\le t<\tau^*}
		\]
		is called a maximal $H^s$ classical solution to \eqref{Target problem SCCF} if the
		following conditions hold:
		
		\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0.79cm]
			\setlength\itemsep{0.2em}
			
			\item  For a.e. $\omega\in\Omega$, and for every $T<\tau^*(\omega)$,

			\item On the event $\{\tau^*<\infty\}$,
			$\limsup_{t\uparrow\tau^*}\|v(t)\|_{H^s}=\infty.$
			
		\end{itemize}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:24:20.645892+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4ec873d06ff22a2b37214214c7389d6627ae122b760d7d702368898982b7647c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:main1 of arXiv:2608.11084, 'Sharp Frobenius-Norm Concentration for Sample Moment Tensors'] Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_N\) be i.i.d. copies of a centered sub-Gaussian random
vector \(X\in\mathbb R^d\) with covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) and
sub-Gaussian constant \(K\). Let \(p\ge 2\) be an integer. Then, for every
\(q\ge1\),
\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\mathbbm{E}
\bigg\|
\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N X_i^{\otimes p}
-
\mathbbm{E} X^{\otimes p}
\bigg\|_{\mathsf F}^q
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
\lesssim_p
K^p
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N}
+
\rho_p(\Sigma)\sqrt{\frac{q\land N}{N}}
+
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N}
\aftergroup\egroup\originalright),
\]
where
\[
\rho_p(\Sigma)
:=
\begin{cases}
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2},
& p \text{ even},\\[3pt]
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-1)/2}\|\Sigma\|^{1/2},
& p \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Moreover, if $X$ is Gaussian, then
\[
\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(\mathbbm{E} \bigg\|
\frac{1}{N}
\sum_{i=1}^N
X_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbbm{E} X^{\otimes p}
\bigg\|_{\mathsf{F}}^q\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)^{1/q}
\asymp_p
\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Sigma)^{p/2}}{\sqrt{N}}
+
\rho_{p,G}(\Sigma)\sqrt{\frac{q}{N}}
+
\|\Sigma\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N},
\]
where
\[
\rho_{p,G}(\Sigma)
:=
\begin{cases}
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{p/2-1}\|\Sigma\|, & p \text{ even},\\[3pt]
\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf{F}}^{(p-1)/2}\|\Sigma\|^{1/2}, & p \text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["entries independent up to symmetry with mean 0 and variance 1 before scaling by 1/sqrt n","moments bounded uniformly in n (finite fourth moment suffices for the semicircle limit of the empirical spectral distribution; the diagonal entries may have a different variance)","the moment method identifies the limit because the semicircle law is determined by its moments (compact support)"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.049288+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_4f1567c38734286426940b4f4f52f264db38c2264b6a25725643dc91aea4918c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"For the semicircle density (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(4 - x^2) on [-2, 2] (mean 0, variance 1), all odd moments vanish and the 2k-th moment equals the Catalan number C_k = (1/(k+1)) binom(2k, k): 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, ... . A semicircle of radius R has 2k-th moment C_k (R/2)^{2k}. In the moment method for a Wigner matrix W = X / sqrt n, where X is real symmetric with independent entries above the diagonal, mean 0 and variance 1, the normalized traces satisfy E tr(W^{2k}) / n -> C_k: expanding the trace as a sum over closed walks of length 2k on the index set, only walks whose edges are each traversed exactly twice and whose underlying graph is a tree survive as n grows, and such walks are counted by C_k; the Catalan numbers determine the semicircle law uniquely because it has compact support. Wigner's theorem then follows from convergence of moments plus a variance bound (or a concentration bound on the trace) giving weak convergence of the empirical spectral distribution in probability.","status":"unverified"}

Then $a^\ast a = |a|^2$ is selfadjoint, and so has a spectral measure $\mu_{|a|^2}$: the unique compactly-supported probability distribution on $\R_+$ whose moments are given by $\int x^k \mu_{|a|^2}(dx) = \tau[(a^\ast a)^k]$ (see \eqref{eq.spectral.meas}).  Denote by $\nu_a$ the push-forward of $\mu_{|a|^2}$ under $x\mapsto\sqrt{x}$; in other words, $\nu_a$ is the spectral measure of $|a|:=\sqrt{a^\ast a}$.

For $z\in\C$, define the {\bf log potential} $U_a\colon\C\to\R\cup\{-\infty\}$ by
\[ U_a(z):= \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\infty \log(x)\,\nu_{a-z}(dx). \]
It is a subharmonic function, and so its (weak) Laplacian is a positive Radon measure.  In this case it is a probability measure: the {\bf Brown measure of $a$}
\[ \mu_a:= \Delta U_a \quad \text{i.e.} \quad
\int_{\C} \psi\,d\mu_a = \int_{\C} \Delta\psi(z)\, U_a(z)\,dz \qquad \forall\,\psi\in C^\infty(\C). \]
The Brown measure is then also uniquely defined by 
\[ \int_{\C} \log |\lambda-z|\,\mu_a(d\lambda) = U_a(z). \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499458+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_4f46b2de22e7549670bcc1dce7b0f972c96bfd2b3336d5d4426cf06f59a598fa","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Weierstrass convergence theorem (a locally uniform limit of holomorphic functions is holomorphic and derivatives converge locally uniformly) has no real-variable analogue and does not upgrade to uniform convergence on the whole domain. (1) Real failure: f_n(x) = sin(n^2 x)/n converges to 0 uniformly on R, but the derivatives f_n'(x) = n cos(n^2 x) do not converge to the derivative of the limit — at x = 0, f_n'(0) = n → ∞ — so uniform convergence of real functions carries no information about derivatives. More dramatically, by the Weierstrass approximation theorem every continuous nowhere differentiable function on [0,1] is a uniform limit of polynomials, so uniform limits of real-analytic functions need not be differentiable anywhere. The complex proof uses the Cauchy estimates, which need holomorphy on a two-dimensional neighborhood: a bound on |g| on a disk controls all derivatives at the center. (2) Only locally uniform: f_n(z) = z^n/n converges to 0 uniformly on all of D, yet f_n'(z) = z^{n-1} has supremum 1 on D for every n and does not converge uniformly on D. So the derivative statement must be quoted with 'uniformly on compact subsets'; deducing a uniform derivative bound up to the boundary from a uniform bound on the functions is a genuine error, and controlling it requires extra input (a larger domain of holomorphy, or boundary regularity). (3) The hypothesis is convergence on compact subsets of the open set, not convergence on the closed set: a sequence converging uniformly on the closed unit disk still gives derivative convergence only on |z| ≤ r < 1 unless the functions are holomorphic on a larger disk.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:25:39.116617+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4f52df7591d276d237c39a099ff651be4172081a5ae7f970158d4c820b49a008","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def: partition procedure in sle of arXiv:2606.13147, 'Scaling limits of the single-curve interface and outermost loops in the planar random fiel'] Fix a sufficiently small constant $\iota>0$, and set
$M=\iota r^{3\kappa}N.$
For a box $\mathsf{B}$, write
$S_\gamma(\mathsf{B}):=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{B}}{\operatorname{dist}}(x,\gamma)^{-1/4}.$
We define the following recursive partition procedure. We first partition $\Lambda_N$ into boxes of side length $M$. Given a current box $\mathsf{B}$, we proceed as follows.

If
$
S_\gamma(\mathsf{B})<M^{7/4},
$
we leave $\mathsf{B}$ unchanged.
If
$
S_\gamma(\mathsf{B})\ge M^{7/4},
$
we divide $\mathsf{B}$ into two sub-boxes according to the following rule. Suppose, after translation and rotation if necessary, that
$
\mathsf{B}=[1,a]\times[1,b],
1\le a\le b.
$
For \(0\le c\le b\), let
$
\mathsf{C}_1(c)=[1,a]\times[1,c],
\mathsf{C}_2(c)=[1,a]\times[c+1,b],
$
with the convention that empty boxes are omitted. We choose \(c\) so that
$
\big|S_\gamma(\mathsf{C}_1(c))-S_\gamma(\mathsf{C}_2(c))\big|
$
is minimized, and replace \(\mathsf{B}\) by the two boxes \(\mathsf{C}_1(c)\) and \(\mathsf{C}_2(c)\).

We repeat this procedure until every current box \(\mathsf{B}\) satisfies
$
S_\gamma(\mathsf{B})<M^{7/4}.
$
The resulting collection of boxes is denoted by
$
\mathsf{B}_1,\ldots,\mathsf{B}_n.
$
Finally, we set
$
\mathsf{B}_i^+=\mathsf{B}_i\cap\Lambda^+,
\mathsf{B}_i^-=\mathsf{B}_i\cap\Lambda^-.
$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f is entire","M(r) denotes the maximum modulus on the circle of radius r"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.483753+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_4f9f621425ba3aa6639c052588aacad670196f81a185514037630e2dd0e75a91","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be a nonconstant entire function and M(r) = max_{|z| = r} |f(z)|. The order of f is ρ = limsup_{r→∞} (log log M(r))/(log r) in [0, ∞]; equivalently ρ = inf{λ ≥ 0 : M(r) ≤ exp(r^λ) for all sufficiently large r}, with the infimum of the empty set taken to be ∞. Constant functions are assigned order 0. If 0 < ρ < ∞ one further distinguishes the type σ = limsup_{r→∞} log M(r)/r^ρ. Examples: every nonconstant polynomial has order 0; exp(z), sin z, cos z and 1/Γ have order 1; exp(z^n) has order n; cos(sqrt z) has order 1/2; exp(exp(z)) has infinite order. If f has finite order ρ and nonzero zeros (a_n) listed with multiplicity, then Σ_n |a_n|^{-s} < ∞ for every s > ρ; the exponent of convergence of the zeros, λ = inf{s > 0 : Σ_n |a_n|^{-s} < ∞}, satisfies λ ≤ ρ, and the inequality can be strict (exp(z) has order 1 and no zeros at all).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:18:13.294453+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_4fe9be5b3a390b33f23aad5959c861507b8ab26e18ed2db78f7a203c0c015431","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:disconnect_interior of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] {amy-cle-resampling}}]

Suppose that $\Gamma$ is a nested ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa}${} in a simply connected domain $D$, and let $\Upsilon_\Gamma$ be its gasket. For each $a\in(0,1)$, $b>0$ there exists $p > 0$ such that the following holds. 

Let $z\in D$ and $j_0\in\mathbf{Z}$ be such that $B(z,2^{-j_0})\subseteq D$. There exists a resampling $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ of $\Gamma$ within $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$ for each $j>j_0$ with the following property. Let $G^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ be the event that $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ has a loop $\widetilde\mathcal {L}$ that
\begin{itemize}
 \item disconnects every point in $\Upsilon_{\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}} \cap B(z,2^{-j})$ from $\partial B(z,2^{-j+1})$,
 \item the gasket and the collection of loops of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ remain the same in each connected component of $\mathbf{C} \setminus \widetilde\mathcal {L}$ that intersects $B(z,2^{-j})$.
\end{itemize}
For $k\in\mathbf{N}$, let $\widetilde G_{z,j_0,k}$ be the event that the number of $j=j_0+1,\ldots,j_0+k$ so that
\[ \mathbf{P}[ G^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j} \,|\, \Gamma ] \geq p\]
is at least $(1-a)k$.  Then
\[ \mathbf{P}[(\widetilde G_{z,j_0,k})^c] = O(e^{-b k}) \]
where the implicit constant does not depend on $z,j_0,k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

A quantizer is \\emph{shared-scale uniform} if every coefficient of a group is stored at the same bit-width on a uniform grid with a single shared scale, so no bits can be re-allocated between coordinates: the per-group \\texttt{INT4} grid of a deployed low-bit kernel (\\texttt{MXFP4} and \\texttt{NVFP4} are shared-scale on a \\emph{non-uniform} element grid, a second axis taken up in \\Cref{sec:format}). {"assumptions":["f ∈ C^1","u is a weak solution which is piecewise C^1 with C^1 shock curves and one-sided traces (the equivalence as stated is for this piecewise-smooth class; Kruzhkov's definition is what governs general L^∞ solutions)","the chord condition must hold at EVERY point of EVERY discontinuity curve","Rankine-Hugoniot alone is not sufficient: it fixes σ but permits inadmissible jumps"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.417666+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_502c4a8cf7e11bf1fd64197cea9e23277293f004895262e4972b802ea4718867","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f ∈ C^1(R) and let u ∈ L^∞(R × (0,∞)) be a weak solution of u_t + f(u)_x = 0 that is piecewise C^1: away from finitely many disjoint C^1 curves x = s_i(t) it is C^1, and it has C^1 one-sided traces u_-(t) (from x < s_i(t)) and u_+(t) (from x > s_i(t)) on each curve. Each curve then satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, σ := s_i'(t) = ( f(u_-) - f(u_+) ) / ( u_- - u_+ ) when u_- ≠ u_+. Such a u is a Kruzhkov entropy solution if and only if at every point of every discontinuity curve the chord condition holds: for every k strictly between u_- and u_+, ( f(k) - f(u_-) ) / ( k - u_- ) ≥ σ ≥ ( f(k) - f(u_+) ) / ( k - u_+ ). Equivalently: if u_+ < u_-, the graph of f on [u_+,u_-] lies on or below the chord joining (u_+,f(u_+)) to (u_-,f(u_-)); if u_- < u_+, the graph of f on [u_-,u_+] lies on or above that chord. If f is strictly convex, this is equivalent to the Lax shock inequalities f'(u_-) ≥ σ ≥ f'(u_+), i.e. to u_- > u_+: a strictly convex flux admits only downward jumps.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.580002+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_503939e72fdf489c347d6441b85be326b2e5fbed44bfca332cdf0722bc122d72","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 13 (CRT scaling limit of the critical cluster; conditional on Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red}) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Assume Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red}, criticality $\rho(M)=1$, irreducibility and aperiodicity as in Theorem~\ref{thm:32}, and in addition that the offspring distributions admit finite exponential moments: $\E[e^{t\deg}]<\infty$ for some $t>0$ (e.g.\ bounded degrees, or Poissonian $g$). Then there is an explicit constant $\Sigma\in(0,\infty)$, computable from the second-moment matrices of the offspring law and the Perron eigenvectors of $M$ (Appendix~\ref{app:miermont}), such that, conditionally on $\{|S|=n\}$,
\[
\Big(S,\ \frac{\Sigma}{\sqrt n}\,d_{\mathrm{gr}},\ \mathrm{unif}_S\Big)\ \xrightarrow{(d)}\ \big(\mathcal T_e,d_e,\mu_e\big)\qquad(n\to\infty)
\]
in the GHP topology, where $d_{\mathrm{gr}}$ is the graph distance on the cluster and $\mathrm{unif}_S$ the uniform probability measure on its vertices. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.543870+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_503a791b1755d53c7385e64d56512fef661f8ac68a58a89821ec3caef72ecfb3","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 30 (Coordinate representation) of arXiv:2603.28734, 'Free energy analyticity of the disordered XY model and Debye screening in the 2D Coulomb g'] Let $G$ be a finite graph and $\beta\in[0,\infty)$.
    Define $\mu_{G,\beta}'$ as the probability measure on
    \[
        \tau:=(\alpha,\omega,\eta)\in [0,\tfrac\pi2]^V\times\{0,1\}^E\times\{0,1\}^E:=\Pi_G
    \]
    with density
    \begin{align}
        &
        \diff\mu_{G,\beta}'(\tau)
        \propto
        \textstyle
        \left(\prod_{u\in V}\diff\alpha_u\right)
        \\
        &
        \qquad\qquad
        \textstyle
        \cdot
        2^{k(\omega)}
        \left(
            \prod_{uv\in \omega}
                (1-\e^{-2\beta(\cos\alpha_u)(\cos\alpha_v)})
            \middle)\middle(
            \prod_{uv\not\in\omega}
                e^{-2\beta(\cos\alpha_u)(\cos\alpha_v)}
            \right)
            \\&
            \qquad\qquad
            \textstyle
            \cdot
            2^{k(\eta)}
            \left(
                \prod_{uv\in \eta}
                     (1-\e^{-2\beta(\sin\alpha_u)(\sin\alpha_v)})
                \middle)\middle(
                \prod_{uv\not\in\eta}
                    e^{-2\beta(\sin\alpha_u)(\sin\alpha_v)}
                \right).
    \end{align}
    Here $k(\rho)$ denotes the number of connected components of $(V,\rho)$.

    Now obtain a sample $\sigma\in(\S^1)^V$ as follows:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Sample $\tau\sim\mu_{G,\beta}'$,
        \item Sample $\xi\in\{-1,+1\}^V$ by flipping a fair coin for each connected component of $\omega$,
        \item Sample $\zeta\in\{-1,+1\}^V$ by flipping a fair coin for each connected component of $\eta$,
        \item Set $\sigma_u:=\xi_u\cos\alpha_u + i\cdot \zeta_u\sin\alpha_u$ for each $u\in V$.
    \end{itemize}
    Then $\sigma\sim\mu_{G,\beta}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["bond percolation on the square lattice Z^2","the Harris half as sketched uses Burton-Keane uniqueness, self-duality, the square-root trick and a planar topological argument","the Kesten half is stated but not proved in this node"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543220+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5050896df8f7fb9dbfa990fc0b0cefbd0928a39e58de37c123d446e63228d84e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For bond percolation on the square lattice Z^2, p_c = 1/2, and moreover theta(1/2) = 0: there is no infinite open cluster AT the critical point. The two halves have separate histories and separate proofs. HARRIS (1960) proved theta(1/2) = 0, which gives p_c >= 1/2. KESTEN (1980) proved that theta(p) > 0 for every p > 1/2, giving p_c <= 1/2. The self-duality of Z^2 bond percolation at p = 1/2 - the dual of the open configuration at parameter p is a configuration at parameter 1 - p on an isomorphic lattice - makes 1/2 the ONLY candidate but does not by itself decide the critical behaviour, which is why the theorem is hard. The corresponding value for SITE percolation on Z^2 is not known; for site percolation on the triangular lattice the answer is 1/2 by the same duality mechanism, and that is the case where conformal invariance at criticality is proved. [Harris (1960); Kesten (1980), Comm. Math. Phys. 74; see Grimmett, Percolation, 2nd ed., Chapter 11, or Bollobas-Riordan, Percolation]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:54:57.544734+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_505cff961fe29adc78b740b001ea81ac013720965efddfef7f16a6e13715fb7e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:conv-immig of arXiv:2412.03325, 'Functional limit theorem for branching processes \\ in nearly degenerate varying environme'] Assume that the BPVEI $(Y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ defined in (equation eq:Y of the paper) satisfies the conditions (C1)--(C3) and (C4) or (C4') holds. Then, for any $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$,
\[
\mathcal{L} ((Y_{A(nt)})_{t \geq  \varepsilon}) 
\stackrel{\mathcal{D}}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{L} ((W(\log t))_{t \geq \varepsilon}),
\]
as $n\to \infty$, 
where $(W(u))_{u\geq \log \varepsilon}$ is a continuous time branching 
process with immigration with initial distribution having g.f.,
\[
\log f_Y(s) 
= 
\begin{cases}
-\sum_{k=1}^{\kappa} 
\frac{2^k\lambda_k}{\nu^k} \left( \log\left( 
1+\frac{\nu}{2}(1-s)\right) +
\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\frac{\nu^i}{i2^i}
(s-1)^i\right), & \nu > 0, \\
\sum_{k=1}^{\kappa} \frac{\lambda_k}{k} (s-1)^k, & \nu = 0,
\end{cases}
\]
with parameters $\alpha = 1+\nu$, $\beta = \sum_{k=1}^{\kappa}(-1)^{k+1}\lambda_k$,
and
\[
\begin{split}
f(s) & = (1+\nu)^{-1} \left(1+\frac{\nu}{2} + \frac{\nu}{2}s^2\right), \\
h(s) & = 1 + \beta^{-1} \sum_{k=1}^{\kappa} \lambda_k (s-1)^k,
\end{split}
\]
offspring and immigration g.f.'s, where $\kappa=K-1$ or $\kappa=\infty$ depending on whether condition (C4) or (C4') holds. The transition generating function of $W$ is given by
\begin{equation*} 
G_y(s, t) = \mathbf{E} \left[ s^{W(t + u)} | W(u) = y \right] = 
\frac{f_Y(s)}{f_Y(h_{e^{-t}}(s))} \left( h_{e^{-t}}(s) \right)^y.
\end{equation*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:33:23.329702+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_50e99db7fab5de34e42901cf169a0e65c9872e5e8b323f985fe2bd615bfa0997","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 3 of arXiv:2506.21829, 'Some notes on Lamperti's recurrence of stochastic sequences'] Assume that \eqref{1}, integrability condition \eqref{2} and assumptions \eqref{4.3}, \eqref{4.4}, \eqref{4.5} and \eqref{4.6} are satisfied.
Then the stochastic sequence is recurrent if, as $x\to\infty$, we almost surely have
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{p\mathsf{E}\{X_{n+1}-X_n~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}>X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}{q\mathsf{E}\{X_{n}-X_{n+1}~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}<X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}\\
&\leq1+\frac{R}{x}+O\left(\frac{1}{x^{1+\epsilon}}\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
where $R(x)=\mathsf{E}\{|X_{n+1}-X_n|~\big|~X_{n}=x, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}$, and $R$ is the limit with probability $1$ of $R(x)$ as $x\to\infty$.
If instead
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{p\mathsf{E}\{X_{n+1}-X_n~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}>X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}{q\mathsf{E}\{X_{n}-X_{n+1}~|~X_n=x, X_{n+1}<X_n, X_{n-1},\ldots, X_0\}}\\
&\geq1+\frac{R\theta}{x},
\end{aligned}
\]
for some $\theta>1$ and almost all large $x$, then the stochastic sequence is transient.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.748203+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5119aefa059987b20f12db27480d76d172e58a0c0cd4c4f5a4252aa1385c07b2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 14 (Renewal--reward CLT) of arXiv:2607.28865, 'First-Passage Percolation on Spread-out line graphs: Microscopic Regime'] Let $\{(X_i,Y_i)\}_{i\ge1}$ be i.i.d.~with $X_i\in\dN$,
\begin{align*}
\E X_1=\mu\in(0,\infty),
\qquad
\E Y_1=\nu\in\dR,
\qquad
\E X_1^2+\E Y_1^2<\infty.
\end{align*}
Define
\begin{align*}
S_m:=\sum_{i=1}^m X_i,
\qquad
R_m:=\sum_{i=1}^m Y_i,
\qquad
N_t:=\max\{m\ge0:S_m\le t\},
\qquad
R(t):=R_{N_t}.
\end{align*}
Then, as $t\to\infty$,
\begin{align}
t^{-1/2}\cdot (R(t)-t\cdot {\nu}/{\mu})
\Longrightarrow
\N(0,\sigma^2),
\end{align}
where $\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{\mu} \var\left(Y_1-\nu/{\mu}\cdot X_1\right)$.
Equivalently,
\begin{align}
t^{-1/2}\cdot (R(t)-\E R(t))
\Longrightarrow
\N(0,\sigma^2).
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.494264+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_513e6ccde40e00de941c0461f711fe6f1ed11768f73c046cd05e56a56bce74a7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 21 (One-hive marginal of the  quadruply augmented double hive law) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] \lab{lem:double-one-hive}
Assume \(\bar a,\bar b,\bar d>0\), and assume either \(\bar f>0\), or
\[
\bar f^2<0,
\qquad
\bar a^2+\bar b^2+\bar d^2+\bar f^2<0.
\]
Let \(p_{\mathrm{dbl}}\) be the density on \(\mathbb D^4\) from
Lemma~\ref{lem:double-maxent}.  Put
\[
T=\bar a^2+\bar b^2+\bar d^2+\bar f^2.
\]
Define the geometric side lengths
\[
a^2=\frac{\bar a^2(T-\bar a^2)}{T},\qquad
b^2=\frac{\bar b^2(T-\bar b^2)}{T},
\]
\[
d^2=\frac{\bar d^2(T-\bar d^2)}{T},\qquad
f^2=\frac{\bar f^2(T-\bar f^2)}{T},
\]
and
\[
c_*^2=
\frac{(\bar a^2+\bar b^2)(\bar d^2+\bar f^2)}{T}.
\]
In the second case these quantities are still positive, since
\(\bar d^2+\bar f^2<-(\bar a^2+\bar b^2)\).
Let \(h_1\) denote the first hive, so that
\[
h_1\in H_n(\alpha,\beta;\nu).
\]
Then the marginal law of \(h_1\) is
\[
\mathcal H_n(a,b,c_*).
\]
Similarly, the marginal law of the second hive is
\(\mathcal H_n(d,f,c_*)\); in the case \(\bar f^2<0\), this is understood
using the symmetry of the three boundary components to place the imaginary
raw parameter in the third slot of Theorem~\ref{thm:gaussian1}.  Moreover,
\(c_*\) is the value of the glued side selected by Lemma~\ref{lem:doublehive}:
it maximizes
\[
x\mapsto
\frac{\Delta_{abx}^2}{abx}\frac{\Delta_{xdf}^2}{xdf}.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\[

Each element of \(\mathbf{T}_j\) is a subtree rooted at a vertex at height \(j\) that admits at least one descendant at height \(h^*\). Note that \(|\mathbf{T}_j|=|\cX_j|=X_j\).

We then write \(\mathsf{T}_1,\ldots,\mathsf{T}_{|\mathbf{T}_j|}\) for a uniform random ordering of the elements of \(\mathbf{T}_j\). Finally, we introduce the labeling map

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.096313+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_521d8b2552ac54fe398b53b3651e9496b3fe562d609da8d501e77cfd5cdd303b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:ricci-removal of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $P_z$ be the rank-one projector onto a unit decomposable bivector and
$C_z=P_z-N^{-1}I_W$.  If $L_z=-2z_{\rm mat}^2$ is the orthogonal
projector onto the plane of $z$, put
\[
 B_z=\frac{L_z-(2/n)I_H}{n-2}.
\tag{2.6.2}
\]
Then the orthogonal curvature decomposition is
\[
 C_z=W_z+X_{B_z},\qquad W_z\in\mathcal W,
 \qquad X_B(u\wedge v)=Bu\wedge v+u\wedge Bv,
\tag{2.6.3}
\]
with no scalar or $\Lambda^4H$ summand, and
\[
 \|B_z\|_\mathrm{op}=\frac1n,\qquad
 \|B_z\|_F^2=\frac{2}{n(n-2)},\qquad
 \|X_B\|_2^2=(n-2)\|B\|_F^2,\qquad
 \|X_B\|_\mathrm{op}\le2\|B\|_\mathrm{op}.
\tag{2.6.4}
\]

In the cumulative moving frame the transported $B_z$ are reverse
martingale differences.  If $\mathfrak B_r$ is their sum, then
\[
 \mathbb E\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^2=\frac{2r}{n(n-2)},\qquad
 \mathbb E\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^4
 \le C\frac{r^2}{n^2(n-2)^2},
\tag{2.6.5}
\]
and, for fixed $c$, uniformly over $r\le cN$,
\[
 \max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_\mathrm{op}=o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\tag{2.6.6}
\]
More quantitatively, for every fixed $L$ and $1\le p\le L\log n$,
\[
 \left(\mathbb E\max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_\mathrm{op}^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le C_{c,L}\left(
 \sqrt{\frac{p+\log n}{n}}+\frac{p+\log n}{n}
 \right)=o(1).
\tag{2.6.6a}
\]
The same martingale satisfies the dimension-free Frobenius estimate
\[
 \left(\mathbb E\max_{r\le cN}\|\mathfrak B_r\|_F^p\right)^{1/p}
 \le C_c\sqrt p,
 \qquad 2\le p\le L\log n.
\tag{2.6.6b}
\]

Finally let $A_i=\operatorname{ad}_{a_i}$.  For traceless symmetric $B$
on $H$ and arbitrary $Z\in\operatorname{End}(W)$, define
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R_i(B,Z)&=\{X_B,[A_i,Z]\}a_i,&
 U_i(B,Z)&=\{X_B,Z\}a_i,\\
 E_i(B,Z)&=\{X_{[a_i,B]},Z\}a_i,&
 \bar E(B,Z)&=N^{-1}\sum_iE_i(B,Z).
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.6.7}
\]
Put $\Psi(T)=\sum_jA_jTa_j$ and
$H_B(Z)=-N^{-1}X_B\Psi(Z)$.  Then the exact two-gradient decomposition is
\[
 \boxed{\mathcal R_i=A_iU_i-(E_i-\bar E)
 -\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j-H_B(Z)},
 \qquad
 \bar E=\frac1N\sum_jA_jV_j+H_B(Z),\qquad V_j=X_BZa_j,
\tag{2.6.8}
\]
and its star-normalized square functions obey
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac1N\sum_i\|U_i\|^2
 &\le\frac{4(n-2)}N\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_j\|V_j\|^2
 &\le\frac{n-2}N\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2,\\
 \frac1N\sum_i\|E_i-\bar E\|^2
 &\le\frac{64}{n-1}\|B\|_F^2\|Z\|_\mathrm{op}^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.6.9}
\]
The residue obeys
\[
 \|H_B(Z)\|
 \le\frac{2\sqrt{n-2}}N\|B\|_\mathrm{op}\|Z\|_2.
\tag{2.6.9a}
\]","status":"unverified"}

sequences of nested intervals are related by this equivalence relation.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.352323+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5310e525d1c3d04c2bef6caeeac83b6c9e99a5bb8f52bec5a90cd4dbd947d4db","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 194 (subsequential limits) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $N\to\infty$ with parameters satisfying Assumption~\ref{a:params}. Then the measures $\Q_N$, as defined by \eqref{e:pm.on.pm.over.paths.Gamma}, are tight. Moreover, for any subsequential limit $\Q$, if $\mu\sim\Q$ and $(\Gamma,\Upsilon,\mathcal{E})\sim\mu$, then $\mathcal{E}\equiv0$. The ``$\frozen$'' variant of the statement also holds. 

\begin{proof}
Write $\E_N$ for expectation with respect to $\Q_N$. We use Assumption~\ref{a:params} throughout. We will argue that $\Gamma^N$ and $\Upsilon^N$ are asymptotically equivalent to
	\[
	\bar{\Gamma}^N
	\equiv \Big(
	\bar{D}^{\RomI},
	Q^{\RomII},Q^{\RomII,\RomIII},C^{\RomIII}, Q^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,,\quad
	\bar{\Upsilon}^N
	\equiv\Big( 
	Y^{\RomII},Y^{\RomIII},Y^{\Ising}
	\Big)\,.
	\]
For the purposes of this proof, it is more convenient to treat $\bar{D}^{\RomI}$ separately, and group together the remaining processes as
	\[
	\bar{f}^N
	\equiv
	\Big(
	Q^{\RomII},Q^{\RomII,\RomIII},C^{\RomIII}, Q^{\Ising},
		Y^{\RomII},Y^{\RomIII},Y^{\Ising}
	\Big)
	\,.\]
By Proposition~\ref{p:drift.kolmogorov}, for $N$ large enough we have
	\beq
	\frac{\E_N[\|
		\bar{D}^{\RomI,N}(t) -
		\bar{D}^{\RomI,N}(s)
		\|^2]}{(t-s)^2}
	\le L^{O(1)}
	\le \mathscr{C}\,.
	\eeq
Meanwhile, by Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}, together with \eqref{e:Q.naive.kolmogorov} and the definition~\eqref{e:def.r} of $C^{\RomIII}$, for $N$ large enough we also have 
	\beq
	\frac{\E_N[\|\bar{f}^N(t)-
		\bar{f}^N
		(s)\|^4]}{(t-s)^2}
	\le L^{O(1)}
	\le \mathscr{C}
	\eeq
for $N$ large enough. We next address the error terms, using Assumption~\ref{a:params}. For any function $f$ on $[0,1]$
we use $\|f\|_\infty$ to denote the supremum norm.
\begin{itemize}
\item It follows by the bound \eqref{e:Q.I.small} from Proposition~\ref{p:qv.kolmogorov}, combined with Doob's $L^2$
martingale inequality, that we have
	\[
	\E_N\bigg[ \Big( \| Z^{\RomI}\|_\infty \Big)^2\bigg]
	\le 4 \E_N[Z^{\RomI}(1)^2]
	= 4\E_N Q^{\RomI}(1)
	\le L^{O(1)} \delta
	\ll1\,,
	\]
recalling that we assumed $\delta\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.
\item It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:D.barD.discrep} that
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
	\Big\|D^\sigma-\bar{D}^\sigma\Big\|_\infty
	\le \frac{L^{O(1)}\eta}{\delta}\ll1\,,
	\]
recalling that we assumed $\eta\ll\delta$.
\item It follows by the bound \eqref{e:bar.D.notI.unif} from Proposition~\ref{p:drift.kolmogorov}
that 
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
	\E_N \| \bar{D}^\sigma\|_\infty
	\ll 1\,,
	\]
using that $\BUCKETS \ll N\delta$.
\item It follows by the bounds \eqref{e:Q.Ising.cross.small},
\eqref{e:qv.error.unif.bound}, and \eqref{e:tildeE.III.unif}
from Proposition~\ref{p:qv.kolmogorov}
that
	\[
	\sum_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}
		\E_N\|\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\Ising}\|_\infty
	+\sum_{\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}}
		\E_N\|E^{\sigma,\tau}\|_\infty
	+ \E_N\|\tilde{E}^{\RomIII}\|_\infty\ll1\,,
	\]
using that $\eta\ll \delta\ll \delta^{1/2}$ and 
$\BUCKETS \ll N\delta \ll N$.
\end{itemize}
Altogether this proves that $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges in probability to the zero path. By passing to a subsequence we can assume that $\mathcal{E}^N$ converges almost surely to the zero path.
 
Now let $J_n(H)$
be the event that $\bar{D}^{\RomI}$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.160651+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53144a8d46bb675c6426a29502ef6aad25df8a850910735bdde4294bf23b9834","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 6 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall the definition of $\Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ from the statement of Proposition~\ref{p:convex.body.polytope.bound.new}. 
Recall $\cD_+$ from \eqref{e:cD-plus}.
Given any $\mu$, define 
    \[
        \cD_{+,\mu}(2) \equiv \Big\{
            \YY = (\BBb,\vvv,\UUu,\www) \in \cD_+ : (\mu, \www) \le 2
        \Big\}\,,
    \]
For $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$ and $\dot{\YY}, \ddot{\YY} \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[\Big|\Surplus(\dot{\YY};\lambda,\mu) - \Surplus(\ddot{\YY};\lambda,\mu)\Big|
        \le
        \frac{4\|\Delta\YY\|_2
            +  6\|\Delta\YY\|_2^{1/2}}{\iota \min\{1,\alpha\}}\,,
    \]
where we abbreviate $\Delta\YY \equiv \dot{\YY} - \ddot{\YY}$. 
That is, $\YY \mapsto \Surplus(\YY;\lambda,\mu)$ is uniformly continuous in $\cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, uniformly in $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$.

\begin{proof}
We will bound separately the differences 
	\baln
	\Delta\Cost
	& \equiv\Cost(\dot{\YY};\lambda) - \Cost(\ddot{\YY};\lambda)\,,\\
	\Delta\Budget
	& \equiv\Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu) - \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)\,.
	\ealn
Note that for any $\xxxx \in \bbR^r$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
    \[
        \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|
        \le \bigg(\sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j |\xxxx_j|^2\bigg)^{1/2}
        \le \|\xxxx\|_2\,.
    \]
    Thus, abbreviating $\Delta\YY
    \equiv(\Delta\vBBb,\Delta\vvvv,\Delta\vUUu,\Delta\vwww)
    \equiv\dot{\YY}-\ddot{\YY}$, we have
    \baln
        |\Delta\Cost|
        &\le \sum_{j=1}^r \lambda_j \bigg\{
            |\Delta\vBBb_j|
            + |\Delta\vUUu_j|
            + \Big|
            (\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+
            \Big| 
            + 2 \Big|(\dot{\vvvv}_j-\dot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}_j-\ddot{\vUUu}_j)_+^{1/2} 
            \Big|
        \bigg\} \\
        &\le \|\Delta\vBBb\|_2
        + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        + \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        	\Big\|_2 
        + 2\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}
        \Big\|_2\,,
    \ealn
    where the operations $x\mapsto x_+$ and $x\mapsto (x_+)^{1/2}$ are applied entrywise.
    Since $x\mapsto x_+$ is a contraction,
    \[
        \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+\|_2
        \le \|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu}) - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})\|_2
        \le \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2 + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2\,.
    \]
Furthermore, since $|a^{1/2}-b^{1/2}| \le |a-b|^{1/2}$ for all $a,b\ge0$, for any vectors $\vec{a},\vec{b}\in[0,\infty)^r$ we can bound
	\[
	\Big(\|\vec{a}^{1/2}-\vec{b}^{1/2}\|_2\Big)^2
	=\sum_{j=1}^r \Big((a_j)^{1/2}-(b_j)^{1/2}\Big)^2
	\le \sum_{j=1}^r |a_j-b_j| = \|\vec{a}-\vec{b}\|_1\,.
	\]
Applying this estimate gives 
    \baln
        &\bigg(\Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2} - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+^{1/2}\Big\|_2\bigg)^2
        \le 
        \Big\|(\dot{\vvvv}-\dot{\vUUu})_+ - (\ddot{\vvvv}-\ddot{\vUUu})_+
        \Big\|_1 \\
        &\qquad \le 
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_1
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_1 
            \le r^{1/2} \Big(
            \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2
            + \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2
        \Big)\,.
    \ealn
    Finally, crudely upper bounding 
$\|\Delta\vBBb\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vvvv\|_2,
        \|\Delta\vUUu\|_2$ by $\|\Delta\YY\|_2$,
    we obtain
    \[
        |\Delta\Cost|
        \le 4 \|\Delta\YY\|_2
        + 2
        \Big(2 r^{1/2} \|\Delta\YY\|_2 \Big)^{1/2} \,.
    \]
This gives a continuity estimate for the $\Cost$ function.

We next turn to the $\Budget$ function.
    For all $\YY  \in \cD_{+,\mu}(2)$, we have
    \[
        0\le \alpha \cdot \Budget(\YY;\mu) \le (\mu,\vwww) \le 2\,,
    \]
    where the intermediate step is by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality.
    Therefore,
    \baln
        \alpha |\Delta\Budget| 
        &= \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2} + 
        \Budget(\ddot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}\Big| 
        \cdot 
        \alpha^{1/2} \Big|
        \Budget(\dot{\YY};\mu)^{1/2}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:15.493454+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5315a14d5e97dd4ffe3a5565200336690752ef5dcc2f635db0d824803f6e9f6e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 12 of arXiv:2512.02538, 'On the spectral geometry of Liouville quantum gravity'] There a.s. exists a family $(\mathbf{p}_t (\cdot ,\cdot))_{t\ge 0}$ of (jointly in all three arguments) measurable functions such that for all $t \ge 0$, for all $x \in \Sigma$,

 \cH_q=(H_n^{\odot q},\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}.
\]

All tensor norms below are the ordinary tensor norms of these scaled coordinates.  The
product transported by the primitive--Fock unitary is the normalized product
\begin{equation}
 u\wtensor_{\mathrm{nor}}v
 =
 \sqrt{\frac{q!}{p!(q-p)!}}\,

 \qquad
 u\in H^{\odot p},\quad v\in H^{\odot(q-p)}.
 
\end{equation}
The raw contractions of Section~\ref{all:sec:infinite-feedback} are ordinary
Hilbert tensor contractions of the scaled coordinates.  The dictionary

 _{\text{Parts II--IV, kernels }f_{n,a,q}}

 \underbrace{(H_n^{\odot q},\ip{\cdot}{\cdot})_{\mathcal U}}
 _{\text{Parts V--VI, coordinates }x_{n,a,q}},
\]
an isometry which carries $\wtensor$ to $\wtensor_{\mathrm{nor}}$ and

 \sum_{a,q}\norm{x_{a,q}}_{\cH_q}^2
 =

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:35:04.198653+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_536bd7c1ff7c9dfdf0d52119fd89b617427aac6937b66c002d5a9671a818d0f0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 13 (Boundary states) of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] A \emph{linear forest} is an acyclic graph whose vertices have degree at
most two.  A \emph{boundary forest} in \(F_m\) is a nonempty edge
subgraph \(\Gamma\subset F_m\) such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \(\Gamma\) is a linear forest;
\item every vertex of degree one belongs to \(\partial F_m\);
\item every connected component contains at least one edge.
\end{enumerate}
Thus every component is a self-avoiding path with two distinct endpoints
in \(\partial F_m\).

An \emph{abstract boundary forest} is a nonempty linear forest whose
vertex set is contained in \(V_0\) and which has no isolated vertices;
equivalently, each connected component is a path containing at least one
edge.  Let \(\cS\) be the finite set of all such abstract boundary
forests.  Thus an element \(\sigma\in\cS\) may consist of one path or of
several vertex-disjoint paths; it records only a possible finite
combination of boundary connections, not an actual walk in \(F_m\).

To pass from the actual boundary forest \(\Gamma\subset F_m\) to its
abstract boundary pattern, consider each component of \(\Gamma\) in
\(F_m\).  List the boundary vertices in the order in which the path meets
them.  Keep only these listed vertices, replace each portion
between two consecutive listed vertices by one abstract edge, and relabel the
retained vertices by \(\iota_m^{-1}\).  This compression operation is
called taking the \emph{boundary trace}.  The resulting nonempty linear
forest on \(V_0\), hence an element of \(\cS\), is the \emph{boundary
state} of \(\Gamma\), denoted by \(\operatorname{tr}_m(\Gamma)\).  It
records which boundary vertices are visited and how consecutive visits
are connected along each path; it does not record the internal vertices
or the lengths of the individual portions.

For \(\sigma\in\cS\), put
\[
  \cC_m(\sigma)
  =
  \{\Gamma\subset F_m:
    \Gamma\text{ is a boundary forest and }
    \operatorname{tr}_m(\Gamma)=\sigma\},
\]
and, for \(\beta\ge0\), define
\begin{equation}
  Z_m^\sigma(\beta)
  =
  \sum_{\Gamma\in\cC_m(\sigma)}
  e^{-\beta\#E(\Gamma)},
  \qquad
  \bZ_m(\beta)
  =
  \bigl(Z_m^\sigma(\beta)\bigr)_{\sigma\in\cS}.
  
\end{equation}
We call \(\bZ_m(\beta)\) the \emph{boundary-state partition vector}.
We adjoin the \emph{empty state} \(\varnothing\) and set
\(Z_m^\varnothing(\beta)=1\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:48:47.287549+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53a63231a14d32986d7b01d953bf29a23589cb9731216344d145a1b7856dcfd9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma gradient TAP of arXiv:2604.20660, 'The Legendre structure of the TAP complexity\\ for the Ising spin glass'] Recall $\mathrm{TAP}$ from (equation def:TAPmu of the paper) and $k_\zeta$ from~(equation def:kqm of the paper).
		Fix $\mathbf{m}\in(-1,1)^N$ and set $q=\frac{1}{N}\Vert \mathbf{m}\Vert^2$.
		Let $\zeta$ be a probability measure on $[q,1]$. Then for every $i\in[N]$:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
			\item (\emph{Exact gradient at the minimizer}) If $\zeta_\mathbf{m}$ is the minimizer in Definition~(def:zetam of the paper), then
			\begin{equation}
				\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})})=-\frac{1}{N}k_{\zeta_\mathbf{m}}(q,m_i).
			\end{equation}
			
			\item (\emph{Exact defect formula and explicit boundary stability}) One has
			\begin{equation}
				-N\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})},\zeta)
				=
				k_\zeta(q,m_i)-m_i\,\xi''(q)\,\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}},
			\end{equation}
			where $\Delta_\zeta^{\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})}}$ is defined in (equation eq:def-Delta of the paper).
			Consequently, if
			\[
			\max_{j\in[N]}|m_j|\le 1-\delta
			\qquad\text{for some }\delta\in(0,1),
			\]
			and
			\[
			\zeta(\{q\})\ge u_0>0,
			\]
			then there exists $C=C(\xi,u_0)<\infty$ such that
			\begin{equation}
				\Bigl|\partial_i \mathrm{TAP}(\mu_N^{(\mathbf{m})},\zeta)+\frac{1}{N}k_{\zeta}(q,m_i)\Bigr|
				\le \frac{C}{N\delta}\,\mathrm{dist}(\zeta_\mathbf{m},\zeta).
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.977676+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53b5ef2e4a0c9b755b0db2166c30ab1590e1fc62ac077e000af7d18efcc6f9f2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 19 of arXiv:2608.12451, '2608.12451'] Fix $\mathsf{S}\in\{\mathsf{P},\mathsf{R}\}$.  Let
$U\in\cC_j^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$ and
$V\in\cC_k^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$.  Then,
\noi
\begin{align}
 \norm{\Gamma(U,V)}_2
 \leq\frac{j+k}{2}\norm{U}_4\norm{V}_4.
 
\end{align}

Let $H=\sum_{j=1}^rH_j$, with
$H_j\in\cC_j^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$, and let $H_t$ be obtained
from the thinning coupling when $\mathsf{S}=\mathsf{P}$ and from the
coordinate-refresh coupling when $\mathsf{S}=\mathsf{R}$.  Without
any lattice assumption,
\noi
\begin{align}
 \cJ_r(H)
 =\lim_{t\downarrow0}
 \frac{\E[(H_t-H)^2\{(H_t-H)^2-1\}]}
 {1-e^{-rt}}.
 
\end{align}
If $H$ satisfies the lattice condition \eqref{cond_La} with shift
$\theta>0$, then $\cJ_r(H)\geq0$.

If $F\in\cC_r^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$ and
$B=\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}B_j$, with
$B_j\in\cC_j^{\mathsf{S}}\cap L^4(\PP)$, then
\noi
\begin{align}
 \abs{\cJ_r(F+B)-\cJ_r(F)}
 \leq84\bigl(1+\norm{F}_4+\eps\bigr)^3\eps,
 
\end{align}
where
$\eps:=\sum_{1\leq j<r}\norm{B_j}_4$.

Assume that a nonnegative quantity $\rho(F)$ satisfies
\eqref{top_rho}, and put
$\mathfrak d(F):=\abs{\cD(F)}+\rho(F)$ as in
\eqref{frak_d}.  Then, without any lattice assumption,
\noi
\begin{align}
 \cJ_r(F)
 \leq4\sqrt{m_2(F)\mathfrak d(F)}+12\mathfrak d(F)
 
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
 |\cJ_r(F)|
 \leq
 4\sqrt{m_2(F)\mathfrak d(F)}
 +16\mathfrak d(F).
 
\end{align}

In the Poisson setting, one has the sharper estimates
\noi
\begin{align}
 \cJ_r(F)
 &\leq4\sqrt{m_2(F)\cP(F)}+8\cP(F).
 
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.376271+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_53b62a4d4b0ea879e3c5457fa6f8ecdb78aba2e92827a95ead2ce3351cd5f4ff","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A sequence (x_n) in a metric space (X, d) is Cauchy if for every epsilon > 0 there is an index N such that d(x_m, x_n) < epsilon for all m, n >= N. The metric space (X, d) is complete if every Cauchy sequence in X converges to a point of X. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, but not conversely in general: the rationals with the usual distance are not complete, while the real line R and Euclidean space R^n are complete. A closed subset of a complete metric space is complete, and a complete subspace of any metric space is closed in it.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:29:08.755493+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53cd53a3c64890c99d77c5c7c432486b23a4395d3088ccd473c393e003538cca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm smasympexGOEGSE of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] There exist universal constants $C,c>0$, and a compactly supported 
distribution $\nu_k$ for every $k\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, such that the following 
hold. Fix any bounded $h\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R})$, and define
$$
	f(\theta):= h(K\cos\theta)
	\qquad\text{with}\qquad
	K := (Cr)^{q_0}\|X_{\rm F}\|.
$$
Then for every $m, N\in \mathbb{N}$ with $m\le\frac{N}{2}$, we have
\begin{multline*}
       \left| \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}} h(X^N)]
	- \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} \frac{\nu_k(h)}{N^k} \right| 
	~\vee~
       \left| \mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}} h(Y^N)]
	- \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} \frac{\nu_k(h)}{(-2N)^k} \right| 
\\
       \le
	\frac{(Cq_0)^{2m}}{m! N^m} \|f^{(2m+1)}\|_{[0, 2\pi]} 
	+
	Cre^{-cN}\big(\sobnorm{h}{0}{(-\infty,\infty)}
		+ \sobnorm{f^{(1)}}{0}{[0, 2\pi]} \big).
\end{multline*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.748711+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_53cecf1b362d10041b0a47312670b1473af05df16737abc8443aa0e0a4561b5c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 20 (Theorem~\ref{thm:micro}-(\ref{thm:sl})) of arXiv:2607.28865, 'First-Passage Percolation on Spread-out line graphs: Microscopic Regime'] Suppose Assumption~\textup{A.\ref{ass:A2}} holds and $0<\ga:=\gc\lc<2$.

    \quad
    t\in\dR.

{"assumptions":["F is continuous","u is continuous on Ω","the equation is written in the form F = 0 with a fixed sign convention"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.110816+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, Hamilton–Jacobi equations","id":"claim_53dfc94ed0a9e05577bb2bf64ec2af288dc9f26b2353c233536514d102e5795c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ be open and F: Ω × ℝ × ℝⁿ → ℝ continuous; consider the equation F(x, u(x), Du(x)) = 0 in Ω. A function u ∈ C(Ω) is a viscosity SUBsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every point x₀ ∈ Ω at which u − φ has a local maximum, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≤ 0. It is a viscosity SUPERsolution if for every φ ∈ C¹(Ω) and every local minimum point x₀ of u − φ, F(x₀, u(x₀), Dφ(x₀)) ≥ 0. It is a viscosity solution if it is both. (Equivalent reformulations: replace 'local' by 'strict local' or 'global' max/min, or use C^∞ test functions, or use super-/subdifferentials D⁺u(x₀) and D⁻u(x₀): the conditions read F(x₀, u, p) ≤ 0 for all p ∈ D⁺u(x₀) and ≥ 0 for all p ∈ D⁻u(x₀).) Every classical C¹ solution is a viscosity solution, and a viscosity solution that is differentiable at x₀ satisfies the equation pointwise there. For time-dependent equations u_t + H(x, Du) = 0 on Ω × (0,T) apply the same definition with the gradient variable (u_t, Du) and test functions of (x,t). SHARP EDGE — the sign of F matters: writing the same equation as −F = 0 interchanges the roles of sub- and supersolutions, so the two forms have DIFFERENT viscosity solutions. Example: on (−1,1) with boundary values u(±1) = 0, the function 1 − |x| is a viscosity solution of |u'| − 1 = 0 but NOT of 1 − |u'| = 0, while |x| − 1 is a viscosity solution of 1 − |u'| = 0 but not of |u'| − 1 = 0 (at the kink x = 0, a concave kink admits only test functions touching from above, and a convex kink only test functions touching from below). Viscosity solutions are in general only continuous, are stable under uniform limits, and for convex H coincide with Lipschitz solutions that are semiconcave; the notion is designed so that comparison/uniqueness theorems hold where classical and a.e. solutions are non-unique.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.348469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5416a777be1cc30c7c8f9a9bebbe4d2ca70960a8272285b96d45fe6a1e694b32","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 162 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $I$ be a finite, nonempty index set. Let 
  \[
    \lt(\Theta, 
    \vec{\hat{Z}}\equiv
    (\hat Z_i)_{i\in I},
    \vec{\tilde{Z}}
    \equiv(\tilde Z_i)_{i\in I}\rt)
  \]
  be a random variable where
  $(\vec{\hat{Z}},\vec{\tilde{Z}})$
  are centered, jointly gaussian, and independent of $\Theta$. 
  Assume that $\vec{\hat{Z}}$ and $\vec{\tilde{Z}}$ are equidistributed,
 and that, for distinct $i,k\in I$,
  \[
    \bbE[\hat Z_i\hat Z_k]
    =\bbE[\tilde Z_i\tilde Z_k]
    =\bbE[\hat Z_i\tilde Z_k]=0.
  \]
Let $F$ and $G$ be measurable functions
such that $F(\Theta,\hat Z)$ and 
$G(\Theta,\hat Z)$ have finite variance, and such that
	\beq
    \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big] = 0 = 
    \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z) 
    	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]\,,
    \eeq
  $\Theta$-almost surely.
Then the covariance between $F(\Theta,\hat{Z})$ and $G(\Theta,\tilde{Z})$ is bounded by
  \beq
    \lt| \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z) G(\Theta,\tilde Z)] \rt|
    \le
    \rho_{\max} \cdot
    \bbE[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2]^{1/2}
    \bbE[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2]^{1/2}\,, 
    
  \eeq
where $\rho_i\in[-1,+1]$ denotes the correlation between $\hat{Z}_i$ and $\tilde{Z}_i$, and 
$\rho_{\max} 
   \equiv\max\{|\rho_i|: i\in i\}$.
 
\begin{proof}
Let $\sigma_i$ denote the standard deviation of $\hat{Z}_i$, and denote
  \[
    \hat W_i \equiv 
    \frac{\hat Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,, \quad
    \tilde W_i 
    \equiv \frac{\tilde Z_i}{\sigma_i}\,,
  \]
which are marginally standard gaussians. It follows from the assumptions that
$(\hat W_i,\tilde W_i)$ are independent over $i\in I$, and $\bbE[\hat W_i\tilde W_i]=\rho_i$.
Let $(h_m)_{m\geq 0}$ denote the orthonormal Hermite polynomials for the
one-dimensional standard gaussian measure. We note that if $W$ and $\tilde{W}$ are marginally standard gaussians, and $(W,\tilde{W})$ is jointly gaussian and $\rho$-correlated, then it is straightforward to verify that
	\beq
	\E[ h_n(W) h_m(\tilde{W})]
	= \ind\{n=m\} \rho^n\,.\eeq
 For a multi-index $\vec n=(n_i)_{i\in I}\in\bbZ_{\ge 0}^I$, define the multivariate Hermite polynomial
  \[
    H_{\vec n}(w)
    \equiv\prod_{i\in I}h_{n_i}(w_i).
  \]
  We expand $F,G$ in the Hermite bases of $\hat W$ and $\tilde W$ respectively, conditional on $\Theta$, to obtain Hermite coefficients $a_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ and $b_{\vec n}(\Theta)$ such that
  \begin{align*}
    F(\Theta,\hat Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}a_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\hat W)\,, \\
    G(\Theta,\tilde Z)
    &= \sum_{\vec n}b_{\vec n}(\Theta)
        H_{\vec n}(\tilde W)\,.
  \end{align*}
  The assumption \eqref{e:conditional-centering} ensures $a_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=b_{\vec 0}(\Theta)=0$, $\Theta$-almost surely.
  Consequently, expanding in the Hermite bases and applying \eqref{e:hermite.corr.ip} gives
  \begin{align*}
    &\bigg|
      \bbE\Big[
        F(\Theta,\hat Z)G(\Theta,\tilde Z) \,\Big|\, \Theta
      \Big]
    \bigg|
    \le
      \sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
         |a_{\vec n}(\Theta)b_{\vec n}(\Theta)|
         \prod_{i\in I}|\rho_i|^{n_i}\\
    &\qquad\le
      \rho_{\max}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        a_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
      \bigg(\sum_{\vec n\neq\vec 0}
        b_{\vec n}(\Theta)^2
        \bigg)^{1/2}
    =\rho_{\max}
      \bbE\Big[F(\Theta,\hat Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}
      \bbE\Big[G(\Theta,\tilde Z)^2 
      	\,\Big|\, \Theta\Big]^{1/2}\,.
  \end{align*}
  Taking expectation over $\Theta$ and again applying the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality proves the conclusion.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Boundary regularity (C^1, or Lipschitz, or finite perimeter) and enough integrability of the field and its derivative up to the boundary.","On an arbitrary bounded open set the statement is false - the boundary can be too wild to carry a normal."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:06:45.870827+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations, vector calculus","id":"claim_544abd1d9e082b813e5e8c51352f287cae66825cd9c5fcd853a1f118dbe89096","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Omega be a bounded open set in R^n with C^1 boundary and outward unit normal nu, and let F be a vector field in C^1(closure of Omega) (or in W^{1,1}(Omega) with an integrable trace). Then the integral over Omega of the divergence of F equals the boundary integral of F dotted with nu with respect to (n-1)-dimensional surface measure. Two standard consequences: integration by parts, the integral over Omega of u_{x_i} v = minus the integral of u v_{x_i} plus the boundary integral of u v nu_i; and Green's identities, for instance the integral over Omega of ( u Laplacian v - v Laplacian u ) equals the boundary integral of ( u times the normal derivative of v minus v times the normal derivative of u ). The theorem extends to Lipschitz domains, where the normal exists at almost every boundary point, and to sets of finite perimeter with the reduced boundary and measure-theoretic normal in place of the classical ones.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:22:46.423015+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_544b0ab65a69238eb286093a8a9952f69bb63ad7dd593d0e1c9470af795aa98a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Causality and extendibility of curves) of arXiv:2609.03101, 'The emergence of the Cauchy horizon from the crease for $3D$ compressible Euler flow'] Let $\mathcal{M} \subset \R^{1+3}$ be an open subset of spacetime on which the fluid variables
	$\vec{\Psi} := \{s,\uprho,v^1,v^2,v^3\}$ are defined and $C^1$,
	and let $\gfour(\vec{\Psi})$ be the acoustical metric defined in \eqref{E:ACOUSTICALMETRICANDMATERIALDER}. Let $\upgamma : I \to \mathcal{M}$ be a $C^1$ curve, where $I \subseteq \R$ is an interval of the form $[a,b], (a,b), [a,b)$, or $(a,b]$ where $-\infty \le a < b \le \infty$.
		\begin{itemize}
			\item We say that $\upgamma$ is $\gfour$-timelike ($\gfour$-null) if $\gfour(\dot \upgamma(s), \dot \upgamma(s)) < 0$ $(\gfour(\dot \upgamma(s), \dot \upgamma(s)) =0)$ for all $s \in I$. We say $\upgamma$ is $\gfour$-causal if it is either $\gfour$-timelike or $\gfour$-null.
			\item We say that $\upgamma$ is \emph{extendible} in $\mathcal{M}$ if at least one of the limits $\lim_{s \to a} \gamma(s)$ or $\lim_{s \to b} \gamma(s)$ exist \emph{in $\mathcal{M}$}. We note that this notion of extendibility is with respect to the \emph{domain} $\mathcal{M}$. 
			\item If $\upgamma$ is not extendible, it is called inextendible.
		\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

For jointly standard normal X,Y with correlation q in (-1,1), define C_g(q)=Cov(g(X),g(Y)) and V=Var_gamma(g). Then C_g(q)=sum_(k>=1) a_k^2*q^k and V=sum_(k>=1) a_k^2. In particular, lim_(q up to 1) [V-C_g(q)]/(1-q)=sum_(k>=1) k*a_k^2, allowing the value +infinity. This sum is finite exactly when g has a weak derivative g_prime in L^2(gamma), that is, g belongs to H^1(gamma); weak derivative means the usual distributional derivative with respect to Lebesgue measure. {"assumptions":["the operator is densely defined but not assumed symmetric or closed","a closure or a core argument is being invoked"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772684+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_54940f80014d70dd9eb95c49c095eba47a53c4de71e730a15c0f74ec018b6e59","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'take the closure of T' presupposes that T is closable, i.e. that x_n ∈ D(T), x_n → 0 and Tx_n → y force y = 0; equivalently (in a Hilbert space) that D(T*) is dense. What fails: without closability the closure of the graph is not a graph, and 'the smallest closed extension' does not exist. Counterexample: H = ℓ², D(T) = finitely supported sequences, T x = (Σ_n x_n) e_1. T is densely defined and linear. Take x^{(k)} = (1/k, ..., 1/k, 0, 0, ...) with k entries: ‖x^{(k)}‖ = 1/√k → 0 while T x^{(k)} = e_1 for every k, so the graph closure contains both (0,0) and (0, e_1) and T is not closable. Consistently, ⟨Tx, y⟩ = (Σ x_n) conj(y_1) is ℓ²-bounded in x only if y_1 = 0, so D(T*) = {y : y_1 = 0} is not dense - exactly the criterion. The same phenomenon occurs for pointwise evaluation f ↦ f(0)g on L²(ℝ) restricted to continuous L² functions. Related traps: (i) an operator can be closable while its closure has strictly larger domain on which a defining formula no longer holds pointwise, so identities proved on D(T) must be re-derived by continuity in the graph norm; (ii) symmetry rescues closability (a symmetric operator is always closable, since T ⊂ T* and T* is closed), which is why this pitfall bites mainly for non-symmetric operators such as first order operators with unbalanced boundary conditions or multiplication-composition operators; (iii) a core argument ('it suffices to verify on a dense subspace') is valid only if the subspace is dense in the graph norm of the closed operator, not merely dense in the ambient space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.773038+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_54a170f683c2fe03b70c7a88e764fe8ab8dc2fc7b3e02b8c7b87103064904edb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem prop2 of arXiv:2608.00295, 'Quadratic Perturbations of Markov Systems'] Let ${\bf A}=(A_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}$ such that   $A_i=(a_{i}^{(s,t)})_{1\leq s,t\leq d}\in M_d(\mathbb{R})$ is a stochastic $d\times d$ matrix for each $1\leq i\leq n$, and ${\bf b}=(b_{i,j})_{1\leq i, j\leq n}$ such that each $b_{i,j}=(\alpha_{i,j}^{(s)})_{1\leq s\leq d}\in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a null-sum vector for each $1\leq i, j\leq n$ (with the convention  that $b_{i,i}=0$ for all $1 \leq i\leq n$).  We define the nonlinear operator 
$$T({\bf A};{\bf b}):\overbrace{\mathbb{R}^d \times  \mathbb{R}^d \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}^d}^{n \text{ times}}\to \overbrace{\mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \times \dots \times \mathbb{R}^d}^{n \text{ times}},$$ 
determined by 
$$T({\bf A};{\bf b})\begin{bmatrix}
v_1\\
v_2\\
\vdots\\
v_n
\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}
{\displaystyle A_1v_1+\sum_{j=1}^n\langle v_1,v_j\rangle b_{1,j}}\\
{\displaystyle A_2v_2+\sum_{j=1}^n \langle v_2,v_j\rangle b_{2,j}}\\
\vdots\\
{\displaystyle A_nv_n+\sum_{j=1}^n \langle v_n,v_j\rangle b_{n,j}}
\end{bmatrix}.$$
The following are equivalent. 
\begin{enumerate}
\item For all the possible combinations of $\pm$ sign of the null-sum vectors $b_{i,j}$ we have that $T({\bf A};{\bf \pm b})$ induces a well defined operator from $\Delta_{d-1}^n$ to  $\Delta_{d-1}^n$. 
\item For each $1\leq i\leq n$ and $1\leq s\leq d$ we have $${\displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n|\alpha_{i,j}^{(s)}|\leq \min_{1\leq t\leq d} \{a_{i}^{(s,t)}\}}.$$  
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.025497+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_54ae114798ca9a256a2c70700fa791a86f298aba79d645fb75c2a110914ca5b2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 16 (Kac's walk applied to the Johnson--Lindenstrauss transform) of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] There is a universal constant $C_{\mathrm{JL}}<\infty$ such that the following holds. Let $n\geq 2$, let $x\in\So{n}$, and let $M\sim\kacdist_{n,T,x}$ be the endpoint of $T$ steps of Kac's walk started from $x$. Let $\mathcal X\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ have $N\geq2$ points, and let $0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2$. Set
\be 
r=\left\lceil \log\frac{N}{\delta}\right\rceil,
\ee
and assume $4r<n$. Let $\ell$ be an integer satisfying
\be 
C_{\mathrm{JL}}\varepsilon^{-2}r\leq \ell<n.
\ee

If
\be 
T\geq
C_{\mathrm{JL}}\,n(4r+\log n)\left(r\log\frac{n}{\varepsilon}+\log\frac{N}{\delta}\right),
\ee
then, with probability at least $1-\delta$ over $M\sim\kacdist_{n,T,x}$,
\be 
(1-\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\leq
\|A_M(x_i-x_j)\|_2^2
\leq
(1+\varepsilon)\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2
\ee
for every pair $1\leq i<j\leq N$.

In particular, for fixed $\varepsilon$ and $N/\delta\leq n^A$, with $A<\infty$ fixed, the usual Johnson--Lindenstrauss target dimension $\ell=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(N/\delta))=O_A(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ \vnote{Isn't the JL target dimension $\epsilon^{-2}\log N$? EDIT: Ah, I see what's going on, $N$ is set to polynomial in $n$. But see below.} is achieved by taking $T\geq C_A n\log^3 n$. \vnote{I am worried that this is not the best illustration of our bound. In particular, when $N$ is polynomial in $n$, the JL embedding dimension $\ell$ is already $O(\log n)$ and so applying the matrix already only costs $O(n\log n)$. Shouldn't we be thinking about very large point sets of size, say $2^{n^{\epsilon'}}$ for some constant $0 < \epsilon' < 1$.} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:07:15.756214+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_54bc151f1da4abc0a9d417c2b9341ca78c23cb6add0cda5142a647ec2cb1b350","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:abstract-square-transversality of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] Let $\nu_{\rm ref}$ be a sigma-finite positive Radon measure on $S$, and let
$(\Lambda_i,\phi_i)_{i=1}^M$ be real eigenpairs of $A_\mu$ with continuous
representatives.  Assume that the following three conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0pt,topsep=0.35em,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt]
\item The eigenpairs satisfy
\begin{equation}
 A_\mu\phi_i=\Lambda_i\phi_i,
 \qquad
 \Lambda_i>0,
 \qquad
 \Lambda_i\ne\Lambda_j\ (i\ne j),
 \qquad
 \left\|\phi_i\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=1.
 
\end{equation}
\item The measures satisfy
\begin{equation}
 \mu\perp\nu_{\rm ref},
 \qquad
 \operatorname{supp}\mu=S,
 \qquad
 \rho=0\ \text{or}\ \rho\ll\nu_{\rm ref}.
 
\end{equation}
\item There exist $c_0>0$, finite signed measures $b_i\ll\nu_{\rm ref}$, and a
linear map
\begin{equation}
 L:
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\phi_1^2,\ldots,\phi_M^2\}
 \longrightarrow\mathcal M_{\rm fin}(S),
 
\end{equation}
such that
\begin{equation}
 L(\phi_i^2)
 =c_0\Lambda_i\phi_i^2\mu-b_i,
 \qquad 1\le i\le M.
 
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
Then, for every $a\in\mathbb R^M$,
\begin{align}
 \sum_{i=1}^Ma_i\Theta_\mu(\phi_i,\phi_i)=0
 &\Longrightarrow a=0,
 \\
 \sum_{i=1}^Ma_i\Lambda_i\Theta_\mu(\phi_i,\phi_i)=0
 &\Longrightarrow a=0.
 
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}
