{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.779036+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6d9b7e1ef52d934dc94f90127d61fd71337f5187524d9f0247be4e1d022a456a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:pseudo-bloch of arXiv:2608.01253, 'The pseudo-quantum representation of \\finite reversible Markov chains'] Let $N=2M$ and let $\{\Sigma_a\}_{a=1}^{d}$, with $d=\tfrac{N(N+1)}2-1$, be a
trace-orthonormal basis of the traceless complex-symmetric matrices, so that
$\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma_a\Sigma_b)=\delta_{ab}$, $\operatorname{Tr}\Sigma_a=0$, and
$\Sigma_a^{T}=\Sigma_a$. Orthonormality here is meant for the bilinear trace form
$\operatorname{Tr}(\Sigma_a\Sigma_b)$, with no complex conjugation, and such a basis exists
because that form is nondegenerate on the complex-symmetric matrices, for instance
the symmetrised units $(E_{ij}+E_{ji})/\sqrt2$ for $i<j$ together with an
orthonormal set of $N-1$ real traceless diagonal matrices work. The
$\Sigma_a$ are complex symmetric, not Hermitian, so they are the bilinear analogue
of the Gell-Mann matrices rather than the matrices themselves. Write

\[
\rho_z=\frac{\operatorname{Tr}\rho_z}{N}\,\mathrm{I}+\sum_{a=1}^{d}r_a(z)\,\Sigma_a,\qquad
r_a(z)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_z\Sigma_a).
\]

Then the coordinate vector obeys the linear flow

\[
\dot r_a(z)=\sum_{b}\Omega_{ab}\,r_b(z),\qquad
\Omega_{ab}=\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(\Sigma_a[K,\Sigma_b]\bigr),\qquad \Omega^{T}=-\Omega.
\]

Hence the flow lies in $\OO(d,\mathbb{C})$ and preserves the bilinear quantity
$\sum_a r_a^{2}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:55:27.263312+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6da9d8a81f978b097e5763afd9fa2e316931f3257b9a7eb8602a3e73fd0072e3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition DefSGP of arXiv:2410.23899, 'Tightness for interlacing geometric random walk bridges'] Fix a set $\Sigma = \llbracket 1, N \rrbracket$ with $N \in \mathbb{N}$ or $N = \infty$ and $T_0, T_1\in \mathbb{Z}$ with $T_0 \leq T_1$. A $\Sigma$-indexed geometric line ensemble $\mathfrak{L} : \Sigma \times \llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket \rightarrow \mathbb{Z}$ is said to satisfy the {\em interlacing Gibbs property} if it is interlacing, meaning that 
$$ L_i(j-1) \geq L_{i+1}(j) \mbox{ for all $i \in \llbracket 1, N - 1 \rrbracket$ and $j \in \llbracket T_0 + 1, T_1 \rrbracket$},$$
and for any finite $K = \llbracket k_1, k_2 \rrbracket \subseteq \llbracket 1, N - 1 \rrbracket$ and $a,b \in \llbracket T_0, T_1 \rrbracket$ with $a < b$ the following holds.  Suppose that $f, g$ are two increasing paths drawn in $\{ (r,z) \in \mathbb{Z}^2 : a \leq r \leq b\}$ and $\vec{x}, \vec{y} \in \mathfrak{W}_k$ with $k=k_2-k_1+1$ altogether satisfy that $\mathbb{P}(A) > 0$ where $A$ denotes the event $$A =\{ \vec{x} = ({L}_{k_1}(a), \dots, {L}_{k_2}(a)), \vec{y} = ({L}_{k_1}(b), \dots, {L}_{k_2}(b)), L_{k_1-1} \llbracket a,b \rrbracket = f, L_{k_2+1} \llbracket a,b \rrbracket = g \},$$
where if $k_1 = 1$ we adopt the convention $f = \infty = L_0$. Then, we have for any $\{ B_i \in \Omega(a, b, x_i , y_i) \}_{i = 1}^k$ that
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}\left( L_{i + k_1-1}\llbracket a,b \rrbracket = B_{i} \mbox{ for $i \in \llbracket 1, k \rrbracket$} \, \vert  A \, \right) = \mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{Inter}, \operatorname{Geom}}^{a,b, \vec{x}, \vec{y}, f, g} \left( \cap_{i = 1}^k\{ Q_i = B_i \} \right).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All stored bits iid uniform signs; M=floor(exp(alpha N))+1","Fixed alpha>0 and 0<=rho<1/2 with 2alpha<I(1-2rho); rho N integral along the limit","One independently sampled uniform Hamming-sphere input per stored pattern","Coordinate-excluded exponential-interaction update, evaluated on each initial corrupted input"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:34:25.143733+00:00","domain":"Demircigil; Heusel; Lowe; Upgang; Vermet; exponential storage; dense associative memory; Hopfield; binary patterns; random corruption; truncated Bernstein proof repair","id":"claim_6dae3d9f578f1079b18da0edfb454f540a55864a57293731e9f178dbf32dfb3b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix 0<alpha<log(2)/2 and rho in [0,1/2) with 2alpha<I(1-2rho), where I(t)=((1+t)log(1+t)+(1-t)log(1-t))/2 and I(1)=log(2). For integers N with rho N integral, let M=floor(exp(alpha N))+1 and let xi^1,...,xi^M be iid uniform patterns in {-1,+1}^N (all bits mutually independent). Conditional on the stored patterns, draw one input sigma^nu independently and uniformly on the Hamming sphere of radius rho N about xi^nu, for every nu. Set T_i(sigma)=sign(sum_mu [exp(xi_i^mu+sum_{j!=i}xi_j^mu sigma_j)-exp(-xi_i^mu+sum_{j!=i}xi_j^mu sigma_j)]). Equivalently T_i(sigma)=sign(sum_mu xi_i^mu exp(sum_{j!=i}xi_j^mu sigma_j)), since the omitted common factor is 2sinh(1)>0. Then P(exists nu exists i: T_i(sigma^nu)!=xi_i^nu) tends to zero as N tends to infinity. The sign at zero may be arbitrary. In particular rho=0 gives simultaneous fixed-point stability of every stored pattern whenever alpha<log(2)/2. This is one random corrupted input per pattern and coordinate evaluation on that initial input, not uniform correction of all Hamming-ball inputs and not a claim about an adaptively changing asynchronous trajectory. Source: Demircigil--Heusel--Lowe--Upgang--Vermet, Theorem 1.3 and Remark 1.4, arXiv:1702.01929v2, PDF p4; model equation (1), PDF p2. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.098386+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6dcb0431074de2ff4749c6c4d362488286b1e92f971577820949395057fd1d11","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:haar-passive-zero of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $V_-$ and $V_+$ be orthogonal $\mathrm{SO}(n)$-modules.  On their
star dilations write $\mathscr T_\pm,\mathscr E_\pm,\mathsf Q_\pm$ and
$\mathscr G_\pm=\mathsf Q_\pm\mathscr T_\pm$ for the maps in (eq:3.2.2 of the paper).
Let $\mathsf M:(V_-)_\star\to(V_+)_\star$ be a typed passive singleton,
so that
\[
 (\mathsf Mh)(i,\theta)=M_i h(i,\theta),\qquad
 \rho_+(R_i(\theta))^*M_i\rho_-(R_i(\theta))=M_i,
 \qquad \sum_iM_i=0.
\tag{3.2.10s$_1$}
\]
Put $\mathsf S^+_{+,-}=\mathsf Q_+\mathsf M\mathscr E_-^*$.
If $\Pi_-$ is the projection onto $V_-^{\mathrm{SO}(n)}$, then
\[
 \boxed{\mathscr G_+^*\mathsf S^+_{+,-}\Pi_-=0.}
\tag{3.2.10s$_2$}
\]
Writing
$\mathsf S^-_{-,+}=\mathscr E_-\mathsf M^*\mathsf Q_+$, applying the
same statement to $\mathsf M^*$ gives the oppositely oriented identity
$\Pi_-\mathsf S^-_{-,+}\mathscr G_+=0$.
Consequently every maximal residual temporal component made only of
passive singleton supernodes is identically zero, term by term in its
weak order and finite residual gaps.  This includes either end component
under the common auxiliary Haar projection of
(lem:haar-residual of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:30:14.147883+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e07f2a2c69a84919c7855920dedbd38eba03f5ecbc58ca2adedcd2d746e572e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem th:poly of arXiv:2608.19358, 'An optimal Poincaré inequality\\for the complex Ginibre log-gas'] Assume that $n\geq2$, and consider the following:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Two symmetric functions, which are polynomials with respect to $z$ and $\bar{z}$:
    \begin{equation}
      S(z)=\sum_{j=1}^n z_j
      \quad\text{and}\quad
      R(z)=\sum_{1\leq j<k\leq n}|z_j-z_k|^2=n\sum_{j=1}^n\left|z_j-\frac{S(z)}n\right|^2.
    \end{equation}
  \item The normalized complex Hermite polynomial\footnote{The Rodrigues
      formula is
      $\mathrm H_{a,b}(s,\overline
      s)=\frac{(-1)^{a+b}}{\sqrt{a!b!}}\mathrm{e}^{|s|^2}\bar\partial_s^{a}\partial_s^{b}\mathrm{e}^{-|s|^2}$.}$\mathrm
    H_{a,b}$ of bidegree $(a,b)$ for $\gamma_1$.
  \item The classical generalized Laguerre polynomial\footnote{Defined by the
      Laguerre equation (equation eq:laguerre of the paper) and normalized by
      $L^{\alpha}_m(0)=\binom{m+\alpha}{m}$. These polynomials are orthogonal
      with respect to the probability distribution
      $\mathrm{Gamma}(\kappa,1)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\kappa)}x^{\kappa-1}\mathrm{e}^{-x}\mathbf{1}_{x\geq0}\mathrm{d}x$.
      However, they are not orthonormal.} $L_m^{(\kappa-1)}$ of degree $m$,
    with $\kappa=\frac{(n-1)(n+2)}{2}$.
  \end{itemize}
  Then for every $a,b,m\in\mathbb N$, the symmetric polynomial
  \begin{equation}
    P_{a,b,m}(z)
    =\mathrm H_{a,b}\bigl(S(z),\overline{S(z)}\bigr)
    L_m^{(\kappa-1)}\bigl(R(z)\bigr)
  \end{equation}
  is an eigenfunction of $A_n$ in the sense that
  \begin{equation}
    -A_nP_{a,b,m}  =\lambda_{a,b,m}P_{a,b,m}
    \quad\text{where}\quad
    \lambda_{a,b,m}=2\frac{\alpha_n}{n}(a+b+2m).
  \end{equation}
  Moreover, the family $\{P_{a,b,m}:a,b,m\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is a basis of the
  polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[S,\overline S,R]$. In particular, this algebra
  is invariant under $A_n$ in the sense that
  $A_n\bigl(\mathbb C[S,\overline S,R]\bigr)\subset\mathbb C[S,\overline
  S,R]$. Furthermore, the elements of the family are mutually orthogonal in
  $L^2(\mu_n)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["P is a product measure (independent coordinates)","A and B are increasing events (van den Berg-Kesten); Reimer's inequality removes this hypothesis","A box B is the disjoint-occurrence event, witnessed by disjoint coordinate sets, not the intersection"],"created_at":"2026-09-02T07:51:33.048828+00:00","domain":"percolation and correlation inequalities (hand-authored statement with hypotheses, 2026-09-02)","id":"claim_6e1b259086d35f04b2f1c00edbbb017feb2ef912f0a7984e0cd00e9e6739eb28","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let P be a product measure on {0,1}^n and let A and B be increasing events. Write A box B for the disjoint occurrence of A and B: the set of configurations omega for which there are disjoint index sets I and J such that every configuration agreeing with omega on I lies in A and every configuration agreeing with omega on J lies in B. Then P(A box B) <= P(A) P(B) (van den Berg and Kesten 1985). This runs in the opposite direction to the Harris-FKG inequality for the plain intersection, P(A and B) >= P(A) P(B); the two are not in conflict because A box B is a subset of A and B. In percolation the standard use is P(two disjoint open paths) <= P(open path)^2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.098312+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e24220f1e54929281d56f5fca37b1cc5fc5b00a3a75044b1501f8ac6d056e8d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:haar-residual of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] Let $V$ be any finite-dimensional orthogonal $\mathrm{SO}(n)$-module,

\[
 \boxed{\mathcal K_V^\ell=\Pi_V+Q_V\mathcal K_V^\ell Q_V.}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:23:05.300717+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e256730514d6bdd7558f3fa3d570bc1759c4d627d8820f64be9e366a63d3c5b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 18 (Projected total-covariance decomposition) of arXiv:2608.21709, 'Posterior Information Dynamics of Diffusion Models for Linear Inverse Problems'] Fix a measurement value $r$ and $t>0$, assume
$\E[\|X_0\|^2\mid R=r]<\infty$, and let $P$ be an orthogonal projector.  With
$m_t^r(X_t)=\E[X_0\mid X_t,R=r]$,
\begin{equation}

\begin{aligned}
\Tr\!\left(P\Cov(X_0\mid r)P\right)
&=
\E\!\left[
\Tr\!\left(P\Cov(X_0\mid X_t,r)P\right)
\,\middle|\,R=r
\right]\\
&\quad+
\Tr\Cov\!\left(Pm_t^r(X_t)\mid R=r\right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The first term is conditional variance that remains after observing the noisy
state; the second is variation of the exact posterior mean across noisy states.
Under the Gaussian noising family, the second term tends to zero as
the channel SNR tends to zero and to
$\Tr(P\Cov(X_0\mid r)P)$ as the channel SNR tends to infinity.  Thus
across-state clean-estimate dispersion is the \emph{resolved} component of a
total-covariance decomposition, not the remaining posterior covariance. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.463164+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e2879df1f45a2244b874b34b20210b465bf580b412d8b57f2e8c93ad21c2097","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 4 (A bounded Brownian perturbation in a mixed equation) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\wt\eta\in(1/\alpha,1)$, let $0<\lambda<1$, let $\kappa\ne0$, and let $r\in L^2(0,T)$ be deterministic. Consider
\[
  b(t,x)=\wt b(t,x)\equiv0,
  \qquad
  a(t,x)\equiv\kappa,
  \qquad
  \wt a(t,x)=\kappa+r(t),
\]
and
\[
  \sigma(t,x)=\wt\sigma(t,x)=1+\lambda\bigl(|x|^{\wt\eta}\wedge1\bigr).
\]
Then the baseline equation contains both the Brownian and stable terms, the perturbed equation is driven by the same two noises, and the stable coefficient is bounded, bounded away from zero, and non-Lipschitz at the origin. For any coupled solution pair satisfying Assumption~\ref{ass:solutions}, the coefficient distances are
\[
  B=0,
  \qquad
  A^2=\int_0^T |r(t)|^2\dd t,
  \qquad
  S=0.
\]
Consequently, if $x_0=\wt x_0$ and $A=\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}<1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:noncritical} gives
\[
  \sup_{0\le t\le T}\E|X_t-\wt X_t|^{\alpha-1}
  \le C\|r\|_{L^2(0,T)}^{\frac{2(\alpha\wt\eta-1)}{\alpha\wt\eta-\alpha+2}}.
\]
Thus, in this mixed Brownian--stable equation, the estimate reduces to the Brownian diffusion error, while the stable coefficient is H\"older and fails to be Lipschitz.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:33:21.477637+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e4ba317c3c02f07a8a926ab6a28de23f447b28130f828e7ba3b6d6957e89135","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2606.21391, 'Extreme points and faces in the moment problem'] Let $(X,\mathcal{F})$ be a measurable space whose $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{F}$ contains all 
singletons in $X$. A \emph{measure} is a countably additive map $\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty)$. 
A measure $\mu$ is \emph{concentrated} on $A\in\mathcal{F}$ if $\mu(X\setminus A)=0$.
A measure $\mu$ is a \emph{probability measure} if its total mass is $\mu(X)=1$. 
Let $P$ be the convex set of probability measures on $(X,\mathcal{F})$. The 
\emph{point measure} at $x\in X$, denoted $\delta_x$, is the measure with values 
$\delta_x(A):=1$ if $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A):=0$ otherwise for every $A\in\mathcal{F}$. 
Let 
\[
P_1:=\{\delta_x: x\in X\}.
\]
A measure $\mu$ is \emph{$k$-atomic} [klerk-laurent19,lasserre10,nie23,schmuedgen17], 
$k\in\mathbb{N}_0$, if $\mu=\lambda_1\delta_{x_1}+\dots+\lambda_k\delta_{x_k}$ for mutually 
distinct points $x_1,\dots,x_k$ in $X$ and strictly positive real weights 
$\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k>0$. A measure is \emph{finitely atomic} if it is $k$-atomic 
for some $k\in\mathbb{N}_0$. Let
\[
P\!_\mathrm{fin}:=
\{\mu\in P : \text{$\mu$ is finitely atomic}\,\}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:37:08.955949+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e55cf06ea9308239f2d44a5ad50b13b8949be43ffa5282bae83bf764ae0b06d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:ci of arXiv:2609.01581, 'Concentration of additive functionals of Stratonovich-type'] Under assumption~(ass:dynamics of the paper), let $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu \in
L^2(\mu)$, and let $\tilde\sigma_A^2$ and $c_A$ be sub-gamma parameters for which
Eq.~(equation eq:uq_general of the paper) holds with $\overline{A}_t \in
\{\overline{\rho}_t(V), \overline{J}_t(U)\}$. 
Fix a confidence level $1-\alpha$, with $\alpha\in (0,1)$, and define
\begin{align}
  r_A(\alpha,t)
  =
  \sqrt{\frac{2\tilde\sigma_A^2}{t}\log\left(\frac{2N_\nu}{\alpha}\right)}
  +
  \frac{c_A}{t}\log\left(\frac{2N_\nu}{\alpha}\right),
  \quad
  N_\nu \equiv \left\|\frac{\mathrm{d}\nu}{\mathrm{d}\mu}\right\|_{L^2(\mu)},
  
\end{align}
where $N_\nu$ is a prefactor encoding the initial condition with $N_\mu=1$.
Then for every $t > 0$,
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(-r_A(\alpha,t) \leq \overline{A}_t - \E^\mu[\overline{A}_t] \leq r_A(\alpha,t)\right)
  \geq 1-\alpha ,
  
\end{align}
that is, with probability of at least $1-\alpha$, under $\mathbb{P}^\nu$, the stationary mean lies in the confidence interval
\begin{align}
  \E^\mu[\overline{A}_t]
  \in
  \left[\overline{A}_t - r_A(\alpha,t),
  \overline{A}_t + r_A(\alpha,t)\right].
  
\end{align}
Moreover, the corresponding one-sided guarantees hold with a smaller radius $r_A^{(1)}(\alpha,t)$, 
obtained from Eq.~(equation eq:ci_radius of the paper) by replacing $2N_\nu$ with $N_\nu$, i.e., 
\begin{align}
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\overline{A}_t - \E^\mu[\overline{A}_t]
  \leq r_A^{(1)}(\alpha,t)\right)
  \geq 1-\alpha,
  \qquad
  \mathbb{P}^\nu\left(\E^\mu[\overline{A}_t] -  \overline{A}_t
  \leq r_A^{(1)}(\alpha,t)\right)
  \geq 1-\alpha.
  
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.345582+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6e9838daad033267a324612fda93794ababb91013b8c4bcf33990c572760ca95","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 138 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If $\psi:\bbR^{d_1}\to\bbR^{d_2}$ is Lipschitz, then $\psi$ preserves $\bbW_2$ convergence.
If $d_1=2,d_2=1$ and $\psi(X,Y)=XY$, then $\psi$ preserves $\bbW_2$ convergence for sequences on which $X$ is uniformly bounded.

\begin{proof}
The first statement follows because $L$-Lipschitz maps increase $\bbW_2$ distances by at most a factor of $L$.
For the second statement, suppose 
$X_N\to X$ and $Y_N\to Y$ in $L^2$, with $|X_N|\leq C$ almost surely for all $N$. 
We will argue that this implies $X_NY_N\to XY$ in $L^2$, and the assertion then follows. First,
the uniform bound on $X_N$ gives
  \[
  \E\Big[(X_NY_N-X_NY)^2\Big]
  \le C^2 \E\Big[(Y_N-Y)^2\Big]
  = o_N(1)\,,
  \]
so $X_NY_N$ and $X_NY$ are close in $L^2$. For $T$ growing sufficiently slowly with $N$, we then bound
  \[
  \E\Big[ (X_NY-XY)^2\Big]
  \le T^2\E\Big[ (X_N-X)^2\Big]
  + 4C^2\E\Big[Y^2; |Y| \ge T\Big]
  \le T^2 o_N(1) + o_T(1)\,,
  \]
where the last term is because $Y^2\in L^1$. Therefore $X_NY$ converges to $XY$ in $L^2$, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:51.726715+00:00","domain":"harmonic analysis / Sobolev embedding","id":"claim_6eb2ea7b6a07326d6e5d6688779ae32153ce28e129f99091ad137afef25da73a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: H^s(R^n) embeds into L^∞(R^n) ∩ C^0 only for s > n/2, strictly; the borderline s = n/2 is excluded. Concrete counterexample, n = 2 (s = 1): u(x) = log log(1/|x|) for 0 < |x| < e^{−1}, extended by 0. Then ∫|∇u|² = 2π ∫_0^{e^{−1}} dr / ( r log²(1/r) ) = 2π < ∞ and ∫ u² < ∞, so u ∈ H¹(R²), yet u is unbounded at the origin. General n: choose f with f̂(ξ) = (1+|ξ|)^{−n} (log(2+|ξ|))^{−1} ≥ 0; then ∫ (1+|ξ|²)^{n/2}|f̂|² dξ < ∞ (radially, ∫ dρ/(ρ log²ρ) converges) so f ∈ H^{n/2}(R^n), while ∫ f̂ dξ = ∞ (∫ dρ/(ρ log ρ) diverges); since f̂ ≥ 0, an L^∞ bound on f would force ∫ f̂ < ∞ (test against a Gaussian approximate identity with positive Fourier transform and use monotone convergence), so f ∉ L^∞. Consequences: an energy-critical argument may not conclude a pointwise bound from the energy norm; ‖u‖_{L^q_t L^∞_x} estimates at the critical regularity generally require Besov spaces, since Ḃ^{n/2}_{2,1} embeds into L^∞ while H^{n/2} does not. This is the same phenomenon that makes the Lebesgue-space wave Strichartz estimates carry the restriction r < ∞ (the Littlewood–Paley summation of the dyadic blocks needs r < ∞, and at r = ∞ one lands in Besov spaces). The failure of the endpoints (q,r) = (2,∞) — Schrödinger in n = 2, wave in n = 3 — is a separate matter, proved by explicit counterexamples of Montgomery-Smith and of Klainerman–Machedon, not a corollary of this embedding failure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:18:13.294721+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ecbc8323de36e2a618c67a1dde402826105a7d6501a410d59a4d8fd1049c06d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:break_loops of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] {amy-cle-resampling}}]

Suppose that $\Gamma$ is a nested ${\rm CLE}_{\kappa}${} in a simply connected domain $D$. For each $a\in(0,1)$, $b>0$ there exists $p > 0$ such that the following holds. 

Let $z\in D$ and $j_0\in\mathbf{Z}$ be such that $B(z,2^{-j_0})\subseteq D$. There exists a resampling $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ of $\Gamma$ within $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$ for each $j>j_0$ with the following property. Let $G^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ be the event that
\begin{itemize}
 \item no loop in $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ crosses the annulus $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$,
 \item denoting $\mathcal {C}$ the loops in $\Gamma$ that cross $A(z,2^{-j},2^{-j+1})$, the collection of loops of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$ remain the same in each connected component of $\mathbf{C} \setminus \bigcup\mathcal {C}$ that is not surrounded by a loop in $\mathcal {C}$ and intersects $B(z,2^{-j})$, and the gasket of $\Gamma$ in these components is contained in the gasket of $\Gamma^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j}$.
\end{itemize}
For $k\in\mathbf{N}$, let $\widetilde G_{z,j_0,k}$ be the event that the number of $j=j_0+1,\ldots,j_0+k$ so that
\[ \mathbf{P}[ G^{\mathrm{res}}_{z,j} \,|\, \Gamma ] \geq p\]
is at least $(1-a)k$.  Then
\[ \mathbf{P}[(\widetilde G_{z,j_0,k})^c] = O(e^{-b k}) \]
where the implicit constant does not depend on $z,j_0,k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Refers to the open problem node open-problem-c0058-a-peeling-algorithm-exploring-site-percolation-on-boltzmann-maps","No independent review; result status attempted_unsolved"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:26:45.042388+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6ee908b5f808cca14f04a9496a7df36b77c5fdd7c0ca2b7a7d3ee18a1cb155de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Design the algorithm and check whether the exploration frontier remains Markov. Result: For bond percolation the peeling frontier is a two-colour boundary (free/blocked edges) and the algorithm peels the edge at the colour change, keeping the unexplored region a Boltzmann map with a boundary of the same type. For site percolation the colour lives on vertices and after peeling a face the newly exposed boundary vertices are uncoloured; the natural algorithm peels the edge whose left endpoint is black and right endpoint is uncoloured, colouring the new vertices as they appear. The unexplored region is then a Boltzmann map with a boundary condition that is a word in {black, white, uncoloured}, and the difficulty is that the length of the black segment is no longer a Markov chain by itself: the future depends on the positions of uncoloured vertices along the boundary. The frontier becomes Markov if one records the boundary word, which is an infinite-dimensional state. On triangulations the problem was solved (Angel-Curien) because degree-3 faces expose at most one new vertex per step, keeping the state finite; for general Boltzmann maps with large faces a peeled face exposes many uncoloured vertices at once. So a Markov site-percolation peeling exists exactly when faces expose boundedly many vertices, i.e. for bounded face degrees, and the general Boltzmann case requires a state space of boundary words; whether the threshold can still be computed from a word-valued Markov chain is the open part. Obstruction: Unbounded face degrees expose many uncoloured boundary vertices at once; the frontier state is a word, not an integer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.617912+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f155acdc0830bd5aeb602e98085e3ef8a1c96bd1fe6b2fcecbea1503a83c8d7","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:W.is.subgaussian of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] Let
\begin{equation}
{\mathcal{H}} =  \{\|I_n+W\|_{\operatorname{op}}\le 4 \}.
    
\end{equation}
If $d \ge (1+\epsilon) n$ for some arbitrarily small constant $\epsilon>0$, then there exists a constant $c>0$ only depending on $\epsilon$ such that 
$\mathbb{P}_0(W \in {\mathcal{H}}^c) \leq \mathop{\rm exp}(-cn)$ 
and,
for any zero-diagonal symmetric matrix $U$,
\[
\mathbb{E}_{X\sim \mathbb{P}_{0}}[\mathop{\rm exp}( \langle U,W\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal H}\rangle)]\le \mathop{\rm exp}\left(\frac{2 \|U\|^2}{d}\right)+1\le 2\mathop{\rm exp}\left(\frac{2\|U\|^2}{d}\right).
\]

\begin{proof}

Recall that $W=XX^\top -I_n$, so 

${\mathcal{H}}$ is implied by the event
$\{\|X\|_{\rm op} \le 2\}$.
Let $Z$ be an $n\times d$ matrix with i.i.d.\ standard gaussian entries, and let $D$ be the $n\times n$ diagonal matrix with diagonal entries $\|z_1\|,\ldots,\|z_n\|$. Then $X$ is equidistributed as $D^{-1}Z$, so we can bound
    \[\|X\|_{\rm op} \le 
    \frac{\|Z\|_{\rm op}}
        {\min_i \|z_i\|}\,.\]
By the standard concentration inequality for Gaussian matrices~[vershynin2010introduction], we have
\[\|Z\|_{\rm op}
\le\sqrt{d} + \sqrt{n}
+t\]
with probability at least $1-2\mathop{\rm exp}(-t^2/2)$. By the standard concentration bound for chi-squared random variables (Lemma~(l:chi.square.lower.tail of the paper)), we have
    \[
    \min\Big\{ \|z_i\|
    : 1\le i\le n\Big\}
    \ge d-(2d)^{1/2} t
    \]
with probability at least $1-n\mathop{\rm exp}(-t^2/2)$.  Taking $t=cn^{1/2}$, we conclude that with probability at least $1-3n\mathop{\rm exp}(-c^2 n/2)$, we have
\[\|X\|_{\rm op} \le \frac{1+(1+c)/\sqrt{1+\epsilon}}{[1-\sqrt{2}c/\sqrt{1+\epsilon}]^{1/2}} \le 2\,,\]
where the last inequality holds by choosing $c$ to be a sufficiently small constant  depending on $\epsilon$. 

Next, let $W_m$ denote the principal submatrix of $W$ formed by the first $m$ rows and columns. We will truncate on the event
$\mathcal H_m= \{\| I_m+W_m\|_{\operatorname{op}}\le 4 \}$.
Note that ${\mathcal{H}}_{m+1} \subset {\mathcal{H}}_{m}$ for all $1 \le m \le n-1$ and $\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}_n$. Abbreviating $u_n$ for the last column of $U$, we can bound
\begin{align*}
     &\ \mathbb{E}_{X\sim \mathbb{P}_{0}}\Big[\mathop{\rm exp}( \langle U,W\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal H}\rangle)\Big]\\
   \le &\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_n}
   \bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg( \sum_{i<j}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)
   \mathbf{1}\{W_n \in \mathcal H_n\}\bigg]+1\\
   \le&\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(
   \sum_{i<j<n}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)\mathbf{1}\{ W_{n-1} \in \mathcal H_{n-1}\} \mathbb{E}_{x_n}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(
   \bigg\langle \sum_{i<n} u_{in}x_i,x_n
   \bigg\rangle
   \bigg)\bigg]\bigg]+1\\
    \le&\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\sum_{i<j<n}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)\mathbf{1}\{W_{n-1}\in \mathcal H_{n-1}\}\cdot \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\frac{ (u_n)^\top (I_{n-1}+ W_{n-1}) u_n}{2d}\bigg)\bigg]+1\\
    \le&\ \mathbb{E}_{x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}}\bigg[\mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\sum_{i<j<n}u_{ij}\langle x_i,x_j\rangle\bigg)\mathbf{1}\{W_{n-1} \in \mathcal H_{n-1}\}\bigg]\cdot \mathop{\rm exp}\left(\frac{2 \|u_n\|^2
    }{d}\right)+1\,,
\end{align*}
where the second-to-last inequality is by Lemma~(lem:beta.mgf of the paper), and the
 last inequality holds because we have $\|I_{n-1}+W_{n-1}\|_{\operatorname{op} }
\le 4$ on the event ${\mathcal{H}}_{n-1}$.
Iterating the above gives the claimed bound.
\end{proof}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a well-defined Dirichlet form and reversible Markov chain with a reference measure mu","a valid Nash-type functional inequality with a specified effective dimension d","for two-sided estimates: matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth bounds on balls","typically also an elliptic Harnack inequality, or comparable regularity, to establish the matching lower heat-kernel bound"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.993577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f33033cc6c015e74e17ecf03f84254fb9e59f13180becd49ac22b25d7db440b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). A Nash inequality on a graph with Dirichlet form E and reference measure mu has the form ||f||_2^{2+4/d} <= C E(f,f) ||f||_1^{4/d} for all f in the domain of the form, where d is an effective dimension parameter. Such an inequality is classically equivalent, by results of Nash and later Carlen-Kusuoka-Stroock, to an on-diagonal heat-kernel upper bound p_t(x,x) <= C' t^{-d/2} for the associated Markov semigroup, and combining it with matching volume-growth and effective-resistance-growth estimates, within the general framework relating resistance growth to heat-kernel decay used for fractal-like and random graphs, yields two-sided sub-Gaussian or Gaussian heat-kernel bounds. On graphs where effective resistance to the complement of a ball of radius n grows like n^zeta and volume grows like n^alpha, this gives sub-Gaussian heat-kernel estimates with off-diagonal decay governed by the exponent alpha+zeta, a technique central to analysis on fractals and on random graphs such as critical percolation clusters or random walk among random conductances. The technique does not give the resistance or volume exponents themselves, which are separate geometric inputs, and a full two-sided heat-kernel estimate typically requires both the Nash-type inequality, giving the upper bound, and a separate lower-bound argument, often via a chaining construction or an elliptic Harnack inequality. Typical failure: Assuming ordinary Euclidean Gaussian heat-kernel scaling, of the t^{-d/2} exp(-|x-y|^2/4t) form, transfers automatically to a random or fractal-like graph without re-deriving the resistance exponent zeta; on structures such as the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or random conductance models with heavy-tailed conductances, the correct scaling is sub-Gaussian with zeta != 1, and using the Euclidean exponent silently mis-states both the walk dimension and the tail behavior of the heat kernel. Canonical reference: Nash, 1958, American Journal of Mathematics; Carlen, Kusuoka and Stroock, 1987, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare; Barlow, 2004, Annals of Probability; Kumagai, Random Walks on Disordered Media and their Scaling Limits, 2014, Springer.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:41.190331+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_6f5cfee93cb76cd8d74924060da891f5b4881b2215fe5aa410d44ee0474d26de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In mathematics, the term homology, originally introduced in algebraic topology, has three primary, closely related usages. First, there is the homology of a chain complex, a sequence of abelian groups, called homology groups, which are regarded as fundamental invariants of the chain complex. Secondly, when one can associate a chain complex to a different mathematical object, one can also associate its homology to that object. Distinct procedures of associating chain complexes to a given object are grouped into homology theories. Finally, homology is important in the study of topological spaces. Under nice conditions in which distinct homology theories for a single topological space produce the same homology groups, one can define a single homology of a topological space. This last notion of homology is closely related to topological ideas frequently discussed in popular mathematics such as the holes of a surface or the cycles of a graph. There is also a related notion of the cohomology of a cochain complex, giving rise to various cohomology theories, in addition to the notion of the cohomology of a topological space.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.094911+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f628d213e948889bebd7b6cc96612958248be05cf576e45b6f16f5b6758c038","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:circuit-primitives of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] For an ordered finite set $S$ of oriented carrier labels, write
$\mathscr H_S=\bigotimes_{u\in S}H_u$, with every factor equipped with
the Euclidean Hilbert norm.  A \emph{normalized Brauer primitive} is a
signed carrier permutation, a wedge reversal, full transpose, a share
turn, a through string, the orthogonal antisymmetrizer, or a cup/cap
normalized so that its operator norm is one.  A share turn is the fixed
signed boundary permutation, possibly followed by full transpose,
induced when a principal pivot reverses one of the two ordered boundary
intervals.  The two coefficient primitives are
\[
 \widehat C_{uv}=\iota_{uv}C\pi_{uv}:H_u\otimes H_v\to H_u\otimes H_v,
\]
where $\pi_{uv}$ is the normalized orthogonal projection and
identification onto $\Lambda^2H$, and $\iota_{uv}=\pi_{uv}^*$; hence
$\widehat C_{uv}$ is zero on $\operatorname{Sym}^2H$ and has norm $K$.
The other coefficient primitive is the restriction/re-expression of
(eq:2.1.3 of the paper) as the Bianchi transfer
\[
 (\Phi_CY)_{ik}=\sum_{m,n}C_{in,mk}Y_{mn},
 \qquad Y\in\Lambda^2H.
\]
The first Bianchi identity identifies the latter with the physical action
of $C$.  A \emph{safe gate} is a typed composite of these primitives,
including the $AA$ words and correctly oriented $AB$ words used below.
Its degree is the number of coefficient primitives.  Thus a degree-$d$
safe gate $G:\mathscr H_S\to\mathscr H_T$ satisfies
$\|G\|_{\rm op}\le K^d$; untouched factors are ancillary identities.

A coefficient box has four darts
$L_{i,0},L_{i,1},R_{i,0},R_{i,1}$.  For a column pairing $q$, a
\emph{packet} is a connected component of the box-incidence graph whose
edges are the $q$-pairs joining different boxes.  A $q$-pair joining the
two darts of one wedge is forbidden and gives zero.  An allowed
\emph{smoothing} chooses at each box either
\[
 h_i^{\parallel}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,0},L_{i,1}R_{i,1}\},\qquad
 h_i^{\times}=\{L_{i,0}R_{i,1},L_{i,1}R_{i,0}\}.
\]
The alternating circuits of $q\vee h$ are the \emph{smoothing
carriers}; adjoining one carrier means adjoining one identity factor
$I_H$.  The smoothing support $\operatorname{supp}_h(i)$ of a box is the
one- or two-element set of $q\vee h$ carriers containing its two
$h$-passages.  A \emph{ported pair comb} on two chosen carriers consists of all
boxes whose smoothing support is that pair, together with every singleton-support box
assigned to it exactly once; removing all other support groups leaves
their boundary darts as linearly ordered typed ports.  These definitions
fix the domains and codomains of every safe word, fold, comb, and
attachment below.

An \emph{ambient rooted ribbon record} $\Gamma$ consists of a common
finite dart set, its coefficient boxes and local wedge signs, a row
pairing $p$, a column pairing $q$, a rooted trace pairing $r$, and the
declared boundary/root data.  Thus $p\vee r$ is the disjoint union of the
original trace circuits in that record; its components, not temporary
proof cuts, receive the normalization bases below.  The more detailed
Weingarten data carried by $\Gamma$ are specified in
(def:ribbon-record of the paper).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:07:15.760628+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f94ffa8dcd385e87271234f98eae453b37f436b5823899a6aa86c6878e3a5bb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:measurable-operator-field-calculus of arXiv:2608.02459, 'Response Calculus for Spectral Simplicity\\ and Joint Eigenvalue Densities'] From the preceding definitions we obtain the following three properties.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:15:36.168836+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6f96cf3350360b3b674906a013981642afa2164edb1dd8ea5b948546eeaf0074","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 12 (Deterministic resolvent comparison) of arXiv:2609.01770, 'Support of Dyson Brownian Motion'] Let \(Y_n\) be a deterministic Hermitian \(n\times n\) matrix, and there exists a constant $K>0$, such that

$E^{\sigma,\tau}$ and $E^{\frozen,\sigma,\tau}$
with $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let
$Q^{\sigma,\tau}=E^{\sigma,\tau}+\tilde{Q}^{\sigma,\tau}$ as in Definitions~\ref{d:Q} and \ref{d:tQ}. Then, for $N$ large enough, we have
	\[\bbE
	\Big|\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le L^{O(1)}\bigg\{\eta\delta^{1/2} + \frac{\BUCKETS\delta}{N}
	\bigg\}
	\]
for all $\sigma,\tau\in\{\RomII,\RomIII,\Ising\}$. The same bound holds with $E^\frozen$ in place of $E$.

to the proof of Corollary~\ref{c:Q.first.quenched}. Recall 
that Lemma~\ref{l:qv.simplification} implies
	\[
	\Big|\Delta E^{\sigma,\tau}(q_d)\Big| 
	\le O\bigg(

	\bigg]\bigg)\,.

	\[\E\Big[\Delta\bar{D}^\sigma(q_d)^2\Big]

{"assumptions":["exactly quadratic loss with symmetric positive semidefinite Hessian","A=G^T H G>0","unbiased iid batch gradients with finite second moment","fixed current theta and one update only"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:45:33.839464+00:00","domain":"optimization.stochastic","id":"claim_6fb37bb81706cd7b2047938ebd218203941edcc87a60a57beca68c7bc19fa0f1","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let L be an exactly quadratic loss with symmetric positive semidefinite Hessian H. At theta let G=grad L(theta) satisfy A=G^T H G>0. Let g_B be the mean of B>=1 iid finite-second-moment gradients with mean G and per-example covariance Sigma. Write C=tr(H Sigma)>=0 and B_noise=C/A. For the update theta_next=theta-eta*g_B, E[L(theta_next)]=L(theta)-eta*||G||^2+(eta^2/2)*(A+C/B), exactly. The unique real minimizing step is eta_opt(B)=||G||^2/(A+C/B)=eta_max/(1+B_noise/B), where eta_max=||G||^2/A. The optimal expected loss decrease is Delta_opt(B)=Delta_max/(1+B_noise/B), where Delta_max=||G||^4/(2*A). If B_noise>0, batch B=B_noise in the continuous interpolation achieves half Delta_max. For a general smooth loss, the source obtains these expressions from a quadratic Taylor model; without a controlled remainder they are not exact guarantees, iteration-complexity bounds, or global convergence rates.","status":"unverified"}

		variance. Let $F$ be convex in each
		coordinate and suppose that, $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely, for every $1\leq i\leq N$,
		\[
			0\leq\partial_i^+F\leq b_i\, ,
		\]
		where the $b_i$ are deterministic. Then there is a universal
		$C<\infty$ such that, for every $L>0$,
		\[
			\mathbb{E}\left[\left(
			F-\mathbb{E} F-\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb{E}[\partial_i^+F]\xi_i
			\right)^2\right]
			\leq CL^2\sum_{i=1}^N\Var(\partial_i^+F)
			+C\eta(L)\sum_{i=1}^Nb_i^2\, ,
		\]
		where, for an independent copy $\xi_1'$ of $\xi_1$,
		\[
			\eta(L)\coloneqq
			\mathbb{E}\left[(\xi_1-\xi_1')^2
			\mathbf{1}_{\{|\xi_1-\xi_1'|>L\}}\right]\, .
		\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["alpha is irrational and satisfies ||q alpha|| >= C q^{-tau} for all integers q >= 1, with C > 0 and tau >= 1","||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer","in part (ii), f is C^infinity on the circle R/Z with mean zero, and the rotation is x -> x + alpha","solutions are sought up to an additive constant; L^2 and distributional solutions are compared by Fourier coefficients"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:09:43.732260+00:00","domain":"Diophantine approximation, small divisors, circle rotations","id":"claim_701f743bb2241950d3a8f90b87a8fd689c27198731a6afd43cc9166321190ecf","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"For a real number t write ||t|| for its distance to the nearest integer. Fix an irrational alpha and suppose alpha is DIOPHANTINE of type (C, tau): there are constants C > 0 and tau >= 1 with

  ||q alpha||  >=  C * q^{-tau}    for every integer q >= 1.

Then:

(i) (the small divisors are only polynomially small) for every nonzero integer q,
      | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 |  =  2 | sin(pi q alpha) |  >=  4 ||q alpha||  >=  4 C |q|^{-tau}.
    The upper bound | e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1 | <= 2 pi ||q alpha|| always holds, so the two sides are comparable to ||q alpha||.

(ii) (solving the cohomological equation) Let R_alpha(x) = x + alpha on the circle T = R/Z and let f be a C^infinity function on T with mean zero. Then the equation u(x + alpha) - u(x) = f(x) has a C^infinity solution u, unique up to an additive constant, given on Fourier coefficients by u-hat(q) = f-hat(q) / (e^{2 pi i q alpha} - 1) for q nonzero. Quantitatively |u-hat(q)| <= |q|^{tau} |f-hat(q)| / (4C), so one loses tau derivatives: in Sobolev scale ||u||_{H^{s - tau}} <= (4C)^{-1} ||f||_{H^s}, and the analogous statement holds in Holder scale with an epsilon loss.

(iii) (how common the hypothesis is) For every tau > 1, Lebesgue-almost every alpha is Diophantine of type (C, tau) for some C = C(alpha) > 0; for tau = 1 the alpha satisfying the condition are exactly the badly approximable ones (bounded partial quotients), a set of Lebesgue measure zero and full Hausdorff dimension; for tau < 1 no alpha satisfies it at all, by Dirichlet's theorem.

WHERE IT FAILS. If alpha is LIOUVILLE (no such C, tau exist), the conclusion of (ii) fails badly: choose q_1 < q_2 < ... with ||q_k alpha|| < q_k^{-k} and define f by f-hat(q_k) = f-hat(-q_k)-bar = ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} and all other coefficients zero. These coefficients decay faster than any power of q_k, so f is C^infinity with mean zero, yet |u-hat(q_k)| >= ||q_k alpha||^{1/2} / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||) = 1 / (2 pi ||q_k alpha||^{1/2}), which blows up faster than any polynomial in q_k. Hence no solution u exists in L^2, and not even a distributional solution exists. So the Diophantine condition is not a technical convenience: it is what separates solvability from non-solvability. Note also that (ii) gives no information at all about the SPEED of ergodic averages by itself, and that the estimates degrade as C -> 0, so any application that needs uniformity must track C and tau explicitly.","status":"unverified"}

Before the precise definition of computable function, mathematicians often used the informal term effectively calculable to describe functions that are computable by paper-and-pencil methods. In the 1930s, several independent attempts were made to formalize the notion of computability:In 1933, Kurt Gödel, with Jacques Herbrand, formalized the definition of the class of general recursive functions: the smallest class of functions that is closed under composition, recursion, and minimization, and includes zero, successor, and all projections. In 1932–33, Alonzo Church created a method for defining functions called the λ-calculus. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.167788+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7047fbc363730689224871ea7b3508059dbfb1af16c2c3095189e1af3a9864bc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 59 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] The set $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ from \eqref{e:sM.Lip} can be expressed as
    \[\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) = \bigcup_{q_0 \in [0,1]}\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0)
    \]
for $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0)$
as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}.
\begin{proof}
    For any $q_0 \in [0,1]$, the inclusion $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ is trivial, so it suffices to prove
    \beq
        \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) \subseteq \bigcup_{q_0 \in [0,1]} \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0)\,.
    \eeq
Consider any sequence $\epsilon_n\downarrow0$. Then, for $\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon)$ defined in \eqref{e:cM.Lip}, we have
    \[ \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) 
    =\adjustlimits
    \bigcap_n \bigcup_{L>0}
    \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha;L,\epsilon_n)
    \,.
    \]
Consider any measure $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$. For any $n\ge 1$, there exists $L_n$ (depending on $\mu,\epsilon_n$) and a sequence of $L_n$-Lipschitz algorithms $(\cA^n_{N_j})_{j\ge 1}$ with 
    \beq
        
        \WERR(\cA^n_{N_j},\mu) =
           \max\bigg\{
            \bbW_2\Big(
            \mu(\cA^n_{N_j}),
            \mu\Big),
            \bbW_2\Big(
            \mu^{\Ising}(\cA^n_{N_j}), \cP(\{\pm 1\})\Big)
        \bigg\} \le \epsilon_n\,.
    \eeq
Abbreviate $\bsig_{n,j} 
\equiv \cA^n_{N_j}(\bG,\bg^\aux)$. 
By passing to a subsequence of the $N_j$, we can ensure that
    \beq
        
	q_0(n,j)
	\equiv \chi_{\cA^n_{N_j}}(0)
	= \frac{\|\bbE\bsig_{n,j}\|^2}{N_j}	
	\stackrel{j\to\infty}
	{\longrightarrow} 
	q_0(n)
    \eeq
    for some $q_0(n) \in [0,1]$.
    Let $q_0 \in [0,1]$ be any subsequential limit of the $q_0(n)$ as $n\to\infty$.
    We will show that $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,q_0)$, from which the result follows.

    By passing to a subsequence of the $\epsilon_n$, we can assume that $q_0(n) \to q_0$ as $n\to\infty$.
    We will show that for $C_1(\alpha)$ as in Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.approx}, 
    $\tilde L_n \equiv 2L_n$, and
    \[\tilde\epsilon_n 
    = \epsilon_n + 2\bigg(
    	C_1(\alpha) \Big[
	|q_0 - q_0^n| + \epsilon_n
	\Big]
	\bigg)^{1/2}\]
    there exists a sequence of $\tilde L_n$-Lipschitz $(\tilde\cA^n_{N_j})_{j\ge 1}$ with
    \beq
        
        \WERR(\tilde{\cA}^n_{N_j},\mu)=

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:16:18.692823+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_705cce3bc3c2f162b4275875c9b9a71f24d78fbec2f616fc38040dcbd9b51005","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 31 (Compatible prefix time) of arXiv:2607.26377, '\textbf{Entire Logarithmic Signatures\\ of Bounded-Variation Paths in Finite Dimensions}'] Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with
$\dim V\geq2$, and let
$\gamma\colon[0,T]\to V$ be a continuous bounded-variation path. Set
\[
l=\log S(\gamma),
\qquad
v=\gamma_T-\gamma_0,
\]
and assume that
\[
R(l)=\infty,
\qquad
v\neq0.
\]
Fix $\ell\in V^*$ such that $\ell(v)=1$, put $W=\ker\ell$, and write
\[
\gamma_t-\gamma_0=x_t v+X_t,
\qquad
x_t=\ell(\gamma_t-\gamma_0),
\qquad
X_t\in W.
\]

Give $W$ an auxiliary Euclidean norm and let $W_{\C}$ be its
complexification. For every finite symmetric set
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$, define the real Hilbert space
\[
E_\Lambda
=
\set{(z_\omega)_{\omega\in\Lambda}
\in\prod_{\omega\in\Lambda}W_{\C}:
 z_{-\omega}=\overline{z_\omega}}
\]
with the norm inherited from the Hilbert direct sum, the decorated
transverse path
\[
B_t^\Lambda(\gamma)
=
\left(
\int_0^t \e^{i\omega x_s}\dd X_s
\right)_{\omega\in\Lambda},
\qquad 0\leq t\leq T,
\]
and the orthogonal map
\[
T_\Lambda\colon E_\Lambda\to E_\Lambda,
\qquad
(T_\Lambda z)_\omega=\e^{i\omega}z_\omega.
\]
Denote by the same symbol the induced graded automorphism of tensor
series, and set
\[
r_t^\Lambda
=S\bigl(B^\Lambda(\gamma)|_{[0,t]}\bigr),
\qquad
h_\Lambda=r_T^\Lambda.
\]

Then there exists $t_*\in[0,T]$ such that, for every finite symmetric
$\Lambda\subset2\pi\Q$,
\begin{equation}
h_\Lambda
=a_\Lambda T_\Lambda(a_\Lambda)^{-1},
\qquad
a_\Lambda=r_{t_*}^\Lambda.
\end{equation}
Equivalently,
\[
r_{t_*}^\Lambda
=h_\Lambda T_\Lambda\bigl(r_{t_*}^\Lambda\bigr)
\]
for every such $\Lambda$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:17:10.022418+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70aaacc132bf006490a2efbd61e694a78c197fa1fcea406ad4ce694db2ff6bdd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 3 of arXiv:2608.17374, '\textbf{On the Pseudo-Mixing of Kac's Walk}'] [Distinguishability With Respect to Fixed Sequences] 
Fix two sequences of distributions $\mu_{n}, \nu_{n}$ that take on values in the set $\mathcal{S}_{n}$, and let $f_{n}$ be a sequence of functions from $\mathcal{S}_{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}$.

We say the sequence $f_{n}$ \textit{weakly} distinguishes $\mu_{n}$ and $\nu_{n}$ if
\be 
\sqrt{\max(\Var_{\mu_{n}}(f_{n}),\Var_{\nu_{n}}(f_{n}))} = O(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |),
\ee 
and \textit{strongly} distinguishes if the LHS is 
$o(|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{n}}[f_{n}] - \mathbb{E}_{\nu_{n}}[f_{n}] |)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f measurable and a.e. finite","|E| < infinity (or E sigma-finite, applied piecewise)","the measure is Borel regular, so that inner regularity by closed sets is available"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751562+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_70f1790178f49b91f5ee0ff4790936831774e34f8e840b54c67bc80f664a49ab","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : R^d -> C be Lebesgue measurable and finite almost everywhere, let E be a measurable set of FINITE measure, and let eps > 0. Then there is a CLOSED set F contained in E with |E \\ F| < eps such that the RESTRICTION of f to F is continuous. Moreover one may take g in C_c(R^d) with g = f on F and sup |g| <= sup |f|. The theorem does not assert that f is continuous AT the points of F as a function on R^d: the indicator of the rationals is nowhere continuous on R, yet it agrees with the zero function off a set of measure zero, and Lusin's F can be taken to be any closed set of irrationals of nearly full measure. Finiteness of |E| may be relaxed to sigma-finiteness by exhausting E, at the price of stating the conclusion with |E \\ F| < eps for each piece. [standard; e.g. Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 2.24]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Two explicitly specified centered covariance-I Gaussian mixture families","0<s sufficiently small; dimension limit before small-SNR expansion","Positive bounded conditional covariance perturbations","Not asserted to satisfy the iid matrix-factor model"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T16:15:57.431274+00:00","domain":"Extensive-rank matrix inference, Gaussian mixtures and high-noise KL expansions","id":"claim_70f4e8e741b41d6bfce9be790f7d9243f6253379eb668f0f080e91fce2b8bc1c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own work, proof draft UNAUDITED; no novelty claim. There are two families of centered, covariance-I_d Gaussian mixtures
whose conditional covariance matrices differ from I_d in operator
norm by O(s), such that, after d->infinity at fixed small s,

 log(1+chi^2(P_s||Q))/d =s^4/2+O(s^8)

for BOTH families (Q=N(0,I_d)), while their normalized KL expansions
are respectively

 D(P_s||Q)/d=s^4/4+O(s^6),
 lim_(d->infinity) D(P_s||Q)/d=s^4/12+O(s^6).

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:28:49.121797+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_70f93b993bb6bb37c7bfcb078034702d78b2e5b7cd400a6962d5b950db4fff82","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:johnson-spectrum of arXiv:2608.18293, 'Critical tensor covariance at the Marchenko--Pastur threshold'] Assume $1\le q<n/2$. Let $A_q$ be the adjacency matrix of the Johnson graph
$J(n,q)$: two $q$-subsets are adjacent when their symmetric difference has size
two. For a $j$-subset $T$, define
\[
  f_T(I)=\1_{\{T\subseteq I\}},
  \qquad |I|=q,
\]
and let $U_j$ be the span of the functions $f_T$ with $|T|=j$. Then
\[
  U_0\subseteq U_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq U_q.
\]
Set $U_{-1}=\{0\}$. If $H_j=U_j\cap U_{j-1}^{\perp}$, then $A_q$ acts on $H_j$ by the scalar
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_j=(q-j)(n-q-j)-j,
  \qquad 0\le j\le q.
  
\end{equation}
In particular, when $q<n/2$, the largest eigenvalue of $A_q$ on the orthogonal complement of the constant vector is
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_1=q(n-q)-n.
  
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.497474+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71012fbc4a10ccd6ccbbd74ad09769b158fb5d1f6cab2bb33003059607417a82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm conformal_invariance_aut_D of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let \( \tau \in \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \). The drift term \( b(\boldsymbol{\theta}, u) \) is a pre-Schwarzian form, satisfying:
\[
b_i = \tau' \widetilde{b}_i \circ \tau + \frac{6 - \kappa}{2} \left(\log \tau'\right)'.
\]
\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] There exists a smooth function \( F(\tau, u): \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathbb{D}) \times \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R} \) such that:
    \[
    \log \psi - \log (\psi \circ \tau) + \frac{\kappa - 6}{2\kappa} \sum_i \log \tau'(\theta_i) = F(\tau, u),
    \]
    where \( F \) satisfies the functional equation:
    
    \begin{equation}
    
    F(\tau_1 \tau_2, u) = F(\tau_1, \tau_2(u)) + F(\tau_2, u).
    \end{equation}

    \item[(ii)] There exists a rotation constant \( \omega \) such that:
    \begin{equation}
    F(A_\theta, 0) = \omega \theta.
    \end{equation}

    If \( \omega = 0 \), \( \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \) suffices to describe conformal invariance, and \( F \) reduces to a map \( \mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D}) \times \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R} \).

    \item[(iii)] Suppose \( F_1(\tau, u) \) and \( F_2(\tau, u) \) correspond to partition functions \( \psi_1 \) and \( \psi_2 \). If their rotation constants \( \omega_1 = \omega_2 \), then there exists a function \( g(u) \) such that:
    \[
   \psi_2 = g(u) \cdot \psi_1.
    \]

    \item[(iv)] For \( \tau \in \widetilde{\mathrm{Aut}}(\mathbb{D}) \), let \( \tau(u) = v \). Decompose \( \tau = T_v \circ A_\theta \circ T^{-1}_u \), where \( u, v \in \mathbb{D} \) and \( \theta \in \mathbb{R} \). Using the relations \( T_u'(u) = \frac{1}{1 - |u|^2} \) and \( T_v'(0) = 1 - |v|^2 \), define:
    \[
    \tau'(u)^{\lambda(u)} \overline{\tau'(u)}^{\overline{\lambda(u)}} := \left(\frac{1 - |v|^2}{1 - |u|^2}\right)^{2 \operatorname{Re}(\lambda(u))} e^{-2 \theta \operatorname{Im}(\lambda(u))}.
    \]
    Then:
    \[
    F(\tau, u) = \log \left(\tau'(u)^{\lambda(u)} \overline{\tau'(u)}^{\overline{\lambda(u)}}\right),
    \]
    satisfy the functional equation ((functional equation for F of the paper)), with rotation constant \( \omega = \operatorname{Im}(\lambda(u)) \).
\end{itemize} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

    \begin{enumerate}

        $F$ is modular in $M|_G$, and $G$ is modular in $M$. Then $F$ is modular in $M$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M|_G$.
        \item If $F, G$ are modular in $M$, then $F \cap G$ is modular in $M$.
        \item If $F$ is modular in $M$, then $(F \vee G)-G$ is modular in $M/G$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.497957+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7136ddb39be635661b82383746e601fad68a079bdd47e3f5f06f6b57b54acc5c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn Monodromy of Coulomb Gas Correlation Differential of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] Let $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j \cdot z_j$ be a divisor on $\mathbb{C}$ with associated Coulomb gas correlation differential
\[
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] = \prod_{j < k} (z_j - z_k)^{\sigma_j \sigma_k}.
\]
This function is multivalued due to the presence of non-integer exponents. Its multivaluedness is described by the \emph{monodromy representation} arising from analytic continuation around branch points.

To illustrate the basic mechanism, consider the case $n = 2$. Then
\[
C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}] = (z_1 - z_2)^{\sigma_1 \sigma_2},
\]
which is analytic in $z_1$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2\}$. If we analytically continue this function as $z_1$ travels once counterclockwise around $z_2$, the function picks up a multiplicative factor of $e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_2}$. 

Thus, the monodromy representation
\[
\rho: \pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2\}, z_1) \longrightarrow \mathbb{C}^*, \quad \rho(C_2) = e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_2}
\]
captures how the function changes under analytic continuation around the singularity at $z_2$, where $C_2$ is the loop encircling $z_2$.

In general, for $\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j \cdot z_j$, the function $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ is analytic in $z_1$ on $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}$. The fundamental group $\pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}, z_1)$ is the free group generated by loops $C_j$ encircling each $z_j$ ($j = 2, \ldots, n$), and the monodromy representation
\[
\rho: \pi_1(\mathbb{C} \setminus \{z_2, \ldots, z_n\}) \to \mathbb{C}^*, \quad \rho(C_j) = e^{2\pi i \sigma_1 \sigma_j}
\]
describes the multiplicative factor acquired by $C_{(b)}[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ when $z_1$ loops around $z_j$ once in the counterclockwise direction.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.652013+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7186db882c863ea9073dea828e7af3f00cab1a8dfbe5aaa44a03333a136d9bd8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 13 ($\ell$-multigraph) of arXiv:2605.07050, 'Universality of the fluctuations of the free energy in generalized Sherrington--Kirkpatric'] We say that a multigraph $\gamma$ with nodes $1, 2, \dots, N$ is an $\ell$-multigraph if any pair of nodes can be connected by at most $\ell$ edges. The multiplicity $m^\gamma_{ij}$ between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is the number of separate edges connecting them, and we let $m^\gamma_{ij} = 0$ if the nodes $i$ and $j$ are not connected. (It is possible that $m_{kk}^{\gamma} > 0$, i.e., self-loops are allowed.) If $m^\gamma_{ij} = 1, 2, 3, 4$, we say that the edge between the nodes $i$ and $j$ is single, double, triple, quadruple, respectively.

The degree of the node $i$ is defined by
\[
	d^\gamma_i = m^\gamma_{ii} + \sum_{j=1}^N m^\gamma_{ij}.
\]
In particular, a single self-loop at the node $i$ increases the degree of the node $i$ by $2$. The size $m^\gamma$ and the length $n^\gamma$ of a multigraph $\gamma$ are defined by
\[
	m^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} m^\gamma_{ij} = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N d^\gamma_i, \quad n^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} > 0),
\]
respectively. The number of the single (respectively, double, triple, quadruple) edges $n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $n_2^\gamma, n_3^\gamma, n_4^\gamma$) is defined by
\[
	n_r^\gamma = \sum_{i\leq j} \indi(m^\gamma_{ij} = r), \quad r=1, 2, 3, 4.
\]
Similarly, the number of the single (respectively, double) self-loops $\tilde n_1^\gamma$ (respectively, $\tilde n_2^\gamma$) is defined by
\[ \tilde n_r^\gamma = \sum_{k=1}^{N}\indi(m^\gamma_{kk} = r), \quad r=1,2.\]

The set of all $\ell$-multigraphs with single and/or double self-loops is denoted by $\caG^\ell$. (The empty graph is a multigraph and included in $\caG^\ell$.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:48:24.296611+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71e0d9ba818881c73222688b9d12a1a5628ea07bb86c0ba813ab26f2112a95b4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem optimaliq>1 of arXiv:2605.10452, 'A secretary for Messrs. Luce and Mallows'] Consider the secretary problem
with either  the  Mallows distribution
or the $P_n^{\mathcal{L}_\text{inv};\{q_n^i\}_{i=1}^n}$-type Luce distribution with  $q=q_n\in(0,\infty)-\{1\}$
in the case that the smallest number is  of highest rank.

\noindent i. Let $q_n=1-\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=0$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{1-e^{-c}}{e-1+e^{-c}}\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent ii.
Let $q_n=1-\frac c{n^\alpha}$, where $c>0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$
M_n^*\sim\frac1c\left(1-\log(e-1)\right)n^\alpha\approx0.459\frac{n^\alpha}c,
$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent iii.
Let $q\in(0,1)$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M^*)$, where
$$
M^*=\begin{cases}&\max\left\{M\ge1: \sum_{j=M}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac 1{1-q}\right\}, \ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge\frac1{1-q};\\
&0,\ \text{if}\ \sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}<\frac1{1-q}.\end{cases}
$$
(If  $\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}=\frac 1{1-q}$, then $M^*-1$ is also optimal.)

\noindent The corresponding limiting probability of success is given by
$$
\begin{cases}&(1-q)(1-q^{M^*})\sum_{j=M^*}^\infty\frac{q^j}{1-q^j}\ge(1-q^{-M^*}),\ \text{if}\ M^*\ge1;\\
&1-q>\frac1e,\ \text{if}\ M^*=0.\end{cases}
$$
This limiting probability is always greater or equal to $\frac1e$ and is
strictly greater than $\frac1e$ for all but at most a countable number of $q$ with no accumulation points in $(0,\infty)$.

\noindent iv. Let $q_n=1+\frac cn$, where $c>0$. Then the asymptotically optimal strategy is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
\begin{equation}
M_n^*\sim n\Big(\frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)\Big),
\end{equation}
 and the corresponding  limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent Also, $\lim_{c\to\infty} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=1$ and $\lim_{c\to0} \frac1c\log\big(1+\frac{e^c-1}e\big)=\frac1e$.

\noindent v.

$$
 and the corresponding limiting probability of success
is $\frac1e$.

\noindent vi. Let $q>1$.  Then the asymptotically optimal strategy  is $\mathcal{S}^\downarrow(n,M_n^*)$, where
$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:36:31.223822+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_71e98425fe4dbb8a7802a7e1bee535b588fa33d6d2fd777225f303dfc5d1e2f2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 17 (Unique Pinkall-modulus limit) of arXiv:2609.00501, 'Uniqueness of Finite-Time Varifold Limits for the M\"obius-Invariant Willmore Flow'] Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:anchored-profile}, orient the
profiles consistently with the reduced flow.  Let
\(\mathcal A_t\in\R/4\pi\mathbb Z\) be the oriented area class
enclosed by \(\gamma_t\), and let \(\mathcal A_T\) be the corresponding area class for
\(\gamma_T\).  Then
\begin{equation}
 
 \mathcal A_t\longrightarrow\mathcal A_T
 \qquad\text{in }\R/4\pi\mathbb Z .
\end{equation}
For \(t\) sufficiently close to \(T\), choose compatible real
representatives such that \(\mathcal A_t\to\mathcal A_T\).  Pinkall's
lattice is
\begin{equation}
 
 \Gamma_t=
 \operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Z}
 \left\{(2\pi,0),
 \left(\frac{\mathcal A_t}{2},\frac{L(\gamma_t)}2\right)\right\},
\end{equation}
and the corresponding modulus is
\begin{equation}
 
 \tau_t=\frac{\mathcal A_t+iL(\gamma_t)}{4\pi}\in\mathbb H .
\end{equation}
It satisfies
\[
 \tau_t\longrightarrow
 \tau_T:=\frac{\mathcal A_T+iL_T}{4\pi}.
\]
Its imaginary part satisfies the quantitative bounds
\begin{equation}
 
 \frac14\leq\operatorname{Im}\tau_T\leq\frac2\pi.
\end{equation}
Consequently the conformal classes
\[
 [\tau_t]\longrightarrow[\tau_T]
 \qquad\text{in }\mathcal M_1=\mathbb H/\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)
\]
have a unique finite-time limit, independent of the approaching time
sequence.  With the orientation induced by the fixed oriented profile

intrinsic oriented conformal class of the limiting \(C^1\) Hopf torus.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:37:51.461737+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_723ad6b0fc4c418480ceff7855f9a1f82bb50dbef869d87ffa6e86fd1b67d24f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 (Long-time behavior in the scalar case) of arXiv:2604.04100, '\LARGE Learning Equilibrium Fluctuation Expansions from Overdamped Langevin Dynamics'] Assume $d=1$. Let $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and let $X_\varepsilon$,  $(\bar{X}_m)_{0\leq m\leq n}$,  $(a_m)_{0\leq m\leq n}$ be as in Proposition \ref{thm-weak-exp-intro}. If we further assume that Assumption \ref{A2} holds, then for every $F \in C^{n+1}(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying \eqref{assump-F}, the following assertions hold:\begin{enumerate}

\item[(i)] The limit
$$
b_0(F) := \lim_{t\to\infty} a_0(t,F)
$$
exists, and satisfies
\begin{equation}
b_0(F) = \mathbb{E}\Bigl[ \lim_{t\to\infty} F\bigl(\bar{X}_0(t)\bigr) \Bigr]
= F(1)\mathbb{P}(\xi_0>0) + F(-1)\mathbb{P}(\xi_0<0).
\end{equation}
\item[(ii)] For each $m \in \{1, \dots, n\}$ and $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$, define
$$
S_{m,i}(t) := \sum_{(j_1,\dots,j_i)\in\mathcal{D}_i^m} \prod_{k=1}^{i}\bar{X}_{j_k}(t),\quad t\ge0.
$$
We adopt the convention that a sum over the empty set is equal to $0$, and hence
$$
S_{m,i}(t):=0
\quad\text{whenever }m<0,\ i<0,\ \text{or } i>m.
$$Then the conditional limits
$$
c_{m,i} := \lim_{t \to \infty}\mathbb{E}[S_{m,i}(t)\mid\xi_0>0],
\quad
\bar{c}_{m,i} := \lim_{t \to \infty}\mathbb{E}[S_{m,i}(t)\mid\xi_0<0]
$$
exist and are uniquely determined by the recursion formula
\begin{equation}
    c_{m,i} = \frac{i-1}{2}c_{m-2,i-2} - \frac{3}{2}c_{m,i+1} - \frac{1}{2}c_{m,i+2}, 
    \quad 
    \bar c_{m,i} = \frac{i-1}{2}\bar c_{m-2,i-2} + \frac{3}{2}\bar c_{m,i+1} - \frac{1}{2}\bar c_{m,i+2},
\end{equation}
with $c_{1,1}=\bar c_{1,1}=0$, $c_{2,2}=\bar c_{2,2}=\frac12$ and the convention that $c_{0,0}=\bar c_{0,0}=1$, and
		$$c_{k,j}=\bar c_{k,j}=0 \quad\text{whenever } (k,j)\notin \{(0,0)\}\cup\{(k,j): k\ge1,\ 1\le j\le k\}.$$ 
The recursion \eqref{eq-c-n-intro} is understood as a nested induction: one first increases the order $m$, and for each fixed $m$, computes $c_{m,i}$ backward in $i$ from $i=m$ to $1$. The same procedure applies to $\bar c_{m,i}$.

\item[(iii)] For each $m \in \{1, \dots, n\}$, the limit
\begin{equation}
b_m(F) := \lim_{t \to \infty} a_m(t,F)
\end{equation}
exists and is given by
\begin{equation}
    b_m(F) = \mathbb{P}(\xi_0>0)\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{c_{m,i}}{i!} F^{(i)}(1)
    + \mathbb{P}(\xi_0<0)\sum_{i=1}^{m} \frac{\bar{c}_{m,i}}{i!}F^{(i)}(-1).
\end{equation}
In particular, $b_m(F)=0$ for all odd $m$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:00:09.358321+00:00","domain":"ensemble learning","id":"claim_725b1291163158659b5a95f154eb99cbd5bf0e3c3895a5a6a7c646f4cd804d39","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In a multi-output stacking problem scored by the mean per-sample relative error $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\|\\hat y_i - y_i\\|/\\|y_i\\|$, the per-output least-squares stack minimises the unweighted squared error, which is dominated by the cases with the largest $\\|y_i\\|$, while the score is dominated by the cases with the smallest. Interpolating the per-output weights toward one pooled simplex weight vector fitted on the relative error therefore improves the score even IN-SAMPLE on the very calibration rows on which least squares is optimal in squared error - the signature that distinguishes an objective mismatch from a generalisation (variance) effect, which can only appear out of sample. Measured on the EMIT lookup-table pool (seed 101, component Y2, 23 members, 932 calibration rows, 285 outputs): in-sample relative error 0.1105 for least squares against 0.1026 at interpolation weight 0.4 (-7.2 percent), the in-sample optimum at the same weight as the out-of-sample optimum (0.1292 to 0.1186), while the in-sample squared error is minimal at least squares (8.8e-5 against 1.2e-4); the out-of-sample gain is +15.9 percent in the smallest-norm quartile of targets and -9.6 percent in the largest, and 45 percent of the least-squares score comes from its worst decile of cases. Consequently no model of the sampling noise of the weight rows reproduces the cross-validated interpolation weight: the known-noise James-Stein amount is 0.00 and the heteroscedasticity-robust amount 0.03-0.05 where cross-validation chooses 0.10-0.40. {"assumptions":["𝔄 is a unital Banach algebra (e.g. bounded operators on a Banach space, or square matrices)","A and B are elements of 𝔄 (bounded operators)","AB = BA"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111181+00:00","domain":"operator theory, matrix analysis, one-parameter groups","id":"claim_72638ddfde3be7c71bd07c8d293de0f5da0036958c9131cd1b17e4853a1f9986","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let 𝔄 be a unital Banach algebra (for instance the algebra B(E) of bounded linear operators on a Banach space E, or the n×n complex matrices), and for A ∈ 𝔄 define exp(A) = e^A := Σ_{k=0}^∞ A^k / k!, a series that converges absolutely in norm for every A (‖A^k/k!‖ ≤ ‖A‖^k/k!), so that ‖e^A‖ ≤ e^{‖A‖}. If A, B ∈ 𝔄 COMMUTE, AB = BA, then e^{A+B} = e^A e^B = e^B e^A. Consequences: for every A and all scalars s, t, e^{(s+t)A} = e^{sA} e^{tA} (the one-parameter group law), e^A is invertible with (e^A)⁻¹ = e^{−A}, e^0 = 1, and t ↦ e^{tA} is norm-differentiable with derivative A e^{tA} = e^{tA} A. If P is invertible, e^{PAP⁻¹} = P e^A P⁻¹. Sharp edges. (1) Commutativity cannot be dropped: for the 2×2 matrices A = [[0,1],[0,0]] and B = [[0,0],[1,0]] one has e^A = I + A, e^B = I + B, so e^A e^B = [[2,1],[1,1]], whereas A + B = [[0,1],[1,0]] gives e^{A+B} = [[cosh 1, sinh 1],[sinh 1, cosh 1]] ≠ e^A e^B (and e^B e^A = [[1,1],[1,2]] ≠ e^A e^B, so the two products differ as well). For non-commuting A, B the product e^A e^B is instead described by the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff series e^{A+B+[A,B]/2+…} when it converges, and by the Lie–Trotter formula e^{A+B} = lim_{n→∞} (e^{A/n} e^{B/n})ⁿ. (2) The converse is false in general: e^A e^B = e^{A+B} does not imply AB = BA (there are non-commuting complex matrices with e^A = e^B = e^{A+B} = I); it does hold for Hermitian (self-adjoint) matrices A, B, because then e^{A+B} Hermitian forces e^A e^B = (e^A e^B)* = e^B e^A, so the positive definite matrices e^A and e^B commute, and hence so do their unique Hermitian logarithms A and B. (3) For UNBOUNDED operators (generators of semigroups) the series definition is unavailable and 'commuting' must be formulated with care (e.g. commuting resolvents / commuting semigroups); this statement is only about bounded operators and Banach algebras.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["α irrational (for the rational case the expansion terminates)","regular (simple) continued fraction with integer partial quotients a_k ≥ 1 for k ≥ 1","||t|| denotes the distance from t to the nearest integer"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:57.492004+00:00","domain":"Diophantine approximation, circle rotations, continued fractions","id":"claim_7271e0510379bbe55262f0b504298ebded2c36c4dd6bb321ac077750203941b8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let α be irrational with regular continued fraction [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...], convergents p_n/q_n (p_{-1} = 1, q_{-1} = 0, p_0 = a_0, q_0 = 1, p_{n+1} = a_{n+1}p_n + p_{n-1}, q_{n+1} = a_{n+1}q_n + q_{n-1}) and complete quotients α_{n+1} = [a_{n+1}; a_{n+2}, ...], so a_{n+1} < α_{n+1} < a_{n+1} + 1. Write ||t|| = dist(t, Z) and δ_n = |q_n α − p_n| (so δ_{-1} = 1).

(1) Exact size and alternating sign. For all n ≥ 0, q_n α − p_n = (−1)^n / (q_n α_{n+1} + q_{n-1}). Hence 1/(q_n + q_{n+1}) < δ_n < 1/q_{n+1}, the errors alternate in sign, δ_n is strictly decreasing, and δ_n = ||q_n α|| for every n ≥ 1 (because q_{n+1} ≥ 2 gives δ_n < 1/2); for n = 0 this holds when a_1 ≥ 2.

(2) The distances obey the same recursion as the denominators: δ_{n-1} = a_{n+1} δ_n + δ_{n+1} for all n ≥ 0. Equivalently δ_n = 1/(α_1 α_2 ··· α_{n+1}).

(3) Closest returns (Lagrange's theorem on best approximations of the second kind). For every n ≥ 0 and every integer q with 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1}: ||q α|| ≥ δ_n, with equality if and only if q = q_n. In dynamical words: for the rotation t ↦ t + α (mod 1), among all times 1 ≤ q < q_{n+1} the orbit of any point comes closest to its starting point exactly at time q_n; the record-breaking (closest-return) times of the orbit are precisely the denominators q_0 (when a_1 ≥ 2), q_1, q_2, ..., and successive closest returns land on alternate sides of the starting point, at distances δ_n.

(4) Growth. q_{n+1} ≥ q_n + q_{n-1}, hence q_n ≥ F_{n+1} (Fibonacci) and q_n ≥ 2^{(n−1)/2} for n ≥ 1; the golden ratio (all a_k = 1) is the slowest case.

Where it fails. For rational α the expansion terminates, the last δ is 0 and the recursion (2) stops. Statement (3) is about ||qα|| = min_p |qα − p| (best approximations of the SECOND kind). For the FIRST-kind problem of minimising |α − p/q| over q ≤ Q, intermediate fractions (p_{n-1} + k p_n)/(q_{n-1} + k q_n) with k > a_{n+1}/2 can also be best approximations, so the two notions must not be conflated. When a_1 = 1 one has q_0 = q_1 = 1, the n = 0 case of (3) is vacuous, and ||α|| equals δ_1, not δ_0.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:31.973825+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7280c27c2b949fd92c0ee3c63e501e2e6b80501cc66fb912945f9639ed0355bb","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2606.11068, '2606.11068'] Let \(S=(S_m)_{m\ge0}\) be a nearest-neighbour motion on \(\mathbb Z\), started
from \(S_0=0\), and let \(\Xi\) be an independent lifetime with tail \(G\).
Define
\[
  D^*:=\max_{0\le k\le \Xi}|S_k|.
\]
Let
\[
  \tau_n:=\inf\{m\ge1: |S_m|=n\},
  \qquad n\ge1,
\]
with the convention \(\inf\varnothing=\infty\). Then
\[
  \Pbb(D^*\ge n)=\E[G(\tau_n)].
\]
If
\[
  D^\to:=\max_{0\le k\le\Xi}S_k,
  \qquad
  \tau_n^+:=\inf\{m\ge1:S_m=n\},
\]
then
\[
  \Pbb(D^\to\ge n)=\E[G(\tau_n^+)].
\]
Analogously, if
\[
  D^\leftarrow:=\max_{0\le k\le\Xi}(-S_k),
  \qquad
  \tau_n^-:=\inf\{m\ge1:S_m=-n\},
\]
then
\[
  \Pbb(D^\leftarrow\ge n)=\E[G(\tau_n^-)].
\]
In the last two identities, we again use the convention \(G(\infty)=0\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact topological space","T: X → X is a map (continuity needed only for the orbit-closure supplement and T(M) = M)","A ⊂ X is nonempty, closed, and T(A) ⊆ A","Zorn's lemma (axiom of choice) is available"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:57:26.111086+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, minimal sets","id":"claim_72825b37190726c07a48638d2ab2de6ae848c0f1fc5cf24098ec659b459ef7be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact topological space and T: X → X a map. Then every nonempty closed set A ⊂ X with T(A) ⊆ A contains a minimal set: a nonempty closed set M ⊆ A with T(M) ⊆ M that has no proper nonempty closed T-invariant subset. In particular (A = X) every compact dynamical system has at least one minimal set. If moreover X is Hausdorff and T is continuous, then M = cl{Tⁿx : n ≥ 0} for every x ∈ M, T(M) = M, and (X metrizable) M carries a T-invariant Borel probability measure by the Krylov–Bogolyubov theorem, so every compact metrizable system has an invariant probability measure supported on a minimal set. The same statement and proof hold for a commuting family (or any semigroup) of maps X → X, with 'invariant' meaning invariant under every map of the family, and for flows. Sharp edges. (1) Compactness cannot be dropped: for the translation T(x) = x + 1 on ℝ, any nonempty closed invariant set A contains, for some a ∈ A, the closed invariant set {a + n : n ≥ 0}, which has the proper closed invariant subset {a + n : n ≥ 1}; so ℝ has NO minimal set, although it has plenty of nonempty closed invariant sets. (2) Existence uses only compactness and Zorn's lemma (the intersection of a chain of nonempty closed sets in a compact space is nonempty by the finite intersection property); continuity of T is needed only for the orbit-closure description and for T(M) = M. (3) Minimal sets need not be unique: the identity map has every single point as a minimal set; a system with a fixed point and a dense orbit (e.g. the doubling map) has minimal sets that are not the whole space. (4) 'Minimal' is with respect to inclusion among closed invariant sets; a nonempty invariant set that is not closed (a single dense orbit) is not a minimal set.","status":"unverified"}

Every continuous real symmetric PSD kernel of rank <=p and diagonal <=R^2 on a nonempty compact X subset R^d admits an explicit raw-input normalized-ReLU-attention transformer for uniform noisy predictive forward KL <=eps, with positive noise s, labels bounded by B, and contexts <=n.
