{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.168080+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_917501103e3120230731cde7a8230b436257d03fc77d1053d4287fe8c93416f9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 61 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have $\sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0)$. 

\begin{proof}
    This is a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$. Then, there exists
    \[
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)
    \]
    such that $\mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta) = \mu$.
    Let $\tilde p$ denote the restriction of $p$ to $[q_*,1] \subseteq [q_0,1]$.
    We will argue that $(b,\sigma,w,\tilde p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered} with $q_*$ in place of $q_0$.
    Indeed, conditions~\ref{it:1.1}, \ref{it:2.1}, \ref{it:3.1}, \ref{it:4.2}, \ref{it:5.1}, and \ref{it:6.1} exactly correspond to assumptions~(\ref{i:IAMP-main-coefs}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-diffusivity}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-p}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-budget}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-endpt}), and (\ref{i:IAMP-main-init}) of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}, while condition~\ref{it:1.1} also provides the additional assumption in Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered} that $w(t,\cdot)$ is even and $\zeta^\Ising$ is symmetric. By Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}, there exists $\iota = \iota(\epsilon)$ with $\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0} \iota(\epsilon) = 0$ such that for all (sufficiently large) $N$, there exists a $C(L,\epsilon)$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ with
    \[
        \max\Big(
            \bbW_2(\mu(\cA_N), \mu),
            \bbW_2(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_N), \cP(\{\pm 1\}))
        \Big) \le \iota
    \]
and
    $\bbE[\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)] = \bzero$.
    This implies $\chi_{\cA_N}(0) = 0$.
    Recalling the definition \eqref{e:cM.Lip.q0}, we have $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))$.
    We have thus shown
    \[
        \cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))\,.
    \]
    Thus, for $\cB_\epsilon$ as defined in \eqref{e:W2.ball.notation},
    \[
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \subseteq \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))\Big)\,.
    \]
    Taking a union over $L>0$ shows
    \[
        \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \subseteq \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;L,\iota(\epsilon))\Big)
        \subseteq \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;L,\tilde\epsilon)\Big)\,,
    \]
    where $\tilde\epsilon = \tilde\epsilon(\epsilon) = \max(\epsilon,\iota(\epsilon))$.
    Since $\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0} \tilde\epsilon(\epsilon) = 0$, taking an intersection over $\epsilon$ yields
    \begin{align*}
        \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0)
        &\stackrel{\eqref{e:measure.classes.simplification.without.L0}}{=}
        \adjustlimits
        \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big) \\
        &\,\,\subseteq
        \adjustlimits \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}}{=} \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0)\,. \qedhere
    \end{align*}
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.953880+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_91bdcd997adca9bb438363c57b1d7d97f25528afc3a7d2892cbd366118e120e4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 11 (Three-point representation of four centered moments) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let \(X\) be a real random variable satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \E X=0,
 \qquad
 \E X^2=v>0,
 \qquad
 \E X^4<\infty.
\end{equation}
Put
\begin{equation}
 a:=\frac{\E X^3}{v^{3/2}},
 \qquad
 b:=\frac{\E X^4}{v^2},
 \qquad
 c:=b-a^2.
\end{equation}
Then \(c\ge1\).  Define
\begin{equation}
 \alpha:=\frac{\sqrt{a^2+4c}-a}{2},
 \qquad
 \beta:=\frac{\sqrt{a^2+4c}+a}{2},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 p_-:=\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha+\beta)},
 \qquad
 p_+:=\frac{1}{\beta(\alpha+\beta)},
 \qquad
 p_0:=1-\frac1c.
\end{equation}
These numbers are nonnegative and sum to one.  If \(Q\) has the three-point
law
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P(Q=-\alpha)=p_-,
 \qquad
 \mathbb P(Q=0)=p_0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb P(Q=\beta)=p_+,
\end{equation}
then \(\widehat X:=\sqrt v\,Q\) satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \E\widehat X^q=\E X^q,
 \qquad q=1,2,3,4.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 |\widehat X|
 \le2\sqrt{\frac{\E X^4}{v}}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.212219+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_91e1404fa676dacdf7afde8eadcf87cffc2f007ea5413a3135ec9cae901ac54c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 11 (Subgaussian Kahane--Khintchine inequality) of arXiv:2608.13687, 'Multiplicative chaos from random multiplicative functions'] Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and fix $(f_i)_{i\in\N}\subset H$.
If $H$ is a real Hilbert space, let $(A_i)_{i\in\N}$ satisfy Case \caseR, and if $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, let $(A_i)_{i\in\N}$ satisfy \caseS.
For any $m\in\N$, 
define  
\[
S_m\coloneqq\sum_{k=1}^m A_k f_k \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sigma_m^2\coloneqq\E\|S_m\|_H^2 =  \sum_{k=1}^m \|f_k\|_H^2 \,.
\]
There exist $c,C>0$ such that for all $m \in \N$ such that  $\sigma_m >0$,
and for all $u\geq 0$,
\begin{align}
        \P(\|S_m\|_H>u)
        \le
        Ce^{-cu^2/\sigma_m^2}\,.
\end{align}
\begin{proof}
A version of the Kahane--Khintchine inequality stated explicitly for Rademacher, Steinhaus, and Gaussian coefficients can be found in \cite[Proposition~6.2.7]{kahane-khintchine-source}\footnote{They call Steinhaus random variables ``complex Rademacher'' random variables.}, which states the bound $\E e^{\delta\|S_m\|_H^2} \leq (1- 2e \delta \E\|S_m\|_H^2)^{-1}$ for all $\delta \in (0, (2e\sigma_m^2)^{-1})$. Equation~\eqref{eq:subgaussian-kahane-khintchine-tail} now follows from taking $\delta = 1/4e\sigma_m^2$ and the Markov inequality.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space","A is measurable","integrability of log^+ ||A|| is the standing hypothesis for the multiplicative ergodic theorem"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438394+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_920354a52c00e42c3e25c80f9069506badd8e398097645124d1386fa4d04f5aa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \\to M_d(\\mathbb{R})$ a measurable matrix-valued function. The linear cocycle generated by $A$ over $T$ is $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x) \\cdots A(Tx)\\,A(x)$ for $n \\ge 1$, $A^0 = I$; it satisfies the cocycle identity $A^{n+m}(x) = A^m(T^n x) A^n(x)$. (If $T$ is invertible and $A(x) \\in GL_d$, one also sets $A^{-n}(x) = A^n(T^{-n}x)^{-1}$.) The cocycle is (forward) integrable if $\\log^+ \\|A\\| \\in L^1(\\mu)$, where $\\log^+ t = \\max(\\log t, 0)$ and $\\|\\cdot\\|$ is any matrix norm; it is two-sidedly integrable if also $A(x)$ is invertible a.e. and $\\log^+\\|A^{-1}\\| \\in L^1$. For $v \\in \\mathbb{R}^d \\setminus \\{0\\}$ the (forward) Lyapunov exponent of $v$ at $x$ is $\\lambda(x, v) = \\lim_{n\\to\\infty} \\frac1n \\log \\|A^n(x) v\\|$ when the limit exists (in $[-\\infty, \\infty)$); more generally $\\bar\\lambda(x, v) = \\limsup$. The function $v \\mapsto \\bar\\lambda(x, v)$ takes finitely many values and satisfies $\\bar\\lambda(x, u + v) \\le \\max(\\bar\\lambda(x,u), \\bar\\lambda(x,v))$, so for each $x$ the sets $\\{v : \\bar\\lambda(x, v) \\le c\\} \\cup \\{0\\}$ are linear subspaces and form a filtration of $\\mathbb{R}^d$. The prototype is the derivative cocycle $A(x) = Df_x$ of a smooth map $f$ on a manifold (trivialised bundle), whose exponents measure exponential rates of divergence of nearby orbits. Warning: $\\|A^n(x)\\|^{1/n}$ and $|\\text{eigenvalues of } A^n(x)|^{1/n}$ are different things; Lyapunov exponents are the growth rates of SINGULAR values of $A^n(x)$, not eigenvalues, and for non-commuting products the two can differ.","status":"unverified"}

The main concerns of Gustave Choquet were in potential theory. {"assumptions":["the axiom of choice (used in step 3 to select orbit representatives; the result is not a theorem of ZF alone)","n >= 3 for the paradox; rigid motions of R^n (isometries); 'pieces' are arbitrary sets, necessarily non-measurable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.480173+00:00","domain":"measure theory and geometry","id":"claim_926a5872eb18b627a0e7fd10743a1293421bfa6309bdf99c41e9eb5a25b9a1d1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Assuming the axiom of choice, the closed unit ball B in R^3 can be partitioned into finitely many pieces which can be reassembled by rigid motions (rotations and translations) into two disjoint copies of B; five pieces suffice (Robinson), and four do not. More generally (the strong form) any two bounded subsets of R^n, n >= 3, with nonempty interior are equidecomposable: one can be cut into finitely many pieces and moved by isometries onto the other. The pieces are necessarily non-measurable, so no contradiction with Lebesgue measure arises - the theorem shows that no finitely additive, isometry-invariant measure defined on ALL subsets of R^3 and normalising the ball can exist. In dimensions 1 and 2 the paradox fails: Banach showed that Lebesgue measure on R and R^2 extends to a finitely additive isometry-invariant measure on all subsets, because the isometry groups of R and R^2 are amenable (solvable), while SO(3) contains a free group on two generators, which is the source of the paradox (Hausdorff, 1914). Tarski's theorem (1929) makes this exact: a group action admits a paradoxical decomposition if and only if it carries no finitely additive invariant probability measure, i.e. it is non-amenable. With choice the result is a theorem; in ZF plus the axiom of determinacy, or in Solovay's model, every set of reals is measurable and the decomposition does not exist.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.360189+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92a1d9662fc1cdf4d1b67078367c48365ebd49b68fc0e169dce8c66a0fd60926","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 252 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If $\bX:\R^{N'}\to\R^N$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $\bg$ is a standard gaussian in $\R^{N'}$, and $\E[\|\bX(\bg)\|^2] = N$, then for any $\delta > 0$, there exists $c(\delta) > 0$ such that 
    \[
    \P\bigg(
    \bigg|\frac{\|\bX(\bg)\|^2}{N} - 1\bigg|
    \ge \delta\bigg)
    \le e^{-c(\delta)N}\,.\]

\begin{proof}
    Since $\bg \mapsto \|\bX(\bg)\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, it follows from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus} that $\|\bX(\bg)\|-\E\|\bX(\bg)\|$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $2L^2$, and satisfies the concentration bound \eqref{e:lip.subgaus}:
    \[
    \P\bigg( \Big|
    \|\bX(\bg)\| - \E\|\bX(\bg)\|\Big| \ge t
    \bigg) \le 2\exp\bigg\{-\frac{t^2}{2L^2}\bigg\}\,.
    \]
It follows that $\|\bX(\bg)\|$ has variance $O(L^2)$, which implies
    \[
     \frac{O(L^2)}{N}
     \ge
    \frac{\E[\|\bX(\bg)\|^2] - ( \E\|\bX(\bg)\|)^2}{N}
    =1- \frac{ ( \E\|\bX(\bg)\|)^2}{N}\,.
    \]
Combining the last two displays gives the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Definition of the specific source model; beta>1,s>0,uniform power-law comparison constants.","Fresh independent Gaussian features and independent Gaussian constant-order label noise; averaged minibatch gradients.","Zero initial iterate and zero initial momentum for the scaling-law protocol."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:47:26.804438+00:00","domain":"Kernel regression and stochastic optimization","id":"claim_92bc45c903189bf192adf6404c4679485e5e9b8150fad2524367d7a2833ca314","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The model used by Wang-Huang-Li-Wu in arXiv:2609.02728 is Gaussian-feature, online least-squares regression. In the covariance eigenbasis, a feature vector phi has centered Gaussian law N(0,H) with H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2,...) positive trace class, lambda_1>=lambda_2>=...>0. A label is y=<phi,theta_star>+epsilon with epsilon~N(0,sigma^2) independent of phi. The target has finite prediction energy sum_j lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2<infinity; the pairing can equivalently be read as its mean-square-convergent Gaussian series. The population risk is R(theta)=E(<phi,theta>-y)^2/2, and the excess risk is Ecal(theta)=sum_j lambda_j*|theta_j-theta_star_j|^2/2=R(theta)-sigma^2/2. Their source/capacity assumptions are beta>1,s>0, lambda_j asymp j^(-beta) and lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2 asymp j^(-(1+s*beta)), where asymp means upper and lower bounds by fixed positive constants, uniform in j. The label-noise standard deviation sigma is bounded above and away from zero by fixed constants (the constant-order noisy setting). At iteration k a fresh IID batch of B examples, independent of all past batches, gives the AVERAGED gradient g(theta;batch)=B^(-1)*sum_i phi_(k,i)*(<phi_(k,i),theta>-y_(k,i)). For a constant eta>0 and constant rho in[0,1), SGD uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch); Polyak uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch)+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)); Nesterov first sets theta_k_la=theta_k+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)) and uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k_la-eta*g(theta_k_la;batch). The source scaling-law analysis takes theta_0=theta_-1=0. For a one-pass data budget D, take T=D/B updates (or integer rounding at the exponent level), and B=D^(b+o(1)) with fixed b in[0,1). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.494853+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92d321365a35e1fdb09d2d7b3b0cda3acab6c8d20c455e3b4fa61147909dfbf1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn rational SLE0 of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] In the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, let $e^{i\theta} \in \partial \mathbb{D}$ be the growth point, and let $u_1, u_2, \dots, u_m \in \overline{\mathbb{D}}$ be marked points. A symmetric double divisor $(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^+, \boldsymbol{\sigma}^-)$ assigns a charge distribution on $e^{i\theta}$ and $\{u_1, \dots, u_k\}$, where
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}^+ = a \cdot e^{i\theta} + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sigma_j \cdot u_j,
\quad \text{and} \quad
\boldsymbol{\sigma}^- = \overline{\boldsymbol{\sigma}^+}|_{\mathbb{D}},
\]
and the total charge satisfies the neutrality condition $\int\boldsymbol{\sigma}=-2$.

We define the rational $\mathrm{SLE}_0[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ Loewner chain as a normalized conformal map $g_t(z)$ with initial conditions $g_0(z) = z$ and $g_t'(0) = e^{-t}$. The evolution of $g_t$ is governed by the Loewner differential equation:
\[
\partial_t g_t(z) = g_t(z) \frac{e^{i\theta(t)} + g_t(z)}{e^{i\theta(t)} - g_t(z)}, \quad g_0(z) = z.
\]

In the angular coordinate, let $h_t(z)$ be the covering map of $g_t(z)$ defined by $e^{i h_t(z)} = g_t(e^{i z})$. Then $h_t(z)$ evolves according to
\[
\partial_t h_t(z) = \cot\left( \frac{h_t(z) - \theta(t)}{2} \right), \quad h_0(z) = z.
\]

The driving function $\theta(t)$ evolves according to
\[
d\theta(t) = \frac{\partial \log \mathcal{Z}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta} \, dt.
\]

where the Coulomb gas partition function is
\begin{equation} 
\mathcal{Z}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \prod_{j < k} \sin\left( \frac{\theta_j - \theta_k}{2} \right)^{\sigma_j \sigma_k} 
\cdot \prod_j e^{\frac{i}{2} \sigma_j (\sigma_0 - \sigma_\infty)\theta_j}.
\end{equation}

The flow $g_t$ is well-defined up to the first time $\tau$ at which $w(t) = g_t(w)$ for some $w$ in the support of $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$. For each $z \in \overline{\mathbb{D}}$, the process $t \mapsto g_t(z)$ is well-defined up to $\tau_z \wedge \tau$, where $\tau_z$ is the first time such that $g_t(z) = e^{i\theta(t)}$. Denote
\[
K_t = \left\{ z \in \overline{\mathbb{D}} : \tau_z \leq t \right\}
\]
as the hull associated with the Loewner chain.

Furthermore, the rational $\mathrm{SLE}_0$ Loewner chain is invariant under Möbius transformations in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D})$ (up to a time reparameterization), due to the conformal invariance of the Coulomb gas correlation. Consequently, rational $\mathrm{SLE}_0[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ in any simply connected domain $\Omega$ is defined by pulling back via a conformal map $\phi: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:33:11.960027+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92e48b9ac631443a82725ec1a098daec22d5d19518ce2027cad21957ceb2ec69","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:romiksniady-main of arXiv:2607.24018, 'Jeu de taquin forests \\ and the inverse infinite RSK correspondence'] \begin{enumerate}

\item The Plancherel measure $P$ is the push-forward of the
infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure $\Lambda$ on
$[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ under the map $\RSK(\cdot)$.

\item The jeu de taquin map $J$ is a measure-preserving
transformation on the Plancherel measure space $(\Omega,
\mathcal{F}, P)$.

\item The jeu de taquin map is intertwined with the shift map $S$
on $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ (defined by $S(z_1,z_2,\ldots)=(z_2,z_3,\ldots)$)
by the map $\RSK(\cdot)$, in the sense that the
relation
\[
J \circ \RSK = \RSK\circ S
\]
holds $\Lambda$-almost surely on $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$. 

\item The RSK map $\RSK(\cdot)$ is an isomorphism between
the two measure-preserving dynamical systems $([0,1]^\mathbb{N},
\mathcal{B}, \Lambda, S)$ and $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P, J)$.

\item The inverse map $\RSK^{-1}(\cdot)$ is given explicitly by
\begin{equation} 
\RSK^{-1}(T) = ( \zeta(T), \zeta\circ J(T), \zeta \circ J^2(T), \ldots)
\quad \textrm{for $P$-almost every }T\in \Omega,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}

\zeta(T) =
1 - F\left(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{x_n-y_n}{\sqrt{T_{x_n,y_n}}} \right),
\end{equation}
where $((x_n,y_n))_{n=0}^\infty$ denotes the jeu de taquin
path associated with $T$ as in (equation eq:jdt-path of the paper) and
$F(u)$ is given by
\begin{equation}

F(u) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-2}^u \sqrt{4-s^2} \, ds
\qquad (-2 \le u \le 2).
\end{equation}
(This statement includes the assertion that the limit in
(equation eq:inverse-rsk-firstcoord of the paper) exists and takes a value in $[-2,2]$
$P$-almost surely.)

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the graph is planar (embeddable in the plane without crossings) and loopless; multiple edges do not matter for colouring","proper colouring: adjacent vertices differ","the proof is computer-assisted; the sketch names the method and the published verifications"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T14:24:13.476890+00:00","domain":"graph theory","id":"claim_92e5db9a713cd3ef2d22a18a59a18840aa7e87870d30226a7a633987fb4d11b1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Every loopless planar graph is properly 4-colourable: its vertices can be coloured with four colours so that adjacent vertices receive different colours. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.653986+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92e64b9f4283d04bc7e5dc9487d38a0b713eb36117e7f749042aa8227931db03","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:restricted of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] An event $A$ is \emph{restricted} to a region $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$ and a time interval $[t_0,t_1]$ if
it is measurable with respect to the $\sigma$-field generated by the particles lying in $X$ at
time $t_0$, their trajectories on $[t_0,t_1]$ and the marks those particles carry on $[t_0,t_1]$.
When the isolation rule is in force, the $\sigma$-field also includes the trajectories on
$[t_0,t_1]$ of the particles lying within distance $2r$ of $X$ at time $t_0$, since these decide
whether those marks are effective.
A particle has \emph{displacement inside} $X'$ during $[t_0,t_1]$ if $X_u(t)-X_u(t_0)\in X'$ for
every $t\in[t_0,t_1]$. An event is \emph{increasing} if it is preserved by adding particles, in
the sense of (prop:mono of the paper)(ii). For an increasing event $E$ restricted to $X$ and $[0,t]$, we
write $\nu_E(\zeta,X,X',t)$ for the probability that $E$ holds when the particles in $X$ at time
$0$ form a Poisson process of intensity $\zeta$ and are conditioned to have displacement inside
$X'$ during $[0,t]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Finite E, orthogonal subspaces H_1, H_2","Evidence is computational on |E| <= 8 only"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T07:36:18.299044+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92f80e4dcf39be1b9857d932b15ffa66cb7d95ccb79f0a2e9b16609e2935e314","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE NUMERICAL EVIDENCE, not a proof. Lyons (ICM 2014, Question 2.8) asks whether for H = H_1 (+) H_2 orthogonal in l^2(E) there is a coupling of the determinantal projection measures P_{H_1}, P_{H_2} whose union has law P_H. Since the cardinalities are dim H_1, dim H_2 and dim H almost surely, the union must be disjoint, and the question is the nonemptiness of the transportation polytope with the three marginals. Exact LP (HiGHS, minimum total violation) on 1360 random pairs of orthogonal subspaces with |E| in {3,...,6} over all dimension splits, on generic instances with |E| = 7 and 8, on Fourier-mode subspaces of cycles of length 5..8, and on star-space splits in the edge space of K_4 found a feasible coupling with zero violation every time (intake raw/C_lyons_q28_lp_check.json and _structured.json). A structural observation: the naive rule 'sample X_1 from P_{H_1} conditioned on X_1 subset C, set X_2 = C minus X_1' does NOT reproduce the P_{H_2} marginal in general (checked on |E| = 4), so the coupling, when it exists, is not the conditional splitting. Open: a general construction.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:19:46.228355+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92fc30ba399813b12bfcb9d15f2d6c797b34a6cc0166f1f2f6535f9e4542a966","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 11 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] For any finite positive semidefinite matrix $Q$, its \textbf{log-determinant entropy} is
\[\rmH(Q) := \log \det Q,\]
with the usual convention that $\log 0 = -\infty$.

If $S$ is any set (not necessarily finite), $Q$ is a positive semidefinite $S$-by-$S$ matrix, and $F$ is a finite subset of $S$, then we define
\[\rmH_Q(F) := \rmH(Q[F]),\]
where $Q[F]$ is the $F$-by-$F$ submatrix of $Q$. (Recall our notation for submatrices from Section~\ref{sec:lin-alg}.)","status":"unverified"}

 p_j\in\R[x_1,\ldots,x_{d},t,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r]
\].
We use the standard convention that the zero polynomial has degree
$-\infty$; thus identically zero atoms are covered by every nonnegative
degree bound below.
The $j$th atom produces the bit
\begin{equation}
 A_j(\bmx,t,\bmmu)
 :=\one_{\{p_j(\bmx,t,\bmmu)>0\}}.
\end{equation}
Finally, choose one Boolean formula tree
$\mathfrak{B}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{s_0})$ as described above, and let
$\mathsf{B}:\{0,1\}^{s_0}\to\{0,1\}$ be the map obtained from its recursive
evaluation.  We say that $\calS$
has an $(s,d_{\mathrm{pol}})$ Boolean-polynomial description in the parameter
$\bmmu$ when, for every $(\bmx,t,\bmmu)$,
\begin{equation}
 \one_{\calS}(\bmx,t,\bmmu)
 =\mathsf{B}\bigl(
 A_1(\bmx,t,\bmmu),\ldots,
 A_{s_0}(\bmx,t,\bmmu)\bigr),
\end{equation}
and, for each fixed $(\bmx,t)$,
\begin{equation*}
 \deg_{\bmmu}p_j(\bmx,t,\cdot)\le d_{\mathrm{pol}},
 \qquad j=1,\ldots,s_0.
\end{equation*}
The integer $s$ is only an upper bound; $s_0$ is the number of leaf

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:15:16.652674+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_93c501d1ba2e2cdeebc1ab59cb29325cbc6ba95e7d96b351198776f7118d36e2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] With the notation above, the normalized energy is nonincreasing and satisfies
\begin{equation}
  e^{-2t}E_{u_0}(X_t)
  \searrow
  \mathscr V_q(Y)
  \qquad
  \text{as }t\to\infty.
  
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{t\to\infty}
  \frac{E_{u_0}(X_t)}{e^{2t}}
  =
  \mathscr V_q(Y),
  \qquad
  E_{u_0}(X_t)
  =
  \mathscr V_q(Y)e^{2t}
  +
  o(e^{2t}).
  
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\(
  0<\mathscr V_q(Y)<\infty.
\)

If \(q\) is Jenkins--Strebel and its vertical foliation is the contracting
foliation of the ray, let
\(
  C_1,\ldots,C_r
\)
be its maximal flat cylinders. Write
\(
  C_i
  \cong
  (0,h_i)\times
  \bigl(\mathbb R/c_i\mathbb Z\bigr),
\)
where the closed vertical trajectories have \(q\)-length \(c_i\), the
transverse height is \(h_i\), and \(\delta_i\) is the core curve of \(C_i\).
Then
\begin{equation}
  \mathscr V_q(Y)
  =
  \frac12
  \sum_{i=1}^r
  \operatorname{Mod}(C_i)\,
  \ell_Y(\delta_i)^2
  =
  \frac12
  \sum_{i=1}^r
  \frac{h_i}{c_i}\,
  \ell_Y(\delta_i)^2.
  
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
  \lim_{t\to\infty}
  \frac{E_{u_0}(X_t)}{e^{2t}}
  =
  \frac12
  \sum_{i=1}^r
  \operatorname{Mod}(C_i)\,
  \ell_Y(\delta_i)^2.
  
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} Boolean, uniform product measure","c is a universal constant","the conclusion bounds only the MAXIMUM influence, not any specific coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_94198fd805d1f2269bd7bd89b92062349f91be394349788a2f4df1ea2bf88af8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} be a Boolean function on the uniform product measure, and define the influence of coordinate i as Inf_i(f) = P( f(X) != f(X^{(i)}) ) where X^{(i)} flips the i-th coordinate. Then there is a universal constant c > 0 with max_{i <= n} Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n / n, where Var(f) = p(1-p) with p = E[f]. This does not bound the TOTAL influence by c Var(f) log n: a dictator f(x) = (1 + x_1)/2 has total influence 1 and Var(f) = 1/4 for every n. The total-influence form of the theorem is sum_i Inf_i(f) >= c' Var(f) log(1/max_i Inf_i(f)) for nonconstant f, with c' > 0 universal, and the maximum bound follows from it. The bound is SHARP up to the constant: the tribes function, a read-once DNF on blocks of size about log_2 n - log_2 log_2 n, is balanced and has all influences of order log n / n. The theorem is about the uniform measure on the cube; the analogous statement for p-biased measures carries an extra factor and is the Friedgut-Kalai sharp-threshold machinery. Note what it does NOT say: it does not bound the influence of any PARTICULAR coordinate, only the maximum, and it says nothing when Var(f) is 0, that is when f is constant. [Kahn, Kalai and Linial (1988); see O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 9]","status":"unverified"}

Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target:1.
General T267 OPEN. This is a precise obstruction to one proof route, not a
counterexample to nonlinear epochwise double descent. Novelty unestablished.

1. Statement
Let Z have ANY initialization-independent probability law on unit vectors in R^3,
and let V be uniform on the unit three-dimensional ball, independent of Z.
Fix 0<nu<=1, 0<tau<=1/4 and any integer m>=1. Independently initialize
 f_m(x;0)=m^(-1/2)sum_(j=1)^m a_j ReLU(W_j.x),
where W_j are iid N(0,I_3), a_j are iid uniform {-nu,nu}, and all are independent.
The SAME network is evaluated at Z+tau V and Z. Conditional on its initialization
put Y_m=E_(Z,V)|f_m(Z+tau V;0)-f_m(Z;0)|^2.
Define the strictly positive Gaussian-box probability
 p=P(1<=G_0<=2, |G_1|<=1, |G_2|<=1)
  =(Phi(2)-Phi(1))*(2Phi(1)-1)^2, for independent standard normals G_i.
Then, uniformly in m and the law of Z,
 E_init Y_m >=nu^2 tau^2 p/5,
 E_init Y_m^2 <=3nu^4 tau^4,
 P_init(Y_m>=nu^2 tau^2 p/10)>=p^2/300.                 (1)
In particular, at a FIXED positive tau the coupled initial-function discrepancy
cannot vanish in probability as width increases, even though initializations
are shared exactly. No training, Gram approximation or kernel-width limit is
needed for this conclusion.

2. Gaussian active-region lower bound
Fix a unit z and choose orthonormal coordinates with first axis z. Rotational
invariance of N(0,I_3) gives the same probability p to
 A_z={1<=W.z<=2, absolute values of the two orthogonal coordinates <=1}.
On this event ||W||<=sqrt(6). For EVERY ||v||<=1 and tau<=1/4,
 W.z>=1 and W.(z+tau v)>=1-tau sqrt(6)>0,
since 6/16<1. Thus both ReLUs are active and their difference is EXACTLY
 tau W.v. Uniform-ball covariance is E VV^T=I_3/5: its radial density is
3r^2 on [0,1], so E||V||^2=3/5, and symmetry divides this equally among axes.
Consequently
 E_(W,V)[ReLU(W.(z+tau V))-ReLU(W.z)]^2
 >=tau^2 E_W[1_(A_z)||W||^2/5]>=tau^2 p/5.            (2)
The integrand is nonnegative, so restriction to A_z is legitimate. This
bound is uniform in z; the orthonormal coordinates need not be chosen jointly
measurably because the pointwise bound is already independent of z.

3. Independent centered heads and the second moment
For fixed z,v put delta_j=ReLU(W_j.(z+tau v))-ReLU(W_j.z), T_j=a_j delta_j.
The T_j are independent centered variables; centering follows from the
independent head sign, without requiring delta_j itself to be centered.
Therefore
 E_init |m^(-1/2)sum_j T_j|^2=nu^2 E_W delta_1^2.
Integrate over (Z,V) and apply (2), using Tonelli, to obtain the first
inequality in (1). There is no 1/m decay in this initial output fluctuation:
the summation has scale 1/sqrt(m), whereas a kernel sample mean has scale 1/m.
The conclusion does not apply to paired antithetic initialization with
identical hidden weights and opposite heads; that violates the iid hypothesis
and can make the initial function identically zero.

4. Fourth moment and a probability lower bound
ReLU is 1-Lipschitz, hence |delta_j|<=tau |W_j.v|. For fixed z,v, write
mu_2=E T_1^2 and mu_4=E T_1^4. Gaussian second and fourth moments give
 mu_2<=nu^2 tau^2 ||v||^2,
 mu_4<=3nu^4 tau^4 ||v||^4.
These Gaussian moments follow by rotating v to a coordinate axis and using
E G^2=1, E G^4=3 (integration by parts for the standard normal density).
In the expansion of E(sum_j T_j)^4, a term survives only if every index
occurs an even number of times. There are m all-equal terms and
6*binom(m,2) two-pair terms. Thus exactly
 E_init |m^(-1/2)sum_j T_j|^4
 =mu_4/m+3(1-1/m)mu_2^2
 <=3nu^4 tau^4 ||v||^4<=3nu^4 tau^4.                 (3)
Jensen on the (Z,V) probability space gives Y_m^2<=E_(Z,V)|D_m(Z,V)|^4,
where D_m is the same initial prediction difference. Integrating (3) proves
the second inequality in (1). All moments are finite by the displayed bounds.

For completeness, the one-sided moment step does not assume concentration.
Set a=nu^2 tau^2 p/5, b=3nu^4 tau^4 and E={Y_m>=a/2}. Then
 E Y_m<=a/2+E[Y_m 1_E]<=a/2+sqrt(b P(E))
by splitting at a/2 and applying Cauchy-Schwarz. Since E Y_m>=a,
P(E)>=a^2/(4b)=p^2/300. This is precisely the last inequality in (1).
It is a probability lower bound, not a conclusion from mean error alone.

5. Consequence for the C022/C023 transfer route
In those constructions Z is uniform on four unit centers. At initialization,
the coupled center-to-ball population L2 error is sqrt(Y_m). It is part of
D_m(T)=max_(0<=k<=T)||F_ball,k(Z+tau V)-F_center,k(Z)||_2,
so D_m(T)>=sqrt(Y_m) for every horizon T, regardless of subsequent updates.
The bound (1) therefore holds for an initial discrepancy inside exactly the
same coupling used there, for every e, every width, and every fixed tau>0.
Directly replacing tau=e^20 by a positive constant cannot retain the
vanishing prediction comparison D_m(T)=o_P(1), let alone o_P(e^5).
More generally, with fixed nu>0 and tau=tau_e<=1/4, any argument that requires
D_m(T)=o_P(e^5) in width-before-scale limits must have tau_e=o(e^5): if not,
a subsequence has tau_e/e^5 bounded below, and (1) gives a fixed positive
probability of D_m(T)/e^5 being bounded away from zero. This is only a
necessary condition for THAT prediction-error route; C022's e^20 radius
satisfies it. It says nothing about optimal radius exponents.

This does NOT prove that actual population-risk differences cannot cancel,
that no alternative nonshrinking-geometry proof exists, or that double descent
fails for fixed-radius input laws. A proof for such laws must analyze their
nonconstant initial function and population dynamics directly, or use an
alternative comparison. The obstruction identifies why the present center
comparison cannot simply be thickened.

6. Finite checks and audit scope
The accompanying exact Fraction script enumerates independent head signs
for several deterministic increment vectors and widths1 through8. It checks
second and fourth moment expansions and detects a deliberately omitted
mixed fourth-moment term. Its paired-head negative control yields zero
initial difference where the independent-head computation is positive.
These checks concern the finite combinatorial step only; they are not an
independent audit of the Gaussian, population or limiting arguments. No Lean
certificate or literature-priority claim is made. Reviewer PASS is pending.

Brain use: q022 returned the standard second-moment technique; its warning
against drawing a probability conclusion from a mean alone is addressed in
Section4. The population Jensen step assumes no independence across inputs.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["gamma the standard Gaussian measure on R^n","f locally Lipschitz (or weakly differentiable) with f and grad f in L^2(gamma)","the constant 1 is sharp; there is no dimension dependence"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628017+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_947309ec928615f9dbb7adf2e8d0772e4ada248270d9924e007bfa120575ef81","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n and let f be locally Lipschitz with f and its gradient in L^2(gamma). Then Var_gamma(f) <= E_gamma[ |grad f|^2 ]. The constant 1 is SHARP and is attained exactly by the affine functions: for f(x) = a . x + b both sides equal |a|^2. The inequality is DIMENSION-FREE - the same constant 1 for every n - which is what makes it useful in high dimension, and it follows from the one-dimensional case by tensorization of the variance. It is strictly weaker than the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality, which implies it by applying the log-Sobolev inequality to 1 + eps f and expanding to second order in eps. Note the direction: the inequality bounds the variance by the gradient energy, so it gives concentration only at the level of variance, not exponential tails; exponential tails require the log-Sobolev inequality and the Herbst argument. [standard; e.g. Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.20]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:04:59.428883+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9496c2e3ea127f8378a01dbda05c168a6f9dcaffcb3d9b635edb255b45a693ee","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:meta-process of arXiv:2605.19835, 'Reemergence of the Epidemic Threshold in SIRS Infections on Connected Stars'] Let $k, \\ell \\in \\mathOrText{\\mathds{N}}_{\\geq 1}$, and let~$G^\\star$ be a \\conStar{k}{\\ell}.\n    Moreover, let $\\varepsilon \\in \\mathOrText{\\mathds{R}}_{>0}$ be a constant, and let $C$ be an SIRS process on a super-graph of~$G^\\star$ (over $n \\in \\mathOrText{\\mathds{N}}_{\\geq 1}$ vertices) with infection rate $\\lambda \\in (0, 1]$ such that $\\lambda \\in \\bigOmega{\\ell^{-1/2+\\varepsilon}}$ and with constant deimmunization rate $\\varrho \\in \\mathOrText{\\mathds{R}}_{> 0}$. For each star $s$ of~$G^\\star$ and each $t \\in \\mathOrText{\\mathds{R}}_{\\geq 0}$, let $A_{s,t}$ be the indicator random variable of the event that~$s$ is active at time $t$. We call the union of these indicator variables over all~$k$ stars the \\emph{meta process} $A$ of $C$. Furthermore, for each $t \\in \\mathOrText{\\mathds{R}}_{\\geq 0}$, let~$X_t$ be the random variable of the number of active stars at time~$t$, and for each $i \\in \\mathOrText{\\mathds{N}}$, let $\\tau(i)$ be the $i$-th time point at which $(X_t)_{t \\in \\mathOrText{\\mathds{R}}_{\\geq 0}} \\eqqcolon X$ changes its value, defining $\\tau(0) = 0$. We call~$X$ the \\emph{simplified meta process} of $C$, and $\\mathopen{}\\mathclose\\bgroup\\originalleft(X_{\\tau(i)}\\aftergroup\\egroup\\originalright)_{i \\in \\mathOrText{\\mathds{N}}}$ the \\emph{discrete version} of $X_t$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["planar first-passage percolation, chi=1/3 fluctuation-exponent conjecture; two campaign threads: (A) a variance-ratio cap (L1') from above needing rho=Q^2/Var=O(1), and (B) a variance lower bound reducing to restricted-min anticoncentration","heuristic framing throughout, not independently refereed at the time of writing; both named ingredients (existence of the per-scale rate rho_L, and a product-beats-growth bookkeeping step) remain open"],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:47:00.008105+00:00","domain":"probability/first-passage percolation","id":"claim_94abbe98ab8d46ca96ae836927b075a4","kind":"heuristic","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the program toward the first-passage percolation fluctuation exponent chi = 1/3, the obstruction that the variance-ratio induction does not start is two-sided rather than one-sided. The upper argument, (L1'), caps the block-increment fluctuation from above and needs alpha = chi through the ratio rho = Q^2/Var = O(1); rho = O(1) needs a variance lower bound that an upper-bound induction cannot supply about itself; and a second argument bounds the same fluctuation from below, reducing that lower bound to restricted-minimum anticoncentration. So the wall is a two-sided sandwich on the block-increment scale - a fixed-point equation whose solution is chi - and a one-directional induction cannot reach a fixed point, which is why it does not start. Proposed escape: carry a window [L, U] on the variance instead of a single value. The ratio R = U/L can contract (the upper leg lowers U given L, the lower leg raises L given U, neither proved about itself), which removes the circularity and reduces the difficulty to one missing ingredient: the lower leg as a per-scale contraction rate rho_L, a restricted-minimum anticoncentration statement weaker-looking than a full variance lower bound. Quantitative floor: the base window R(0) ~ n/log^2 n is polynomially large and only about log n scale steps are available, so the contraction must be at most about 1/2 at every step, not merely have a product below 1. Status: heuristic at the sandwich framing (the equivalence of the two sides holds at the level the block-sum argument needs, not as a formal if-and-only-if); the existence of rho_L and the bookkeeping by which the product beats the growth are open, chi = 1/3 is not proved, and a referee reading is owed.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T03:42:25.818267+00:00","domain":"probability, trees, ergodic theory","id":"claim_94db0dee1d2ddaa48514c8d55f228d27c4d573e1cf1e757815403f5e1e40d56c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (version 19 August 2026), Question 17.18 (p. 575) asks whether a consistent equivariant flow rule admitting a stationary measure EQUIVALENT to Galton-Watson measure must induce an ergodic Markov chain; their Proposition 17.17 proves it when all child weights are strictly positive, and Exercise 17.22 gives a non-ergodic example whose stationary measure is only absolutely continuous, so equivalence is the point of the question. Our result (id P0033, 2026-09-08): NO. Take Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5 (mean 12/5) and an isomorphism-invariant colour in {0,1} defined by AND at two-child vertices and OR at three-child vertices; both preserve unanimity, so every vertex has at least one child of its own colour, and the flow chooses uniformly among those. Galton-Watson measure is stationary, the root colour is invariant along the chain and takes each value with probability 1/2 - a non-constant invariant function, hence no ergodicity - and the stationary measure equals Galton-Watson measure, trivially equivalent to it. The colour exists because F(p) = (3/5) p^2 + (2/5)[1 - (1-p)^3] fixes 1/2, and r_n = E[q_n^2] satisfies r_{n+1} = 3/10 + (3/5) r^2 + (2/5) r^3 whose increment factors as (r - 1/2)[(2/5) r^2 + (4/5) r - 3/5], driving r_n from r_0 = 1/4 up to 1/2 and giving E[q(1-q)] = 0. Verification as the source words it: the step the proof leaves implicit, and which was checked, is that Galton-Watson really is stationary - it holds because, conditioned on the children's colours, the child subtrees are independent, each distributed as Galton-Watson conditioned on its own colour, so the chosen subtree is exactly GW given colour = c, the uniform choice adds no bias, and mixing over c returns GW. Prior art unchecked; the tree-automaton and factor-of-iid literature is where to look. Galton-Watson with P(D=2) = 3/5, P(D=3) = 2/5 consistent equivariant flow rule choosing uniformly among same-coloured children","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is an open subset of R^N","u belongs to W^{1,p}(Omega) for the chain rule to apply","k > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250886+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, Sobolev spaces, truncation method","id":"claim_94ec221464adf6dc620b348214224d1a08fe5b06010d5e14cd92e3e805a01a53","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For $k > 0$ the truncation at level $k$ is $T_k(s) = \\max(-k, \\min(k, s))$, $s \\in \\mathbb{R}$: it equals $s$ for $|s| \\leq k$ and $\\pm k$ outside. $T_k$ is Lipschitz with constant 1, odd, and $T_k(0) = 0$. Chain rule (Stampacchia): if $\\Omega \\subset \\mathbb{R}^N$ is open and $u \\in W^{1,p}(\\Omega)$, $1 \\leq p \\leq \\infty$, then $T_k(u) \\in W^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ with $\\nabla T_k(u) = \\nabla u \\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{|u| < k\\}}$ almost everywhere; if $u \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ then $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$, and $|T_k(u)| \\leq \\min(|u|, k)$. In particular $\\nabla u = 0$ a.e. on every level set $\\{u = c\\}$. Companion functions: the positive part $u^+ = \\max(u,0)$ and $G_k(u) = u - T_k(u)$ (the part of $u$ beyond level $k$); all such compositions satisfy the same chain rule $\\nabla(\\phi \\circ u) = \\phi'(u)\\nabla u$ a.e. for piecewise $C^1$ Lipschitz $\\phi$ with finitely many corners (with $\\phi(0) = 0$ to stay in $W_0^{1,p}$). The truncation method uses $T_k(u)$ (or $G_k(u)$) as a test function in a weak formulation; because it is bounded by $k$ it is admissible against $L^1$ right-hand sides, and $\\int_\\Omega |\\nabla T_k(u)|^p$ measures the energy of $u$ on the set where $|u| < k$. Sharp edges: the chain rule needs $\\phi$ Lipschitz (a merely continuous or unbounded-derivative $\\phi$ can leave $W^{1,p}$); for a function that is only in $L^1_{loc}$ with no Sobolev regularity, $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}$ for all $k$ is a genuine extra hypothesis, and this is exactly the class in which entropy solutions of $L^1$-data problems live.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A small parameter: bubble (SAW), triangle (percolation) or square (lattice trees) diagram small at criticality","Above the upper critical dimension: d > 4 (SAW), d > 6 (percolation), d > 8 (lattice trees)","Nearest-neighbour models need d >= 5 (SAW) or d >= 11 (percolation) with current methods"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.968648+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9508af6f4f512cf74f16f4606c7b7ceb7dd262c959d7295040f6340ccc642962","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The lace expansion writes the two-point function of self-avoiding walk, Bernoulli percolation, oriented percolation or lattice trees as a renormalised random-walk Green function plus a correction series: for SAW, c_n(x) = sum_y D(y) c_{n-1}(x - y) + sum_{m=2}^{n} sum_y pi_m(y) c_{n-m}(x - y), with pi_m the alternating-sign lace coefficients obtained by inclusion-exclusion over self-intersections (for percolation the analogous expansion is in terms of pivotal bonds and sausages). The expansion is an exact identity; its use requires a bootstrap showing the coefficients are small in a norm controlled by a random-walk diagram: the bubble diagram for SAW (finite for d > 4), the triangle diagram for percolation (finite for d > 6) and the square diagram for lattice trees (d > 8). Proved regimes: nearest-neighbour SAW for d >= 5 (Hara-Slade), spread-out SAW for d > 4, nearest-neighbour percolation for d >= 11 (Fitzner-van der Hofstad) and spread-out percolation for d > 6 (Hara-Slade). Conclusions there: mean-field exponents (gamma = 1, eta = 0, beta = 1 and delta = 2 in bounded-ratio senses), Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limits, and asymptotic expansions of critical points. It gives nothing at or below the upper critical dimension, and for nearest-neighbour percolation in 7 <= d <= 10 there is no small parameter, so the expansion holds only as an identity, not as a bound. Typical failure: Applying the expansion's mean-field conclusions (eta=0, Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limit) to a model at or below its upper critical dimension without re-verifying the triangle or bubble condition; the coefficients pi_m are not shown small there, the bootstrap can fail to close, and the diagrammatic control silently assumed at the outset is exactly the open problem, which is why four-dimensional nearest-neighbor percolation mean-field behavior remains open despite the spread-out and high-dimension cases being resolved. Canonical reference: Hara and Slade, 1990, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Madras and Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk, 1993, Birkhauser.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.162901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9566de8788a2dd2f4f3bf959669521d315f4faf5a42e798e2177a0b45ef154f2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 22 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall $F^{\rii}$ from \eqref{e:F.rii}
    and $F^{\riii}$ from \eqref{e:F.iii}. 
    For sufficiently large $N$, for all $t\in \R$,
    \[
        \P(F^{\rii}(k) \ge t)
        \le \P
        \bigg(
        F^{\riii}(k,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))
         + \frac{\epsilon'}{5} \ge t
        \bigg) + e^{-cN} \,.
    \]
That is, $F^{\riii}(k)$ approximately stochastically dominates
$F^{\rii}(k)$.

\begin{proof} Condition on any realization of $\bG$. Recall that
$F^\rii(k)$ is defined by \eqref{e:F.rii}
as the average of $F^\ri$ over $k$ orthogonal replicas, maximized over $S_\perp(k)$. Recall moreover that $F^\ri$ is defined by summing \eqref{e:F.B}--\eqref{e:F.w}, where we rewrote \eqref{e:F.B} and \eqref{e:F.U} in \eqref{e:F.B.rewrite} and \eqref{e:F.U.rewrite} above.
\begin{itemize}
\item Considering \eqref{e:F.U.rewrite}, 
note that $\bXi^\ell \hat{\bx} / \sqrt{N}$ is a standard gaussian in $\R^M$, independent of the gaussian process $\{\bXi^\ell \by^\ell : (\hat{\bx}, \by^\ell) = 0\}$.
Thus, the quantity inside
the maximum defining $F^\rii(k)$
(see \eqref{e:F.rii}),
as a process indexed by $\by^{1:k}$, remains distributionally unchanged if we replace each $\bXi^\ell \hat{\bx} / \sqrt{N}$ with $\bz^\ell$, which corresponds to replacing $F_U$ with $\bar{F}_U$. 
\item Considering \eqref{e:F.B.rewrite}, we can set
     \[
        \tbmeta^j
        = \frac{1}{|B_j|^{1/2}}
        \sum_{a\in B_j}
        \bmeta^{\ell,a}\,,
    \]
and note that the $\tbmeta^j$ are i.i.d.\ standard gaussian vectors in $\R^N$.
\end{itemize}
This shows that
    \begin{align*}
    F^{\rii}(k)&
       \stackrel{d}{=}
       \sup\bigg\{
       \frac{1}{k} \sum_{\ell=1}^k
     \bigg[
       \bar{F}_B(\tbmeta^\ell,\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))
       +F_v(\bG,\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)) \\
 &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad 
       +\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N}
       \bar{F}_U(\bG,\bz^\ell,\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))
       +F_w(\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)) \bigg]
        : \by^{1:k}
    \in S_\perp(k)
       \bigg\} \,.
    \end{align*}
Enlarging the domain from $S_\perp(k)$ to $S_+(k)$ can only decrease the above supremum. Finally, the difference between the quantity inside the above supremum, versus the quantity inside the supremum \eqref{e:F.iii} (with $\cB = \hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)$),
is upper bounded by
    \baln
        &\lt|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1 \rt|
        \frac{1}{k}
        \sum_{\ell=1}^k
        \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hU_j}{MN|B_j|}
        \bigg(
            \sum_{a\in B_j}
            (\bz^\ell)_a \barbg^a,
            \by^\ell
        \bigg)^2 \\
        &\le \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1 \bigg|
        \frac{1}{k}
        \sum_{\ell=1}^k
        \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hU_j}{MN|B_j|}
        \|\bz^\ell(B_j)\|^2
        \|\bG^{B_j}\|_{\op}^2
        \|\by^\ell\|^2\,.
    \ealn
    By standard estimates, we have $\|{\bz^\ell(B_j)}\|^2 \le 2|B_j|$ with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$.
    Combined with the estimate $\|\bG^{B_j}\|_{\op} \le C\sqrt{N}$ from \eqref{e:wishart.bound.repeated}, and $\|\by^\ell\| = \sqrt{N}$, we find that the last display is
        \[
    \le O(1)
    \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1 \bigg|
    \le \frac{\epsilon'}{5}\,,
    \]
where the last inequality holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ by
 Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T is continuous","the supremum is over T-invariant Borel probability measures; it need not be attained"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438290+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_95cd3f5a581ee5b3b33c5ba6ef9422e6da7205ab57a2fb35db6f9be50cdf92b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T: X \to X$ be a continuous map of a COMPACT metric space and let $M(X, T)$ be the (nonempty, by Krylov-Bogolyubov) set of $T$-invariant Borel probability measures. Then
$$h_{top}(T) = \sup\{ h_\mu(T) : \mu \in M(X, T) \},$$
and the supremum may be restricted to ERGODIC invariant measures. The inequality $h_\mu(T) \le h_{top}(T)$ for every invariant $\mu$ is Goodwyn's half; the existence, for every $c < h_{top}(T)$, of an invariant $\mu$ with $h_\mu(T) > c$ is the Dinaburg-Goodman half (Misiurewicz's proof below). Both sides may be $+\infty$. A measure attaining the supremum is a measure of maximal entropy; it need NOT exist for a general continuous $T$ (there are continuous maps, and even homeomorphisms, with $h_{top} < \infty$ and no measure of maximal entropy), but it exists whenever $\mu \mapsto h_\mu(T)$ is upper semicontinuous, e.g. for expansive maps and for $C^\infty$ maps of compact manifolds. The variational principle is the case $\varphi = 0$ of the variational principle for topological pressure, $P(T, \varphi) = \sup_\mu \{ h_\mu(T) + \int \varphi\,d\mu \}$.

WHERE IT FAILS OR NEEDS CARE. (1) Non-compact $X$: the statement depends on which notion of topological entropy is used; for the Bowen metric entropy on a non-compact space the supremum over invariant measures can be strictly smaller, and $M(X,T)$ may be empty (translation on $\mathbb{R}$). (2) The supremum need not be a maximum (see above). (3) Restricting to a non-invariant measure is meaningless: $h_\mu(T)$ is defined only for invariant $\mu$. (4) The principle relates ENTROPY to entropy; it does not say that a generic point has orbit-growth rate $h_{top}$, nor that the measure of maximal entropy is unique (uniqueness = intrinsic ergodicity, a much stronger property that holds e.g. for topologically mixing shifts of finite type but fails for many systems).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.865328+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_95d2b07675c0ad1811873e44deb8ef7a44b824d1b1acb342afcf15b87074cca1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:weighted-bipartite-graph of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] Let $G=(I,J,M)$ be a weighted bipartite graph, where
\[
M\in\mathbb R^{I\times J}.
\]
We call $I$ the left vertex set and $J$ the right vertex set. We declare that
\begin{align}

\quad
\Leftrightarrow
\quad
M_{ij}\ne0
\end{align}
and, when $(i,j)$ is an edge, its weight is $M_{ij}$.

\[

\]

Hence TV is at least $r_L^k/2$, and reaching TV<=1/4 requires $k\\ge\\log2/(-\\log r_L)\\sim\\lambda\\log2\\,L^2/(2\\pi^2)$. Check: The multiplier is the integral of lambda*exp(-lambda*t)*exp(-(1-cos(theta))*t) over positive t. Equivalently it is the resolvent eigenvalue of the walk generator. For zero particles the state space is a singleton and mixing takes zero steps. Obstruction: One particle has density tending to zero, so this does not prove the positive-fixed-density lower bound or the supercritical upper bound. Neither is claimed solved.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:56:17.350956+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_96027ba99f974b0687326acd85db9973cfc6afa77a4001809717ec87c7567825","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop P:only-easy-consequences of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take any half-space pre-landscape $\mathcal{M}^\rho$ continuously extended to $\mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$. Let $\mathcal{K}^\rho(x, s; y, t) = \mathcal{M}^\rho(x, s; y, t) + \frac{(x-y)^2}{(t-s)}$ for any $(x,s;y,t)\in \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textup{(Modulus of continuity, analogue of [DOV]).} For any $b \ge 2, \epsilon \le 1$, define
$$
K^\epsilon_b = \{(x, t; y, t + s) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow : s \in [\epsilon, b], \text{and } |t|, x, y \le b \}.
$$
For two points $u_i = (x_i, t_i; y_i, s_i)\in K^\epsilon_b$, $i = 1, 2$, let 
\begin{align*}
    \tau &= \tau(u_1, u_2) = \|(t_1, s_1) - (t_2, s_2)\|_2, \\
    \xi &= \xi(u_1, u_2) = \|(x_1, y_1) - (x_2, y_2)\|_2.
\end{align*}
Then if $\tau^{1/3} + \xi^{1/2} \le \min(\epsilon/b, 1/(\rho \vee 0))$, we have
$$
|\mathcal{K}^\rho(u_1) - \mathcal{K}^\rho(u_2)| \le M \left(\tau^{1/3}\log^{2/3}(\tau^{-1}) + \xi^{1/2}\log^{1/2}(4b\xi^{-1}) \right),
$$
with a random variable $M$  satisfying
$\mathbb{P}(M > a) \le b^{4}[(b/\epsilon)^{10} + (\rho \vee 0)^{10}] \exp(-ca^{3/2})$
for all $a > 0$. Here $c>0$ is a universal constant.
\item \textup{(Shape bound, analogue of [DOV]).} Fix $\rho_0 > 1$ and assume $\rho < \rho_0$. Then there exists $c > 0$ depending on $\rho_0$ such that the following holds. For all $u = (x, t; y, t + s) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$ with $s \le \rho_0$, we have
$$
\left|\mathcal{K}^\rho(u) \right|\le M s^{1/3} \log^2\left(\frac{2\|u\|_2}{s}\right),
$$
where $M > 0$ is a random variable satisfying
$\mathbb{P}(M > a) \le 2\exp(-ca^{3/2})$
for all $a > 0$.
\item \textup{(Metric composition holds everywhere, analogue of [DOV])}
For each $u = (x, r;y, t) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$ and $s \in (r, t)$, define
	$f_{u, s}(z) = \mathcal{M}^\rho(x,r;z,s)+\mathcal{M}^\rho(z,s;y,t)$. Then on an event of probability $1$, $\mathcal{M}^\rho$ satisfies the metric composition law
	\begin{equation}
	
	\mathcal{M}^\rho(u)=\max_{z \in \mathbb R} f_{u, s}(z)
	\end{equation}
	for every $u = (x, r;y, t) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$ and $s \in (r, t)$. Moreover, for any compact set $K \subset \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$, there exists a random variable $B_K$ such that for all $u = (x, r;y, t) \in K$ and $s \in (r, t)$, the set where $f_{u, s}$ attains its maximum is contained in the interval $[-B_K, B_K]$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.257406+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_96047941d9dfb72124a35d8e0927b187c93ad108c4d7275a0ad1119af3d69862","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 63 of arXiv:2605.23308, 'Convergence rate estimates for semigroups and heat kernels associated with resistance form'] Fix $x,y\in F,\;y_n\in F_n,\;t>0,\;\kappa\in [1/2,1],\;p_0,p,q\in [1,\infty],$ and $\alpha\in (0,\alpha_0)$.
\begin{itemize}
  \item [$\rm{(i)}$]Under the conditions $1_{\kappa,p_0}$ and $2_{\kappa,p,q}$, we have that

  &\quad\times \Bigl\{ d_{\rm{H}}(F,F_n)+d_{\rm{H}}(F,F_n)^{\kappa}+d(y,y_n)+d_{\BL^{\kappa}}(\mu,\mu_n)\Bigr\}\\
  &+L(t)\Bigl\{\mu(B(x,4r+\rho))+(1+\rho^{-\kappa})d_{\BL^{\kappa}}(\mu,\mu_n)\Bigr\}r\\
  &+M(t)c_1(\varepsilon,\kappa,p_0)\mu(B(x,r))^{1/p_0}d_{\rm{H}}(F,F_n)^{\kappa},
\end{align*}
where $f_r:=1_{B(x,r)}:F\to [0,1]$ and $\overline{P_{\varepsilon}f_r}$ is a McShane extension with exponent $\kappa$, and 
  $\varepsilon\in (0,1],\;\rho\in (0,\infty),\;r\in [d_{\rm{H}}(F,F_n),\infty),$ and $\delta\in (0,r)$.
  \item [$\rm{(ii)}$]Moreover, if the assumption $\rm{(A3)}$ is additionally satisfied, then it holds 
  for $\varepsilon,\rho\in (0,1),\;\xi\ge d_{\rm{H}}(F,F_n),$ and $0<r<\eta<1$ that

  \lesssim&L(t)\mu\left( B\left(x,\eta\right)\right)\eta+M(t)\exp[-c(\eta-r)^{1+\beta}/\varepsilon^{\beta}]\\
  &+\g{c}{sg2,n}\Bigl\{c_2(\alpha,\varepsilon,\kappa,p)\mu(B(x,r))^{1/p} +c_3(\alpha,\varepsilon,\kappa,q) \mu(B(x,r))^{1/q}\Bigr\}\\
  &\quad\times \Bigl\{ d_{\rm{H}}(F,F_n)+d_{\rm{H}}(F,F_n)^{\kappa}+d(y,y_n)+d_{\BL^{\kappa}}(\mu,\mu_n)\Bigr\}\\
  &+L(t)\Bigl\{\mu(B(x,\eta+\xi+\rho))+(1+\rho^{-\kappa})d_{\BL^{\kappa}}(\mu,\mu_n)\Bigr\}(\eta+\xi)\\
  &+M(t)c_1(\varepsilon,\kappa,p_0)\mu(B(x,r))^{1/p_0}d_{\rm{H}}(F,F_n)^{\kappa}.
\end{align*}
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:31:57.857005+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9668287f3bd74338b1807081c9198d70221d955edbcdc0d6b707fe8489542221","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:improvedBernstein of arXiv:2510.01021, '\Large Random Matrices, Intrinsic Freeness, and Sharp Non-Asymptotic Inequalities\relatedv'] Let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ be random independent symmetric matrices satisfying $\mathbb{E} Y_i=0$, and such that $\|Y_i\|\leq R$, for all $i\in[n]$, almost surely. \[
\mathbb{E} \left\| \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i  \right\| \leq 2\sigma + C \Big( v^{\frac12}\sigma^{\frac12}(\log d)^\frac34 + R^{\frac13}\sigma^{\frac23}(\log d)^\frac23 + R \log d \Big),

and
\[
\mathbb{P}\left[  \left\| \sum_{i=1}^n Y_i  \right\| \geq 2\sigma + C \Big( v^{\frac12}\sigma^{\frac12}(\log d)^\frac34 + \sigma_\ast t^{\frac12}+ R^{\frac13}\sigma^{\frac23}t^\frac23 + R t \Big)    \right] \leq de^{-t}

{"assumptions":["p, q probability mass functions on one finite set","p(A) > 0 and q(A) > 0","total variation is half the L1 distance"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:13:40.804747+00:00","domain":"total variation and couplings of finite probability laws","id":"claim_96788e32b7dc3e972356e5ee47f8562428e089141e06a6ce5f93c02ce9f3d9b2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let p and q be probability mass functions on a finite set S and A a subset of S with a = p(A) > 0 and b = q(A) > 0. Let c be the total variation distance between the conditional laws p(.|A) and q(.|A), d = d_TV(p, q), M = max(a, b) and m = min(a, b). Then max(|a - b|, M c) <= d <= 1 - m(1 - c), and for every a, b in (0, 1] and c in [0, 1] both ends are attained on a finite set. When the conditional laws are disjoint (c = 1) this gives M <= d <= 1 and no more: d = 1 - sum over x outside A of min(p_x, q_x), so d = 1 exactly when the restrictions of p and q to the complement of A are also disjoint. For example p = (1/2, 0, 1/2), q = (0, 1/2, 1/2) and A = {1, 2} give c = 1 and d = 1/2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["k algebraically closed; the curves are projective and have no common component","intersection multiplicity is the local-ring dimension (equivalently Fulton's axiomatic multiplicity)","over non-closed fields or in affine coordinates only the upper bound mn on the number of points holds"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626765+00:00","domain":"algebraic geometry","id":"claim_9689091d3f27a70eb1bd6d2e53f2f98d9030885135749952fef3396e0d0e9bcd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let C and D be projective plane curves over an algebraically closed field k, defined by homogeneous polynomials F, G in k[X, Y, Z] of degrees m and n with no common factor (the curves share no component). Then C and D meet in exactly mn points of the projective plane P^2(k) when each intersection point P is counted with its intersection multiplicity I_P(C, D) = dim_k O_P / (F, G) (the local ring at P modulo the ideal of the two curves); in particular they meet in at least one and at most mn distinct points. The multiplicity is at least m_P(C) m_P(D), the product of the multiplicities of the two curves at P, with equality exactly when the curves have no common tangent at P. {"assumptions":["K is a compact metric space","F is a uniformly bounded family in C(K)","F is equicontinuous on K"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.377034+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_969621bacd8c4d8d1d18dc91064c5582eb98fa2cd21ef76831aadd2757e586da","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K be a compact metric space and let F be a family of real- or complex-valued continuous functions on K. Suppose F is (i) uniformly bounded: there is M with |f(x)| <= M for all f in F and all x in K, and (ii) equicontinuous: for every epsilon > 0 there is delta > 0 such that d(x, y) < delta implies |f(x) - f(y)| < epsilon for every f in F simultaneously. Then every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on K (to a continuous limit); equivalently, F is relatively compact in C(K) with the supremum norm. Conversely, a relatively compact subset of C(K) is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. (Pointwise boundedness plus equicontinuity already implies uniform boundedness on compact K; the classical statement on K = [a,b] is the special case.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.211673+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_96d41c51d74c33eb55f3eba30f7fb65c3d0270d0b9ef2e7eadb4f20d454a78e4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2608.13687, 'Multiplicative chaos from random multiplicative functions'] Consider $(A_p)_p$ in  Case \caseS or Case \caseR.
There exist constants $c, C>0$ such that for any finite set of primes $B$, and for any  $\{\phi_p\}_p \subset \C$ in Case \caseS or $\{\phi_p\}_p \subset \R$ in Case \caseR, there exists a coupling of $\langle\phi A\rangle_B$ with a  Gaussian $Z_{B}$ such that 
\[
  \mathrm{Cov}(Z_B) = \mathrm{Cov}\langle\phi A\rangle_B\,,
\]
and, letting $\Delta_{B} \coloneqq |\langle\phi A\rangle_B - Z_{B}|$, we have the first moment bound
\begin{align} 
  \E \Delta_{B} \leq C \min\bigg( V_{B}^{1/2} \,,\, \frac{T_{B}}{V_{B}} \bigg)
\end{align}
and the tail bound
\begin{align}
  \P(\Delta_{B} > u ) \leq Ce^{-c u^2/V_B}
\end{align}
for all $u\geq 0$, where we use the interpretation that $1/V_B \coloneqq 0$ if $V_B = 0$.

\begin{proof}
Since the case $V_B = 0$ is trivial, we assume throughout the proof $V_B>0$. Moreover, it is quick to show $\E\Delta_B \leq C V_B^{1/2}$: we simply take the independent coupling between $\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B$ and $Z_B$ (they are realized as independent random variables on the same probability space). Then $\E\Delta_B \leq \E|\langle\phi A\rangle_B| + \E|Z_B| \leq C V_B^{1/2}$ by Jensen's inequality.

To prove \eqref{eq:block-coupling-expectation}, it  remains to show $\mathbb{E}\Delta_B \le CT_B/V_B$. 
The proofs are identical in Case \caseS and Case \caseR, so for concreteness we take $A_p = \alpha_p$ iid Steinhaus.
We  apply \cref{lem:berry-esseen} in dimension $k=2$, identifying $\C$ with $\R^2$.  Observe 
$\Cov \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B = \tfrac12 V_B \id$. 
Letting $X_p \coloneq \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \phi_p \alpha_p$, we then have 
\[
\sum_{p \in B} \Cov(X_p) = \id \qquad\text{and}\qquad
\sum_{p\in B} \E |X_p|^3 = \big(\tfrac{2}{V_B}\big)^{3/2} \,T_B\,. 
\]
The third-moment condition of \cref{lem:berry-esseen} then becomes, for some constant $c>0$,
\begin{equation}
T_B/V_B^{3/2}\leq c
\end{equation}

Suppose first that \eqref{eq:third-mom-condition-proof} is satisfied.  Then \cref{lem:berry-esseen} yields a Gaussian vector $Z\sim \cN(0,\id)$ with
\begin{align}
  \Big|\P\Big( \Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B\Big|  \leq r \Big) - \P (|Z| \leq r )\Big|\ll \frac{1}{(1+r)^3} \frac{T_B}{V_B^{3/2}}
\end{align}
for all $r\geq 0$.
Observe that the $W_1$ distance between two rotationally-symmetric random variables is bounded by the $W_1$ distance between their norms: the same uniform random variable can be used for both angles, taken independently of the norms. 
We may then use the formula \eqref{eq:vallender}
to compute
\begin{align*}
  W_1\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B, Z\Big) \le W_1\Big(\Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B\Big|, |Z| \Big) = \int_0^{\infty} \Big| \P\Big(\Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}} \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B\Big| \leq r\Big) - \P(|Z| \leq r) \Big| \ll \frac{T_B}{V_B^{3/2}}\,.
\end{align*}
Scaling each random variable by $\sqrt{V_B/2}$ yields $W_1(\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B, Z_B) \ll T_B/V_B$, where $Z_B = \sqrt{V_B/2} Z$ and therefore $\Cov \langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B = \Cov Z_B$. This completes the proof of \eqref{eq:block-coupling-expectation} when \eqref{eq:third-mom-condition-proof} holds.

If \eqref{eq:third-mom-condition-proof} does not hold, i.e.,
$T_B/V_B^{3/2} > c$,
then the independent coupling of $\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B$ and $Z_B$ yields 
\[
  \E\Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}}(\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B - Z_B)\Big| \leq  \E\Big|\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{V_B}}\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B\Big| + \E |Z| \leq C'
\]
for some constant $C'>0$. Choose $C$ such that $C' < cC < T_B/V_B^{3/2}$. It follows that 
\[
  E\Delta_B \leq C V_B^{1/2} \frac{T_B}{V_B^{3/2}} = C \frac{T_B}{V_B}\,.
\]

The tail bound \eqref{eq:block-coupling-tail} follows from the triangle inequality and Hoeffding's inequality. Choose any coupling such that \eqref{eq:block-coupling-expectation} holds, and write
\[
\P(\Delta_B >u) \leq \P(|\langle\phi\alpha\rangle_B| > u/2) + \P(|Z_B|> u/2)\,.
\]
Fix any finite mesh of angles  (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.161845+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97106abd4033274e1b7b80450f58f510f15be0af5ab0bb57db151ea3e1c2915f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 14 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any $(\lambda,\mu) \in \Lambda$, 
there exists a closed $\cD_\mu$-polytope $P$ such that
    \beq
       K_1 \equiv S_\star(\lambda,\mu)[\epsilon']
        \subseteq P
        \subseteq S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
        	\frac\epsilon5,\frac\epsilon2\bigg) 
	\equiv K_2\,,
    \eeq
where $K_1,K_2$ are both
 $\cD_\mu$-convex bodies.

\begin{proof}
Note that $\Cost(\YY;\lambda)$, $(\|\BBb\|_2)^2$, and $-\Budget(\YY;\mu)$ are all convex functions of $\YY\in\cD_\mu$. (This uses the fact that for $\YY \in \cD_\mu$, the input to the $(\cdot)_+$ in $\Cost(\YY;\lambda)$ is always nonnegative.) This immediately implies that $K_2$ is a $\cD_\mu$-convex body. It also implies that $S_\star(\lambda,\mu)$ is a $\cD_\mu$-convex body, and therefore so is its $\epsilon'$-neighborhood $K_1$.

We now turn to the construction of the polytope $P$. Lemma~\ref{l:S.star.nbd.in.S.star.eps} gives
    \beq 
        K_1 \subseteq S_\star\bigg(\lambda,\mu;
        		\frac\epsilon5,\frac{\epsilon}{3}
		\bigg)
        \subseteq (K_2)^\circ\,,
    \eeq
    where $(K_2)^\circ$ denotes the interior of $K_2$ relative to the topology of $\cD_\mu$. We let $C$ denote the boundary of $K_2$ relative to the topology of $\cD_\mu$, that is,
	\[
	C\equiv \partial K_2
	\equiv K_2 \setminus (K_2)^\circ\,.
	\]
Note that $C$ is a compact set in the topology of $\cD_\mu$. It follows from \eqref{e:S.star.nbd.in.S.star.eps.consequence} that $K_1$ and $C$ are disjoint.

Recall from \eqref{e:D.mu.affine.closure} that we use $\mathcal{F}_\mu$ to denote the affine closure of $\cD_\mu$.
For each $\YY\in C$, by the (strict) hyperplane separating theorem, there exists an open half-space $U_\YY$ of $\mathcal{F}_\mu$ such that $\YY\in U_\YY$ and $U_\YY\cap K_1=\emptyset$. Then $V_\YY\equiv \cD_\mu \cap U_\YY$ is open in the $\cD_\mu$-topology, and we have an open cover
	\[
	C\subseteq
	\bigcup_{\YY\in C} V_\YY\,.
	\]
Since $C$ is compact, this must admit a finite subcover, so there exists finite $S\subseteq C$ such that
	\[
	C\subseteq
	\bigcup_{\YY\in S} V_\YY\,.
	\]
Let $A_\YY \equiv \mathcal{F}_\mu\setminus U_\YY$, a closed half-space of $\mathcal{F}_\mu$. It follows that we can express $A_\YY = \mathcal{F}_\mu \cap H_\YY$ where $H_\YY$ is a closed half-space of the full space $\R^{3r+s}$. We then define the closed $\cD_\mu$-polytope 
	\[
	P\equiv
	\cD_\mu\cap
	\bigg( \bigcap_{\YY\in S} H_\YY
	\bigg)\,.
	\]
Since each $U_\YY$ is disjoint from $K_1$, each $H_\YY$ must contain $K_1$, so we have $K_1\subseteq P$.
On the other hand, since 
	\[
	\cD_\mu \setminus P
	= \cD_\mu \cap 
	\bigg( \bigcup_{\YY\in S} U_\YY
	\bigg)
	\supseteq C\,,
	\]
we see that $P$ does not intersect $C$. Since $P$ is convex, it must be fully contained in either $(K_2)^\circ$ or
$(\cD_\mu\setminus K_2)^\circ$.
Since we already saw that $K_1\subseteq P$, the former must hold, so $P\subseteq K_2$ as claimed.\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:17:33.988198+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_972c739154c7e2110889a4975117f4b3dd1b77d6106c90295eaf4331c4898e73","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 4 of arXiv:2609.03386, 'Twisted Gradient Flow Approach to Vegetation-Rainfall-Bushfire Interactions Model'] For every $\delta \in (1,\infty)$ and $\bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega)$ the bilinear form  
$(\cdot,\cdot)_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}:L^2(\Omega) \times L^2(\Omega) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined by (\ref{Equation-2-18}) is a quasi-variational inner
product on $L^2(\Omega)$.\\
\indent
Moreover, for each $\delta \in (1,\infty)$ the class of inner products 
$\{(\cdot,\cdot)_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}}\,;\,\bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega)\}$ satisfies the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}\leftskip6pt
\item[(1)] There exist constants $C_1>0$ and $C_2>0$ such that

\begin{equation*}
\delta^{-\frac{1}{2}} C_1 \|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le \|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}$}}} \le \delta^{\frac{1}{2}} C_2 \|v\|_{L^2(\Omega)}, 
\quad \forall v \in L^2(\Omega),~\forall \bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega).
\end{equation*}

\item[(2)] There exists a constant $C_3>0$ such that 

\begin{equation*}
\left| \|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}_1$}}}^2-\|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}_2$}}}^2 \right| 
\le \delta^3 C_3 \|\bar{z}_1-\bar{z}_2\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \|v\|_{\text{{\tiny $\delta,\!\bar{z}_1$}}}^2, 
\quad \forall \bar{z}_1,\bar{z}_2 \in L^2(\Omega),\,\forall v \in L^2(\Omega).
\end{equation*}

\end{enumerate}
where for every $\delta \in (1,\infty)$ and $\bar{z} \in L^2(\Omega)$ we set

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.397124+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9739eb0e75593e2c95007cdf00188d8ee52693da3ab680e344f398fd24707878","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 2. dfn eq: restriction of a measure to a closed ball of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{The vague metric $d_{V}^{S, \rho_{S}}$}]
  We denote the set of Radon measures on $S$ by $\mathcal{M}(S)$.
  For $\mu \in \mathcal{M}(S)$,
  we write $\mu^{(r)}$ for the restriction of $\mu$ to $S^{(r)} \coloneqq \closure (B_{S}(\rho, r))$, 
  that is,
  $\mu^{(r)}$ is a finite Borel measure given by
  \begin{equation}  
    \mu^{(r)}(\cdot) 
    \coloneqq
    \mu|_{S^{(r)}}(\cdot)
    =
    \mu \left( \cdot \cap S^{(r)} \right).
  \end{equation} 
  We then define, for each $\mu, \nu \in \mathcal{M}(S)$,
  \begin{equation}
    d_{V}^{S, \rho_{S}}(\mu, \nu)
    \coloneqq
    \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-r} \left( 1 \wedge d_{P}^{S}(\mu^{(r)}, \nu^{(r)}) \right) dr.
  \end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:09.850529+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_974f993ea55dbb51cf199b61cd33a42054dbbddaf02c8c5467ece11aa1fdcab6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 2 of arXiv:2605.18751, '\mytitle'] Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be probability measures on \(E\), with likelihood ratio \(\ell\) as in~\eqref{def.ell}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]

\item \emph{Usual stochastic order} ($\st$): \(P\st Q\) if
\(\bar F_P(x)\le\bar F_Q(x)\) for every \(x\in E\).

\item \emph{Hazard-rate order} ($\hr$): \(P\hr Q\) if \(\bar F_P(x)/\bar F_Q(x)\) is nonincreasing wherever \(\bar F_Q(x)>0\) (equivalently, \(h_P(x)\ge h_Q(x)\) wherever both hazard rates are defined).

\item \emph{Likelihood-ratio order} ($\lr$): \(P\lr Q\) if \(\ell\) is nonincreasing on \(\supp(P)\cup\supp(Q)\).

\item \emph{Relative log-concavity} ($\lc$): when \(\supp(P)\) is an interval contained in \(\supp(Q)\), \(P\lc Q\) if \(\log\ell\) is concave on \(\supp(P)\).
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F a class of measurable functions with values in a bounded interval [a, b] (for the two-sided form with the stated constant the class should be closed under negation or one accepts an extra factor; see the references)","the sample is i.i.d. from P; delta in (0, 1)","measurability of the suprema (a countable class, or the usual separability assumptions) is assumed throughout"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:40:13.706434+00:00","domain":"statistical learning theory","id":"claim_97839b3fb5a128a097b064c2e4b18409edd68bbc82e49a4901fe22e9f110c5d0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"DEFINITIONS. Let F be a class of measurable functions f: X -> [a, b], let S = (X_1, ..., X_n) be an i.i.d. sample from a distribution P on X, and let sigma_1, ..., sigma_n be independent Rademacher signs, independent of S. The empirical Rademacher complexity of F on S is R_hat_S(F) = E_sigma [ sup_{f in F} (1/n) sum_{i=1}^{n} sigma_i f(X_i) ], and the Rademacher complexity is R_n(F) = E_S [ R_hat_S(F) ]. Write P f = E f(X) and P_n f = (1/n) sum_i f(X_i). THEOREM. For every delta in (0, 1), with probability at least 1 - delta over the sample, simultaneously for all f in F: P f - P_n f <= 2 R_n(F) + (b - a) sqrt( log(1/delta) / (2n) ), and also P f - P_n f <= 2 R_hat_S(F) + 3 (b - a) sqrt( log(2/delta) / (2n) ) (a bound computable from the data). If F is closed under negation (f in F implies -f in F), the two-sided version sup_{f in F} |P f - P_n f| <= 2 R_n(F) + (b - a) sqrt(log(2/delta) / (2n)) holds with probability at least 1 - delta (for a general F apply the one-sided bound to F and to -F, each with delta/2, which replaces R_n(F) by R_n(F union -F)). Since E sup_f (P f - P_n f) <= 2 R_n(F), a class is uniformly Glivenko-Cantelli whenever R_n(F) -> 0. Standard values of R_n: a finite class bounded by B has R_n <= B sqrt(2 log |F| / n) (Massart); a class of indicators of VC dimension d has R_n <= sqrt(2 d log(e n / d) / n) and in fact O(sqrt(d / n)) (Dudley); linear predictors x -> <w, x> with ||w||_2 <= Lambda on inputs with ||x||_2 <= r have R_n <= Lambda r / sqrt(n); and for L-Lipschitz phi, R_n(phi o F) <= L R_n(F) (Ledoux-Talagrand contraction), which is how the bound passes from a class of predictors to a class of losses. In learning, with f the loss of a hypothesis, the theorem says the true risk of EVERY hypothesis in the class exceeds its empirical risk by at most 2 R_n plus a term of order sqrt(log(1/delta)/n), the modern replacement for VC bounds when the class is not a class of sets.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:18:19.220183+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97a72a1847f5a25f10ab1d841c3f1b73d0d91735389913491d547e16332d393e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 17 of arXiv:2608.29075, 'The 2-Monoidal Structure of Symmetric Sequences'] Let $(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ be a 2-monoidal category. A \textit{double monoid} in $\catname{C}$ is an object $A$ equipped with morphisms
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=scriptsize]
	{A \square A} & A && I & A && {A \circ A} & A && {J } & A,
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow[from=1-7, to=1-8]
	\arrow[from=1-10, to=1-11]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    which turn $A$ into a monoid in both $(\catname{C},\square,I)$ and $(\catname{C},\circ,J)$, and make the following diagrams commute.
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{(A \circ A) \square (A \circ A)} && {(A \square A) \circ (A \square A)} \\
	{A \square A} & A & {A \circ A}
	\arrow["{\zeta_{A,A,A,A}}", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	{J \square J} & {A \square A} && {I \circ I} & {A \circ A} \\
	J & A && I & A
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\mu_J}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5]
	\arrow[from=1-5, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\Delta_I}", from=2-4, to=1-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\[\begin{tikzcd}
	& A \\
	I && J
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{{\iota_J = \epsilon_I}}"', from=2-1, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=1-2]
\end{tikzcd}\]
    Dually, one can define \textit{double comonoids}. 

    A morphism between two double (co)monoids is a morphism of the two underlying (co)monoids. 
    
    The categories of double (co)monoids in the 2-monoidal category $(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ are denoted by $\text{dMon}(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$ and by $\text{dComon}(\catname{C},\square, I, \circ, J)$, respectively.","status":"unverified"}
