{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.617359+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97cfdf3e416a43739095433521fe7ee6020f77b8448968cb0fd114be07910a2e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:beta.mgf of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] Let $x$ is sampled uniformly at random from the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then $x$ is zero-mean and subgaussian with variance proxy $1/d$.

\begin{proof}
Fix a vector $v\in\mathbb{R}^d$.
Let $t=\|v\|$. Then $Z=\langle v,x\rangle/t$ is a symmetric random variable, and
    \[
    B=Z^2\sim\operatorname{Beta}\bigg(\frac{1}{2},
        \frac{d-1}{2}\bigg)\,.
    \]
It follows from the moment-generating function of the beta distribution that
    \[
    \mathbb E_x[\mathop{\rm exp}(\langle v,x\rangle)]
    = \mathbb E [\mathop{\rm exp}(tZ)]
    = 1 + \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{t^{2k}}{(2k)!}
        \prod_{r=0}^{k-1} \frac{1+2r}{d+2r} 
    \le 1 + \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{t^{2k}}{k! (2d)^k}
    = \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\frac{\|v\|^2}{2d}\bigg)\,,
    \]
which proves the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.431561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97e3804b3bd38df4c13bb36d47f9c369e4c2f55b1ab653dbdcb41f9e1e5abb51","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 4. dfn: resistance forms of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] [{Resistance form and resistance metric, [Kigami_12_Resistance]}] 
  
  Let $F$ be a non-empty set.
  A pair $(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})$ is called a \textit{resistance form} on $F$ if it satisfies the following conditions.
  \begin{enumerate} [label=(RF\arabic*), leftmargin = *]
    \item 
          The symbol $\mathcal{F}$ is a linear subspace of the collection of functions $\{ f : F \to \mathbb{R} \}$ 
          containing constants,
          and $\mathcal{E}$ is a non-negative symmetric bilinear form on $\mathcal{F}$
          such that $\mathcal{E}(f,f)=0$ if and only if $f$ is constant on $F$.
    \item 
          Let $\sim$ be the equivalence relation on $\mathcal{F}$ defined by saying $f \sim g$ if and only if $f-g$ is constant on $F$.
          Then $(\mathcal{F}/\sim, \mathcal{E})$ is a Hilbert space.
    \item
          If $x \neq y$, then there exists a function $f \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $f(x) \neq f(y)$.
    \item 
          For any $x, y \in F$,
          \begin{equation} 
            R_{(\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{F})}(x,y)
            \coloneqq
            \sup
            \left\{
            \frac{|f(x) - f(y)|^{2}}{\mathcal{E}(f,f)}
            :
            f \in \mathcal{F},\
            \mathcal{E}(f,f) > 0
            \right\}
            < \infty.
          \end{equation}     
    \item
          If $\bar{f}\coloneqq  (f \wedge 1) \vee 0$,
          then $\bar{f} \in \mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{E}(\bar{f}, \bar{f}) \leq \mathcal{E}(f,f)$ for any $f \in \mathcal{F}$.
  \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:05:09.629919+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97e92b713f5fb0ae485923c164806f6eca2dc22232484a3f8e3e4538afc5727a","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:tech_extent_lowerbound of arXiv:2411.03609, 'Asymptotically optimal Wasserstein couplings for the small-time stable domain of attractio'] Let $\bm{Y}$ be a nonzero pure-jump L\'evy process on $\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\psi_{\bm{Y}}(\bm{u})$ denote its L\'evy-Khintchine exponent and $\nu_{\bm{Y}}$ its L\'evy measure.\\
{\normalfont(a)} If $\bm{Y}$ has finite variation and nonzero drift with direction $\bm{u}_*\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then $|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant cx$ for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $x>0$.\\
{\normalfont(b)} Suppose there exist a locally finite measure $\rho$ on $(0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with
\[
\nu_{\bm{Y}}(A)
\geqslant \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}\int_{(0,\infty)}\1_A(x\bm{v})\rho(\mathrm{d} x)\sigma(\mathrm{d}\bm{v}),
\qquad A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d_{\bm{0}}).
\]
Define $\Upsilon(x):=\int_{(0,x)}r^2\rho(\mathrm{d} r)$ for $x>0$, and, given any $c\in (0,1)$, suppose that $C_{c,\bm{u}_*}\coloneqq\{\bm{v}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}:|\langle \bm{u}_*,\bm{v}\rangle|\geqslant c\}$ has positive $\sigma$-measure $m:=\sigma(C_{c,\bm{u}_*})>0$ for some $\bm{u}_*\in \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. Then we have
\[
|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant \frac{c^2m}{3}r^2\Upsilon(x^{-1})
\qquad\text{for all }x>0.
\]
In particular, if $c_\delta:=\inf_{x\in(0,1)}x^{\delta-2}\Upsilon(x)>0$ for some $\delta\in(0,2)$, then $|\psi_{\bm{Y}}(x\bm{u}_*)|\geqslant (c_\delta c^2m/3)x^{\delta}$, $x>1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:43:16.153150+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97eadd3bbdbc643b6ff10222c41881b0ecca7b3efcfbff2369bdef82e1989b9f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 3 of arXiv:2604.13819, 'Convolution, cumulants and infinitesimal generators in the formal power series ring'] For $t\in \mathbb{R}\setminus \mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$, we define the \emph{$t$-deformed cumulants} $\{\kappa_{i}^{t}(A)\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}}$ of $A \in U$ by
$$
C^t[A](z) \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^\infty \kappa_i^t(A)z^i \coloneqq -\frac{z}{t} \frac{d}{dz}\log \left(1+ \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{t^{k}}{(t)_{\underline{k}}} a_{k} z^{k} \right).
$$
If $A\in U_d$ for some $d\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}$, we define the \emph{$d$-deformed cumulants} $\{\kappa_{i}^{d}(A)\}_{i \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge1}}$ by
$$
C^d[A](z) \coloneqq \lim_{t\to d} C^t[A](z)\coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^\infty \kappa_i^d(A)z^i  = -\frac{z}{d} \frac{d}{dz}\log\left(1+ \sum_{k=1}^d \frac{d^{k}}{(d)_{\underline{k}}} a_{k} z^{k}\right).
$$
We call $C^t[A](z)$ the \emph{$t$-deformed cumulant transform} of $A$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.726474+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97ecd6839d292e7e8bebfc938bfd5f9fd869e6026c28b5977e0597fb6725f65a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5 of arXiv:2605.02002, 'Glauber dynamics for random field Ising models on bounded degree graphs and MLSI'] Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$, $G=(V,E)$ be a graph that has $\alpha$-stretched exponential growth, and the RFIM measure $\mu_G$ satisfies $\operatorname{WSM}(C)$ for some $C>0$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.994414+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_97efde84c687734e23b1ce3ae8052542c0c176f8db17c62eaa957917a20a6546","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 42 (Physical fourth-moment theorem: exact zero stratum) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let $q\ge2$ and
\[
 X_{n,a}=I_q^{W_n}(f_{n,a}),
 \qquad
 \sup_n\sum_{a=1}^dq!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2<\infty.
\]
Write $\Sigma_n=\Cov(X_n)$, fix a free ultrafilter $\mathcal U$, and put
\[
 \xi_a=[f_{n,a}]_{\mathcal U}\in\cH_q,
 \qquad
 \Sigma=\Ulim\Sigma_n,
 \qquad
 \kappa_{n,a}=\E[X_{n,a}^4]-3\E[X_{n,a}^2]^2.
\]
The represented terminal has the intrinsic splitting
\begin{equation}
 T_a=\mathbb U_q^{-1}\xi_a
 =A_a^{\phys}+G_a^{\phys},
 \quad
 A_a^{\phys}=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cD_q}\xi_a,
 \quad
 G_a^{\phys}=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cK_q}\xi_a.
 
\end{equation}
The following conditions are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 \item $\displaystyle\sum_{a=1}^d\mathfrak Q_q(\xi_a)=0$,
 equivalently $\Ulim\sum_a\kappa_{n,a}=0$;
 \item for every $a$ and $1\le r<q$,
 $
  \Ulim\norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,a}}=0
 $;
 \item $\xi_a\in\cK_q$ for every $a$, equivalently
 $P_{\cD_q}\xi=0$;
 \item $A^{\phys}=0$ (equivalently, the limiting active part of
 the reduced Hilbert--Stein trajectory vanishes) and the represented
 laws converge along $\mathcal U$ to $N_d(0,\Sigma)$;
 \item for every $a$,
 $
  \Ulim\E[X_{n,a}^4]=3\Sigma_{aa}^2
 $.
\end{enumerate}
When these conditions hold, every mixed proper contraction also
vanishes:
\begin{equation}
 \Ulim\norm{f_{n,a}\otimes_rf_{n,b}}=0
 \qquad(1\le r<q,\ 1\le a,b\le d).
 
\end{equation}
Moreover, there is a finite constant $C_{q,d}$, depending only on
$(q,d)$, such that for every $n$ and $t\in\R^d$,
\begin{equation}
 \left|
  \E e^{it\cdot X_n}
  -e^{-\frac12t^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_nt}
 \right|
 \le C_{q,d}|t|^2
 \left(\sum_{a=1}^d\kappa_{n,a}\right)^{1/2}.
 
\end{equation}
Componentwise, the exact carré-du-champ comparison is
\begin{equation}
 \frac1{3q}\kappa_{n,a}
 \le
 \Var\bigl(\Gamma(X_{n,a},X_{n,a})\bigr)
 \le
 \frac{q-1}{3q}\kappa_{n,a}.
 
\end{equation}
Thus the fourth cumulants detect exactly, and not merely sufficiently,
the disappearance of the decomposable physical sector.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.597312+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_98007bbba924d317f1529fa9ec85d0495b68301a6ac218d272ee8607835c0fd5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary C:parabolic-profile of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take $\kappa \in (0, 1/2)$ and $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n/m \in [\kappa, \kappa^{-1}]$. $$

$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:30.018391+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_980620c96ab93eac9e1e85545da0740e30be70f545956f34f3f387204b3d2594","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 37 of arXiv:2605.05864, 'Classification and Metrization of Classes of Smooth measures'] \rm
 
 A \([0,\infty]\)-valued function
 $A_t(\omega),\ t \ge 0,\ \omega \in \Omega$
 is a PCAF if the following hold:
 \begin{itemize}
  \item[(A.1)] for each $t \ge 0$, $A_t(\cdot)$ is $\c{F}_t$-measurable,
  \item[(A.2)]
       there exist a set $\Lambda \in \c{F}_{\infty}$ called a defining set, and
       an exceptional set $N \subset E$ such that $\b{P}_x(\Lambda) = 1$
       for any $x \in E \setminus N$ and $\theta_t \Lambda \subset \Lambda$
       for any $t > 0$, and moreover,
       for each $\omega \in \Lambda$, ${A}_0(\omega) = 0$,
       $|A_t(\omega)| < \infty$ for any $t < \zeta(\omega)$,
       $A_t(\omega) = {A}_{\zeta(\omega)}(\omega)$ for any
       $t \ge \zeta(\omega)$ and
       \begin{align}
	{A}_{t + s}(\omega) = {A}_s(\omega) + {A}_t(\theta_s \omega),\
	\text{for any $t,s \ge 0$},
       \end{align}
  \item[(A.3)]
       for each $\omega \in \Lambda$, the map
       $t \mapsto {A}_t(\omega)$ is non-negative and continuous on
       $[0,\infty)$, where $\Lambda$ is the set defined in the above condition.
 \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.424079+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9809e645bc9e28115b11fb82e0dde50272f41350eee9cbad8b8820531cc3eb72","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:Gaussian-variational of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:gaussian-variational}
There exists \(L_0<\infty\) such that, for every fixed \(L>L_0\),

\begin{align}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\Phi_{N,L}^G(V,\varepsilon,f)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:25:05.623004+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_980f53748b8ce0d37dc630ae56da82e5d0ce9a7f3cdc8488d7fe4fee5b6c60e3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (General mixed-Sellke fluid limit) of arXiv:2608.22122, '2608.22122'] Under the stochastic construction and notation of Section~\ref{sec:model}, for every finite \(T>0\),
\[
\sup_{0\leq t\leq T}
\left\|
\bigl(s_N(t),\iota_N(t),r_N(t),A_N(t)\bigr)
-

\right\|
\xlongrightarrow{\Pp}0
\]
as $N\to\infty.$

The deterministic limit is characterized by the  initial-value problem
\[
\dot A(t)
=

and

Equivalently,

\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:09:23.967955+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_98159da2a12dfb20089c8a77b9f494f81797e02b77f3e887535a315a94c64943","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 13 of arXiv:2607.22416, 'A multi-player optimal stopping game based on a spider Brownian bridge'] Suppose that $p=0.5$, $\mathcal{G}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{1}$ are given by $\mathcal{G}_{1}(z)=z - \alpha$ and $\mathcal{L}_{1}(z)=  \theta z$, and that $\mathcal{G}_{2}$ and $\mathcal{L}_{2}$ are given by $\mathcal{G}_{2}(z)=-z - \alpha$ and $\mathcal{L}_{2}(z)=  -\theta z$.

{"assumptions":["entries of Z i.i.d., mean 0, variance 1, finite fourth moment (necessary for the edge statements)","||Sigma_n|| bounded; spectral distribution of Sigma_n converges to H; p/n -> c in (0, infinity)","the interval [a, b] is outside the supports of the finite-n laws for all large n (not only outside the limiting support)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T09:21:49.109871+00:00","domain":"random matrix theory","id":"claim_98405d3e08a3062d8207dc22178a18452e909979f29e46ab7d8122c66d7b17e8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S_n = \\frac{1}{n} X_n^T X_n$ with $X_n = Z_n \\Sigma_n^{1/2}$, where $Z_n$ is $n \\times p$ with i.i.d. entries of mean $0$, variance $1$ and finite fourth moment, $\\Sigma_n$ is positive semidefinite with $\\|\\Sigma_n\\|$ bounded, $p/n \\to c \\in (0, \\infty)$, and the spectral distribution of $\\Sigma_n$ converges weakly to $H$. Let $F^{c,H}$ be the limiting spectral distribution of $S_n$ (the Marchenko-Pastur-Silverstein law) and let $[a, b]$ be a closed interval, $a > 0$, lying outside the support of $F^{c,H}$ and outside the supports of $F^{c_n, H_n}$ for all large $n$ (the finite-$n$ laws built from $c_n = p/n$ and $H_n$). Then almost surely no eigenvalue of $S_n$ lies in $[a, b]$ for all $n$ large enough: $\\mathbb{P}(\\text{no eigenvalue of } S_n \\text{ in } [a, b] \\text{ for all large } n) = 1$. Corollary (Bai-Yin 1993, the case $\\Sigma = I$): $\\lambda_{\\max}(S_n) \\to (1 + \\sqrt c)^2$ and, for $c < 1$, $\\lambda_{\\min}(S_n) \\to (1 - \\sqrt c)^2$ almost surely - the Marchenko-Pastur edges - and the finite fourth moment is necessary for the largest eigenvalue to converge. Consequence used throughout: an eigenvalue of a sample covariance strictly above $\\sigma^2(1 + \\sqrt c)^2$ (by a fixed margin) cannot come from an identity-covariance bulk, which is what licenses the bulk edge as a detection threshold in the spiked model, in Gavish-Donoho denoising, and in the median-based noise estimate.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["fixed design X of full column rank","independent errors with mean zero and possibly different variances","finite fourth moments of errors and regressors; (1/n) X'X -> positive definite; p fixed as n -> infinity for the consistency statement"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T05:50:37.943831+00:00","domain":"regression","id":"claim_985b54f9338db3244323dab66f1613e14302710ac7bfd8d3569800bb347b6e0c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $y = X\\beta + \\varepsilon$ with $X$ an $n \\times p$ design of full column rank (treated as fixed), $E[\\varepsilon] = 0$, and $\\operatorname{Var}(\\varepsilon) = \\Omega = \\operatorname{diag}(\\omega_1^2, \\dots, \\omega_n^2)$ - independent errors whose variances may differ across observations. With $r = y - X\\hat\\beta$ the residuals, the estimator $\\hat V_{\\mathrm{HC0}} = (X^T X)^{-1}\\big(\\sum_i r_i^2 x_i x_i^T\\big)(X^T X)^{-1}$ is consistent for $\\operatorname{Var}(\\hat\\beta)$ in the sense that $n\\,\\hat V_{\\mathrm{HC0}} - n\\operatorname{Var}(\\hat\\beta) \\to 0$ in probability as $n \\to \\infty$ with $p$ fixed, under finite fourth moments of the errors and of the regressors (the rows $x_i$ bounded or with $\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_i \\|x_i\\|^4 = O(1)$) and $\\frac{1}{n}X^T X \\to$ a positive definite limit. {"assumptions":["X is a set and mu* is defined on the entire power set of X","for the construction: E contains the empty set and some countable subfamily of E covers X, so that every subset has at least one admissible cover","rho maps E into [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0; no additivity or monotonicity of rho is assumed","countable, not arbitrary, families are used in the subadditivity axiom"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402410+00:00","domain":"measure theory, Caratheodory construction","id":"claim_9861570c368e84c1c207e946455b7453e592c4255152ddc4ad3423bc0df71072","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a set. A function mu* from the FULL power set of X to [0, +infinity] is an OUTER MEASURE if (1) mu*(empty set) = 0, (2) it is monotone: A contained in B implies mu*(A) <= mu*(B), and (3) it is countably subadditive: mu*(union over n >= 1 of A_n) <= sum over n >= 1 of mu*(A_n) for every countable family of subsets A_n of X, MEASURABLE OR NOT. Note that subadditivity is part of the definition in the abstract setting; the mathematical content lies in the fact that the standard constructions produce it. CONSTRUCTION FROM A COVERING FAMILY (a gauge): let E be a family of subsets of X containing the empty set and covering X by countably many of its members, and let rho : E -> [0, +infinity] with rho(empty set) = 0. Define mu*(A) = inf { sum over k >= 1 of rho(E_k) : E_k in E for all k and A contained in the union of the E_k }, with the convention that the infimum of the empty set is +infinity. Lebesgue outer measure on R^n is the case where E is the family of boxes (or open boxes, or cubes) and rho is the elementary volume. A set A is CARATHEODORY MEASURABLE for mu* if mu*(T) = mu*(T intersect A) + mu*(T minus A) for every test set T; these sets form a sigma-algebra on which mu* restricts to a complete countably additive measure (Caratheodory's theorem). CAUTIONS: an outer measure is defined on all subsets but is in general NOT additive on disjoint sets; it is not a measure on the power set; and the Caratheodory criterion, not the mere inequality in (3), is what recovers additivity.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:13:49.971936+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9877467e026f00b612e50d498a661006fbc979653968f984138cef41b06c4d6f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eq:deftildeupsilon of arXiv:2411.07157, 'Rough differential equations in the flow approach'] We define the family of elementary differentials $(\Upsilon^{\tau}: \tau\in\mathfrak{T})$, with $\Upsilon^{\tau} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\tau]$, by using an induction in $\tau$. 
For the base case, we define  $\Upsilon^{\circ} = \big( \Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}\big)_{r \in \N} \in \prod_{r \in \N} \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\circ_{r}]$ by setting, in analogy with (equation eq:elem_diff1_base of the paper), 
\[
\Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}(x_{r}) = V(x_{r})\;.
\]
It is clear that one indeed has $\Upsilon^{\circ_{r}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\circ]$. 
In other words, we could have just fixed a single $r \in \N$, applied the above formula, and then defined $\Upsilon^{\circ} = \pi_{\circ,\circ_{r}} \Upsilon^{\circ_{r}}$ and our construction would be well-defined in that it didn't depend on our initial choice of $r$. 

We now proceed to the inductive step. 
Suppose we have $\tau=[\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k]$, where $k > 0$, the $\tau_1,\dots,\tau_k$ are unlabelled, and $[\cdot]$ denotes joining the roots of unlabelled trees at a new unlabelled root. 
Our inductive assumption is that we have been given $\Upsilon^{\circ} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\raisebox{+0.05ex}{\includegraphics[scale=1.5]{figures/Xi.pdf}}]$, and $\Upsilon^{\tau_{j}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}_j]$ for $1 \leqslant j \leqslant k$.

Next, fix any labelled $\underline{\tau} \in \tau$, and choose any labelled $\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k$ with $\underline{\tau}_j \in \tau_j$, such that $\underline{\tau} = [\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k]_{r}$ (here we use the notation of (equation eq:product_of_trees of the paper), and $r = r(\underline{\tau})$).
For every $\underline{\sigma}\in \{\circ_{r}, \underline{\tau}_1,\cdots,\underline{\tau}_k\}$, we first set
\begin{equs}
   \Upsilon^{\underline{\sigma}} \eqdef \iota_{\sigma,\underline{\sigma}} \Upsilon^{\sigma}\in\text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\sigma}]\,.
\end{equs}
We then define $\Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}} \in \text{${\mcb{B}}$}[\underline{\tau}]$ in analogy with (equation eq:elem_diff1 of the paper) by setting
\begin{equ}
\Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau})})
=
\big( \mathrm{d}^{k} \Upsilon^{\circ_r}(x_{r(\underline{\tau})}) \big) \big[ \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}_{1}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_1)}),\cdots, \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}_{k}}(x_{N(\underline{\tau}_k)}) \big]\,,
\end{equ}
and finally we can set
\begin{equ}
\Upsilon^{\tau} \eqdef
\pi_{\tau,\underline{\tau}} \Upsilon^{\underline{\tau}}\;.
\end{equ}
In the next lemma we verify that $\Upsilon^{\tau}$ as defined above is well-defined, in that it does not depend on how we realised $\tau$ as the labelled tree $[\underline{\tau}_1,\dots,\underline{\tau}_k]_{r}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.375169+00:00","domain":"general topology","id":"claim_987a713ab2d41c965d796f3285a70f19fefacd5934de0e8382701f1d12d8b510","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A collection B of subsets of a set X is a basis (base) for a topology on X if (i) every point of X lies in at least one member of B, and (ii) whenever a point x lies in the intersection of two members B1, B2 of B, there is a member B3 of B with x in B3 and B3 contained in the intersection of B1 and B2. The topology generated by B consists of exactly those subsets U of X such that every point of U lies in some member of B contained in U; equivalently, the open sets are precisely the unions of subfamilies of B. Conversely, given a topological space (X, T), a subcollection B of T is a basis for T exactly when every open set is a union of members of B.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["all F_k lie in the SAME fixed chaos of order n >= 2","E[F_k^2] -> sigma^2 > 0","the equivalence is FALSE for sequences not confined to one chaos"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.543836+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_987c81863f8063bc739cd937cd38fc426cd1f16bcd26e3a30b1ba5274965a462","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix an integer n >= 2 and let F_k = I_n(f_k) be a sequence living in the SAME n-th Wiener chaos, with E[F_k^2] = n! ||f_k||^2 converging to sigma^2 > 0. Then the following are EQUIVALENT: (i) F_k converges in distribution to N(0, sigma^2); (ii) E[F_k^4] -> 3 sigma^4; (iii) the contractions satisfy || f_k contracted with f_k at r indices || -> 0 for every r = 1, ..., n-1. The theorem replaces the infinitely many moment conditions of the method of moments by a SINGLE fourth-moment condition. The hypothesis that the chaos order n is FIXED and the same for every k is essential and is the standard misquotation: for a general sequence of random variables, or for a sequence whose chaos order drifts, matching the fourth moment says nothing about normality - the fourth moment of a suitable two-point law is also 3 times the square of its variance. Also essential is sigma^2 > 0; degenerating variance is excluded. The quantitative form is due to Nourdin and Peccati via Malliavin-Stein: for F in the n-th chaos with E[F^2] = sigma^2, the total variation distance to N(0, sigma^2) is bounded by a constant depending only on n times the square root of ( E[F^4] - 3 sigma^4 ), so the fourth cumulant controls the rate as well as the limit. [Nualart and Peccati (2005), Ann. Probab. 33; Nourdin and Peccati (2009); see Nourdin and Peccati, Normal Approximations with Malliavin Calculus, Theorem 5.2.7]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.744319+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_98b69e2fa8508940af6a1fbb1117af0e4f28eb9d10d8d89c31b39210aabbe69a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The language $H$ equals the well-defined concatenation $J.G$.
  \begin{proof}
    To every word $w \in H$ there is a \emph{coupon-counting
    function} $f_w\colon \{ 0, 1, \ldots, \lvert w \rvert \} \to \N$
    that tracks the current number of distinct coupons held.
    This means $f_w(0) = 0$ and $f_w(\lvert w \rvert) = m$.
    Choose the smallest $k$ for which $f(k) = m$ and let
    $j$ be the word formed from the first $k$ letters in $w$.
    Then $w$ has the decomposition $j.g$ for some word $g$
    of length $\lvert w\rvert - k$.
    But since $f(k) = f(\lvert w \rvert) = m$,
    each occurrence of $\D_i$ in $g$ must be eventually followed
    by $\C_i$. Hence $g \in G$. There can be no decomposition $j = u.v$
    with $u \in H$ and $v \neq \varepsilon$ because $k > 0$ was selected minimally.
    This establishes $j \in J$ and $w \in J.G$. Thus $H \subseteq J.G$.

    To show $J.G \subseteq H$, take some $j.g \in J.G$ and
    consider the coupon-counting function $f_{j.g}$.
    Then $f_{j.g}(\lvert j \rvert) = m$ but $g$
    recovers all coupons it drops,
    so $f_{j.g}(\lvert j\rvert + \lvert g \rvert) = 
    f_{j.g}(\lvert j \rvert) = m$. We conclude
    $j.g \in H$ and $H = J.G$.

    We could not have selected a longer word $j' \in J$ in the first
    paragraph because $j' = j.u$ would hold with $u \neq \varepsilon$.
    This gives the contradiction $j' \notin J$.
    So, the factorisation of words $w \mapsto (j, g)$ is unique;
    $J$ and $G$ are well-defined for concatenation.
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.499252+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_98c8bf02b194191751d59e544407d2b5ddcfe2816446a87e8a3d6e57a9ae7c3e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"(1) U ≠ C is essential: there is no biholomorphism from C onto D, since any holomorphic map C → D is bounded, hence constant by Liouville's theorem. C and D are the two conformal types of simply connected Riemann surfaces with the sphere. (2) Simple connectivity is essential and is not repaired by 'the domain has no holes that matter'. The punctured disk D minus {0} is not conformally equivalent to D: a biholomorphism F : D minus {0} → D would be bounded, hence extend holomorphically to 0 with |F(0)| ≤ 1; the extension maps the disk into D by the open mapping theorem, so F(0) = F(z1) for some z1 ≠ 0, and openness near both points contradicts injectivity on D minus {0}. Likewise two annuli {1 < |z| < R} and {1 < |z| < R'} are conformally equivalent only when R = R': conformal type has a modulus, so 'both are doubly connected' is not enough. (3) The conclusion is interior. The Riemann map need not extend continuously to the boundary, and when it does it need not be injective there. For the slit disk U = D minus [0,1) (which is simply connected), the inverse of the Riemann map extends continuously to the closed disk, but each point of the open slit is the image of two boundary points, so no homeomorphism of the closures exists. The correct boundary statement is Carathéodory's theorem: if U is bounded by a Jordan curve, then the Riemann map extends to a homeomorphism of the closed domains. (4) Normalization: the map is unique only after fixing F(z0) = 0 and F'(z0) > 0; without it the family of Riemann maps is a three-real-parameter family (compose with any automorphism of D).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:35:19.875197+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_98de3550e564e494cc44cf9a8e2c05a05b8422d924aa0d891a71d9af9ed4384d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn slith of arXiv:2608.27939, 'Entropy and domination for quasi-Hitchin representations'] For a closed surface $S$ and a maximal lamination $\lambda$, let $\rho:\pi_1(S) \to \mathrm{PSL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be an $n$-pleated representation (as in Definition (defn:pleat of the paper)), pleated along $\lambda$, with an associated $\rho$-equivariant limit map $\xi$ that assigns flags in $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the endpoints of leaves of $\tilde{\lambda}$. The \textit{slithering map} compatible with $\xi$  $$\Sigma:\tilde{\Lambda}^2 \to \mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$$ defined on the space of pairs of leaves of $\lambda$, such that $\Sigma(g_1,g_2)$ is a matrix in $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{C})$ that takes the transverse pair of flags associated with the endpoints of a leaf $g_2$ to that of a leaf $g_1$ (oriented in parallel), satisfying
\[
\Sigma(g,g)=\mathrm{id}, \qquad
\Sigma(g_1,g_3)=\Sigma(g_1,g_2)\Sigma(g_2,g_3),
\]
whenever $g_2$ separates $g_1$ from $g_3$. When $g_1$ and $g_2$ share an endpoint, $\Sigma(g_1,g_2)$ is the unique unipotent transformation that fixes the flag at the common endpoint and takes the flag at the other endpoint of $g_2$ to the flag at the other endpoint of $g_1$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(F_n) increasing, F_infinity generated by their union","Y integrable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.627314+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_990c757f8a69205734bf9eaa5f8523ff03979cc297993560b1152fd27fd6f9f2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (F_n) be an increasing filtration with F_infinity the sigma-algebra it generates, and let Y be in L^1. Then E[Y | F_n] converges almost surely and in L^1 to E[Y | F_infinity]. Taking Y = 1_A for A in F_infinity gives LEVY'S 0-1 LAW: P(A | F_n) -> 1_A almost surely, so the conditional probability of any event in the limit sigma-algebra converges to 0 or 1. Applied to a tail event of an independent sequence, where F_n is generated by the first n variables and P(A | F_n) = P(A) by independence, this yields Kolmogorov's 0-1 law as a corollary. The theorem is about an INCREASING family; the corresponding statement for a decreasing family is Levy's downward theorem and needs its own proof. The limit is conditional on F_infinity and not on F - the two differ, and writing E[Y | F] would be wrong unless F_infinity = F up to null sets. [standard; e.g. Williams, Probability with Martingales, Theorem 14.2]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:44.527059+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_991e7971736502bc06092723e17af2cf349bf02434680cca634a33b35e30ccf9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 3 of arXiv:2604.01748, 'Largest-loop-first loop-erased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^{4}$'] Let $m \ge 0$ be an integer. A sequence of points 
 $$\lambda = [\lambda(0), \lambda(1), \cdots, \lambda(m)] \subset \mathbb{Z}^{d}$$ is called a path of length $m$ if $|\lambda(k) - \lambda(k+1)| = 1$ for all $0 \le k \le m-1$. We write $\text{len}\, (\lambda) = m$ for the length of $\lambda$. For $0 \le a \le b \le m$, we set $\lambda[a,b] = [\lambda(a), \lambda(a+1), \cdots, \lambda(b)]$ to denote the portion of the path $\lambda$ between times $a$ and $b$. Furthermore, $\lambda$ is said to be a simple path if $\lambda(j) \neq \lambda(k)$ for all $0 \le j < k \le m$.

     Let $\lambda_{1} = [\lambda_{1}(0), \cdots, \lambda_{1}(m_{1})]$ and $\lambda_{2} = [\lambda_{2}(0), \cdots, \lambda_{2}(m_{2})]$ be two paths in $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ of lengths $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$, respectively, and suppose that $\lambda_{1}(m_{1}) = \lambda_{2}(0)$. We define the concatenation of $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$, denoted by $\lambda_{1} \oplus \lambda_{2}$, by
$$\lambda_{1} \oplus \lambda_{2} = [ \lambda_{1} (0), \cdots , \lambda_{1} (m_{1}) , \lambda_{2} (1), \cdots , \lambda_{2} (m_{2})]. $$
    Then $\lambda_{1} \oplus \lambda_{2}$ is a path of length $m_{1}+m_{2}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149419+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity theory","id":"claim_994ea180f3136425e554f422a5cd28077f4672f5e5871e28d1685f524f0bcfca","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Three hypotheses of the De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theorem are load-bearing, and each fails concretely. (1) Scalar. The theorem is false for systems: De Giorgi (1968) exhibited, for n >= 3, a linear elliptic system with bounded measurable coefficients satisfying the Legendre-Hadamard and even the strong ellipticity condition whose weak solution is u(x) = x |x|^{-gamma} for an explicit gamma with 1 < gamma < n/2 - a solution in H^1 that is unbounded, hence not even locally bounded, let alone Hoelder. So a referee must check that an application of De Giorgi-Nash-Moser or of Moser's Harnack inequality is to a single equation, not to a system, and that the maximum-principle-based truncations used in the proof are available. (2) The energy class u in H^1_loc. A distributional solution whose gradient is only in L^p for some p < 2 need not be bounded. In the plane take A(x) = I + (mu - 1) x x^T/|x|^2 with mu > 1 (uniformly elliptic, bounded, measurable, discontinuous only at the origin). In polar coordinates div(A grad u) = (1/r) d/dr ( r mu u_r ) + (1/r^2) u_{theta theta}, so u = r^s cos(theta) solves the equation away from 0 exactly when mu s^2 = 1. The choice s = -1/sqrt(mu) in (-1,0) gives u = r^{-1/sqrt(mu)} cos(theta), which is unbounded at 0, lies in W^{1,p}_loc precisely for p < 2/(1 + 1/sqrt(mu)) < 2, and is a distributional solution across the origin (the flux through small circles tends to 0 because s > -1). (3) The Hoelder exponent depends on the ellipticity ratio and cannot be improved to Lipschitz. The same coefficients with s = +alpha, i.e. mu = 1/alpha^2, give the H^1 solution u = r^alpha cos(theta) of a uniformly elliptic equation with ellipticity ratio alpha^{-2}: it is exactly C^{0,alpha} at the origin and no better. Hence the exponent alpha(n, Lambda/lambda) in the theorem must degenerate to 0 as Lambda/lambda tends to infinity, and 'bounded measurable coefficients give Lipschitz solutions' is false. Gradient bounds require continuity (or Dini/Hoelder continuity) of the coefficients.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the walk is on the incipient infinite cluster or a similarly statistically self-similar critical random graph","a known or boundable volume-growth exponent d_f for balls in the cluster","a known or boundable effective-resistance-growth exponent reflecting the bottleneck/dangling-end structure","typically also requires the cluster's law to have appropriate scale-invariance, or at least comparable behavior across scales"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_995bb1851ff2b7c32ba0e7dcdd60e02e63ccc5cf1891c73d2c0eefad0e85bbb6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For simple random walk on the incipient infinite cluster of critical percolation, or more generally on critical random media with anomalous volume growth, Kesten's argument establishes subdiffusive behavior, that the walk's typical displacement after n steps is of order n^{1/d_w} with walk dimension d_w > 2 rather than the diffusive n^{1/2}, by combining a volume-growth estimate showing balls of radius r typically contain of order r^{d_f} points, with d_f the fractal (volume) dimension of the cluster, and an effective-resistance estimate R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) of order r^{zeta}, reflecting the long dangling ends and low-conductance bottlenecks characteristic of the critical cluster. The expected exit time from a ball of radius r is then of order r^{d_f+zeta} (volume times resistance: the Einstein relation d_w = d_f + zeta), so the displacement is of order n^{1/(d_f+zeta)}, subdiffusive when d_f + zeta > 2; the Nash/heat-kernel machinery or a direct expected-exit-time computation turns the two estimates into bounds. In balls of the intrinsic (graph) metric with unit conductances R_eff(0, B(0,r)^c) <= r, so zeta <= 1 there: for the high-dimensional incipient infinite cluster the intrinsic volume grows as r^2 and the resistance as r, giving d_w = 3. The argument does not give the exact value of the subdiffusivity exponent in most dimensions, only bounds, with the precise exponent known rigorously only in specific settings such as sufficiently high dimension or tree-like/hierarchical models, and it is specific to critical (not subcritical or supercritical) percolation geometry, where the fractal, tree-like structure with many bottlenecks is essential to the argument. Typical failure: Assuming the subdiffusivity exponent established for one setting, such as high-dimensional or tree-based incipient infinite clusters where exact computation is possible, transfers to two-dimensional critical percolation, where the exact random-walk dimension remains a major open problem; volume-growth and resistance-growth exponents are model- and dimension-specific quantities that must be independently estimated rather than imported across models with superficially similar critical geometry. Canonical reference: Kesten, 1986, Annales de l'Institut Henri Poincare, Probabilites et Statistiques; Barlow, Jarai, Kumagai and Slade, 2008, Communications in Mathematical Physics.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.542424+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9983acdd24bab7573598cbe43c588211e9e1d72227253d0cb43782e29ec19a49","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Fix d >= 2 and let E(Z^d) be the set of nearest-neighbour edges of the integer lattice. Assign to each edge e an independent random weight tau_e >= 0 with common distribution F; the collection (tau_e) is the environment. The PASSAGE TIME of a finite lattice path gamma is T(gamma) = sum over the edges of gamma of tau_e, and the passage time between vertices x and y is T(x,y) = inf over finite paths from x to y of T(gamma). T is a random pseudometric on Z^d: it is symmetric, satisfies the triangle inequality, and vanishes on the diagonal, but T(x,y) = 0 is possible for x != y when F has an atom at 0. A GEODESIC from x to y is a path attaining the infimum. Geodesics need not exist for a general F, and when F(0) is at least the critical probability p_c(d) the infimum can be 0 and attained by infinitely many paths; when F(0) < p_c a geodesic exists almost surely for every pair, and it is almost surely unique for every pair when F is continuous, since ties then have probability 0. The standing notation in the literature is T(0, x) for the point-to-point time, mu or g for the time constant, chi for the fluctuation exponent and xi for the wandering exponent; the store already records that those exponents are DEFINED differently by different theorems and are not interchangeable. [standard; e.g. Auffinger, Damron and Hanson, 50 Years of First-Passage Percolation, Chapters 1 and 4]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Burgers' equation f(u) = u^2/2 in one dimension","Weak solutions are only required to satisfy the integral identity; jumps must satisfy Rankine-Hugoniot but may still be inadmissible","Uniqueness is restored by the Kruzhkov entropy inequalities (equivalently, for piecewise smooth solutions, by Oleinik's chord condition at each jump)"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418611+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_99a13816dfad50d260100b726c1812dec833cb5ab9500c5108e4748d4cdc77db","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: uniqueness in Kruzhkov's theorem is for ENTROPY solutions; the integral (weak) formulation alone, even with Rankine-Hugoniot satisfied at every jump, does not determine the solution. Counterexample 2 (Burgers with u0 = 0 for x < 0, u0 = 1 for x > 0): the stationary-in-shape expansion shock u = 0 for x < t/2, u = 1 for x > t/2 satisfies Rankine-Hugoniot, but the entropy solution is the rarefaction u = 0 for x ≤ 0, u = x/t for 0 ≤ x ≤ t, u = 1 for x ≥ t. In both cases the wrong solutions create information (characteristics emanate from the shock) instead of destroying it, and they are not vanishing-viscosity limits. Auditor's check: a proof that constructs 'a' weak solution and then calls it 'the' solution — or that computes shock speeds from Rankine-Hugoniot without verifying admissibility — is incomplete; check Oleinik's chord condition at every jump (for convex flux: the state must jump DOWN as x increases).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["rows i.i.d. with finite twelfth moments (the Ledoit-Wolf condition)","M/n -> c in (0,1) for the stated form; the population spectral distribution has compact support (Ledoit-Peche take it bounded away from zero)","the sample eigenvalues are distinct (they are, almost surely)"],"created_at":"2026-09-05T06:40:20.562774+00:00","domain":"covariance estimation / random matrix theory","id":"claim_99cacf9752b7e70bfc79fa5a079c62ca089650407d9a61a19b42983a5a0f9318","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $S = n^{-1} X^T X = \\sum_{i=1}^M \\lambda_i u_i u_i^T$ be the sample covariance of $n$ i.i.d. rows in $\\mathbb{R}^M$ with population covariance $\\Sigma$, and let $M/n \\to c \\in (0,1)$. Among rotation-equivariant estimators $\\sum_i d_i u_i u_i^T$ the Frobenius-optimal choice is the oracle $d_i^* = u_i^T \\Sigma u_i$, whose large-dimensional limit is $\\lambda_i / |1 - c - c\\lambda_i \\breve m_F(\\lambda_i)|^2$ with $\\breve m_F(\\lambda) = \\lim_{\\eta \\downarrow 0} m_F(\\lambda + i\\eta)$, $m_F(z) = \\int dF(t)/(t - z)$ the Stieltjes transform of the limiting sample spectral distribution $F$ (Ledoit-Peche 2011). Writing $\\operatorname{Im} \\breve m_F(\\lambda) = \\pi f(\\lambda)$ and $\\operatorname{Re} \\breve m_F(\\lambda) = \\pi H_f(\\lambda)$, $H_f(x) = \\pi^{-1} \\mathrm{PV}\\!\\int f(t)/(t - x)\\,dt$, the oracle reads $\\tilde d_i = \\lambda_i / \\big[(\\pi c \\lambda_i f(\\lambda_i))^2 + (1 - c - \\pi c \\lambda_i H_f(\\lambda_i))^2\\big]$. Ledoit and Wolf (2020) estimate $f$ and $H_f$ from the sample eigenvalues themselves with the Epanechnikov kernel $\\kappa(x) = \\tfrac{3}{4\\sqrt5}(1 - x^2/5)^+$ and the eigenvalue-proportional bandwidth $h_j = \\lambda_j n^{-1/3}$: $\\tilde f(x) = M^{-1}\\sum_j \\kappa((x - \\lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$ and $\\tilde H_f(x) = M^{-1}\\sum_j H_\\kappa((x - \\lambda_j)/h_j)/h_j$, where $H_\\kappa(x) = -\\tfrac{3x}{10\\pi} + \\tfrac{3}{4\\sqrt5\\pi}(1 - x^2/5)\\log\\big|\\tfrac{\\sqrt5 - x}{\\sqrt5 + x}\\big|$. The resulting estimator $\\hat\\Sigma = \\sum_i \\tilde d_i u_i u_i^T$ has no tuning constant, is positive definite when $c < 1$, and its Frobenius loss (and its minimum-variance-portfolio loss) converges to the oracle's; for $c > 1$ a separate formula handles the $M - n$ null eigenvalues.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:42:39.077695+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_99d0309b697d8047602eaa18a2648c7871cb9153900bd62de68b3851ce305e8d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm A. thm: convergence coupling for fused resistance spaces of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] Let $(F_{n}, R_{n}, \rho_{n}),\, n \geq 1$ and $(F, R, \rho)$ be rooted compact resistance metric spaces.

$Y\in C^\alpha([0,T];W)$ and
$Y'\in C^\alpha([0,T];\mathcal{L}(V,W))$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:37:25.961606+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9a0ed5bf760729c612bf8d7e8875ae75b38e6a3024f1ae5a7928790100fb8a1f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2 of arXiv:2608.29713, '\textbf{A Cartan geometry from a correspondence space in Riemannian geometry}'] A Cartan geometry $(q:\mathcal{P}\to M,\omega)$ of type $(\operatorname{Euc}(n),O(n))$ canonically determines a Riemannian metric $g$ on $M$ by
$$
g_{x}(v,w):=\left\langle \phi_{u}(v),\phi_{u}(w)\right\rangle,
\qquad v,w\in T_{x}M,
$$
where $u\in\mathcal{P}$ is any point with $q(u)=x$. Moreover, after fixing the canonical orthonormal basis $(E_{1},\ldots,E_{n})$ of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, the map
\[
\mathcal{P}\longrightarrow \mathcal{F}_{g}(M),
\qquad
u\mapsto\big(\phi_{u}^{-1}(E_{1}),\ldots,\phi_{u}^{-1}(E_{n})\big),
\]
is an isomorphism of $O(n)$-principal fiber bundles over $M$.
Here the right action on $\mathcal F_g(M)$ is the usual one:
\[
(e_1,\ldots,e_n)\cdot A
=
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i A_{i1},
\ldots,
\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i A_{in}
\right),
\qquad A=(A_{ij})\in O(n).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.495231+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9a373311faced9b1e270a6dbf43f9089e656bc02abaa3d735fb9068f7c3b3f5b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm Loewner coordinate change in angular coordinate of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] In angular (trigonometric) coordinates, suppose $\gamma(0) = \theta \in \mathbb{R}$ and let the marked points be $\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_n \in \mathbb{C}$. Let $\gamma(t)$ be the curve generated by the deterministic Loewner chain:
\begin{equation}
\partial_t h_t(z) = \cot\left( \frac{h_t(z) - \theta_t}{2} \right), \qquad \dot{\theta}_t = b\left( \theta_t ; h_t(\theta_1), \ldots, h_t(\theta_n) \right),
\end{equation}
with initial condition $h_0(z) = z$ and $\theta_0 = \theta$, where $b : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{C}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a smooth vector field.

Let $\tau : \mathcal{N} \to \mathbb{H}$ be a conformal map defined on a neighborhood $\mathcal{N}$ of $\theta$ such that $\gamma[0,T] \subset \mathcal{N}$ and $\tau(\partial \mathcal{N} \cap \mathbb{R}) \subset \mathbb{R}$. Define the image curve $\widetilde{\gamma}(t) := \tau(\gamma(t))$ for $t \in [0, T]$, and let $\widetilde{h}_t$ denote the conformal map associated with $\widetilde{\gamma}[0, t]$.

Define the conformal coordinate change
\[
\Psi_t := \widetilde{h}_t \circ \tau \circ h_t^{-1}.
\]

Then the image conformal map $\widetilde{h}_t(z)$ satisfies the evolution equation:
\begin{equation}
\partial_t \widetilde{h}_t(z) = \cot\left( \frac{\widetilde{h}_t(z) - \widetilde{\theta}_t}{2} \right) \cdot \left[ \Psi_t'(\theta_t) \right]^2, \qquad \widetilde{h}_0(z) = z,
\end{equation}
where the new driving function is
\[
\widetilde{\theta}_t := \widetilde{h}_t \circ \tau \circ h_t^{-1}(\theta_t) = \Psi_t(\theta_t), \quad \widetilde{\theta}_0 = \tau(\theta).
\]

Moreover, the curve $\widetilde{\gamma}(t)$ is parameterized so that its unit disk capacity satisfies
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{hcap}(\widetilde{\gamma}[0, t]) = 2 \sigma(t), \qquad \text{where} \quad \sigma(t) := \int_0^t \left| \Psi_s'(\theta_s) \right|^2 \, ds.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:30:14.145694+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9a45b9b24a3dfd2219e5e8c2033ea782d3df6e05de2cfd7ce3cd22c3f69a70a0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem th:split of arXiv:2608.19358, 'An optimal Poincaré inequality\\for the complex Ginibre log-gas'] Consider the complex line $L=\mathbb{C}(1,\ldots,1)\subset\mathbb{C}^n$, and
  its orthogonal complex hyperplane $L^\perp\subset\mathbb{C}^n$. Let
  $\varphi_n(z)=c_n^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{-n|z|^2}|V_n(z)|^2$, $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$,
  be the density of the complex Ginibre log-gas $\mu_n$. Then
  $z=\operatorname{proj}_L(z)+\operatorname{proj}_{L^\perp}(z)=S(z)v+W$ where
  $S(z)=z_1+\cdots+z_n$, $v=(1/n,\ldots,1/n)$ and $W=z-S(z)v$, for all
  $z\in\mathbb{C}^n$, and
  \begin{equation}
    \varphi_n(z)=\mathrm{e}^{-|S(z)|^2}\varphi_n(W).
  \end{equation}
  In probabilistic terms, if $\mathbf{Z}\sim\mu_n$ then
  $\mathbf{S}=\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbf{Z}_k$ and
  $\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{Z}-(\mathbf{S},\ldots,\mathbf{S})/n$ are independent

  \[
    \mathbf{R}=n|\mathbf{W}|^2\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\kappa,1)

  \]
  when $n\geq2$, while $\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{Z}$, $\mathbf{W}=0$, and

{"assumptions":["R>=72; d>=2","Independent standard Gaussian inputs","LSI convention Ent(f^2)<=2 C_LS E||grad f||^2","Fixed exceptional observation; not a typical-observation guarantee","Score-only input model for the information-obstruction consequence"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T20:12:05.583953+00:00","domain":"posterior sampling and functional inequalities","id":"claim_9a4cfee7532e1d359fb034449676f341a43f25f9d713fd07004d3bd13051134c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"DRAFT, proof (unaudited), T411-w740-C002/C003 v1. Let d>=2 and R>=72, T_R(z)=z+(z-R)_+, and let Z,W,Z2,...,Zd be independent standard Gaussians. Set P0=Law(Z+W,Z2,...,Zd) and P1=Law(T_R(Z)+W,Z2,...,Zd). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.317229+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9a9a7b9208547e6f0c04ede1265f12a244a2a346e801a831712fef3dc31bf404","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:higher-dimensional-coding of arXiv:2607.25616, 'Stealthy point processes and lattice induction'] Let $d\geq2$, and let $Z$ be a standard Borel space equipped with

\[

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-24T23:47:01.939466+00:00","domain":"boolean functions/fourier analysis","id":"claim_9a9adddb76424d3b96eb917c2d999d1a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[DERIVED + CHECKED 09-08 07:3x] Bernoulli 2/3: rescaling a block by v=(3/2)^n w turns Q^2 into a RIESZ PRODUCT with ratio 3/2, and the criterion's coefficient c(n) is its Fourier coefficient at frequency (3/2)^(n+1). That frequency is provably NOT in the product's spectrum - if (3/2)^(n+1) = sum eps_i (3/2)^i with eps in {0,+-1} then 3^(n+1) = sum eps_i 3^i 2^(n+1-i), and mod 3 induction forces every eps_i = 0 (brute-forced n=1..9 too). So |c(n)| is pure window leakage rather than a spectral line, which is why it measures ~0.08 not order one. LIMIT: summing leakage over the 3^(n+1) characters overshoots by 2^n (the linearising failure), and the nearest line can sit within 2^-(n+1), so a proof needs a COUNT of near-coincidences, not an exactness statement","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.096419+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9b1afa08cb1432c416d963cee443bdd6994471bd1a5eb173411bb5775883801e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:ribbon-record of arXiv:2608.29403, 'Kac's Walk on Rotation Matrices Mixes in $\boldsymbol{\Theta(n^2)}$ Steps:\\ A Proof Disco'] A rooted orthogonal-Weingarten ribbon record $\Gamma$ of degree $m$
consists of the dart set
$\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\{L_0,L_1,R_0,R_1\}$; its coefficient boxes and
color labels; perfect matchings $p,q,r$ giving the row,
coefficient-column, and rooted trace wiring; all local wedge and
direct/cross signs; the distinguished root boundary; and the following
orthogonal-Weingarten path data.

Partition the darts into the independent Haar-color classes
$\mathscr H_\Gamma$ (there is one class when all entries come from one
Haar matrix).  If $a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma$ contains $m_a$ coefficient
occurrences, put $k_a=2m_a$, so it has $2k_a=4m_a$ darts, and denote by
$p_a,q_a$ the restrictions of $p,q$.  The rooted dart order chooses a
deterministic relabelling $\sigma_a$ with
$\sigma_a\cdot e_{k_a}=p_a$, where
\[
 e_k=\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\},\ldots,\{2k-1,2k\}\},
\]
and put
$\mathfrak m_a=\sigma_a^{-1}\cdot q_a\in\mathcal P_2(2k_a)$.
The orthogonal Weingarten graph has vertex set
$\bigsqcup_{j\ge0}\mathcal P_2(2j)$.  At level $j$ it has a solid arrow
\[
 \mathfrak n\longrightarrow(i,2j-1)\cdot\mathfrak n,
 \qquad 1\le i<2j-1,
\]
and it has a dashed arrow
$\mathfrak n\dashrightarrow\mathfrak n^\downarrow$ when
$\{2j-1,2j\}\in\mathfrak n$, where $\mathfrak n^\downarrow$ is
obtained by deleting that pair.  The record chooses, for every $a$, one
\emph{individual} path $\gamma_a$ from $\mathfrak m_a$ to the empty
pairing.  It uses exactly $k_a$ dashed arrows; write $s_a$ for its number
of solid arrows.  If $\mu_a$ is the coset type of $\mathfrak m_a$, define
\[
 d_a:=|\mathfrak m_a|=k_a-\ell(\mu_a)
      =k_a-\#(p_a\vee q_a),
 \qquad
 g_a:=s_a-d_a\ge0,
 \qquad
 g_{\rm Wg}:=\sum_{a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma}g_a.
\]
Thus $g_{\rm Wg}$ is the total number of solid arrows beyond shortest
orthogonal-Weingarten paths; unlike the unitary excess, it need not be
even.

Let $w_\Gamma$ be the scalar coefficient of this chosen product path,
including the bounded local wedge and direct/cross coefficients.  Write
$\operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}$ for the typed raw
contraction determined by the record and its circuit state, and put
\[
 F_\Gamma=\#(p\vee r),\qquad
 \ell_\Gamma=\#(p\vee q)
      =\sum_{a\in\mathscr H_\Gamma}\#(p_a\vee q_a),\qquad
 \omega_\Gamma=n^{F_\Gamma}w_\Gamma,\qquad
 \mathcal A_\Gamma=w_\Gamma
       \operatorname{Contr}^{\rm raw}_{\Gamma,\tau}.
\]
Thus $w_\Gamma$ is a scalar coefficient, not the value or norm of an
open contraction; $\omega_\Gamma$ merely expresses the same coefficient

{"assumptions":["N is a positive integer","X takes values in the positive divisors of N","X | n means that X divides n"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T06:15:55.496081+00:00","domain":"finite discrete probability on a divisibility-ordered state space","id":"claim_9b4afd82d145ae84baff796fea99bb85c487e52b15a9c1e12afbbb4884bbb5d6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let N be a positive integer and X a random variable with values in D(N); put F(n) = P(X | n) for n | N (the event that X divides n). Then P(X = n) = sum_{d | n} mu(n/d) F(d), with mu the arithmetic Moebius function. Conversely, a real function F on D(N) equals n -> P(X | n) for some law on D(N) if and only if F(N) = 1 and every value p(n) = sum_{d | n} mu(n/d) F(d) is nonnegative. Monotonicity cannot replace nonnegativity: on D(6), F(1) = 0, F(2) = F(3) = 3/5, F(6) = 1 is order-preserving with F(6) = 1, yet p(6) = F(6) - F(2) - F(3) + F(1) = -1/5.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A square over a field (R or C in the numerical statements)","unit lower triangular L fixes the normalisation; L D U variants move the diagonal into D"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479562+00:00","domain":"numerical linear algebra","id":"claim_9b87fdf50aa592bb2dcee21b2e13402fec32970a0b5820f287442e30505c9e85","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A be an n x n matrix over a field. A has a factorisation A = L U with L unit lower triangular (ones on the diagonal) and U upper triangular if and only if every leading principal submatrix A_k = A[1..k, 1..k], k = 1, ..., n - 1, is invertible (for invertible A this is equivalent to all n leading principal minors being nonzero); when it exists the factorisation is unique for invertible A, and u_kk = det A_k / det A_{k-1}. In general, for every A there is a permutation matrix P with P A = L U (Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting: at each step the row with the largest remaining entry in the pivot column is swapped into the pivot position); for invertible A the factors are then unique given P. The elimination costs 2 n^3 / 3 flops; solving A x = b afterwards costs 2 n^2 by one forward and one back substitution; the determinant is the product of the u_kk times the sign of P. Partial pivoting is backward stable in practice (the growth factor is bounded by 2^{n-1} in the worst case, attained by Wilkinson's example, but is small on almost all matrices), whereas elimination without pivoting can be unstable on matrices with small pivots even when A is well conditioned. Symmetric positive definite matrices need no pivoting (Cholesky); diagonally dominant matrices need none either.","status":"unverified"}

Thus, let us suppose we have controls $(q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfying the $(\alpha,q_0,L,\epsilon)$-$\sii$ conditions, which drive processes $X,Y$ as in

Let $\tilde q_* = q_0$, so that condition~\ref{it:8.2} is satisfied, and $(\tilde p,\tilde \zeta,\tilde \zeta^\Ising) = (p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$. We will couple $\tilde{X}(q_0)=X(q_*)$ and 
$\tilde{Y}(q_0)=Y(q_*)$. 
From the
definition \eqref{e:filt.X.Y} of $\cF_X$ and $\cF_Y$, we can write
\begin{align*}
        b_t &= b_t( (B(s))_{s\in[q_*,t]},U,X(q_*)), \\
        \sigma_t &= \sigma_t( (B(s))_{s\in[q_*,t]},U,X(q_*)), \\

    \end{align*}
where the $\sigma_t,b_t,w_t$ on the right-hand sides are measurable functions.
We then let $(\tilde{b},\tilde{\sigma},\tilde{w})$ be defined by
$(\tilde b_t,\tilde \sigma_t,\tilde w_t) = (0,1,1)$ for $t\in [q_0,q_*)$, and
    \begin{align*}

        \tilde{X}
        (q_0)

        &= \sigma_t( (B(s))_{s\in[q_*,t]},U,

        \tilde{Y}(q_0)

for $t\in [q_*,1]$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:48:02.411883+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9b9af4ae5833e3581d9a96a9dca7fdb7045e70b277e0f22f8d46dcd2cad2f182","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lma:realformsign of arXiv:2608.26564, 'Real ideal points, Conway spheres, and left-orderable Dehn fillings'] Let $R_\theta = \left(\begin{smallmatrix}\cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.

{"assumptions":["T is measurable","invariance is expressed through preimages T^{-1}A"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.437948+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, foundations","id":"claim_9ba1defc34ee3afb4584a993f111afbfc82e7640f9230052afb1810248d72dbf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable map $T: X \\to X$ is measure-preserving if $\\mu(T^{-1} A) = \\mu(A)$ for every $A \\in \\mathcal{B}$ (preimages, not images: $T$ need not be injective, and for non-invertible $T$ the condition $\\mu(TA) = \\mu(A)$ is neither implied nor required). The system is a probability-preserving system when $\\mu(X) = 1$. A set $A$ is (strictly) invariant if $T^{-1}A = A$, and invariant mod $\\mu$ if $\\mu(T^{-1}A \\,\\triangle\\, A) = 0$; every set invariant mod $\\mu$ differs from a strictly invariant set by a null set. $T$ is ergodic if every invariant set has measure $0$ or full measure; equivalently (for a probability measure) every measurable $f$ with $f \\circ T = f$ a.e. is a.e. constant; equivalently every set $A$ with $T^{-1}A \\subset A$ mod $\\mu$ (or $T^{-1}A \\supset A$ mod $\\mu$) has measure 0 or 1. The invariant $\\sigma$-algebra $\\mathcal{I} = \\{A : T^{-1}A = A\\}$ is what the ergodic averages converge to conditional expectations onto. Ergodicity is not the same as mixing (mixing implies ergodic, not conversely: an irrational rotation of the circle is ergodic but not mixing), and it is not preserved by passing to powers ($T^2$ may fail to be ergodic when $T$ is, e.g. the rotation by $1/2$ on two points).","status":"unverified"}

Shmalo, Outer vertex-isoperimetry of regular plane tessellations (18 September 2026) proves that for an infinite (d,f)-regular plane tessellation G with finite d, f >= 3, 1/d + 1/f <= 1/2 and face degree f >= 5, the outer vertex-isoperimetric constant equals the edge-isoperimetric constant: h_V(G) = h_E(G) = (d-2) sqrt(1 - 4/((d-2)(f-2))); in particular h_V(H_{5,5}) = sqrt(5). The law of X is invariant under all permutations of V if and only if q(A) = P(A subset of X) depends only on |A|, say q(A) = a_|A|. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:04:30.586318+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9bf81268db63460dfa0081b97a618074479a959a5d18cf9529625b343c35f874","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:eta-kappa of arXiv:2411.10419, 'Lower bounds on the top Lyapunov exponent for linear PDEs driven by the 2D stochastic Navi'] For any $ \mathbf{q} > 2$ and $ \kappa \in (0, 1] $, we set $\hat M_i = (M_0 - i) \vee \kappa^{-\mathbf{q}}$ and define the  time $ \eta$ as follows:

\begin{equs}[e:def-tau-sigma-i]

Define
$$ \mu = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{i=1}^r X_i \right] = \sum_{i=1}^r \frac{1}{\lambda_i}, \quad \quad \lambda_* = \min_{i \in [r]} \lambda_i. $$

For each \(n\geq 1\), once the new vertex \(n+1\) has chosen its parent \(p_{n+1}\), it inherits the bit of its parent with probability \(1-q\) and flips it with probability \(q\), independently of the tree growth and all previous broadcasting steps. Equivalently,
	\[

	\]
	where \((Z_n)_{n\geq 2}\) are independent \(\{-1,1\}\)-valued random variables satisfying
	\[
	\mathbb P(Z_n=-1)=q,

	\mathbb P(Z_n=1)=1-q.
	\]
	The parameter \(q\in[0,1]\) is called the bit-flip probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["examples use Lebesgue measure on [0,1] and a one-point space of infinite measure","statements about (L^infinity)* use the axiom of choice via Hahn-Banach","the degenerate exception in (1) is a measure that is a finite sum of atoms of finite measure"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.553548+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_9c99a22f279aba04c24062eeaa629c6222d83b8f4cd18106908536d318f9894e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The identification of the dual of L^p has two genuine exceptions. (1) p = infinity fails in general: apart from the degenerate case of finitely many atoms all of finite measure (where L^1 = L^infinity is finite-dimensional and the duality is trivially true), L^1 is a proper closed subspace of (L^infinity)*. On [0,1] with Lebesgue measure, C[0,1] embeds isometrically in L^infinity (for continuous functions the sup norm equals the essential sup norm); extend the evaluation functional h -> h(0) from C[0,1] to a norm-one functional Lambda on L^infinity by Hahn-Banach. If Lambda were integration against some g in L^1, then taking continuous h_n with h_n(0) = 1, 0 <= h_n <= 1, supported in [0, 1/n], dominated convergence would give int h_n g -> 0 while Lambda(h_n) = 1. (Concretely, (L^infinity)* is the space of finitely additive bounded measures absolutely continuous with respect to mu.) (2) p = 1 without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) fails: let X = {pt} with mu({pt}) = infinity. Then L^1(mu) = {0}, so (L^1)* = {0}, while L^infinity(mu) is one-dimensional; the canonical map L^infinity -> (L^1)* is not injective, let alone onto. (3) For 0 < p < 1 and mu nonatomic (e.g. Lebesgue on [0,1]) the dual is trivial: (L^p[0,1])* = {0}, so no duality/Hahn-Banach argument survives below p = 1. {"assumptions":["two-dimensional planar lattice model satisfying the FKG inequality","translation invariance and, in the classical gluing constructions, reflection symmetry of the lattice","an a priori lower bound on square-crossing probabilities, which is a hypothesis to be separately established, not a free consequence of RSW","independence, or at least positive association, of the underlying edge or site variables"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T16:00:40+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9ca68baa0660aa59223fcaebbdec10b169d0c2892b9d78d08095d1f75675fc1d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). In two-dimensional critical or near-critical percolation, RSW theory states that if crossing probabilities of n x n squares are uniformly bounded away from 0 as n grows, then crossing probabilities of rho n x n rectangles, for any fixed aspect ratio rho, are also uniformly bounded away from 0 by a constant depending on rho but not on n. The matching bound away from 1 needs the same input for the dual model (at criticality on a self-dual lattice it follows by duality); a lower bound for the primal model alone does not give it, since in the supercritical phase both crossing probabilities tend to 1. The classical proof glues together several square-crossing events using the FKG inequality and translation and reflection symmetry of the lattice. RSW estimates are the essential multi-scale input for proving arm-exponent bounds, conformal-invariance-adjacent results, and, via the Duminil-Copin-Tassion approach, for establishing sharpness of the phase transition without relying on exact self-duality. RSW does not by itself prove existence of a scaling limit as n -> infinity, does not give the exact value of any crossing probability, only two-sided bounds; and the classical form required exact self-duality (p=1/2 on the square lattice), so extending the theory to general planar lattices or to p != 1/2 required a genuinely new, duality-free argument (Tassion, 2016). Typical failure: Assuming that RSW-type bounded-away-from-0/1 crossing estimates transfer automatically to a new planar model merely because it is monotone and planar; RSW requires either exact self-duality or the more robust but still nontrivial Tassion-style construction, and models without FKG, or with strong enough long-range dependence, can fail to admit the needed gluing arguments even though they look superficially similar to Bernoulli percolation. Canonical reference: Russo, 1978, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Seymour and Welsh, 1978, Annals of Discrete Mathematics; Tassion, 2016, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:11:57.330086+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cbcd78b7765e37629a4e4c04458e9267e4d0fa65711078f1ccbdb64fb956a06","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 (Hydrodynamic limit) of arXiv:2607.23640, '{\sl Non-equilibrium fluctuations of a two-species exclusion process with slow boundary }'] Let \(\{\mu^n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}\) be a sequence of probability measures on \(\Omega_n\) associated with \(\bm\rho_0\).

	\[
	\lim_{n\to\infty}

	\left(
	\left|
	X_k^{n,t}(f_k)

{"assumptions":["X is a Banach space","A is densely defined (automatic in reflexive X under the range condition)","A is dissipative","a range condition: Ran(λ_0 − A) = X (or dense) for some λ_0 > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771500+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, operator semigroups, evolution equations","id":"claim_9cc7074f8de110e84e704f7481a4bebc14d6b3c2eb606e5b71dc671682f7125e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a Banach space and A: D(A) ⊂ X → X linear and densely defined. (1) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for every λ > 0, and A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (2) If A is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) is merely dense for some λ_0 > 0, then A is closable, its closure Ā is dissipative with Ran(λ − Ā) = X for all λ > 0, and Ā generates a contraction C_0-semigroup. (3) Conversely, if A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup, then A is densely defined, closed, Ran(λ − A) = X for all λ > 0, and A is dissipative in the strong sense that Re⟨Ax, x*⟩ ≤ 0 for every x ∈ D(A) and every x* ∈ J(x). (4) If X is reflexive, a dissipative A with Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > 0 is automatically densely defined. (5) Hilbert space corollary: if A is densely defined and closed and both A and A* are dissipative, then A generates a contraction C_0-semigroup; and a densely defined symmetric operator S with S ≤ 0 that is self-adjoint generates the contraction semigroup e^{tS}. Quasi-contractive version: if A − ω is dissipative and Ran(λ_0 − A) = X for some λ_0 > ω, then A generates a C_0-semigroup with ‖T(t)‖ ≤ e^{ωt}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.199499+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cdd95b748fea298de1a2af88b5ce1ac2dba3e772343b6d54cc9e46d419d944e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 132 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $u,v$ be real numbers such that $v\geq u^2 - \bar{\lambda}$, and let $P_1,P_2>0$.
Set
\beq
    \sigma 
    \equiv
    \bigg(
    \frac{P_1v + 2
    (P_1P_2)^{1/2}
    u+P_2}{P_1+P_2}
    \bigg)^{1/2}
\eeq
Then we have the bound
\beq
  u^2 + \Big((v-u^2 + 2\bar{\lambda})^{1/2}-1\Big)^2 
  \ge \bigg(1+\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)(\sigma-1)^2\,.
\eeq
Given any $\sigma\ge0$, if we let $(u,v)$ be defined by the equations
	\[
	u^2 = \frac{P_2}{P_1}(\sigma-1)^2 
	= v-\sigma^2 + 2\bar{\lambda}\,,
	\]
then $(u,v)$ achieves equality in both \eqref{e:sigma.of.u.v} and \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound}. 

\begin{proof}
Denote $\tilde{v}\equiv v-u^2 + 2\bar{\lambda} \ge0$. The above definition of $\sigma$ can then be rewritten as
	\beq    
	(P_1+P_2)\sigma^2
	= P_1 \tilde{v}  +
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)^2\,.
	\eeq
Consider optimizing the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} subject to the constraint 
\eqref{eq:LM-constraint}: the Lagrangian is
	\[
	\mathscr{L}
	= u^2 + \Big(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1\Big)^2 
	+ \lambda
	\bigg\{
	(P_1+P_2)\sigma^2
	- P_1 \tilde{v}  -
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)^2
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The Lagrangian stationarity conditions are
	\begin{align*}
	0&=\frac{\partial\mathscr{L}}
		{\partial u}
	= 2u - 2\lambda (P_1)^{1/2}
	\Big( (P_1)^{1/2} u + (P_2)^{1/2}
	\Big)\,\\
	0&=\frac{\partial\mathscr{L}}
		{\partial\tilde{v}}
	= 1-\frac{1}{\tilde{v}^{1/2}}
	- \lambda P_1\,.
	\end{align*}
Simplifying the above equations gives
	\[
	u
	= \bigg(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)^{1/2}
	 \frac{\lambda P_1}{1-\lambda P_1}
	=
	\bigg(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)^{1/2}
	(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)
	\,.
	\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:LM-constraint} gives $\sigma^2=\tilde{v}$. Substituting this back into the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} gives
	\[
	u^2 + (\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)^2
	= \bigg(1+ \frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)
	(\tilde{v}^{1/2}-1)^2
	= \bigg(1+ \frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)
	(\sigma-1)^2\,,
	\]
so \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} holds with equality in the case of an interior stationary point. It remains to check the boundary case $\tilde{v}=0$. In this case we have
	\[
	\sigma
	=\bigg|\bigg( \frac{P_1}{P_1+P_2}\bigg)^{1/2} u
	+\bigg( \frac{P_2}{P_1+P_2}\bigg)^{1/2}\bigg|
	\equiv
	\Big| (A_1)^{1/2} u + (A_2)^{1/2}
	\Big|\,,
	\]
with $A_1+A_2=1$. The desired bound \eqref{eq:u-v-to-sigma-bound} then simplifies to
	\begin{align*}
	u^2 + 1
	&= \bigg(\frac{-(A_2)^{1/2}\pm\sigma}{(A_1)^{1/2}}\bigg)^2+1
	= \frac{A_2 + \sigma^2
		\pm 2 (A_2)^{1/2}\sigma}{A_1}
		+1
	= \frac{1+\sigma^2
		\pm 2 (A_2)^{1/2}\sigma}{A_1}
	\\
	&\ge
	\frac{1 + \sigma^2-2\sigma}{A_1}
	= \bigg(1+\frac{P_2}{P_1}\bigg)(\sigma-1)^2\,,
	\end{align*}
which gives the bound for the boundary case $\tilde{v}=0$. This concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:35:04.199426+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9cfe0ebeca0342ec2e95769900db90cd9b07740f4ca08a3dc4c7102a0fcfbe80","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 (Regular polygonal \(N\)-gaskets) of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] Let \(N\ge3\) with \(4\nmid N\).  Identify \(\R^2\) with \(\mathbb C\), and put
\[
  q_j=\exp(2\pi\mathrm i j/N),
  \qquad
  V_0^{(N)}=\{q_j:j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\}.
\]
Let \(F_0^{(N)}\) be the cycle on \(V_0^{(N)}\).  Write
\[
  k_N=\lfloor N/4\rfloor,
  \qquad
  \ell_N=N-4k_N,
  \qquad
  s_N=k_N+1,
\]
and define
\[
  \rho_N
  =
  \frac{\sin(\pi/N)}
       {\sin(\pi/N)+\sin((2s_N-1)\pi/N)},
  \qquad
  \Psi_j^{(N)}(x)=q_j+\rho_N(x-q_j).
\]
The attractor of the \(N\) homotheties
\(\{\Psi_j^{(N)}:j\in\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\}\) is the
\emph{regular polygonal \(N\)-gasket}.  Its finite graphs and its one-sided graph
are denoted by \(F_m^{(N)}\) and \(F_\infty^{(N)}\).  In the construction
\eqref{eq:finite-graphs}, the
indices are relabeled by \(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z\), the root is
\(O=q_0\), and \(\Psi_0^{(N)}\) is the map fixing \(O\).  The number
\(\rho_N\) is the \emph{first-contact
ratio}~\cite[Section~7]{TysonWu2006}.
When \(4\mid N\), two consecutive first-level fractal cells in the
first-contact construction share a non-degenerate line segment.  Since
\(V_0^{(N)}\) is finite, this intersection cannot equal the intersection
of their boundary vertex sets.  Thus \textup{(NF4)} fails, so this
construction is not a nested fractal and is excluded from the definition.","status":"unverified"}
