{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:07:35.022614+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a4a66c5ef2226c51ee2d48c031c804bf32596f1676b64aa001aab18fe4e7a945","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 56 of arXiv:2609.02878, '2609.02878'] Let \(U\subset Y^{\rm rv}\) be a Zariski-open product region.  Suppose
\[
 q_i\longrightarrow q_\infty\in U,
 \qquad x_i\in F_{q_i},
 \qquad t_i\nearrow T.
\]
Set \(\tau_i=T-t_i\) and assume that
\begin{equation}
             \tau_i|\Rm(g(t_i))|_{g(t_i)}(x_i)\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{equation}
Choose nested coordinate sets
\[
 q_\infty\in V_0\Subset V_a\Subset V_b\Subset V\Subset U
\]
and holomorphic coordinates \(w=(w^1,\ldots,w^m)\) on \(V\).  After
discarding finitely many terms, assume that \(q_i\in V_0\).

Then there are \(\sigma_j\searrow0\) and a subsequence
\(i(j)\nearrow\infty\) such that the pointed flows
\begin{equation}
 \widehat g_j(t)
 =\frac{1}{\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}}
   g\bigl(t_{i(j)}+\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}t\bigr),
 \qquad
 -\frac{t_{i(j)}}{\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}}\le t\le0,
\end{equation}
have the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.4em]
\item Equipped with the point conjugate heat kernels based at
$(x_{i(j)},0)$, the flows converge in $\mathbb F$, and smoothly on the
full regular spacetime, to a connected noncollapsed K\"ahler shrinking
soliton \(\mathcal Z\).  Write \((Z,g_Z)=\mathcal Z_{-1}\) and
\[
 d\nu_{Z,-1}=(4\pi)^{-(m+1)}e^{-f_Z}\,dV_{g_Z}
\]
for its distinguished shrinker probability measure.  Its normalized
Nash entropy satisfies
\[
 \mathcal N(Z):=
 \int_{\Reg Z}f_Z\,d\nu_{Z,-1}-(m+1)<0.
\]

\item On the localized convergence charts, the maps
\begin{equation}
 \widehat H_j
 =\frac{(w-w(q_{i(j)}))\circ\pi}
        {\sqrt{\sigma_j\tau_{i(j)}}}
\end{equation}
converge smoothly on compact subsets of the regular spacetime to a map
$H_Z$.  Its time-$-1$ restriction extends uniquely to a globally
Lipschitz holomorphic map $H_Z:Z\to\C^m$ satisfying on $\Reg Z$
\begin{equation}
 \nabla^{g_Z}dH_Z=0,
 \qquad
 c|a|^2\le |d(a\cdot H_Z)|_{g_Z}^2\le C|a|^2
 \quad(a\in\C^m).
\end{equation}

\item The time-$-1$ space is smooth.  More precisely, there exists
\(L\in\mathrm{GL}(m,\C)\), with no target translation, such that
\begin{equation}
 Z\cong\C^m\times\PP^1,
 \qquad LH_Z=\operatorname{pr}_{\C^m},
\end{equation}
where $\PP^1$ carries the round metric normalized by
$\Rc(g_{S^2})=\frac12g_{S^2}$.

\item The convergence is realized on a regular exhaustion by embeddings
$\Psi_j$ for which
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_j^*\widehat g_j(-1)\longrightarrow g_Z,
 \qquad
 \widehat H_j\circ\Psi_j\longrightarrow H_Z
\end{equation}
smoothly on compact subsets of \(Z=\Reg Z\).  For every \(U'\Subset Z\)
and all sufficiently large \(j\),
\begin{equation}
 \Psi_j(U')\cap\widehat H_j^{-1}(0)
 =\Psi_j(U')\cap F_{q_{i(j)}}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:37:51.455188+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a4e28d6cdd4d92c110f57ca72319e6fc1d7f01f7d035dba4fd6ddd731e6626bd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 4 of arXiv:2604.03777, 'Equilibrium fluctuations for a multi-species particle system with long jumps'] Let $\gamma \geq 3/2$, $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\kappa \in\R$.

\begin{equation}

\begin{align*}
& \mathcal{M}_t(H) := \mathcal{Z}_t(H) - \mathcal{Z}_0(H) - \mathcal{I}_t(H) + \kappa_{\gamma} \mathcal{B}_t(H),  \quad \mathcal{N}_t(H) :=[ \mathcal{M}_t(H)]^2  -2  D_3 t \;    \mathcal{P}^{\gamma} H,
\end{align*} 
 are continuous martingales with respect to the canonical filtration 
generated by $(\mathcal{Z}_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$, where the processes $(\mathcal{I}_t)_{t\in[0,T]}$ and

satisfies items (1) and (2) with $\kappa$,

\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:57:59.663321+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a521a73f68a79e41c548a6f2c09f0df35b059c9076a37cf796292e3ae0fdd109","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X_1, X_2, ... be iid real random variables with mean 0 and variance 1, and let S_n = X_1 + ... + X_n. The law of the iterated logarithm states that, almost surely, limsup_{n -> infinity} S_n / sqrt(2 n log log n) = 1 and liminf_{n -> infinity} S_n / sqrt(2 n log log n) = -1. So for every eps > 0, S_n crosses (1-eps) sqrt(2 n log log n) infinitely often but exceeds (1+eps) sqrt(2 n log log n) only finitely often, pinning the almost-sure growth rate strictly between the CLT scale sqrt(n) and O(sqrt(n log n)). Due to Khinchin (bounded case, 1924) and Hartman-Wintner (general iid finite-variance case, 1941).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Homogeneous Poisson process in R^d, d large","LPS tree criterion; continuum lace expansion (both to be verified against the papers)"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T07:36:18.335047+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a57f98ccc1d666d33da3d1f3ca215528a435526bfb43599a4502245d6d547bb4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE CONDITIONAL RESOLUTION, author-recorded, sources not re-fetched. Aldous-Steele (2004) ask whether the minimal spanning forest of a homogeneous Poisson process in R^d is connected for d >= 3 and suspect it is not in high dimension. Lyons-Peres-Schramm's criterion (Ann. Probab. 2006) makes the free MSF a single tree when there is no percolation at criticality and the infinite cluster is unique above criticality; for the Poisson-Boolean (Gilbert) model uniqueness above criticality is classical and absence of percolation at the critical radius in high dimensions follows from the lace expansion for the random connection model (Heydenreich-van der Hofstad-Last-Matzke 2019). If the LPS criterion transfers verbatim to Poisson point processes, the MSF IS a single tree for d large, the reverse of the source's suspicion. Two verifications remain: the exact hypotheses of the LPS criterion in the continuum, and the exact statement of the high-dimensional continuum result. Treat as a lead with sign, not a theorem.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.746840+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a5abe4b7b2f1bbaf1c1f7056fab6f5392aea2c743002878883712dc250b6d979","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 24 of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] If $p = \omega(1/m)$ then
  $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$ converges
  in law to an exponential distribution
  with rate $1$.
  \begin{proof}
    Fix $t < 0$ and recall definition \eqref{eq:extra term}.
    The reciprocal of the
    moment-generating function of
    $p\,(1-p)^m\,(T_{m,p} - T_{m,0})$ is
    \begin{align*}
      \frac{1}{I_{m,p}(p\,(1-p)^m\,t)}
      &=
      (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^1 p\,m
      \left(1-x\right)^{m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m\,(-t))-m}
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx \\
      &=
        (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^1 p\,m
      \left(1 + x\,t\,p\,m\,(1-p)^m\right)
      \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx + o(1)
    \intertext{where we have used the binomial approximation
      $(1-x)^\alpha = 1 - \alpha \, x + O(\alpha^2)$, uniform in $x$,
      and a first-order expansion
      $m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m \, (-t)) - m = p\,m\,(1-p)^m\,(-t)
      + O(p^2\,m\,(1-p)^{2m})$.
      Together these give
      $(1-x)^{m\exp(p\,(1-p)^m\,(-t)) - m}
      = 1 + x\,t\,p\,m\,(1-p)^m + O(p^2\,m^2\,(1-p)^{2m})$.
      This error suffices because, upon distribution to form another integral,
      we are left with a trivial term
      $O(p^3\,m^3\,(1-p)^m) \int_0^1 \left(1-p\,x\right)^{m-1} dx =
      O((p\,m)^3 \, e^{-2pm}) = o(1)$, which we have written above.
      The remaining steps involve the dominated convergence theorem:
      }
      &=
        (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \int_0^{pm}
      \left(1 + x\,t\,(1-p)^m\right)
      (1-x/m)^{m-1}\, dx + o(1)\\
      &= (1-p)^{-m} - (1-p)^{-m} \underbrace{\int_0^{pm} 
          \left(1-x/m\right)^{m-1} dx}_{1-(1-p)^m}\\
      &\quad\, -
        {\underbrace{\int_0^{pm}
          x\,t
          \left(1-x/m\right)^{m-1} dx}_{t+o(1)}} + o(1) \\
      &= 1 - t + o(1).
    \end{align*}

where $Z(x)$ is the normalizing constant
\[

+\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\psi(y)\right)\nu(dy)
\;=\;\exp\!\big(-\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}\phi(x)\big).
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

    A family $\mathcal{E}\subset \mathcal{P}(S\times S)$ is called a \emph{coarse structure} on $S$ if it satisfies the following five conditions (see Section \ref{subsection:notation} for notation):
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\diag(S) \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E^\dagger \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E_1 \cup E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E_1, E_2 \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E_1\circ E_2\in \mathcal{E}$.
        \item $E \in \mathcal{E}$ implies $E' \in \mathcal{E}$ for each $E' \subset E$.
    \end{enumerate}
    The pair $(S, \mathcal{E})$ is called a \emph{coarse space} and 
    each element of $\mathcal{E}$ is referred to as an \emph{coarse entourage} or simply an \emph{entourage}.
    An entourage $E\in \mathcal{E}$ is called \emph{symmetric} if the equality $E=E^\dagger$ holds.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.650989+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a64cf7e6408816fb0d1491dd7b47309217f1fe8391795753ce1e4823d8a86492","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Discrete-discrete coupling of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] \label
 {def:discrete_discrete_coupling}

  Let $Y^L_0 = (y^L_0, (\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0))$ and
  $\tilde Y^L_0 = (\tilde y^L_0, (\tilde \sigma^1_0, \tilde
  \sigma^2_0))$ in $\{1, \ldots, L\} \times \Sigma$ be given. Now turn to
  constructing a coupling between two discrete processes $Y^L$ and
  $\tilde Y^L$ with respective initial states $Y^L_0$ and
  $\tilde Y^L_0$. Let $s^1, s^2, \tilde s^1, \tilde s^2$ be four
  independent Markov jump processes with the transition rates of
  figure (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2016 of the paper)
  (resp. (fig:single_speed_transition_rates_slowman_2017 of the paper)) and
  respective initial states
  $\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0, \tilde \sigma^1_0, \tilde
  \sigma^2_0$. Define

  set
\begin{align*}
  \sigma^i(t) = s^i(t) \text{ for all } t \ge 0, \quad \quad \tilde \sigma^i(t) = \tilde s^i(t) \text{ for } t < \tau_i \text{ and } \tilde \sigma^i(t) = s^i(t) \text{ for } t \ge \tau_i.
\end{align*}

Let $N_1^L$ and $N_2^L$ be two independent Poisson clocks with
parameter $\gamma_L = (L-1) / \ell$ independent of
the~$\sigma^i$. Finally, set
$Y^L = \mathcal Y (\sigma^1, \sigma^2, N_1^L, N_2^L, y^L_0, L)$ and

Edgar Gilbert introduced the other model contemporaneously with and independently of Erdős and Rényi. In the model of Erdős and Rényi, all graphs on a fixed vertex set with a fixed number of edges are equally likely. In the model introduced by Gilbert, also called the Erdős–Rényi–Gilbert model, each edge has a fixed probability of being present or absent, independently of the other edges. {"assumptions":["U ⊂ C is open and connected","f is holomorphic on U","f is not constant on U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.482048+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_a6b99002ecb79eae7c982d9fde341aac0683db46b4f620776ddcbf4a03879dbe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U be a connected open subset of C and f : U → C holomorphic and not constant. Then f(V) is open for every open V ⊂ U. More precisely, if z0 is in U and f - f(z0) has a zero of order m ≥ 1 at z0, then for every sufficiently small r > 0 there is δ > 0 such that every w with 0 < |w - f(z0)| < δ has exactly m preimages (counted with multiplicity, in fact m distinct simple preimages when r is small enough) in the disk |z - z0| < r. Consequences: a nonconstant holomorphic function on a connected open set cannot have locally constant modulus, real part, or argument, and an injective holomorphic map has nonvanishing derivative and holomorphic inverse. Connectedness can be replaced by: f is nonconstant on every connected component of U.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a Hilbert space (complete)","a is sesquilinear and bounded on all of H × H","a is coercive: Re a(u,u) ≥ α‖u‖² with α > 0, on the whole space H","F is a continuous (conjugate-)linear functional on H"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771728+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, elliptic PDE, variational methods","id":"claim_a6ce6929f12d5ce7339c07a63e3bc2c50cf5e81c49bcf05a5a388b1517ad79ba","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a real or complex Hilbert space and a: H × H → K (K = ℝ or ℂ) a sesquilinear form (bilinear in the real case, linear in the first and conjugate linear in the second argument in the complex case) such that: (boundedness) |a(u, v)| ≤ C‖u‖‖v‖ for all u, v ∈ H with C < ∞; (coercivity) Re a(u, u) ≥ α‖u‖² for all u ∈ H with α > 0. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:19:46.230089+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6daeea6a634ba135f17653f65a2f4b1bc0272ae1e7a068528c16331ba36eb5b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 20 of arXiv:2507.08909, 'Annealed almost periodic entropy'] A \textbf{partial positive semidefinite} matrix with \textbf{block sizes} $k$, $\ell$ and $m$ is a $5$-tuple

{"assumptions":["independent (product) Bernoulli measure, possibly with coordinate-dependent parameters","A is a monotone (increasing) event depending on finitely many coordinates","differentiability in p, automatic for finite-dimensional product measures"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.974074+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6e95b98b55e5073a7f62110341ac5fe86d89ae81b909d71bb1c753c13feb7de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the product measure mu_p on {0,1}^E with each coordinate independently open with probability p and an increasing event A depending on finitely many edges, Russo's formula states d/dp mu_p(A) = sum_{e in E} mu_p(e is pivotal for A), where e is pivotal for A at a configuration omega if flipping the state of e changes the indicator of A. When different edges carry different parameters p_e, the analogous statement is d/dp_e mu(A) = mu(e is pivotal for A). This identity converts questions about how quickly an event's probability crosses a threshold into questions about counting or bounding pivotal edges, which is the basic engine behind sharp-threshold theorems when combined with the Margulis-Russo framework and tools such as hypercontractivity, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm influence bound, or the OSSS inequality. Russo's formula does not by itself give sharp thresholds; it requires monotonicity of A, since non-monotone events need a more complex signed-pivotal generalization; and it is stated for independent-coordinate measures, so applying it to dependent measures such as the random-cluster model requires a separate Glauber-dynamics-based generalization rather than the naive product-measure formula. Typical failure: Using Russo's formula on a non-monotone event without its signed-pivotal generalization, or applying the plain product-measure version of the formula to a dependent measure such as a random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure, where the correct analogue requires the generator of an associated Glauber dynamics rather than a simple coordinatewise derivative; both errors produce a derivative formula that looks structurally similar but is simply wrong. Canonical reference: Russo, 1981, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Margulis, 1974, Problemy Peredachi Informatsii; Grimmett, Percolation, second edition, 1999, Springer, Chapter 2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.994065+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6f0f9ae991e501982155aabb678eeaf75543488ad65d2195e541dec2e32c168","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 39 (Identification of the Hilbert--Stein and primitive--Fock splittings) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let
\[
 X_{n,a}=I_q(f_{n,a}),
 \qquad
 \sup_n\sum_{a=1}^{d}q!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2<\infty,
\]
choose $R>0$ with
$R^2\ge\sup_n\sum_aq!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2$, and run the spectrally reduced
feedback on $x_{n,a,q}=\sqrt{q!}\,f_{n,a}$ from the zero module.  Along every
subsequence on which the covariance and all the finitely many proper
self-contraction norms converge, one may extract a further subsequence
and choose a sufficiently slow diagonal $J(n)\to\infty$ such that, with
the corresponding active and
residual Wiener polynomials $A_n^{[J(n)]},B_n^{[J(n)]}$,
\[
 (A_n^{[J(n)]},B_n^{[J(n)]})
 \Longrightarrow(A_{\mathrm{FF}},G_{\mathrm{prim}}),
 \qquad X_n\Longrightarrow A_{\mathrm{FF}}+G_{\mathrm{prim}},
 \qquad
 G_{\mathrm{prim}}\indep A_{\mathrm{FF}}.
\]
If $\xi_a=[f_{n,a}]_{\mathcal U}\in\cH_q$, then, in the terminal
primitive--Fock representation,
\begin{align}
 A_{\mathrm{FF},a}
 &=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cD_q}\xi_a,
 \\
 G_{\mathrm{prim},a}
 &=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cK_q}\xi_a.
 
\end{align}
The second term belongs to the first Gaussian chaos over $\cK_q$; the
first is the orthogonal sum of all weighted sectors containing at least
two primitive particles.  In particular the split is intrinsic relative
to the represented packet and ultrafilter, and
\begin{equation}
 \Cov(G_{\mathrm{prim}})_{ab}
 =\ip{P_{\cK_q}\xi_a}{P_{\cK_q}\xi_b}_{\cH_q}
 =q!\,\Ulim\ip{p_{n,a}}{p_{n,b}},

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T : X -> X is continuous","M(X,T) carries the weak-star topology and is nonempty (guaranteed by Krylov-Bogolyubov)","h*(T) = 0 (asymptotic h-expansiveness); h-expansiveness and expansiveness are sufficient special cases","h_mu(T) is the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of the measure-preserving system (X, mu, T)","the existence corollary uses the variational principle, which itself needs only compactness and continuity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090700+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy, measures of maximal entropy","id":"claim_a77bafb383fb156acf97fdf0ec6338f3cdb7ec81469c4cf42ee27a80550d59df","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact metric space, T : X -> X continuous, and let M(X,T) be the set of T-invariant Borel probability measures with the weak-star topology, a nonempty compact convex metrisable set. Suppose T is ASYMPTOTICALLY h-EXPANSIVE, i.e. its tail entropy h*(T) = lim as eps -> 0 of sup over x of h(T, Gamma_eps(x)) vanishes; this holds in particular when T is h-expansive, and a fortiori when T is expansive. THEN the entropy map mu -> h_mu(T) is upper semicontinuous on M(X,T): whenever mu_k -> mu weak-star inside M(X,T), limsup_k h_{mu_k}(T) <= h_mu(T). CONSEQUENCES: an upper semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its supremum, so by the variational principle a measure of maximal entropy exists and h_top(T) = max over mu in M(X,T) of h_mu(T); the entropy function is then a bounded, affine, upper semicontinuous function on a Choquet simplex, which is what makes the theory of maximal measures and of symbolic extensions run. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) some hypothesis of this kind is necessary. For a general continuous map the entropy map need not be upper semicontinuous and a measure of maximal entropy need not exist; this is why smoothness matters - Newhouse proved that C^infinity diffeomorphisms of compact manifolds are asymptotically h-expansive and therefore always carry maximal measures, while for finite smoothness there are counterexamples. (ii) The conclusion is strictly one-sided and cannot be improved to continuity even for expansive systems: in a mixing shift of finite type the periodic-orbit measures, all of entropy 0, are weak-star dense, so they converge to the measure of maximal entropy and the entropy map is not lower semicontinuous. (iii) Compactness of X (hence of M(X,T)) is what converts upper semicontinuity into existence of a maximiser; on a noncompact space the existence conclusion fails even when the map is upper semicontinuous. (iv) The implication is stated in one direction only: upper semicontinuity of the entropy map is a strictly weaker property than asymptotic h-expansiveness, so do not run the criterion backwards.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["two independent centered Gaussian fields on a common finite or suitably truncated index set","existence and enough regularity of the covariance functions to differentiate the interpolated expectation under the integral","a consistent-sign comparison, or specific structural relation, between the two covariance kernels","the test functional F smooth with the correct sign of mixed partial derivatives for the interpolation identity to yield a useful inequality rather than an uncontrolled remainder"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.986351+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7b6b7b2b6ff3d35232e25a83c85018f52e970e60f45507e62d94c80f06513bc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For two independent centered Gaussian fields X, Y indexed by a common finite (or suitably truncated) set T with covariance functions C_X, C_Y, Kahane's interpolation forms Z(t,u) = sqrt(u) X(t) + sqrt(1-u) Y(t) for u in [0,1] and computes d/du E[F(Z(.,u))] for a smooth test function F, obtaining an integral expression involving (C_Y(s,t) - C_X(s,t)) times a mixed second derivative of F, evaluated against the law of Z(.,u). When C_X <= C_Y pointwise (or the relevant difference has a consistent sign) and F is chosen with matching sign of mixed partials, this yields a comparison inequality between functionals of X and Y, an approach that both generalizes Slepian-type comparisons and, in the Gaussian multiplicative chaos literature, is used to show that different regularizations of a log-correlated field, such as the two-dimensional Gaussian free field, converge to the same limiting chaos measure regardless of the approximation scheme, a key technical step in constructing Liouville quantum gravity measures. It does not apply to non-Gaussian fields, it requires the two fields being compared to be independent for the interpolation construction itself, and the sign or convexity conditions on F needed to obtain a clean inequality must be verified case by case rather than assumed. Typical failure: Applying the interpolation to fields that are not independent, or to a family of regularizations whose covariance difference does not have a consistent sign across the whole index set, which is common when comparing regularizations of a log-correlated field near its singular set; either error breaks the monotonicity the interpolation is meant to exploit, and the resulting comparison can go in the wrong direction with no explicit error term to control it. Canonical reference: Kahane, 1986, Annales des Sciences Mathematiques du Quebec; Robert and Vargas, 2010, Comptes Rendus Mathematique; Berestycki, 2017, Electronic Communications in Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform (or explicitly known-bias) product measure on {-1,1}^n or {0,1}^n","f in the relevant L^p space, typically boolean or bounded","the noise parameter rho within the sharp Bonami-Beckner range 0<=rho<=sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))","a well-defined Fourier-Walsh expansion, i.e. finite n or a suitable limiting argument"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.984732+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7cdeeca3ae5af431b85d8b03bcd9758e011331b5617840dca263851d2163174","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For f: {-1,1}^n -> R with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_S hat{f}(S) chi_S and the noise operator T_rho, which independently resamples each coordinate to a fresh uniform sign with probability (1-rho)/2, the Bonami-Beckner inequality states ||T_rho f||_q <= ||f||_p whenever 1 <= p <= q and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1)). Equivalently, T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} hat{f}(S) chi_S, and the inequality forces the Fourier weight of f on high-degree levels to decay geometrically once rho<1, giving sum_S rho^{2|S|} hat{f}(S)^2 <= (E[|f|^p])^{2/p} for suitable p. This is the central tool converting L^2 Fourier information into higher-moment (typically L^4) control, and it underlies the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem on the existence of an influential coordinate, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm noise-sensitivity theorems, and Friedgut's junta theorem for low-influence functions. It does not directly give influence bounds without further combination with such machinery, and the sharp constant and range of rho given here hold for the uniform measure on {-1,1}^n; biased-p product measures or non-product (dependent) measures require different, generally weaker, p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractive inequalities. Typical failure: Applying the sharp uniform-measure {-1,1}^n hypercontractive constant to a biased-p product measure or to a dependent measure such as the random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure without switching to the correct p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractivity inequality, whose constants generally degrade as p approaches 0 or 1; this silently invalidates quantitative noise-sensitivity conclusions claimed for critical percolation at p != 1/2 or for genuinely non-product models. Canonical reference: Bonami, 1970, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Beckner, 1975, Annals of Mathematics; O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, 2014, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} Boolean, uniform product measure","c is a universal constant","the conclusion bounds only the MAXIMUM influence, not any specific coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628283+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7d3fa81d9e828619a0897ad9b5e1de549e37211c93fe093b3a6f7e2f0ac728c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} be a Boolean function on the uniform product measure, and define the influence of coordinate i as Inf_i(f) = P( f(X) != f(X^{(i)}) ) where X^{(i)} flips the i-th coordinate. Then there is a universal constant c > 0 with max_{i <= n} Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n / n, where Var(f) = p(1-p) with p = E[f]. Equivalently the TOTAL influence satisfies sum_i Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n. The bound is SHARP up to the constant: the tribes function, a read-once DNF on blocks of size about log_2 n - log_2 log_2 n, is balanced and has all influences of order log n / n. The theorem is about the uniform measure on the cube; the analogous statement for p-biased measures carries an extra factor and is the Friedgut-Kalai sharp-threshold machinery. {"assumptions":["No finiteness, countability or uniformity assumption on the family;","values in the extended reals are allowed."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:01:51.298864+00:00","domain":"real analysis, topology","id":"claim_a7d6b373429f32266ad5157b4e9a016da414a695cb09150843502c65cad89b8f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and let (f_i) be an arbitrary family of functions on X with values in the extended reals. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149018+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_a7ff9de16f2bbefc6c4fe4f5adbe349d50f8611965c390800f138c4833c83567","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: c <= 0 in the nondivergence convention Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu (equivalently c >= 0 in the divergence convention -div(A grad u) + b.grad u + cu). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:29:08.782564+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7ff9e6e768db2042daa88a08e9773bc148ad4eca5417690be72deb9a539e69a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn subexp of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] An \emph{operator space} is a closed subspace of a 
$C^*$-algebra. A finite-dimensional operator space $\mathbf{W}$ is called
\begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
\itemsep\smallskipamount
\item 
\emph{exact} if for every $C>1$, there exists $S\in\mathbb{N}$ and a
linear embedding $u:\mathbf{W}\to\mathrm{M}_S(\mathbb{C})$ such that
for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $x\in \mathbf{W}\otimes\mathrm{M}_N(\mathbb{C})$, we have
$$
	\|(u\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\| \le
	\|x\| \le C\|(u\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\|;
$$
\item \emph{$C$-subexponential} if there exists
$D_N\in\mathbb{N}$ with $D_N=e^{o(N)}$ and a linear embedding 
$f_N:\mathbf{W}\to\mathrm{M}_{D_N}(\mathbb{C})$ such that
for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $x\in \mathbf{W}\otimes\mathrm{M}_N(\mathbb{C})$, we have
$$
	\|(f_N\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\| \le
	\|x\| \le C\|(f_N\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\|.
$$
\end{enumerate}
An operator space $\mathbf{W}$ is called exact or $C$-subexponential if 
every finite-dimensional subspace of $\mathbf{W}$ is exact or 
$C$-subexponential, respectively. The subexponential constant of an
operator space
$\mathbf{W}$ is $C(\mathbf{W}) := \inf\{C:\mathbf{W}\text{ is }C\text{-subexponential}\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X integrable with X in an open interval I almost surely","phi convex on I","E[phi(X)^-] < infinity, so that E[phi(X) | G] is defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752623+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a82c08a702478464e662ccbbaeeea30b77120ba9b85679d10ca8d340f884bc36","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be an integrable random variable taking values almost surely in an open interval I of R, let phi : I -> R be convex, and let G be a sub-sigma-algebra. If phi(X) is integrable, or more generally if E[phi(X)^-] < infinity so that E[phi(X) | G] is well defined in (-infinity, +infinity], then phi(E[X | G]) <= E[phi(X) | G] almost surely. Taking G trivial recovers the unconditional Jensen inequality. Two hypotheses do real work: X must lie in the interval where phi is convex, and some one-sided integrability of phi(X) is needed for the right-hand side to be defined. Convexity cannot be weakened to midpoint convexity without measurability, and the inequality REVERSES for concave phi. A standard consequence is that for a convex phi and a martingale (M_n), the process phi(M_n) is a submartingale whenever it is integrable. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.1.10]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.403343+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a846b8468b125845887a8b7a2039c5031569c5ea5176313bbdb4f380293ca852","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 3 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] Let $u_{\mathrm{init}}\in L^{1}(\Omega;L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))$
be nonnegative and $\mathcal{F}_{0}$-measurable.
A stochastic kinetic solution of the obstacle problem for \eqref{eq:main} is a pair $(u,\nu)$, where $u\in L^{1}(\Omega\times[0,T];L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))$ is a nonnegative, $L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})$-valued $\mathcal{F}_{t}$-predictable function, and $\nu$ is a predictable Radon measure on $Q_T$ satisfying the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] Almost surely $u\leq \psi$, and $\mathbb{E}[\nu(Q_T)]<\infty$.

\item[(ii)] Preservation of mass: almost surely for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
    -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u(x,s)\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\mathrm{d}\nu(x,s)=\phi(0)\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_{\mathrm{init}}\mathrm{d}x.
\end{align}
\item[(iii)] The initial condition: almost surely
\begin{align}
\lim_{\tau\to0}\frac{1}{\tau}\int_0^{\tau}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}|u(x,t)-u_{\mathrm{init}}(x)|\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}t=0.
\end{align}
\item[(iv)]  $\sigma(u)\in L^{2}(\Omega;L^{2}(Q_T))$, \quad $g(u)\in L^{1}(\Omega;L^{1}(Q_T;\mathbb{R}^d))$.

\item[(v)] For every $K\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
[(u\land K)\lor(1/K)]\in L^{2}(\Omega\times[0,T];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))).
\]
\end{itemize}
Furthermore, there exists a kinetic measure $q$ satisfying the following three properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(vi)] Almost surely as a nonnegative measure, $q$ satisfies
\[
\delta_{0}(\xi-u)\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u|^{2}\leq q\quad\text{on}\quad\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T].
\]
\item[(vii)] (Vanishing)
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\big[q(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times[N,N+1]\times[0,T))\big]=0.
\]
\item[(viii)] For every $\phi\in C_{c}^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$, the kinetic function $\chi$ of $u$ almost surely satisfies
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u)\nabla u\cdot(\nabla\phi)(x,u,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma^{\prime}(u)]^{2}\nabla u+\sigma(u)\sigma^{\prime}(u)F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla\phi)(x,u,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}q(x,\xi,s)-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u,s)\nabla\cdot g(u)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma(u)\sigma^{\prime}(u)\nabla u\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma^{2}(u)F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}       \int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,\psi,s)\mathrm{d}\nu(x,s)-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u,s)\nabla\cdot(\sigma(u)f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k}.\nonumber
\end{align}
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces over the same field","T is a bounded linear operator from X to Y"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571248+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_a8d654dd18a265403bd8a3b84aa51c1024872fabf26f962e91167e35b5920dca","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y) a bounded linear operator. T is a Fredholm operator if (a) its kernel ker T is finite-dimensional and (b) its range ran T has finite codimension, i.e. the quotient vector space Y / ran T is finite-dimensional. The index of a Fredholm operator is the integer ind T = dim ker T - dim(Y / ran T). The range of a Fredholm operator is automatically closed (a bounded operator between Banach spaces whose range has finite algebraic codimension has closed range), so texts that add 'ran T is closed' to the definition define the same class. For Fredholm T one has dim(Y / ran T) = dim ker T', where T': Y' -> X' is the Banach-space adjoint, so ind T = dim ker T - dim ker T'. Examples on l^2: an invertible operator has index 0; the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is injective with range of codimension 1, so ind S = -1, and its adjoint (the backward shift) has index +1; I + K with K compact has index 0. The set of Fredholm operators X -> Y is written Phi(X,Y).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["R associative with identity; 'semisimple' means semisimple as a left module over itself (equivalent to the right-module version)","the division rings need not be commutative (the real quaternions H occur, e.g. in R[Q_8])"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479831+00:00","domain":"ring theory and representation theory","id":"claim_a8dff8cc7fd1ebc995d2f1c2cd5a96f7c66d395874540b73e9f3e7c21eab6fcc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"A ring R (associative, with 1) is semisimple - every left R-module is a direct sum of simple modules, equivalently R is a finite direct sum of simple left modules, equivalently R is left Artinian with zero Jacobson radical - if and only if R is isomorphic to a finite product of matrix rings over division rings: R = M_{n_1}(D_1) x ... x M_{n_r}(D_r). The integers r and n_i and the division rings D_i (up to isomorphism) are determined by R: r is the number of isomorphism classes of simple left R-modules, and the simple module S_i = D_i^{n_i} has End_R(S_i) = D_i (opposite conventions aside). A simple left Artinian ring is a single matrix ring M_n(D). Consequences: for a finite group G and a field k of characteristic not dividing |G| (Maschke), the group algebra k[G] is semisimple, so k[G] = prod M_{n_i}(D_i); over an algebraically closed field the D_i are k itself, the n_i are the degrees of the irreducible representations, r is the number of conjugacy classes, and |G| = sum n_i^2. A commutative semisimple ring is a finite product of fields. Wedderburn's little theorem (finite division rings are fields) then gives: a finite semisimple ring is a product of matrix rings over finite fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Continuous-time rate-one simple walks; one initial particle per vertex.","n>=3 and coalescence occurs on occupying the same vertex."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364725+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a9084c7ddee91d83c2907916bc18b221f7d93355453213ec33d244da82d105d6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked, no independent read.] This is an exactly solved adjacent case of Open Problem 14.12 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). For n>=3 let C_n be the simple cycle on n vertices. Start a particle at every vertex. Each particle independently jumps at rate one to a uniformly chosen neighbor, and particles merge on meeting. Let T_coal be the first time only one particle remains. Then E[T_coal]=(n^2-1)/6. If P is the cycle's discrete-time simple-walk matrix, define its mean spectral hitting-time quantity K=sum_{j=2}^n 1/(1-lambda_j(P)); then K=(n^2-1)/6 also. Thus E[T_coal]=K exactly. Its relaxation time tau_2=1/(1-cos(2pi/n)) satisfies tau_2/K -> 3/pi^2, so this family has the equality conclusion even though the small-relaxation-time hypothesis in the source problem fails. In the extracted optional-stopping proof, EC in a stopping-time subscript denotes the random coalescence time; the final displayed EC denotes its expectation. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["F=p Uniform[a,b]+(1-p)G","0<p<1","a<b finite","G bounded support","Established Wang-Wang monotone density criterion"],"created_at":"2026-10-14T17:25:04.867375+00:00","domain":"probability; constant-sum couplings","id":"claim_a9109f1fe05ce8c0fb40bac309f8b6ea54ec31d8d96415b0ec609c2290165534","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); D0007-C008 v1; audits pending. If F=p Uniform[a,b]+(1-p)G with 0<p<1, a<b finite and G bounded-support, then F is n-completely mixable for every sufficiently large integer n. Symmetry is unnecessary and the uniform interval need not contain mean(F). Put ell=b-a, c=(a+b)/2, m=E_G[X], R=B-A for an interval [A,B] supporting G, C=|c-m|+R, and K0=ceil(max(2,6C/ell,2+2C/ell)). Every n>=ceil(K0/p) works. Cyclic quantile strata couple residual coordinates with sum discrepancy at most R. Therefore a bounded law with a positive density lower bound on just one subinterval is eventually n-CM. This does not cover densities with essential infimum zero on every interval; general D0007 remains unresolved. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.349462+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a92498367fe58854a9a798399bcf45fca47089064441a3fc5204baf9947d404f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 170 (quenched second moment bounds for $Y^{\RomI}$ and $Y^{\RomI,\frozen}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $N$ large enough, we have
	\beq
	\max\bigg\{
	\bE\Big[\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big]
	: 0 \le d\le \dmax-1
	\bigg\}
    \le L^{O(1)} \delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2
    \,,
    \eeq
with $\MAX_N$ as in Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}. The same bound holds with $\vY^\frozen$ in place of $\vY$. 

\begin{proof} It follows using
Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} that
	\[\bE\Big(
	\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big)
	\le \bE\Big( \Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))^2\Big)
	+ O(\eta)\bigg\{ \bE\Big| \Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	+ \eta\bigg\}\,.\]
From the spatial rerandomization (Definition~\ref{d:rerand}), the index $a(q_{d+1})$ is a uniformly random sample from $[M]$, even if we condition on the gaussian disorder. Thus we can apply Proposition~\ref{p:X.second.mmt.quenched} with $a(q_{d+1})$ in place of $\hat{a}$. Together with Jensen's inequality and \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound}, it implies

    + \eta^2\Big\}
    \le L^{O(1)}\delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2\,,
	\]
using that $\MAX_N\ge1$ and $\eta\ll\delta$ from Assumption~\ref{a:params}. This proves \eqref{e:Y.I.second.quenched}, and the analogous bound for $Y^{\frozen,\RomI}$ follows by the same argument.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356775+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a995d06274ddf557e5d3170e4d4483f83f08209bad25e038d38c0297bc13eb05","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 236 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $1\le \fq < \fp$ and $C > 0$, the spaces $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ and $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric,
are compact.

\begin{proof}
	We will show compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$, as compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$ is proved analogously.
	It suffices to show that every sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ has a subsequence converging in $\bbW_\fq$ to a measure in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$.
	Consider any such sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$.
	The set of measures $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ is clearly tight, so by Prohorov's theorem there exists a weakly convergent subsequence $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$. 
Let $\mu$ be its weak limit. By Skorokhod's theorem, we can find a coupling of random variables $X_j\sim\mu_{n_j}$ and $X\sim\mu$ such that
$X_j\to X$ almost surely. Then, by Fatou's lemma, we have
	\[
		\|\mu\|_{L^\fp}^\fp 
	=\E[|X|^p]^{1/p}
		\le
		\liminf_j \E[|X_j|^p]^{1/p}
		= \liminf_{j\to\infty} \|\mu_{n_j}\|_{L^\fp}^\fp
		 \le C\,,
	\]
	so $\mu \in \cP_\fp(\R,C)$. 
	It remains to show $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$ converges to $\mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
	 Note that for any $\nu \in \cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, Markov's inequality implies
	\[
	\nu(|x|>K) 
	\le \frac{1}{K^\fp}\int
		|x|^\fp \,d\nu
		 \le \frac{C}{K^\fp}\,.
	\]
Combining this with H\"older's inequality gives
	\beq
		\int_{|x|>K} |x|^\fq \,d\nu
		\le \nu(|x|>K)^{1 - \fq/\fp} \bigg(
			\int |x|^\fp \,d\nu
		\bigg)^{\fq/\fp}
		\le \frac{C}{K^{\fp - \fq}}\,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq.tail} and the weak convergence $\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$,
	\begin{align*}
		\limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\bigg|
		&\le \limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			\,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			 \,d\mu
		\bigg|\\
		&\qquad + \limsup_{j\to\infty} \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		+ \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\le \frac{2C}{K^{\fp-\fq}}\,.
	\end{align*}
	Since $K$ was arbitrary, we infer the convergence of $\fq$-th moments
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\E[|X_j|^p]
		=\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		= \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		= \E[|X|^p]\,.\]
This implies that the random variables $\{X_j\}$ are uniformly integrable, so
	\begin{align*}
	&\bbW_\fq(\mu_{n_j}, \mu)^\fq
	\le \E[|X_j-X|^\fq]\\
	&\le\E\Big[
	\max\{|X_j-X|,2K\}^\fq\Big]
	+\E\Big[|X_j| ; |X_j|\ge K\Big]
	+ \E\Big[|X| ; |X|\ge K\Big]
	\\
	&\le o_j(1) + o_K(1)+ o_K(1)\,.
	\end{align*}
Since the left-hand side does not depend on $K$, we conclude that
$\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:17:04.325711+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a9a6489d85aac88ef9b490e2b4ae58bbb2831720cd67044d10e32b7cfa43ce1d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition cond:subcrit of arXiv:2606.01866, 'Phase Transition of a Semiflexible Membrane in Two Dimensions'] \label[proposition]{thm:massiveanalysis}

    & {\cal A}\mathop{\buildrel\Delta\over=}\phi (\ell_t^2-\ell_{tt})-\sum_{j,k=1}^n

       & {\cal B}\mathop{\buildrel\Delta\over=}{\cal A}\Psi+(\phi {\cal A}\ell_t)_t\!-\! \sum_{j,k=1}^n\!({\cal A}

# Target 1: scalar three-token self-attention under joint training

Version 1, unaudited. Own work; novelty not established globally.
This extends the scalar family, not arbitrary vector-valued token geometry.

## Data, model and conclusions

For each i=1,...,n, n>=2, take a label y_i in {-1,+1} and three distinct
signed token values c_ij. Their minimum m_i is negative, maximum M_i positive,
and the FIRST token c_i1 is positive. Let raw tokens x_ij=y_i c_ij and use
the actual first token x_i1 as the self-attention query. With jointly trained
scalar head v and scalar attention weight p, signed prediction is v h_i(p),

 h_i(p)=sum_j c_ij exp(zeta_i c_ij p)/sum_j exp(zeta_i c_ij p),
 zeta_i=c_i1>0.

The loss is average logistic loss. Let
 H=max_i max(|m_i|,|M_i|), D=max_i zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2,
 eta_*=min(2/H^2,1/(2D)).

For every fixed eta in (0,eta_*], simultaneous GD in (v,p) has precisely
three possible limits: the unique finite saddle (0,p_bar), where
mean_i h_i(p_bar)=0; matching-positive escape v,p->+infinity; or
matching-negative escape v,p->-infinity. The saddle's global stable set is
planar null. Both escaping basins are open and nonempty. Their hard selections
are respectively the maximum signed token in EVERY example and the minimum
signed token in EVERY example. No interior token, or mixed pattern of extrema,
is a hard-selection limit in this scalar model. On escaping trajectories
p=O(log |v|), loss->0 and the normalized joint directions are (+1,0),(-1,0).
The corresponding minimum signed margins, normalized by sqrt(v^2+p^2),
are Gamma_+=min_i M_i and Gamma_-=min_i(-m_i).

In addition, for EVERY eta>0 the regions
 Q_+={v>0,p>max_i rho_i}, Q_-={v<0,p<min_i rho_i},
where h_i(rho_i)=0, are forward invariant and satisfy the same respective
escape/margin conclusions. Thus if Gamma_+>Gamma_-, the inferior basin is
open and positive measure even without a step-size restriction. A sufficient
strict inequality is M_i+m_i>0 for every example.

## Scalar softmax link estimates

Write alpha_ij(p) for the three softmax weights. Direct differentiation gives
h_i'=zeta_i[sum alpha_ij c_ij^2-h_i^2]
     =zeta_i sum_{j<l} alpha_ij alpha_il(c_ij-c_il)^2>0.
Also |h_i|<=H, h_i'<=zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2<=D, and h_i tends to m_i,M_i
at the two infinities. Thus each root rho_i exists uniquely.

Let delta be the minimum over i of zeta_i times either adjacent gap of its
sorted three token values. It is strictly positive. For p>=0, the total
softmax mass on nonmaximum tokens is <=2 exp(-delta p).
Variance is no larger than the second moment about the maximum token,
so h_i'(p)<=2D exp(-delta p). Reflecting yields the same upper bound
2D exp(-delta |p|) for p<=0. Every h_i is real analytic, strictly increasing,
bounded, and has exponentially decaying derivative.

## Full-plane trapping and escape

For g_i=(1+exp(v h_i(p)))^-1 put F=mean g_i h_i and G=mean g_i h_i'>0.
GD is v_+=v+eta F, p_+=p+eta vG. The following estimates are identical
to those needed in proof 005, now established for genuine three-token links:

 -H^2/4<=F_v<=0,
 F(0,p)=mean h_i(p)/2=:F_0(p), 0<F_0'<=D/2, G<=D.

There is a unique mean root p_bar. Set u=p-p_bar, A=H^2/4.
In v,u>0, v_+>=(1-eta A)v+eta F_0(p)>0 and p increases; reflecting gives
invariance in v,u<0. In a bad quadrant v>0,u<0, v decreases and u increases
until it exits or converges to the saddle. Double crossing would require

 (1-eta A)v<=eta(D/2)|u|<=eta^2 D^2 v/2,

impossible since eta A<=1/2 and eta D<=1/2. The other bad quadrant is the
reflection. An axis point other than the saddle enters a good quadrant after
one step. A bad-quadrant orbit staying there is bounded and monotone; continuity
of increments gives vG=F=0 at its limit, hence the saddle.

Consider a positive good-quadrant orbit. If p had a finite limit P and v were
bounded, compactness would give G bounded below; Delta p->0 would force v->0,
but F_0(P)>0 contradicts convergence of v to zero. If v were unbounded and
P<=R:=max rho_i, an example with root R has h_j(p)<=0 and therefore g_j>=1/2.
On the compact p interval its derivative is bounded below, so
Delta p>=eta d v/(2n), contradicting finite P. If P>R, eventually all links
are >=c>0; v then increases without bound and
Delta p/Delta v>=d v/H again contradicts finite P. Thus p->infinity.
Eventually all h_i>=c, forcing v->infinity (bounded v would keep the g_i
uniformly positive). Negative escape follows by reflection using -h_i(-p).

This proof also applies directly within Q_+ or Q_- at any eta>0: both
coordinates are monotone from the start and all signed links are positive
after reflection. Only the full-plane trapping argument uses eta_*.

## Rates, margin, and the null exceptional set

On a positive escaping trajectory, h_i>=c>0 eventually, so
Delta p<=eta D v exp(-cv)->0. Moreover
Delta p/Delta v<=2D v exp(-delta p)/c.
Once Delta p<=1, the mean value theorem gives
Delta exp(delta p)<=C v Delta v. Telescoping against v^2 gives
exp(delta p)<=C'(1+v^2), so p=O(log v). Reflection proves the other branch.
Loss and normalized margin limits now follow. For any parameter pair,
the endpoint bounds and sqrt(v^2+p^2)>=|v| show the normalized minimum
margin cannot exceed max(Gamma_+,Gamma_-); the larger branch attains it.

At the saddle, the update Jacobian is
[[1-eta A_s,eta B_s],[eta B_s,1]],
where A_s=mean h_i(p_bar)^2/4<=A and B_s=mean h_i'(p_bar)/2 in (0,D/2].
Its determinant >=7/16 and det(DT-I)<0: one eigenvalue lies in (0,1),
the other exceeds 1. The analytic update map has a Jacobian determinant
not identically zero; the zero set is null. Away from that set its local
inverse maps preserve null sets. By a countable cover, preimages of null
sets are null. The local stable-manifold theorem and countably many iterated
preimages therefore give a null global stable set. Each escaping basin is
the union of preimages of its open good quadrant, hence open. This is the
same null-preimage argument detailed in proofs/003 and 005, not an assumption
that the GD map is globally invertible.

## Which locally optimal selections, and comparison with prior art

For p->+infinity only the largest signed c_ij can dominate; for p->-infinity
only the smallest can dominate. Because all zeta_i>0 these choices must be
consistent across examples. At finite p all weights are strictly positive,
so an interior token cannot become a hard selection. For a fixed v>0, the
maximum-token pattern is the only locally optimal feasible hard selection;
for fixed v<0 the minimum-token pattern is the only one. Both are stable
under joint training, by the open basins above. The minimum pattern can
nevertheless be inferior when comparing the two JOINT normalized margins.

Tarzanagh et al., 2306.13596, Definition 2 (PDF p.5) compares the chosen token
score only to its active SVM neighbors, with a FIXED head. Their Theorem 3
(PDF p.6) gives convergence from cones C_{mu,R} around such locally optimal
directions. It already includes a three-token illustration immediately after
the theorem. The present scalar result is not the discovery of that phenomenon:
it classifies the scalar joint-head basins and excludes mixed/interior hard
patterns in this stated geometry. General vector-valued three-token locally
optimal selections and their joint-head basins remain open here.

## Explicit distinct mixed-label witness

Take signed triples (3/2,1/4,-1/2) and (3/2,1/8,-1), with labels +1,-1.
Raw triples are (3/2,1/4,-1/2),(-3/2,-1/8,1); actual first-token queries
are 3/2,-3/2. Both zeta_i=3/2. H=3/2, D=75/8, eta_*=4/75.
Gamma_+=3/2 and Gamma_-=1/2. The conditions are strict and persist in an
open neighborhood of these data. This witness is illustrative; the theorem
covers the whole family above rather than just this isolated case.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:07.031970+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aad1c342f4931e8eb7d7fd673ef23041a1a43e6d0cbdf8ded2c58958e4e4c86c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:one-point-gaussian-regression of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Under the hypotheses and notation of
		Proposition~(prop:one-point-conditional-hessian of the paper), whenever
		\(m=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(r,x)\), write
		\[
		u(r,m):=\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(r,x)
		=\frac1{\partial_{mm}h_\zeta(r,m)}.
		\]
		Set \(e=\mathbf{m}/\sqrt{Nq}\), and let \(P\) be the orthogonal
		projection onto \(\mathbf{m}^\perp\). Define
		\[
		z_i
		:=
		\xi''(q)\left(
		\frac{b_i}{\xi'(q)}-\partial_m u(q,m_i)
		-2\zeta(\{0\})m_i
		\right).
		\]
		There exist a GOE matrix \(W_N\), with off-diagonal entries of
		variance \(N^{-1}\), and a standard Gaussian vector \(g_N\) in
		\(\mathbf{m}^\perp\), independent of \(W_N\), such that, under
		\(\mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{m},f_N}\) and relative to
		\(\mathbb R e\oplus\mathbf{m}^\perp\),
		\begin{equation}
			\nabla_-^2F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})

			\begin{pmatrix}

				Py_N&C_N
			\end{pmatrix}
			+o(1),
		\end{equation}
		where the error converges to zero in operator norm in probability,
		and
		\begin{equation}
			C_N
			=
			P\left(
			\sqrt{\xi''(q)}\,W_N
			-\operatorname{diag}\left(
			\frac1{u(q,m_i)}
			+\frac{\xi''(q)}N\sum_{j=1}^Nu(q,m_j)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.774470+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aaf5b9b1b62827a32ec6f5199485e2d1de8f146393db87469eb999cb20440202","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 29 (Careless uniform exponential tails and moments) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] Let $Y_n:=\mu_nT_{n,p}$ in the fixed-$p$ careless collector started from the empty collection, where
\[
        \mu_n=\Pbb_{\nu_n}(K_0<n,K_1=n)
\]
is the stationary-entry flux into the post-loss completion state.  There are constants $C,c\in(0,\infty)$, depending only on $p$, such that
\[
        \Pbb(Y_n>x)\le C e^{-cx},
        \qquad x\ge0,
\]
for all sufficiently large $n$.  Consequently, for every fixed $r\ge1$,
\[
        \Ebb Y_n^r\longrightarrow \Ebb Z^r=r!,
        \qquad Z\sim\Exp(1).
\]
In particular,
\[
        \Ebb T_{n,p}\sim \frac{1}{\mu_n},\qquad
        \Var(T_{n,p})\sim \frac{1}{\mu_n^2}.
\]
Together with Theorem~\ref{thm:careless-sharp-constant}, this gives the explicit constant
\[
        \mu_n\sim \frac{1}{(q;q)_\infty}
        \frac{n!}{n^n}q^{n(n+1)/2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
        \Ebb T_{n,p}
        \sim (q;q)_\infty\frac{n^n}{n!}q^{-n(n+1)/2},
\]
and
\[
        \Var(T_{n,p})
        \sim (q;q)_\infty^2\left(\frac{n^n}{n!}\right)^2q^{-n(n+1)}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.134109+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_ab09a2c6051a4049fa8a2429dd73e7b3cd9ba24b6ee241a42e79d2fdc03080e9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. With R_r the block conditional variances, put D_m = (-1)^(m+1) Delta^m R_0 for 1 <= m <= n, and let H_<m be the functions whose Hoeffding components of order m or more vanish. Then D_m = binom(n, m)^(-1) sum_{k=m}^n binom(k, m) W_k and D_m <= dist_2(f, H_<m)^2 <= binom(n, m) D_m; so D_m = 0 if and only if f lies in H_<m. With nonzero tail, the left inequality is an equality exactly when all the tail mass sits at order n, and the right one exactly when it sits at order m. The same holds with Q_r, the average over |A| = r of E[(f(X) - f(X^(A)))^2], since Q_r = 2 R_r: for m = 1 it reads Var(f) <= (1/2) sum_i E[(f(X) - f(X^(i)))^2].","status":"unverified"}

  where $H_m$ is the $m^\text{th}$ harmonic number

  \[

  \[

  If $p = \omega(1/m)$ then

  \]
  In particular, for $p$ constant,
  \begin{align*}

    $\E [T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}] = \lim_{t \uparrow 0} I_{m,p}'(t)$.
    With the knowledge 
    \begin{equation}
      
      \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left( 1 - x \right)^{m \exp(-t) - m}
      = \log\left(\frac{1}{1-x}\right) \, m \, e^{-t}
      \left( 1 - x \right)^{m \exp(-t) - m},
    \end{equation}
    we differentiate the integral expression of

    \begin{align}
      \notag

      \log\left( \frac{1}{1-x} \right) dx\\

{"assumptions":["the operator is compact on a Hilbert space","self-adjointness or normality is what the eigenbasis conclusion needs","for a general compact operator only the Riesz-Schauder conclusions and the singular value decomposition are available"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573312+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory of compact operators","id":"claim_ab876a6af8757c91d5eb78a56fd013d6691bfc416c7fa2ac4c3ae96614531a82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators (an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, real eigenvalues tending to 0, ||T|| = max |eigenvalue|, min-max characterisation of eigenvalues) requires self-adjointness or at least normality. Compactness alone gives only the Riesz-Schauder picture: the nonzero spectrum consists of eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity accumulating only at 0, and the set of such eigenvalues may be empty. The standard counterexample is the Volterra operator on L^2([0,1]), (V f)(x) = integral from 0 to x of f(t) dt, which is Hilbert-Schmidt (kernel k(x,t) = 1 for t < x, 0 otherwise) hence compact, but has no eigenvalues at all: V f = lambda f with lambda nonzero forces f to be absolutely continuous with f' = f/lambda and f(0) = 0, so f = 0; and V f = 0 forces f = 0 a.e. Thus sigma(V) = {0}, spectral radius 0, while ||V|| = 2/pi; the singular values of V are 1/((n + 1/2) pi), n >= 0, so V is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, and the moduli of its eigenvalues (all zero) are nowhere near its singular values. Consequences for an auditor: (a) 'compact, so expand in eigenfunctions' is invalid without normality; the right substitute is the Schmidt decomposition in singular values, which always exists; (b) 'compact, so the spectral radius equals the norm' is false; (c) Rayleigh-quotient and min-max formulas for eigenvalues are statements about self-adjoint operators and become statements about singular values otherwise; (d) Mercer-type positivity conclusions require a self-adjoint positive kernel, not just an L^2 kernel.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:44:39.738155+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_abc2b1b0293d18399580279211cbf559774e5b066d59d58cbb0c0201674f864b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 4 (Interior regularity under Engelbert--Schmidt conditions) of arXiv:2608.29854, '2608.29854'] Assume \eqref{eq:ES}, let $\cV$ be an admissible form domain with
associated operator $A$, let $q:I\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Borel,
and recall the strongly continuous semigroup $(T_t^q)_{t\ge0}$ from
\Cref{prop:L2-semigroup}. Let $f\in L^2(I,\mu)$.  For every $t>0$, $T_t^qf$ admits a unique
continuous representative, which we identify with $T_t^qf$.
Furthermore, the following statements hold with $u(t,x)=T_t^qf(x)
$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},ref=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item
For every $k\in\N_0$, $\partial_t^ku$ and
$\partial_x\partial_t^ku$ exist on $(0,\infty)\times I$ and are jointly
continuous there. 

\item
For every $t>0$, $\partial_xu(t,\cdot)\in\AC_{\loc}(I)$, and for almost every $x\in I$,
\begin{equation}
  \partial_tu(t,x)
  =
  a(x)\partial_{xx}u(t,x)
  +b(x)\partial_xu(t,x)-q(x)u(t,x).
\end{equation}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.746675+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac3037a6545d598ace0d73333207f847ead87e2c92fde615e4c950e935c6689d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 23 (Subcritical shape) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] Suppose $p = o(1/m)$.   $(T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0})/m \stackrel{P}{\to} 0$ as $m \to \infty$.
  It follows that $(T_{m,p} - m \log{m})/m$ converges

    The first claim follows by observing that $\PP(T_{m, 0} = T_{m, p}) = (1-p)^m \to 1$.
    Then Proposition~\ref{thm:classical mgf convergence}
    confirms $m^{-t}\,M_{T_{m,0}}(t/m) \to \Gammaop(1-t)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.199182+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac3b35e8d69c8916a75f31a260dd4f7e833a3c597539ff4b35fbe5e35e24ce2c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 130 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $X^1$ and $X^2$ be solutions to SDEs
    \[
    dX^i(t)
    =
    b^i(t,X^i(t))\,dt
    +
    \sigma^i(t,X^i(t))\,dB_t\,,
    \]
such that $X^1(q_*)$ and $X^2(q_*)$ are equidistributed.
Suppose for some finite constant $\oL$ that the SDE coefficients $b^i$ and $\sigma^i$ are uniformly bounded by $\oL$, and moreover are $\oL$-Lipschitz in the space coordinate. Lastly suppose
	\[
    \sup_{(t,x)\in [q_*
    ,1]\times \mathbb R}
    \bigg\{
    \Big|b^1(t,x) - b^2(t,x)\Big|
    +
 	\Big|\sigma^1(t,x)-\sigma^2(t,x)\Big|
    \bigg\}
    \le \epsilon\,.
    \]
Then the marginal laws of $X^1$ and $X^2$ are close in $L^2$-Wasserstein distance for all time: more precisely, there is a coupling of $X^1$ with $X^2$ under which
	\[
	\sup\bigg\{
	\E\bigg[\Big(X^1(t)-X^2(t)\Big)^2\bigg] 
	: t\in[q_*
        ,1]
	\bigg\} \le 
	C(\oL) \epsilon^2\,,
	\]
where $C(\oL)$ denotes a constant depending only on $\oL$.

\begin{proof}
Couple $X^1$ and $X^2$ with the same Brownian motion $B$, and same initial value (almost surely). For this coupling let $Z(t) = X^1(t)-X^2(t)$, and $E(t) = \E[Z(t)^2]$. By It\=o's formula, for any
$0\le t\le t'\le1$, we have
	\[
	E(t')-E(t)
	=\E \int_t^{t'} \bigg\{
		2 Z(s)
		\Big(b^1(s,X^1(s))-b^2(s,X^2(s))
		\Big)
	+\Big( \sigma^1(s,X^1(s))
		-\sigma^2(s,X^2(s))
		\Big)^2
		\bigg\}\,ds\,.
	\]
For $s\in[q_*,1]$, using that $b^1$ and $b^2$ are $\epsilon$-close to one another, and $\oL$-Lipschitz in the space coordinate, gives
	\[
	\Big|b^1(s,X^1(s))-b^2(s,X^2(s))
	\Big|
	\le \oL\Big| X^1(s)-X^2(s)\Big|
		+ \epsilon
	=\oL |Z(s)|
		+ \epsilon\,.
	\]
A similar bound holds with $\sigma^i$ in place of $b^i$. It follows that 
for $[t,t']\subseteq[q_*,1]$, we have
	\[
	E(t')-E(t)
	\le 3
	\E \int_t^{t'}
	\Big(\oL |Z(s)| + \epsilon\Big)^2\,ds
	\le 6 \bigg\{
	\oL^2 \int_t^{t'} E(s)\,ds
	+ \epsilon^2 (t'-t)
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The claimed bound follows from Gr\"onwall's inequality. More precisely, we can use the form stated in \cite[Lem.~6.1]{MR1071170} which says that if for all $t\in[q_*
    ,1]$ we have
	\[
	E(t) \le a(t) +\int_{q_0}^t b(s) E(s)\,ds
	\]
with $a,b$ continuous nonnegative functions, then it holds that
	\[
	E(1)
	\leq 
	E(q_*)
	+
	\int_{q_*
        }^1
	a(s)b(s)
	\exp
	\lt(
	\int_s^1 b(r)\,dr
	\rt)\,ds.
	\]
In our setting $E(q_*)=0$, $b(t)=6\oL^2$, and $a(t)=6\epsilon^2(t-q_*)$. Therefore
$a(1) \le 6\epsilon^2$, and the claimed bound follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["N>=3,K>=2,1<=r<K,0<=s,t<=r integers","One arbitrary and one systematic context, remaining contexts known S; source uniform contexts then uniform truths","Known truth identities from actual untagged factual samples and optional verifier; all compatible supports/orientations allowed","Robust source exact-level zero miscalibration; arbitrary generators"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:03:49.822810+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; robust calibration; truth support identification","id":"claim_ac4030be2b43ae3f012bf4d5561467d93512ee60948bd24529927d6d06add842","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical, priority and target-scope audit pending. # Neutral truth/false bundles defeat the smaller-count hypothesis

T379-C016 v2, proof (unaudited), exact checks PASS; independent audit pending.
Targets 1/2: auxiliary-route failure, no target score claimed.

For every integer m>=5 and N>=3 set K=3m,r=3(m-1),d=1. In the two
variable contexts L,R suppose the known truth unions have sizes
s=2(m-1),t=r, respectively. There are N-2 fixed known S contexts.
No partition tags are supplied. Both orientations remain compatible:
if L is A its r-support contains C_L of size s; if R is A its support
is exactly C_R of size r. Such unions have positive probability from
actual untagged factual samples with ell=0, e.g. one occurrence of
every known truth, n=s+r. The identities can be permuted within each
context without affecting the construction or source probabilities.

Put lambda=1/(NK). Partition the variable-context atoms as follows:

* B: all K-s=m+2 atoms outside C_L and two atoms outside C_R;
* T: all s known L truths and any s of the known R truths;
* Z: the remaining m-1 known R truths and its one remaining outside atom.

B has m+4 atoms; T has 4(m-1); Z has m. In either orientation and
for EVERY compatible residual L support, their source masses are

 p(B)=lambda*(m+2),
 p(T)=lambda*(4m-2),
 p(Z)=lambda*m.

For B, if L is A its residual true count is r-s=m-1, so
p(B)=(m-1)/(Nr)+2/(NK)=lambda*(m+2). If R is A the same mass comes
from K-s systematic L atoms and no R truths. T's mass is always
s/(Nr)+s/(NK). Z's mass is (m-1)/(Nr)=m/(NK) when R is A and is
also m/(NK) when R is S. This checks invariance directly from p.

Define g as the uniform coarsening of these groups:

 g(B atom)=lambda*(m+2)/(m+4)=q,
 g(T atom)=lambda*(2m-1)/(2(m-1)),
 g(Z atom)=lambda,
 g(fixed S atom)=lambda.

The total is one and all probabilities are nonnegative. Equal lambda
scores merge Z and fixed S; their source masses remain invariant.
Thus g is source Mis_infinity=0 for every compatible world, not just
on average or conditional on a correct orientation prediction.

If L is A all three false atoms lie in B, giving H_L=3q.
If R is A two false atoms lie in B and one in Z, giving H_R=2q+lambda.
Since q<lambda, the worst-world false mass is

 max H=lambda*(3m+8)/(m+4).                              (1)

C016 v1 conjectured that the smaller known count alone gives the exact
value. Here h=s yields that conjectured value

 V_small=3lambda*(m+1)/(m+2).

The actual feasible worst risk (1) is strictly smaller, by

 V_small-max H=lambda*(m-4)/((m+2)(m+4))>0.               (2)

For m=5,N=3 these are 2/35 versus 23/405, gap 1/2835.
This refutes the entire proposed smaller-count formula; it does not
establish the optimal risk in this family. In particular the nine
complete small-alphabet score-partition checks were consistent with
the conjecture but insufficient to prove it. No general lower bound
was promoted from those computations.

The neutral Z group contains truths and possible falsehoods in exactly
the systematic true-density ratio. Its p mass is orientation-invariant
even though the known truth counts are unequal. This mechanism is
invisible to a rule that discards all surplus known truths. A general
unequal-count frontier must account for invariant weighted count
identities, not merely the minimum count or posterior risk ordering.
This is a route obstruction, not a solution of the unrestricted target.
Primary calibration basis: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2.

Verification: logs/neutral_bin_counterexample_check.json records 33
exact rational parameter cases and 582 compatible-world source-bin
calibration checks. It exhausts residual L supports for m=5,6,7;
larger m use the displayed general cardinality proof plus one
representative support, without claiming exhaustive enumeration there.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:11:44.390798+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac6146d5527c068866123e3c43ea099b3a42e1a25fb30a22c26668d252f973e4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5 ({\cite[Theorem 1) of arXiv:2609.03171, 'Factorization patterns and fields of definition of $\ell$-torsion points on the Jacobians '] {Xing}}]
The possible characteristic polynomials of abelian varieties of dimension three over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ (where $q=p^k$) are all $f(t) \in \mathbb{Z}[t]$ of degree six satisfying one of the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
    \item $f(t)=t^{6}+a_{1}t^{5}+a_{2}t^{4}+a_{3}t^{3}+a_{2}qt^{2}+a_{1}q^{2}t+q^{3}$ whose roots are Weil numbers, $v_p(d(0))/k \in \mathbb{Z}$ for any irreducible factor $d(t)$ of $f(t)$ in $\mathbb{Q}_{p}[t]$, and the polynomial $t^{3}+a_{1}t^{2}+(a_{2}-3q)t+a_{3}-2qa_{1}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$.
    
    \item $f(t)=(t^{2}+\beta t+q)^{3}$, where $\beta$ is equal to either:
    \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
        \item $\beta=aq^{1/3}$ with $3 \mid k$, $p \nmid a$, and $|a| < 2q^{1/6}$.
        \item $\beta=\pm q^{2/3}$ with $q=8$ or $27$.
    \end{enumerate}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627182+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_ac75738e8e3dabce1159fdd76643746f5142db1f8704a7114eee97125f9e99b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A function f: [a, b] -> R has bounded variation if its total variation V(f; [a, b]) = sup over all partitions a = x_0 < x_1 < ... < x_n = b of sum_{i=1}^{n} |f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})| is finite; the space of such functions is BV[a, b]. Facts (Jordan, Lebesgue): (1) f is of bounded variation if and only if f = g - h with g and h nondecreasing on [a, b] (Jordan decomposition; one may take g(x) = V(f; [a, x]), the variation function, and h = g - f, both nondecreasing); (2) a BV function is bounded, has one-sided limits at every point, has at most countably many discontinuities, all of them jumps, and is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere with f' integrable and integral_a^b |f'(x)| dx <= V(f; [a, b]), with equality if and only if f is absolutely continuous; (3) monotone functions and Lipschitz functions are BV (a Lipschitz function with constant L has V <= L (b - a)), while a continuous function need not be: x sin(1/x) on (0, 1] (extended by 0) has infinite variation, and the Cantor function is continuous, nondecreasing, BV, yet has f' = 0 almost everywhere with total variation 1 (so it is not absolutely continuous); (4) BV[a, b] is a Banach space under ||f|| = |f(a)| + V(f; [a, b]); (5) f is BV exactly when the Riemann-Stieltjes integral integral_a^b g df exists for every continuous g, and then g -> integral g df is a bounded linear functional on C[a, b] of norm V(f; [a, b]) - the Riesz representation of the dual of C[a, b] (normalised BV functions correspond to finite signed Borel measures). In higher dimensions BV functions are those whose distributional gradient is a finite vector measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149510+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity, L^p theory","id":"claim_ac7bfef65ba08df89da6d269b48b216132d2600e11e7ada5844f2602810376eb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in the Calderon-Zygmund theory for Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu the leading coefficients must be continuous (uniform continuity on the relevant compact set), or at least of vanishing mean oscillation; only then does the freezing-and-absorption step work for every 1 < p < infinity. Mere measurable uniform ellipticity is not enough, and the failure is not a technicality: both the estimate and uniqueness fail. Counterexample (Gilbarg-Serrin type): on the unit ball B_1 in R^n, n >= 2, fix lambda in (0,1) and set a^{ij}(x) = delta^{ij} + beta x_i x_j/|x|^2 with 1 + beta = (n-1)/(1 - lambda) > 0. These coefficients are bounded, symmetric, uniformly elliptic (eigenvalues 1 with multiplicity n-1 and (n-1)/(1-lambda)) and continuous except at the origin. For radial u, D_{ij}u = u''(r) x_i x_j/r^2 + (u'(r)/r)(delta_{ij} - x_i x_j/r^2), hence Lu = (1 + beta) u'' + (n-1) u'/r, and u(x) = |x|^lambda gives Lu = r^{lambda - 2} [ (1 + beta) lambda(lambda - 1) + (n-1) lambda ] = 0. Now w = |x|^lambda - 1 lies in W^{2,p}(B_1) for every p < n/(2 - lambda), lies in W^{1,p}_0(B_1) for those p, satisfies Lw = 0 almost everywhere, and is not identically zero (w(0) = -1). Consequences: the Dirichlet problem is not uniquely solvable in W^{2,p} intersect W^{1,p}_0 for p < n/(2 - lambda), so no global estimate ||w||_{W^{2,p}} <= C ||Lw||_{L^p} can hold there; the maximum principle also fails for such strong solutions (w attains its minimum -1 at an interior point while Lw = 0 and w = 0 on the boundary). Note n/(2 - lambda) < n and lambda may be taken as close to 1 as desired, so the failure reaches every exponent below n. What survives with only measurable coefficients: the Aleksandrov-Bakelman-Pucci estimate and Krylov-Safonov theory, both of which require the solution to be in W^{2,n}_loc - which is exactly the class this example escapes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357576+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac81b303f3d1341ca273c97542be91edbaf419690548b6ea7476e7328eb55d4a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 242 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\phi \in C_b(\R,\R)$ and define the domain
	\[
		\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha) = \Big\{
			\mu \in \cP_2(\R,C'(\alpha)) : \bbW_1(\mu, \ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \le 1
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Then the function
	\[
		f_\phi(\mu) \equiv \int \phi\,d\mu
	\]
	is uniformly continuous on $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ equipped with the $\bbW_1$ metric.

\begin{proof}
The set $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ is clearly closed with respect to the $\bbW_1$ metric. By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_2(\R,C'(\alpha))$ endowed with the $\bbW_1$ metric is compact, so $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ is also compact. It thus suffices to show that $f_\phi$ is continuous. In fact, since we are on a metric space, it suffices to show that $f_\phi$ is sequentially continuous. To this end,  consider any sequence $\mu_n$ in $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ converging to $\mu$ in $\bbW_1$. Then $\mu_n$ also converges weakly to $\mu$. Since $\phi$ was assumed to be a bounded continuous function, we obtain 
	 \[\lim_{n\to\infty} f_\phi(\mu_n) = f(\mu)\,.\]
Therefore $f_\phi$ is indeed continuous, which concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752423+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_ad0f3a207b3c5379410429f086bcbbeb1babd7dfb64560bd3c03ab098d3b5d3e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:26:26.807268+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ad2577d53d461574b2aa13e7c5473ca3510eb25e4462f7d955d961221f62d0ed","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:read-k of arXiv:2608.06159, 'Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi Graphs:\\[0.5ex] Gaussian Winner '] {gavinsky2015tail}}]
    
     Let \(\{\rY_j\}_{j\in[r]}\) be a read-\(k\) family of indicator random variables with \(p_j \coloneqq\P(\rY_j=1)\), and denote their average by \(\bar p \coloneqq r^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^r p_j\).
    If \(0<\bar p<1\), then
    \begin{subequations}
    \begin{align}
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\ge (\bar p+\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p+\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le1-\bar p,
    \\
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\le (\bar p-\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p-\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le\bar p.
    \end{align}
    \end{subequations}
    where the Kullback-Leibler divergence is defined as
    \[
    \D_{\mathrm{KL}}(u\|v)\coloneqq
    u\log(u/v)+(1-u)\log((1-u)/(1-v)).
    \]
    We use the standard convention \(0\log0=0\) at \(u\in\{0,1\}\).
    If \(\bar p\in\{0,1\}\), all the indicators are almost surely constant and
    the corresponding tail statements are trivial. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space","1 <= p < infinity (the statement is false for p = infinity)","for p = 1: mu sigma-finite (or localizable) for surjectivity; mu semifinite for isometry","scalars real or complex"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.552519+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_adee9ce43c73105fd97da47f2239ef349918c1fc447cc025fb6cb07edd000262","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p < infinity with conjugate exponent p'. (a) If 1 < p < infinity, then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^{p'}(mu) onto the dual space (L^p(mu))*, for an arbitrary measure space.
